items.title: Elon Musk takes a dig at Waymo's pet collision history and says Tesla Robotaxi has a solution
items.summary: Elon Musk said Waymo's robotaxis are "pet destroyers." PATRICK PLEUL/POOL/AFP via Getty Images Waymo has previously caught flak for its robotaxis colliding with stray animals. Elon Musk took jabs at Waymo, calling the robotaxis "pet destroyers." Musk said Tesla gave itself challenges to solve the problem of robotaxis running over animals. Elon Musk took a dig at his robotaxi rival, Waymo , calling the vehicles "pet destroyers," and said Tesla Robotaxi has solved the issue of avoiding stray pets. During a livestreamed interview at an event hosted by Tesla Owners of Silicon Valley on Saturday, Musk called out Waymo for its reported collisions with animals. "What a lot of people don't know is that Waymos are like pet destroyers," Musk said, laughing. "Well, maybe Waymo's made some improvements on that front, but they do run over a lot of pets, and we don't want to run over pets." Waymo has gotten flak over animal collisions before, most notably after its run-in with a beloved bodega cat in a San Francisco neighborhood back in October 2025. The feline, named KitKat, died after it was run over by Waymo's rear right tire, video obtained by The New York Times showed. That is not Waymo's first collision with an animal. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration's Standing General Order requires autonomous vehicle companies like Waymo to report qualifying crashes. NHTSA data showed that between July 2025 and July 2026, Waymo reported at least 9 crashes involving animals, 6 of which Waymo described as domestic animals. A Waymo spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment. Tesla's robotaxi service also reported a collision involving an animal during the same time period, but the incident involved a supervised robotaxi. Tesla also operated a smaller fleet, and most of its unsupervised operations were concentrated in one city: Austin. Musk said during the virtual interview that Tesla Robotaxi will be able to detect roaming pets at night. "We have these challenges of literally like: gray kittens on a gray tarmac with tar seams at night in low visibility. And it's like, 'Can we not run over the kittens,' type of thing," he said. Musk added that Tesla will deploy the update, though he did not specify when. Have a tip on Tesla or Waymo? Contact this reporter via email at lloydlee@businessinsider.com or Signal at lloydlee.71. items.title: Creating a permutation test, two ways
items.summary_html:
[This article was first published on From the bottom of the heap — R posts, and kindly contributed to R-bloggers]. (You can report issue about the content on this page here) Want to share your content on R-bloggers? click here if you have a blog, or here if you don't.

In my last post on permute, I looked at ordered set partitions and the new formula interface for plots and blocks. This time I want to show two helpers for the next part of writing a permutation test: taking those permutations and doing something with them.

permutations() gives you the shuffled values directly. permutator() gives you a function that hands out the next set of observation indices each time you call it. Both use the same permutation machinery underneath, so we can use them to build the same test in two slightly different ways.

These functions are in the development version of permute. To follow along, install it from my R-universe:

install.packages("permute", repos = c(
  "https://gavinsimpson.r-universe.dev",
  "https://cloud.r-project.org"
))
Something different from jackals

Let’s use PlantGrowth, which comes with R. It records dried plant weights under a control and two treatment conditions:

library("permute")
data(PlantGrowth, package = "datasets")

aggregate(weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth, FUN = mean)
  group weight
1  ctrl  5.032
2  trt1  4.661
3  trt2  5.526

The group means differ, but is that more variation than we’d expect if plant weights were unrelated to the treatments? We can use the overall F statistic from a linear model to measure how different the groups are. Larger values mean more variation between groups relative to the variation within them.

I’ll wrap that calculation in a small function, because we’ll be doing it quite a few times:

f_stat <- function(weight, group) {
  fit <- lm(weight ~ group)
  unname(summary(fit)$fstatistic[["value"]])
}

observed <- with(PlantGrowth, f_stat(weight, group))
observed
[1] 4.846088

This is an overall test across the groups. It doesn’t tell us which particular treatments differ.

For the permutation test, we’ll leave the group labels in place and shuffle the weights among them. Under the null hypothesis, we’re assuming those weights are exchangeable across the treatment groups.

Give me the shuffled values

Usually, shuffleSet() returns permuted indices, which we then use to rearrange our data. permutations() does that indexing step for us:

ctrl <- how(nperm = 9999)

set.seed(42)
shuffled <- permutations(PlantGrowth$weight, control = ctrl)

dim(shuffled)
[1] 9999   30

Each row contains one shuffled version of the weight vector. Columns correspond to the original observation positions, so we can pair every row with the unchanged PlantGrowth$group vector. Here are the first few values from a few rows:

as.matrix(shuffled)[seq_len(3), seq_len(5)]
     [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5]
[1,] 6.03 4.50 4.17 5.37 5.14
[2,] 4.81 5.87 5.12 5.29 4.53
[3,] 5.14 4.53 4.50 4.17 6.03

Those are plant weights, ready to use. as.matrix() just removes the extra permutation metadata for this little look.

Now fit the model for each row in shuffled and collect the F statistics:

null_values <- apply(shuffled, 1, f_stat, group = PlantGrowth$group)

That’s our permutation distribution. The -value is the proportion of results at least as large as the observed F statistic, including the observed result itself:

tol <- sqrt(.Machine$double.eps)
p_value <- (1 + sum(null_values >= observed - tol)) /
  (length(null_values) + 1)

c(F = observed, p_value = p_value)
       F  p_value 
4.846088 0.014200

The small tolerance lets us count ties despite minor numerical differences in the model fits. Adding one to the numerator and denominator includes the observed statistic in this Monte Carlo test. We count the upper tail because larger F statistics are more extreme; there’s no need to double the result for a test of differences in either direction.

We can also have a look at the data and the permutation distribution:

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
boxplot(weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth,
        xlab = "Group", ylab = "Dried plant weight",
        col = "grey85")
hist(null_values, breaks = 40, main = "",
     xlab = "F statistic after shuffling weights",
     col = "grey85", border = "white")
abline(v = observed, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
par(old_par)

Plant weights by group (left) and the permutation distribution of the F statistic (right). The red line marks the observed F statistic.

The observed value sits out in the right tail. For this unrestricted permutation test, there’s evidence of differences among the treatment groups. The p-value is estimated from random permutations, so it will vary with the seed and the number we request.

permutations() works with an atomic vector, rather than a whole data frame. If you give it a factor, it returns the shuffled character labels. It also follows the usual shuffleSet() rules about checking and complete enumeration, so the number of returned rows can differ from the number requested for small permutation spaces. Use the size of the returned object in subsequent calculations, as we did above.

One permutation at a time

Sometimes a loop1 is a more convenient place to fit a model, collect several results, or keep track of progress. That’s one situation where permutator() comes in.

Calling it creates a function. Calling that function returns the next permutation of observation indices. I’ll reset the seed so that we use the same set we used above:

set.seed(42)
next_perm <- permutator(nrow(PlantGrowth), control = ctrl)

null_iter <- numeric(attr(next_perm, "nperm"))

for (b in seq_along(null_iter)) {
  i <- next_perm()
  null_iter[b] <- f_stat(PlantGrowth$weight[i], PlantGrowth$group)
}

Here i contains indices, so PlantGrowth$weight[i] does the shuffling. The iterator’s "nperm" attribute tells us how many permutations are actually in the set; we use that to allocate the results vector.

Once we’ve used all of the permutations, another call returns NULL:

next_perm()
NULL

An iterator remembers how far you’ve got. If you run the loop again with this exhausted iterator, it won’t start over; create a fresh one first.

Did the two approaches give us the same F statistics?

all.equal(null_values, null_iter)
[1] TRUE

They did. We reset the seed and used the same design, so both helpers worked through the same underlying index permutations. We can calculate the -value from the loop results in exactly the same way:

p_iter <- (1 + sum(null_iter >= observed - tol)) /
  (length(null_iter) + 1)

c(values = p_value, iterator = p_iter)
  values iterator 
  0.0142   0.0142

One detail to keep in mind: permutator() generates and stores the permutation matrix when you create the iterator. It hands out rows one at a time, but it isn’t generating them lazily or removing the need to store the index matrix.

Reusing a set

You can also pass an existing index matrix to permutator(). This is useful when you want several calculations to use exactly the same permutations, or want to revisit a saved set later:

set.seed(42)
indices <- shuffleSet(nrow(PlantGrowth), control = ctrl)

next_perm <- permutator(perms = indices)
i <- next_perm()
head(PlantGrowth$weight[i])
[1] 6.03 4.50 4.17 5.37 5.14 6.11

Creating another iterator over that matrix starts from the beginning:

replay <- permutator(perms = indices)
identical(i, replay())
[1] TRUE

Supply either perms or the generation arguments such as n, nset, and control. The matrix passed to perms must contain observation indices, such as those returned by shuffleSet(). The shuffled weights from permutations() aren’t interchangeable with that matrix.

For a single vector and a short calculation, I like permutations() with apply(). When the calculation fits more naturally in a loop, or I want to reuse a saved set of indices, permutator() is handy. Both leave the choice of permutation design with how(), so the same workflow extends to restricted designs when the data call for them. The package manual has the details, and feedback is welcome on the issue tracker.

Footnotes

  1. Yes, I know apply is just a loop…︎

items.title: Alibaba Qwen Introduces QwenGyre: Elastic Reinforcement Learning RL for XLong-Horizon Agents
items.summary: Alibaba’s Qwen team has introduced QwenGyre , an elastic reinforcement learning RL framework for extreme-long-horizon agent training. QwenGyre is an online reinforcement learning system from Alibaba that trains coding agents through unmodified, black-box harnesses. It targets rollouts that run for hours and process close to 1M tokens. The QwenGyre elastic RL framework was used on Qwen’s flagship Qwen 3.8 2.4T model. It rests on 2 core ideas. It moves idle GPUs between rollout and training. It also turns branching agent histories into bounded training samples. TL;DR Size: A training framework, not a model. Tested on Qwen 3.6 122B and Qwen 3.8 2.4T ( A95B per Qwen ), with ~700K tokens per rollout. Runs on: Multi-node GPU clusters. The 122B runs used 24 to 32 nodes; the 2.4T run used 192 nodes (4 cells of 48). GPU model not disclosed. Megatron trains, SGLang serves rollouts. Performance: 1.38x to 1.78x faster than Async, 1.21x to 1.85x faster than Colocate, at matched scores. Best: 1.85x end-to-end speedup over Colocate on TerminalBench. Worst: Only 1.21x over Colocate on the 2.4T model, where many queries ran near the timeout. Bottom line: Best: NL2RepoBench rises from 52.5% to 58.5% in 48 steps. Worst: the paper links no public code release. What problem does QwenGyre solve? The research team defines ‘XLong-horizon’ tasks as agent runs spanning hours and hundreds of model and tool interactions. Examples include generating full repositories from specs, as in NL2Repo-Bench . Two problems appear at this scale: First, rollouts have long tails. In a Colocate setup, training waits for the slowest execution while GPUs idle. In an Async setup, fixed GPU pools cannot lend spare capacity to each other. Second, harnesses like Claude Code compact context, spawn sub-agents and retry. One execution becomes a branching tree, not a single trajectory. Expanding every path duplicates shared prefixes and inflates training cost. How does the Elastic Scheduler work? QwenGyre splits GPUs into cells that share a training layout. Each cell can serve rollouts or host a full training replica. A core cell owns the authoritative weights and optimizer state. Satellite cells join training later. The scheduler tracks a rollout waterlevel: queued and running executions. As executions finish, cells switch to training once the remaining cells can still serve all live work. Model calls are rerouted through a proxy, so the harness keeps running. Key mechanics: KV-cache blocks migrate over RDMA during rerouting, reducing prefix recomputation. Satellites pull core weights through Mooncake’s Transfer Engine and join an ongoing batch. Streaming training lets cells claim micro-steps as data becomes ready. Average role switches took 8.52 s (rollout to training) and 3.46 s (training to rollout). How does the Trajectory Processor build training samples? A proxy records exact token IDs and behavior log-probabilities using token-in, token-out (TITO) . Calls are stored as prefix-shared trajectory trees . Partial scoring: Timed-out executions are still scored on their preserved workspace. Evaluator failures are excluded, never treated as a zero reward. Bounded sampling: At most 5 trajectories per execution are kept, ranked main > main-summary > sub-agent > sub-agent-summary. Deduplication: Shared targets count once, and only policy-generated tokens are trained. Fair weighting: Losses average within each execution, so extra branches do not inflate its weight. A cap of 5 matched uncapped training scores while cutting forward-backward time by 25.2%. Training uses an adapted GSPO with 16 rollouts per group. How fast is QwenGyre? Benchmark results All runs used Claude Code 2.1.220 as the harness, with equal GPU budgets and matched staleness. Workload (model) vs Async vs Colocate NL2RepoBench (Qwen 3.6 122B, 48 steps) 1.42x to 1.53x 1.36x to 1.47x DeepSWE (Qwen 3.6 122B, 24 steps) 1.569x to 1.572x 1.610x to 1.824x TerminalBench (Qwen 3.6 122B, 24 steps) 1.383x to 1.430x 1.809x to 1.849x NL2RepoBench (Qwen 3.8 2.4T, 48 steps) 1.78x 1.21x On the 2.4T model, QwenGyre finished 48 steps in 75.42 hours. Async took 134.55 hours and Colocate took 91.47 hours. Evaluation pass rate rose from 52.48% to 58.54%. && How does QwenGyre compare with other agentic RL frameworks? Feature QwenGyre veRL AReaL Agent Lightning Developer Alibaba Qwen ByteDance Seed + community Tsinghua IIIS + Ant Group Microsoft License Not disclosed Apache-2.0 Apache-2.0 MIT GPU placement Elastic cells, switch mid-rollout Flexible device mapping, HybridEngine resharding Fully asynchronous Not disclosed Black-box harness Yes, via proxy Not disclosed Yes, via base_url swap Yes, near-zero code change Training / rollout Megatron / SGLang FSDP, Megatron / vLLM, SGLang Megatron, FSDP, Archon / vLLM, SGLang Not disclosed Largest stated scale Qwen 3.8 2.4T 671B models Not disclosed Not disclosed Headline speedup Up to 1.85x vs Colocate Not disclosed 2.77x vs synchronous (v0.3) Not disclosed Public code Not disclosed Yes Yes Yes Speedups come from each project’s own setup and are not directly comparable. Key Takeaways QwenGyre moves GPUs between rollout and training without stopping live agents. Trajectory trees cap samples at 5 per execution and train shared prefixes once. Timed-out runs still get scored on their partial work. Up to 1.85x faster than Colocate and 1.78x faster than Async. Qwen 3.8 2.4T NL2RepoBench improved from 52.5% to 58.5% in 48 steps. Check out the full QwenGyre paper on arXiv and Qwen’s announcement post . All credit goes to the researcher of this project. Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well.
items.summary_html:
Alibaba’s Qwen team has introduced QwenGyre, an elastic reinforcement learning RL framework for extreme-long-horizon agent training. QwenGyre is an online reinforcement learning system from Alibaba that trains coding agents through unmodified, black-box harnesses. It targets rollouts that run for hours and process close to 1M tokens. The QwenGyre elastic RL framework was used on Qwen’s flagship Qwen 3.8 2.4T model. It rests on 2 core ideas. It moves idle GPUs between rollout and training. It also turns branching agent histories into bounded training samples.

TL;DR
  • Size: A training framework, not a model. Tested on Qwen 3.6 122B and Qwen 3.8 2.4T (A95B per Qwen), with ~700K tokens per rollout.
  • Runs on: Multi-node GPU clusters. The 122B runs used 24 to 32 nodes; the 2.4T run used 192 nodes (4 cells of 48). GPU model not disclosed. Megatron trains, SGLang serves rollouts.
  • Performance: 1.38x to 1.78x faster than Async, 1.21x to 1.85x faster than Colocate, at matched scores.
  • Best: 1.85x end-to-end speedup over Colocate on TerminalBench.
  • Worst: Only 1.21x over Colocate on the 2.4T model, where many queries ran near the timeout.
  • Bottom line:
    • Best: NL2RepoBench rises from 52.5% to 58.5% in 48 steps.
    • Worst: the paper links no public code release.
What problem does QwenGyre solve?

The research team defines ‘XLong-horizon’ tasks as agent runs spanning hours and hundreds of model and tool interactions. Examples include generating full repositories from specs, as in NL2Repo-Bench.

Two problems appear at this scale:

  • First, rollouts have long tails. In a Colocate setup, training waits for the slowest execution while GPUs idle. In an Async setup, fixed GPU pools cannot lend spare capacity to each other.
  • Second, harnesses like Claude Code compact context, spawn sub-agents and retry. One execution becomes a branching tree, not a single trajectory. Expanding every path duplicates shared prefixes and inflates training cost.
How does the Elastic Scheduler work?

QwenGyre splits GPUs into cells that share a training layout. Each cell can serve rollouts or host a full training replica. A core cell owns the authoritative weights and optimizer state. Satellite cells join training later.

The scheduler tracks a rollout waterlevel: queued and running executions. As executions finish, cells switch to training once the remaining cells can still serve all live work. Model calls are rerouted through a proxy, so the harness keeps running.

Key mechanics:

  • KV-cache blocks migrate over RDMA during rerouting, reducing prefix recomputation.
  • Satellites pull core weights through Mooncake’s Transfer Engine and join an ongoing batch.
  • Streaming training lets cells claim micro-steps as data becomes ready.
  • Average role switches took 8.52 s (rollout to training) and 3.46 s (training to rollout).
How does the Trajectory Processor build training samples?

A proxy records exact token IDs and behavior log-probabilities using token-in, token-out (TITO). Calls are stored as prefix-shared trajectory trees.

  • Partial scoring: Timed-out executions are still scored on their preserved workspace. Evaluator failures are excluded, never treated as a zero reward.
  • Bounded sampling: At most 5 trajectories per execution are kept, ranked main > main-summary > sub-agent > sub-agent-summary.
  • Deduplication: Shared targets count once, and only policy-generated tokens are trained.
  • Fair weighting: Losses average within each execution, so extra branches do not inflate its weight.

A cap of 5 matched uncapped training scores while cutting forward-backward time by 25.2%. Training uses an adapted GSPO with 16 rollouts per group.

How fast is QwenGyre? Benchmark results

All runs used Claude Code 2.1.220 as the harness, with equal GPU budgets and matched staleness.

items.title: Anthropic is making a $100 million bet on deployed AI engineers, and it seeks 5 key attributes
items.summary: Anthropic's developer conference in May. Don Feria/AP Content Services for Anthropic Anthropic is putting $100 million into a new training program for other companies' workers. The push is an effort to create more "deployed engineers," who can ramp up AI usage at companies. Executives explained the program and described the ideal forward-deployed engineer. Forward-deployed engineers are all the rage in AI, and Anthropic is going to other companies to train up top talent. The AI company announced a $100 million investment into an FDE training initiative earlier this month. It's a quasi-fellowship that engineers from other firms have already begun applying for. They'll attend four-day on-site intensives and then complete 12-week "residencies" working with Anthropic's Claude tools at their own companies. The company says it hopes to train 10,000 people through the program by the end of 2027. As Anthropic approaches its gigantic initial public offering , it's using the new training model to get more of the corporate world used to AI — and ramp up Claude spending. Job postings for FDEs have boomed over the last couple of years, as more companies buy software from AI firms and need help deploying it. Two Anthropic executives leading the push told Business Insider that their customers see AI's advances, notice competitors grabbing market share, and feel pressure to change their own work. "Everybody understands the model capability is expanding extremely fast," said Shambhavi Shambhavi, Anthropic's head of go-to-market strategy and operations for partnerships. "So, what can be done with the technology is greatly appreciated by the customers." Enter the FDE — which Anthropic calls "Frontier Deployed Engineers," rather than the standard " forward-deployed engineer " title that Palantir helped popularize . Both roles essentially mean someone with deep technical expertise in AI and the mandate to create new modes of work at a company. Shambhavi and Steve Corfield, Anthropic's head of global business development and partnerships, broke down the FDE role as they see it and how Anthropic hopes to set a "gold standard" with its new skills push. Anthropic execs say FDEs are curious Shambhavi said that the best FDEs have four main attributes. They are familiar with agentic AI systems. They're good problem-solvers. They're excellent communicators. And they're experienced, skilled engineers. Corfield tacked on a point he thinks helps Anthropic thrive: "You've got to be super, super curious. If you walk around this organization, everybody talks about curiosity." Communication is particularly important, Shambhavi said. She said that as companies try to overhaul entire workflows and approach agentic AI holistically, someone who can navigate the interpersonal dynamics goes a long way. "Our own Frontier Deployed Engineers work with these kinds of problems day in and day out," Shambhavi said. "And so we kind of applied the mindset of, we need to take this skill and bring it to our customers and partners and to the top engineers in those organizations, so that they can derive the benefits from Claude." Anthropic wants to set the 'gold standard' for AI skills Engineers who can expand their teams' use of AI have become a hot commodity in Silicon Valley. Salesforce, a major Anthropic partner , announced a plan in May to recruit 1,000 early-career workers into "AI builder" roles. Anthropic's program, in Corfield's view, goes a step above other industry attempts to recruit and train FDEs. Combined with other company initiatives to teach people AI, he hopes Anthropic will set "the gold standard for AI skilling." The first cohorts have begun in New York and San Francisco, including engineers from Accenture, Bain, Novo Nordisk, and other organizations. Companies nominate engineers for the training, and Anthropic interviews candidates. If they're accepted, they work for the four-day residency on a "simulated environment," an agentic system that they have to learn how to build and deploy. Then they take a practical test, before returning to their companies while staying in touch with Anthropic mentors for 12 more weeks. Anthropic is still building its assessments throughout the program. Shambhavi said they'll focus on "what does a great FDE look like" — articulation, problem solving, coding skills. Corfield said corporate customers wanted a program like this to help them figure out how to deploy Claude more effectively, and the holdup isn't motivation. "This is a skills gap problem, and that creates a market problem," he said. "What we're trying to do is fill that gap," he added. Have a tip? items.title: “A major overhaul”: OpenCode 2.0 puts its terminal, desktop, and web apps on one shared service
items.summary: OpenCode 2.0 is getting a formal unpacking today, some three months after its public beta launch . The sizable architectural upgrade introduces a shared background service connecting its terminal, web and desktop interfaces, alongside a rebuilt API, a new embeddable SDK, and support for running subagents and shell commands in the background. In a blog post published on Monday, Anomaly , the company behind the open-source coding agent, calls the release a “major overhaul,” adding that it drew on the experiences of “millions of daily users” to build a more adaptable system capable of supporting an expanding range of agent capabilities. Anomaly has, in fact, been iterating on version 2.0 over the past few months, including publishing a detailed technical account of its revamped plugin architecture and hot-reloading capabilities in September. However, the drawn-out rollout has caused some confusion among developers, with questions about whether version 2.0 was officially stable yet, and complaints about missing release notes , even as updates kept shipping. Monday’s announcement, alongside the official changelog’s switch to the 2.x series , effectively signals that version 2 is now OpenCode’s main release. In tandem, the company is also offering a broader explanation of the technical decisions behind the upgrade. OpenCode’s story so far OpenCode is an open-source coding agent. By way of a brief recap, OpenCode’s origins lie in the world of serverless development. Anomaly founders Jay V and Frank Wang previously created Serverless Stack ( SST ), an open-source framework for building and deploying applications on Amazon Web Services (AWS). Dax Raad , another prominent figure in OpenCode’s development, was also part of the SST team. Since its 2025 debut, OpenCode has gained a fervent following among developers looking for greater freedom over the AI models powering their coding tools. That became particularly pertinent in January when Anthropic began preventing third-party agents from using Claude Pro and Max subscription credentials, forcing affected developers to find alternative ways of accessing Claude or switch providers. As Janakiram MSV reported for The New Stack in May, these restrictions coincided with a surge of interest in OpenCode, which allows developers to switch between competing AI models. Today, the OpenCode GitHub repository has accumulated north of 212,000 stars and almost 30,000 forks. More broadly, there are signs of growing commercial interest in this category of coding agents. In July, Anaconda acquired Kilo , another such open-source coding agent that allows developers to choose their preferred AI provider. Interestingly, Kilo had already rebuilt its command-line interface and VS Code extension using OpenCode, demonstrating how the latter was finding a role inside other developer tools. With version 2.0, Anomaly has laid out how it has reworked OpenCode’s underlying architecture to accommodate a wider range of use cases. Arguably, the most significant change concerns how the coding agent runs, and how its different interfaces connect to it. One service, multiple interfaces Anomaly says the plumbing for a client/server setup has been in OpenCode from the start, though few beyond power users went out of their way to use it. With version 2.0, the server now starts automatically as a single background process on the developer’s machine, allowing OpenCode’s terminal, browser and desktop interfaces to communicate with the same underlying service. This means developers can access and manage their coding sessions through different interfaces, while the service handles the underlying execution. Scripts built using OpenCode’s programmatic client can also automatically discover and connect to the local service, making it useful for scheduled tasks, while developers can additionally expose the service to other machines and pair it with external applications. “Developers can now start a session in OpenCode’s terminal interface, continue working on it through the desktop or web app, and have their own scripts connect to the same underlying service”. The long and short of this is that developers can now start a session in OpenCode’s terminal interface, continue working on it through the desktop or web app, and have their own scripts connect to the same underlying service. OpenCode’s shared background service These architectural changes are accompanied by a ground-up redesign of OpenCode’s API, which Anomaly concedes was built piecemeal while the industry was still figuring things out. “The old API grew haphazardly as we and the world collectively learned what agents are and should be,” the company writes in its blog post. “It was bad.” “The old API grew haphazardly as we and the world collectively learned what agents are and should be. It was bad.” And so the new API gives the agent greater control over its own environment. For example, it can create a Git worktree for a new task, transfer an existing session into that worktree, or identify and interrupt another session that has become stuck. Developers can also access the API through a new @opencode/client package, which supports standard JavaScript and Effect. Agents manage their own sessions Another addition is an embeddable SDK , distributed as @opencode/sdk , that allows developers to incorporate OpenCode directly into their own applications. It uses the same underlying code as OpenCode’s CLI, the company notes, enabling developers to create customized versions of the agent for servers or environments such as Cloudflare Durable Objects. These implementations can communicate with existing OpenCode clients through its standard server protocol, although Anomaly says the SDK remains under development. Code Mode and background execution OpenCode 2.0 also changes how agents interact with external tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). A feature dubbed Code Mode allows agents to write JavaScript that calls multiple tools and processes their results within a single execution. Built around a lightweight JavaScript interpreter in the @opencode/codemode package, it converts MCP servers and OpenAPI endpoints into functions that agents can invoke programmatically. For example, an agent could retrieve bug reports from GitHub, extract the relevant information and create corresponding issues in Linear, without having to make a separate model round trip for each operation. The implications are particularly significant for developers connecting agents to large numbers of external services, where tool definitions can consume substantial portions of a model’s available context. Anomaly is making Code Mode the default for all MCP servers in version 2.0, arguing that it makes extensive integrations more practical. “This means you can add a thousand of them with minimal context bloat and your agent will discover and compose them to get things done,” the company writes. Code Mode connects MCP tools Meanwhile, OpenCode is introducing background execution for both subagents and shell commands, allowing developers to continue interacting with the primary agent while other operations are underway. A developer could, for instance, delegate a code review to a subagent running a different AI model while continuing to work on the main task. Similarly, lengthy shell operations, such as running tests or building an application, can execute asynchronously, with the primary agent receiving a notification when they finish. Developers can also use a keyboard shortcut to move an existing foreground task into the background if it takes longer than expected. Subagents and commands run concurrently Rounding out the release are changes to OpenCode’s plugin architecture. Anomaly says it has implemented more than 80 internal plugins, covering most of the functionality introduced in version 2.0, as part of an effort to improve the reliability and maintainability of its plugin API. Terminal interface plugins have also been promoted from experimental to stable, while support for hot reloading means OpenCode can create and start using a new plugin during an active session, without requiring a restart. There are, however, some compatibility implications for existing users. Plugins developed for OpenCode 1.0 won’t work with version 2.0, while integrations built around the previous server API will need updating. Existing OpenCode 1.x users can upgrade to version 2.0 by running opencode upgrade --major from the command line or entering /update in the terminal interface. According to the October 11 release notes , updates are no longer installed automatically, meaning users must initiate the upgrade themselves.

items.title: Airtable's new owner is laying off a 'large part' of its team
items.summary: Layoffs have hit Airtable. Illustration by Idrees Abbas/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images A "large part" of Airtable's workforce is being laid off, the company's new owner said. Bending Spoons' product leader said smaller teams and AI features are central to its new strategy. Cut employees will leave by the end of the week with "substantial separation packages," he said. Big layoffs are coming to Airtable. Airtable's new owner, Italian tech conglomerate Bending Spoons, said Monday it is laying off a "large part" of the software company as it reshapes the business around smaller teams and AI features. In an X post , Federico Simionato, Bending Spoons' product leader, said the cuts were not a reflection of employees' work but of the company's "deep belief that small teams ship more and better." "To everyone leaving: thank you. If you're hiring, these are excellent people and worth a call," Simionato said. Bending Spoons announced in August that it was acquiring Airtable , the spreadsheet and database app, for $1.28 billion. It was not immediately clear how many people would be affected by the layoffs. A Bending Spoons spokesperson said they were "not able to share additional details on the number of individuals impacted." Airtable product lead Alessandro Savarese said in a blog post on the company's website that the employees being cut will leave by the end of the week with "substantial separation packages." Layoffs have hit Airtable.

Illustration by Idrees Abbas/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images

  • A "large part" of Airtable's workforce is being laid off, the company's new owner said.
  • Bending Spoons' product leader said smaller teams and AI features are central to its new strategy.
  • Cut employees will leave by the end of the week with "substantial separation packages," he said.

Big layoffs are coming to Airtable.

Airtable's new owner, Italian tech conglomerate Bending Spoons, said Monday it is laying off a "large part" of the software company as it reshapes the business around smaller teams and AI features.

In an X post, Federico Simionato, Bending Spoons' product leader, said the cuts were not a reflection of employees' work but of the company's "deep belief that small teams ship more and better."

"To everyone leaving: thank you. If you're hiring, these are excellent people and worth a call," Simionato said.

Bending Spoons announced in August that it was acquiring Airtable, the spreadsheet and database app, for $1.28 billion.

It was not immediately clear how many people would be affected by the layoffs. A Bending Spoons spokesperson said they were "not able to share additional details on the number of individuals impacted."

Airtable product lead Alessandro Savarese said in a blog post on the company's website that the employees being cut will leave by the end of the week with "substantial separation packages."

"At Bending Spoons, we've seen firsthand how smaller, faster-moving teams with streamlined responsibilities can have an outsized impact, and we have the same ambitions at Airtable," Savarese wrote. "We intend to make Airtable a better product while providing our customers with an exceptional level of reliability and support."

Savarese said the company will focus on improving Airtable's core platform and investing in AI features.

Laid-off Airtable employees may already have some job prospects: X product engineer Mridul Singhai responded to the job-cuts announcement in a post, saying X will "continue to hire & grow people who want to commit."

items.title: Epic Games reportedly pivoting to "AI first" game development model
items.summary: Epic Games is shifting to an "AI first" development strategy for its collaboration with the Walt Disney Company, letting AI models write all the code and guide all the artwork for an upcoming shooter. That's according to a Bloomberg report , which cites unnamed people familiar with the project who commented on the significant pivot in internal development at the Unreal Engine maker. Human developers will be tasked with managing and guiding code and art assets generated by models such as Anthropic's Claude, according to internal Epic employee messages viewed by Bloomberg. That means "no more hand-written code" and art assets "generated with full AI workflows," according to the report. The $1.5 billion collaboration between Epic and Disney, announced in early 2024 , was slated to release a Marvel- and Star Wars-themed shooter in March 2027. That project has now been delayed indefinitely amid the AI-related shakeup and understaffed, slower-than-expected development thus far, according to the report. Read full article Comments

items.title: 22 romance books to read while you wait for Emily Henry's next novel
items.summary: Emily Henry in September 2026. Cindy Ord/WireImage/Getty Images Emily Henry announced her next novel, "Modern Classic," will be published on April 6, 2027. Henry's novels are romantic and sexy, often leaving readers wanting more. You can read similar romance novels to help pass the time while you wait for Henry's next book. Emily Henry fans are in luck. On September 22, Henry revealed her next romance novel will be released on April 6, 2027. She unveiled the title, "Modern Classic," by posting it on movie theater marquees across the US and UK. "Modern Classic" will be Henry's seventh romance novel to date. She smashed onto the romance scene in 2020 with " Beach Read " and has written five more books since then, each of which has made The New York Times' bestseller list. Henry's summer romance books often approach love with a sense of honesty and fun that the genre needs to thrive. Her characters may be enemies who find themselves living next door to each other or best friends who are scared to risk it all for something more, as was the case in " People We Meet on Vacation ," which was turned into a Netflix film released in January 2026. Henry has yet to release a cover or description for "Modern Classic," but the marquee announcement and title have fans wondering whether the book will have anything to do with movies. It will be a while, though, before readers know for sure. Luckily, there are plenty of other romance books to pass the time with, including Henry's earlier works if you haven't read — or reread — them yet. "Beach Read" by Emily Henry Penguin Random House In Henry's 2020 novel "Beach Read," which is being adapted into a film , author January Andrews is in a writing rut. She can't seem to think of her next big idea for a romance novel, so she decides to retreat to the beach house she inherited from her father, hoping inspiration will strike. To her dismay, January discovers Augustus Everett, an acclaimed literary author who happens to be her college archnemesis, is living next door. January plans to steer clear of Augustus for the duration of summer — until she finds out he's having writer's block, too. They decide the solution to their problem is for each of them to try their hand at each other's writing style. Augustus will have to show January the ropes of capital-L literature, and she'll have to make him fall in love with writing about love. However, falling for Augustus was never part of the plan. As you dive into "Beach Read," it's easy to see how it turned Emily Henry into a household name. "People We Meet On Vacation" by Emily Henry "People We Meet on Vacation" by Emily Henry. Berkley No one expected Alex and Poppy to become best friends less than Alex and Poppy. After a fateful road trip in college, free-spirited Poppy and buttoned-up Alex become inseparable. To keep their friendship alive after graduation, the pair agreed to take a trip together every summer, exploring a new place side by side. The trip is Poppy's favorite week of the year, but when "People We Meet on Vacation" begins, they haven't been on a trip — or spoken — in two years, distance growing between them after one night changes everything. As Poppy feels more bogged down than ever by her life in New York, she knows reuniting with Alex would make everything better. So Poppy proposes one more trip, hoping a week together can get their friendship — and her life — back on track. Will Poppy or Alex be willing to face the feelings that sent them running from each other in the first place? "Book Lovers" by Emily Henry "Book Lovers" by Emily Henry. Penguin Random House "Book Lovers" is Henry's third summer romance book , and it's both an epic love story and an ode to books themselves. Nora Stephens doesn't think anything is missing in her life. She loves her job as a literary agent, her apartment in New York, and living near her sister, Libby, and her nieces. When Libby asks Nora to escape to Sunshine Falls, North Carolina, for a month, Nora can't say no, especially since Libby is several months pregnant at the time. Libby has big dreams of small-town romance for Nora during their getaway, but instead of finding a local man to have a fling with, Nora keeps running into Charlie Lastra, a grumpy New York editor she's never gotten along with. Despite their less-than-romantic history, Charlie and Nora keep crossing paths in Sunshine Falls, making the ever-growing list of things they have in common harder to ignore. And when Nora discovers her life as she knows it is about to change, Charlie might be the exact thing she needs. "Happy Place" by Emily Henry "Happy Place" by Emily Henry. Penguin Random House Henry is at her best in "Happy Place," a novel that ruminates on what it means to fight for love. Harriet has spent her entire adult life loving Wyn. Their relationship consumes her, and the fact that she met him through her best friends, Sabrina and Cleo, only makes her love him more. Between Wyn and her friends, Harriet found the family she had always wanted in college, and she plans to spend her entire life with them. When Wyn abruptly breaks up with her after she starts her medical school residency, Harriet is heartbroken and terrified she's going to lose everyone she loves. She manages to avoid telling Sabrina and Cleo what happened for five months, planning to burst their bubble on their annual group trip to Maine . Then Wyn shows up, telling her they'll have to pretend to be a couple for the duration of the trip, since it's the last vacation the group will ever spend in the house they've loved for years. Harriet doesn't want to cause her friends pain, so she's willing to torture herself for a week. All she has to do is stop herself from asking Wyn what went wrong for seven days, but as his displays of fake affection start to feel more and more real, Harriet might have to face her fear of rocking the boat if she wants a true chance at happiness. "Funny Story" by Emily Henry "Funny Story" by Emily Henry. Berkley In "Funny Story," Daphne Vincent thought she had everything figured out. She was going to marry her doting fiancé, Peter, quietly thrive at her dream children's librarian job, and settle down in his hometown of Waning Bay, Michigan. Then, Peter leaves her for his childhood best friend , Petra, leaving Daphne at a crossroads. As she tries to recalibrate her entire future, Daphne moves in with Petra's ex, Miles Nowak, a wild spirit with whom she doesn't think she has much in common. She plans to avoid Miles as much as she can in their tiny apartment . Then, a night of drinking leads the pair to realize they may be able to help each other get over their breakup embarrassment if they let their exes think there's more between them than just a shared living space . Daphne knows their plan is temporary, but when she starts to develop real feelings for Miles, she may have to rethink everything she knows about what it means to be in love. "Great Big Beautiful Life" by Emily Henry "Great Big Beautiful Life" by Emily Henry. Penguin Random House Henry's latest book, "Great Big Beautiful Life," takes place in the summer and features a love story, but it marks a departure from her typical romances. Journalist Alice Scott is ready for the biggest challenge of her career to date: convincing the elusive heiress Margaret Ives to let her write her biography. Sunny-dispositioned and thoughtful Alice is sure she can make Margaret comfortable enough to share the story of why she disappeared from public life years ago. However, when she arrives in Little Crescent Island, Georgia , to meet Margaret, she finds she'll be competing against Hayden Anderson, a grumpy and inconveniently handsome writer who happened to win a Pulitzer Prize for his last biography, to tell Margaret's story. Beating out Hayden for the role might be an uphill battle, but Alice isn't going down without a fight, even after she realizes Margaret is picking and choosing what she tells each of them after getting them to sign strict NDAs. And as they try to unweave Margaret's history, it will become more and more difficult for Alice and Hayden to ignore the heat between them. "Honey & Spice" by Bolu Babalola "Honey & Spice" by Bolu Babalola. HarperCollins Bolu Babalola's "Honey & Spice" doesn't feel like a debut novel, as she writes romantic chemistry with a deftness Henry herself may envy. Kiki Banjo has made a name for herself at Whitewell University with her radio show "Brown Sugar." She's staked her reputation on her ability to suss out players, warning her peers in the African-Caribbean Society against dating men who aren't worth their time. Then she risks it all by kissing Malakai Korede in front of everyone after writing him off as "The Wastemen of Whitewell" on her show. Kiki is terrified her show is going to slip through her grasp, so she makes a deal with Malakai to pretend to be a couple in the hopes that Kiki can save her show and Malakai can change his reputation on campus. Kiki expects the duration of their fake romance to be torture, but as she and Malakai eat, study, and spend time together, she's unsettled to discover there seems to be more to him than meets the eye. Will Kiki be willing to let go of her preconceived notions for a chance at something real? "The Seven Husbands of Evelyn Hugo" by Taylor Jenkins Reid "The Seven Husbands of Evelyn Hugo" by Taylor Jenkins Reid. Simon & Schuster Like Henry, Taylor Jenkins Reid is a master at writing about yearning and epic love, as is obvious in "The Seven Husbands of Evelyn Hugo." Monique Grant's career as a magazine writer is at a standstill when famous — and famously private — film star Evelyn Hugo says she wants to do a tell-all interview with Monique, and only Monique. Monique doesn't understand why Evelyn would want to work with her of all people, but she can't say no, especially when Evelyn starts opening up to her about her path to fame and the forbidden love that changed the course of her life. Monique feels like Evelyn has handed her the opportunity of a lifetime. When she finds out why Evelyn chose her for the tell-all, Monique will have to face truths about their shared history she never expected. If you've already read Henry's "Great Big Beautiful Life," you'll swoon for "The Seven Husbands of Evelyn Hugo." "The Two Lives of Lydia Bird" by Josie Silver Penguin Random House Lydia Bird's life is turned upside down when the love of her life, Freddie, dies in a car accident . After months of mourning and wanting to go back in time, Lydia begins to move on with the help of her sister and Freddie's best friend. Then she's given a way to return to her old life with Freddie, a life where the tragedy never occurred. Her heart is pulled in two directions as she struggles to choose between going back to the familiar and embracing the unknown, where someone new wants to love her. Poignant and fresh, Josie Silver's "The Two Lives of Lydia Bird" is a story of love and hope that strikes a similar tone to Henry's works. "The Wedding Date" by Jasmine Guillory Penguin Random House On the night before Drew Nichols is set to be a groomsman in his ex-girlfriend's wedding, he gets stuck in an elevator with the pretty and funny Alexa Monroe, the first bright spot in what he believes will be an unbearable weekend. Impulse leads him to ask her to be his date to the wedding , and the duo surprises themselves by having more fun together than they bargained for. They plan to part ways after the wedding, neither interested in a long-distance relationship, but fate might have other plans for them. Jasmine Guillory writes about romance with reverence and joy, making "The Wedding Date" an ideal read for Henry lovers. "In Five Years" by Rebecca Serle Simon and Schuster Dannie Kohan's plan is on track. In one day, she performs well at the job interview of a lifetime and agrees to marry her long-term boyfriend. Then, when she goes to sleep that night, she wakes up five years in the future, with a different man beside her and his ring on her finger. Dannie has only one hour in the future before she's yanked back to the present, and she tries to push the experience aside as a vivid dream. Then, she meets the man from her dream four and a half years later and discovers he's dating her best friend. Dannie will have to confront what she really wants and decide whether she's willing to change her plans to find true happiness. Rebecca Serle's "In Five Years" explores time, grief, and all-consuming love, both romantic and platonic, in the same way Henry's books do, challenging readers to ask how far they would go for true happiness. "Normal People" by Sally Rooney Amazon Although Sally Rooney's beloved "Normal People" has a darker tone than Henry's books, the protagonists, Connell and Marianne, have a chemistry and a yearslong history that Henry fans will love. Connell and Marianne meet in high school, when Connell is a popular jock, and Marianne is, well, the opposite. The two bond despite their differences, setting them on a course that will shape their lives, drawing them back to one another over and over again. Rooney's novel shows the inevitability of love, finding words for the often inexplicable reasons people need each other. You can also stream the Hulu series once you finish the book. "One Golden Summer" by Carley Fortune "One Golden Summer" by Carley Fortune. Penguin Random House Like Henry, Carley Fortune captures the angst and ecstasy of summer love in "One Golden Summer." Alice can trace back her successful photography career to one photo: a candid shot of three teenagers on a bright yellow speedboat. She captured the shot during the one summer she spent at Barry's Bay with her Nan when she was 17, and it shifted the trajectory of her life. Fifteen years later, Alice should be living her dream as a professional photographer , but six months after a breakup, she feels stuck and uninspired. When Nan breaks her hip, Alice thinks spending another summer at Barry's Bay might be good for them both. Her vision of a tranquil summer with her grandmother gets upended by Charlie Florek, one of the teens from Alice's famous photo. The glimpse of Charlie that she got across the lake all those years ago was intriguing, but adult Charlie is so devastatingly handsome and thoughtful that he almost scares Alice. As they spend the summer together, Charlie heals wounds in Alice that she didn't know were there. If he lets her in, Alice might just do the same for Charlie. "Heated Rivalry" by Rachel Reid "Heated Rivalry" by Rachel Reid. Carina Press Ilya Rozanov and Shane Hollander are supposed to hate each other. Not only have they been competing against each other in hockey since they were 18, but they're also total opposites. Canadian Shane is cautious and focused, while Russian wild card Ilya isn't afraid to embrace his bad boy reputation on the ice. They have one big thing in common, though: the secret hookups they can't seem to resist every time they see each other. If the world found out about their relationship, both Ilya and Shane's careers could be in jeopardy, but they may decide it's worth the risk for a chance at something real with each other. Rachel Reid's "Heated Rivalry" was adapted into a hit TV show, so you can stream the series if you want more from the characters when you finish the book. "Love & Other Words" by Christina Lauren "Love & Other Words" by Christina Lauren. Simon & Schuster Christina Lauren has written dozens of books, and their 2018 novel "Love & Other Words" is perfect for Henry fans who love friends-to-lovers plots. Macy Sorensen has been white-knuckling her way through life for nearly a decade, but she's content with the safe world she's constructed for herself. A pediatric resident and newly engaged to a kind man who makes her feel mostly nothing, Macy thinks her heart is safe from the turmoil she experienced in her adolescence — until Elliot Petropoulos literally walks back into her life. Macy met Elliot as a teen shortly after her mother died, and he quickly became her center of gravity as she visited the small town he called home on weekends. Christina Lauren tells their story from the past and present, showing readers how they became fast friends over books and adolescent secrets, how they fell into life-changing love, and the wreckage they were both left with when it all fell apart. After 10 years of no contact, Macy may finally be ready to tell Elliot why she went radio silent on him after one fateful night. They'll both have to decide if they can move on from the pain of the past for a chance at a joy-filled future, together. "The Seven Year Slip" by Ashley Poston "The Seven Year Slip" by Ashley Poston. Penguin Random House Achingly romantic and surprisingly funny, "The Seven Year Slip" by Ashley Poston is about meeting the right person at the wrong time, literally. Clementine West has been adrift since her beloved aunt died. She thought living in the Upper East Side apartment she inherited from her would make her feel closer to her, as the apartment's magic had always drawn her in. Instead, she feels like she's just waiting for her aunt to walk through the door. Then, one day, Clementine comes home to find a man she doesn't know standing in her kitchen. Except, he thinks the apartment is his , for the summer anyway. He exists seven years in the past, staying in the apartment over the summer while Clementine and her aunt were in Europe. Clementine isn't ready to be hurt by love again, but she might not be able to keep up her defenses against the sweet chef staying the summer. And if she does let herself fall, will they work together if she finds him again in the now? "Just for the Summer" by Abby Jimenez "Just for the Summer" by Abby Jimenez. Hachette Justin and Emma are having the same dating problem. Everyone they date meets their soulmate immediately after they break up with them. When Emma sees Justin's viral Reddit post about his problem, she reaches out, and they decide to go on a date in hopes of breaking their curse. Emma, a traveling nurse, plans to stay in Minnesota for the summer and enjoy a fling with Justin during her short stay. The last thing either expects is to get immediately attached, especially when they both have family members counting on them come fall. Despite their best-laid plans, Emma and Justin's curse might have been leading them to each other all along in "Just for the Summer" by Abby Jimenez. "Seven Days in June" by Tia Williams "Seven Days in June" by Tia Williams. Hachette To the world, romance novelist Eva Mercy and acclaimed literary author Shane Hall have nothing to do with each other. That's because the only two people who know their books are inspired by each other are Eva and Shane. For their entire careers, Shane and Eva have been writing secret love letters to each other, as the week they spent as teens glued to each other's sides in a rush of love still haunts them both years later. They finally come face-to-face again when they both speak on a Brooklyn literary panel, and despite the years since they've seen each other, their chemistry is undeniable. Eva doesn't trust Shane after the way things went down between them, though, and as a single mom, she can't risk getting hurt again. Still, Eva has always been curious to know why Shane disappeared, and reuniting with him might be the key to breaking her writer's block. The second-chance romance in Tia Williams' "Seven Days in June" will hit the spot for Henry's fans. "Deep End" by Ali Hazelwood "Deep End" by Ali Hazelwood. Penguin Random House Ali Hazelwood is a prolific romance author, and the coming-of-age story and yearning in "Deep End" will scratch the itch for lovers of Henry's books. Nearly every moment of Scarlett Vandermeer's life at Stanford is accounted for. She spends her days in the pool as a member of the diving team or studying, laser-focused on achieving her goal of getting into medical school. A relationship or even a fling is the last thing on Scarlett's mind. Then, she finds out Lukas Blomqvist, Stanford's world champion swim captain who thrives on control, has similar interests to her when it comes to intimacy, and she thinks she might be able to make time in her busy schedule for something casual. Lukas and Scarlett agree to explore their attraction together, deciding not to tell almost anyone about their arrangement. Scarlett doesn't think keeping her relationship with Lukas to herself will be a problem until she realizes the last thing she feels about him is casual. "Same Time Next Summer" by Annabel Monaghan "Same Time Next Summer" by Annabel Monaghan. Penguin Random House "Same Time Next Summer" by Annabel Monaghan offers another take on second-chance romance. Sam's family's beach house on Long Island was her happy place in her childhood. She spent every summer there, and she was never happier than she was with her toes in the sand. Then, at 17, Wyatt broke her heart, and Sam couldn't face a summer there without him. She hasn't been back for more than a long weekend since. At 30, Sam is making the trek from the city back to the beach, and she isn't the girl she was at 17. She's determined to succeed at her high-powered job and plan the perfect wedding with her fiancé, Jack, whose tendency to over-schedule their lives has become a comfort. Only when she arrives, Sam discovers that Wyatt has returned to the house next door, and the entire adult life she created for herself begins to crumble. As old feelings come rushing back, Sam will have to take stock of who she is, who she wants to be, and who she really wants to live her life with. "The Wedding People" by Alison Espach "The Wedding People" by Alison Espach. Macmillan When Phoebe Stone arrives at the Cornwall Inn in Rhode Island, she's dressed to the nines and doesn't intend to ever check out. Her plans immediately go awry, though, when she discovers the entire hotel has been rented out for a wedding , and the attendees immediately assume she's one of the wedding people. Soon, Phoebe has no choice but to participate in the wedding festivities, especially because she and the bride keep telling each other their darkest secrets. After months of depression, the fanfare and plot twist of a stranger's wedding might show Phoebe her own path forward. Slightly more melancholy in tone than Henry's works but still beautifully romantic, "The Wedding People" by Alison Espach is about the surprises life can bring when you least expect it. "The Deal" by Elle Kennedy "The Deal" by Elle Kennedy. Bloom Books If you're looking for another romance work that has been adapted for the screen, you can check out "The Deal" by Elle Kennedy, known as "Off Campus" on Amazon Prime. Hannah Wells is thriving at Briar University. She's killing it in her music classes, and she has the best friend a girl could ask for. Her crush, Justin, has no idea she's into him, though, and Hannah doesn't know where to start on figuring out how to flirt or date. Enter Garrett Graham, a hockey captain bound for the NHL. His GPA is in trouble, though, and Hannah is the only one who can help. The duo strikes a deal, with Hannah agreeing to tutor Garrett in school if he helps her make Justin jealous with a fake relationship. Garrett expects that pretending to date Hannah will be a breeze, but when he develops real feelings for her, he'll have to come up with a new plan to get the girl.
