Between Wyn and her friends, Harriet found the family she had always wanted in college, and she plans to spend her entire life with them.

When Wyn abruptly breaks up with her after she starts her medical school residency, Harriet is heartbroken and terrified she's going to lose everyone she loves. She manages to avoid telling Sabrina and Cleo what happened for five months, planning to burst their bubble on their annual group trip to Maine.

Then Wyn shows up, telling her they'll have to pretend to be a couple for the duration of the trip, since it's the last vacation the group will ever spend in the house they've loved for years. Harriet doesn't want to cause her friends pain, so she's willing to torture herself for a week.

All she has to do is stop herself from asking Wyn what went wrong for seven days, but as his displays of fake affection start to feel more and more real, Harriet might have to face her fear of rocking the boat if she wants a true chance at happiness.

"Funny Story" by Emily Henry
"Funny Story" by Emily Henry.

Berkley

In "Funny Story," Daphne Vincent thought she had everything figured out. She was going to marry her doting fiancé, Peter, quietly thrive at her dream children's librarian job, and settle down in his hometown of Waning Bay, Michigan.

Then, Peter leaves her for his childhood best friend, Petra, leaving Daphne at a crossroads. As she tries to recalibrate her entire future, Daphne moves in with Petra's ex, Miles Nowak, a wild spirit with whom she doesn't think she has much in common.

She plans to avoid Miles as much as she can in their tiny apartment. Then, a night of drinking leads the pair to realize they may be able to help each other get over their breakup embarrassment if they let their exes think there's more between them than just a shared living space.

Daphne knows their plan is temporary, but when she starts to develop real feelings for Miles, she may have to rethink everything she knows about what it means to be in love.

"Great Big Beautiful Life" by Emily Henry
"Great Big Beautiful Life" by Emily Henry.

Penguin Random House

Henry's latest book, "Great Big Beautiful Life," takes place in the summer and features a love story, but it marks a departure from her typical romances.

Journalist Alice Scott is ready for the biggest challenge of her career to date: convincing the elusive heiress Margaret Ives to let her write her biography.

Sunny-dispositioned and thoughtful Alice is sure she can make Margaret comfortable enough to share the story of why she disappeared from public life years ago. However, when she arrives in Little Crescent Island, Georgia, to meet Margaret, she finds she'll be competing against Hayden Anderson, a grumpy and inconveniently handsome writer who happened to win a Pulitzer Prize for his last biography, to tell Margaret's story.

Beating out Hayden for the role might be an uphill battle, but Alice isn't going down without a fight, even after she realizes Margaret is picking and choosing what she tells each of them after getting them to sign strict NDAs. And as they try to unweave Margaret's history, it will become more and more difficult for Alice and Hayden to ignore the heat between them.

"Honey & Spice" by Bolu Babalola
"Honey & Spice" by Bolu Babalola.

HarperCollins

Bolu Babalola's "Honey & Spice" doesn't feel like a debut novel, as she writes romantic chemistry with a deftness Henry herself may envy.

Kiki Banjo has made a name for herself at Whitewell University with her radio show "Brown Sugar." She's staked her reputation on her ability to suss out players, warning her peers in the African-Caribbean Society against dating men who aren't worth their time.

Then she risks it all by kissing Malakai Korede in front of everyone after writing him off as "The Wastemen of Whitewell" on her show. Kiki is terrified her show is going to slip through her grasp, so she makes a deal with Malakai to pretend to be a couple in the hopes that Kiki can save her show and Malakai can change his reputation on campus.

Kiki expects the duration of their fake romance to be torture, but as she and Malakai eat, study, and spend time together, she's unsettled to discover there seems to be more to him than meets the eye. Will Kiki be willing to let go of her preconceived notions for a chance at something real?

"The Seven Husbands of Evelyn Hugo" by Taylor Jenkins Reid
"The Seven Husbands of Evelyn Hugo" by Taylor Jenkins Reid.

Simon & Schuster

Like Henry, Taylor Jenkins Reid is a master at writing about yearning and epic love, as is obvious in "The Seven Husbands of Evelyn Hugo."

Monique Grant's career as a magazine writer is at a standstill when famous — and famously private — film star Evelyn Hugo says she wants to do a tell-all interview with Monique, and only Monique. 

Monique doesn't understand why Evelyn would want to work with her of all people, but she can't say no, especially when Evelyn starts opening up to her about her path to fame and the forbidden love that changed the course of her life. Monique feels like Evelyn has handed her the opportunity of a lifetime.

When she finds out why Evelyn chose her for the tell-all, Monique will have to face truths about their shared history she never expected.

If you've already read Henry's "Great Big Beautiful Life," you'll swoon for "The Seven Husbands of Evelyn Hugo."

"The Two Lives of Lydia Bird" by Josie Silver

Penguin Random House

Lydia Bird's life is turned upside down when the love of her life, Freddie, dies in a car accident. After months of mourning and wanting to go back in time, Lydia begins to move on with the help of her sister and Freddie's best friend.

Then she's given a way to return to her old life with Freddie, a life where the tragedy never occurred. Her heart is pulled in two directions as she struggles to choose between going back to the familiar and embracing the unknown, where someone new wants to love her. 

Poignant and fresh, Josie Silver's "The Two Lives of Lydia Bird" is a story of love and hope that strikes a similar tone to Henry's works.

"The Wedding Date" by Jasmine Guillory

Penguin Random House

On the night before Drew Nichols is set to be a groomsman in his ex-girlfriend's wedding, he gets stuck in an elevator with the pretty and funny Alexa Monroe, the first bright spot in what he believes will be an unbearable weekend.

Impulse leads him to ask her to be his date to the wedding, and the duo surprises themselves by having more fun together than they bargained for. They plan to part ways after the wedding, neither interested in a long-distance relationship, but fate might have other plans for them. 

Jasmine Guillory writes about romance with reverence and joy, making "The Wedding Date" an ideal read for Henry lovers.

"In Five Years" by Rebecca Serle

Simon and Schuster

Dannie Kohan's plan is on track. In one day, she performs well at the job interview of a lifetime and agrees to marry her long-term boyfriend. Then, when she goes to sleep that night, she wakes up five years in the future, with a different man beside her and his ring on her finger.

Dannie has only one hour in the future before she's yanked back to the present, and she tries to push the experience aside as a vivid dream. Then, she meets the man from her dream four and a half years later and discovers he's dating her best friend. Dannie will have to confront what she really wants and decide whether she's willing to change her plans to find true happiness. 

Rebecca Serle's "In Five Years" explores time, grief, and all-consuming love, both romantic and platonic, in the same way Henry's books do, challenging readers to ask how far they would go for true happiness.

"Normal People" by Sally Rooney

Amazon

Although Sally Rooney's beloved "Normal People" has a darker tone than Henry's books, the protagonists, Connell and Marianne, have a chemistry and a yearslong history that Henry fans will love.

Connell and Marianne meet in high school, when Connell is a popular jock, and Marianne is, well, the opposite. The two bond despite their differences, setting them on a course that will shape their lives, drawing them back to one another over and over again.

Rooney's novel shows the inevitability of love, finding words for the often inexplicable reasons people need each other. You can also stream the Hulu series once you finish the book.

"One Golden Summer" by Carley Fortune
"One Golden Summer" by Carley Fortune.

Penguin Random House

Like Henry, Carley Fortune captures the angst and ecstasy of summer love in "One Golden Summer."

Alice can trace back her successful photography career to one photo: a candid shot of three teenagers on a bright yellow speedboat. She captured the shot during the one summer she spent at Barry's Bay with her Nan when she was 17, and it shifted the trajectory of her life.

Fifteen years later, Alice should be living her dream as a professional photographer, but six months after a breakup, she feels stuck and uninspired. When Nan breaks her hip, Alice thinks spending another summer at Barry's Bay might be good for them both.

Her vision of a tranquil summer with her grandmother gets upended by Charlie Florek, one of the teens from Alice's famous photo. The glimpse of Charlie that she got across the lake all those years ago was intriguing, but adult Charlie is so devastatingly handsome and thoughtful that he almost scares Alice.

As they spend the summer together, Charlie heals wounds in Alice that she didn't know were there. If he lets her in, Alice might just do the same for Charlie.

"Heated Rivalry" by Rachel Reid
"Heated Rivalry" by Rachel Reid.

Carina Press

Ilya Rozanov and Shane Hollander are supposed to hate each other. Not only have they been competing against each other in hockey since they were 18, but they're also total opposites. Canadian Shane is cautious and focused, while Russian wild card Ilya isn't afraid to embrace his bad boy reputation on the ice.

They have one big thing in common, though: the secret hookups they can't seem to resist every time they see each other. If the world found out about their relationship, both Ilya and Shane's careers could be in jeopardy, but they may decide it's worth the risk for a chance at something real with each other.

Rachel Reid's "Heated Rivalry" was adapted into a hit TV show, so you can stream the series if you want more from the characters when you finish the book.

"Love & Other Words" by Christina Lauren
"Love & Other Words" by Christina Lauren.

Simon & Schuster

Christina Lauren has written dozens of books, and their 2018 novel "Love & Other Words" is perfect for Henry fans who love friends-to-lovers plots.

Macy Sorensen has been white-knuckling her way through life for nearly a decade, but she's content with the safe world she's constructed for herself. A pediatric resident and newly engaged to a kind man who makes her feel mostly nothing, Macy thinks her heart is safe from the turmoil she experienced in her adolescence — until Elliot Petropoulos literally walks back into her life.

Macy met Elliot as a teen shortly after her mother died, and he quickly became her center of gravity as she visited the small town he called home on weekends. Christina Lauren tells their story from the past and present, showing readers how they became fast friends over books and adolescent secrets, how they fell into life-changing love, and the wreckage they were both left with when it all fell apart.

After 10 years of no contact, Macy may finally be ready to tell Elliot why she went radio silent on him after one fateful night. They'll both have to decide if they can move on from the pain of the past for a chance at a joy-filled future, together.

"The Seven Year Slip" by Ashley Poston
"The Seven Year Slip" by Ashley Poston.

Penguin Random House

Achingly romantic and surprisingly funny, "The Seven Year Slip" by Ashley Poston is about meeting the right person at the wrong time, literally.

Clementine West has been adrift since her beloved aunt died. She thought living in the Upper East Side apartment she inherited from her would make her feel closer to her, as the apartment's magic had always drawn her in. Instead, she feels like she's just waiting for her aunt to walk through the door.

Then, one day, Clementine comes home to find a man she doesn't know standing in her kitchen. Except, he thinks the apartment is his, for the summer anyway. He exists seven years in the past, staying in the apartment over the summer while Clementine and her aunt were in Europe.

Clementine isn't ready to be hurt by love again, but she might not be able to keep up her defenses against the sweet chef staying the summer. And if she does let herself fall, will they work together if she finds him again in the now?

"Just for the Summer" by Abby Jimenez
"Just for the Summer" by Abby Jimenez.

Hachette

Justin and Emma are having the same dating problem. Everyone they date meets their soulmate immediately after they break up with them.

When Emma sees Justin's viral Reddit post about his problem, she reaches out, and they decide to go on a date in hopes of breaking their curse.

Emma, a traveling nurse, plans to stay in Minnesota for the summer and enjoy a fling with Justin during her short stay. The last thing either expects is to get immediately attached, especially when they both have family members counting on them come fall.

Despite their best-laid plans, Emma and Justin's curse might have been leading them to each other all along in "Just for the Summer" by Abby Jimenez.

"Seven Days in June" by Tia Williams
"Seven Days in June" by Tia Williams.

Hachette

To the world, romance novelist Eva Mercy and acclaimed literary author Shane Hall have nothing to do with each other. That's because the only two people who know their books are inspired by each other are Eva and Shane.

For their entire careers, Shane and Eva have been writing secret love letters to each other, as the week they spent as teens glued to each other's sides in a rush of love still haunts them both years later.

They finally come face-to-face again when they both speak on a Brooklyn literary panel, and despite the years since they've seen each other, their chemistry is undeniable. Eva doesn't trust Shane after the way things went down between them, though, and as a single mom, she can't risk getting hurt again.

Still, Eva has always been curious to know why Shane disappeared, and reuniting with him might be the key to breaking her writer's block.

The second-chance romance in Tia Williams' "Seven Days in June" will hit the spot for Henry's fans.

"Deep End" by Ali Hazelwood
"Deep End" by Ali Hazelwood.

Penguin Random House

Ali Hazelwood is a prolific romance author, and the coming-of-age story and yearning in "Deep End" will scratch the itch for lovers of Henry's books.

Nearly every moment of Scarlett Vandermeer's life at Stanford is accounted for. She spends her days in the pool as a member of the diving team or studying, laser-focused on achieving her goal of getting into medical school.

A relationship or even a fling is the last thing on Scarlett's mind. Then, she finds out Lukas Blomqvist, Stanford's world champion swim captain who thrives on control, has similar interests to her when it comes to intimacy, and she thinks she might be able to make time in her busy schedule for something casual.

Lukas and Scarlett agree to explore their attraction together, deciding not to tell almost anyone about their arrangement. Scarlett doesn't think keeping her relationship with Lukas to herself will be a problem until she realizes the last thing she feels about him is casual.

"Same Time Next Summer" by Annabel Monaghan
"Same Time Next Summer" by Annabel Monaghan.

Penguin Random House

"Same Time Next Summer" by Annabel Monaghan offers another take on second-chance romance.

Sam's family's beach house on Long Island was her happy place in her childhood. She spent every summer there, and she was never happier than she was with her toes in the sand. Then, at 17, Wyatt broke her heart, and Sam couldn't face a summer there without him. She hasn't been back for more than a long weekend since.

At 30, Sam is making the trek from the city back to the beach, and she isn't the girl she was at 17. She's determined to succeed at her high-powered job and plan the perfect wedding with her fiancé, Jack, whose tendency to over-schedule their lives has become a comfort.

Only when she arrives, Sam discovers that Wyatt has returned to the house next door, and the entire adult life she created for herself begins to crumble. As old feelings come rushing back, Sam will have to take stock of who she is, who she wants to be, and who she really wants to live her life with.

"The Wedding People" by Alison Espach
"The Wedding People" by Alison Espach.

Macmillan

When Phoebe Stone arrives at the Cornwall Inn in Rhode Island, she's dressed to the nines and doesn't intend to ever check out. Her plans immediately go awry, though, when she discovers the entire hotel has been rented out for a wedding, and the attendees immediately assume she's one of the wedding people.

Soon, Phoebe has no choice but to participate in the wedding festivities, especially because she and the bride keep telling each other their darkest secrets.

After months of depression, the fanfare and plot twist of a stranger's wedding might show Phoebe her own path forward.

Slightly more melancholy in tone than Henry's works but still beautifully romantic, "The Wedding People" by Alison Espach is about the surprises life can bring when you least expect it.

"The Deal" by Elle Kennedy
"The Deal" by Elle Kennedy.

Bloom Books

If you're looking for another romance work that has been adapted for the screen, you can check out "The Deal" by Elle Kennedy, known as "Off Campus" on Amazon Prime.

Hannah Wells is thriving at Briar University. She's killing it in her music classes, and she has the best friend a girl could ask for. Her crush, Justin, has no idea she's into him, though, and Hannah doesn't know where to start on figuring out how to flirt or date.

Enter Garrett Graham, a hockey captain bound for the NHL. His GPA is in trouble, though, and Hannah is the only one who can help. The duo strikes a deal, with Hannah agreeing to tutor Garrett in school if he helps her make Justin jealous with a fake relationship.

Garrett expects that pretending to date Hannah will be a breeze, but when he develops real feelings for her, he'll have to come up with a new plan to get the girl.

items.title: GPUs on Kubernetes are bring-your-own-everything, starting with the bill
items.summary: If you run a Kubernetes platform, you’ve probably got at least one Grafana dashboard for resource visibility on your workloads. It shows what a container asked for versus what it used, making it relatively easy to point at the deployment that requested four cores and is only using half of one. If you break it down by namespace you get a rough idea which team is consuming what, which is what teams have been doing for CPU and memory for years and it mostly works. Then people started putting workloads on GPUs and a lot of what we assumed would carry over didn’t. Almost every piece of visibility you take for granted on CPU and memory, GPUs make you build yourself. Your own metrics, your own accuracy, your own rules for splitting the bill. Which is what stings the most, since the GPU is the most expensive line on the bill. Bring your own metrics With CPU and memory, the kernel already tracks usage per container for you, so getting a per-pod number is basically free. GPUs on the other hand, don’t give you that. The tool everybody starts with, NVIDIA’s DCGM exporter, reports at the physical device level by default. This is fine when one pod has a GPU to itself, but the second you start sharing a GPU across pods, with time-slicing or MPS, DCGM gives every pod sharing that GPU the same value. So if three pods are sharing one GPU, all three look like they’re using the whole thing, and when you add it up you get 300% of a GPU that doesn’t exist. With time-slicing or MPS, the driver exposes a single set of counters for the whole GPU, so DCGM has no per-pod data to attribute and cannot distinguish which workload consumed what. The numbers still plot nicely on a graph, but teams build full dashboards and reports on values that are blatantly wrong but hard to notice. Bring your own rightsizing math On the CPU side we’re all used to millicores, overcommitting, bursting, a CPU limit that just throttles you, a memory limit that gets you OOM killed but GPUs throw most of that out. A GPU shows up as a whole-number resource, nvidia.com/gpu: 1. You ask for whole GPUs, your request and your limit have to match, and there’s no overcommitting at the scheduler. The fractional sharing you need for inference happens underneath the scheduler through time-slicing or MIG, and Kubernetes requests don’t fit in neatly. So the basic rightsizing premise, comparing what a workload requested against what it’s using and reclaiming the difference, barely exists for GPUs when you start. You end up having to work out how much of a GPU’s capacity a workload got before you can even have the waste conversation. Bring your own guardrails The NVIDIA container runtime looks at an environment variable called NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES , and the base CUDA container images ship with it set to all. In a normal setup the device plugin overrides that and injects only the GPUs a pod was actually allocated. But if nothing overrides it or the container runtime is configured to honor the env var from the container, a pod can end up seeing and grabbing every GPU on the box no matter what Kubernetes thinks it handed out. So what the scheduler recorded as allocated and what ran on the hardware can diverge significantly. If you want the real number, you have to look at what’s happening at the process level and line it up against what Kubernetes thinks it did. Bring your own definition of utilization When a CPU graph says 80%, you pretty much know what you’re looking at, but GPU utilization is squishier. The usual metric tells you a kernel was running on the GPU for some slice of the sample window. It won’t tell you how much of the actual compute or memory bandwidth you burned. You can watch GPUs sit at 100% utilization while the compute is barely doing anything. And a lot of the time the thing that runs out first is memory, because frameworks like vLLM grab most of the GPU at startup whether they need it or not. Work out early which signal means something for your workloads, whether that’s compute occupancy, memory footprint, bandwidth, or power. If you rely on that big headline number, you can reach the wrong conclusion. Bring your own attribution NVIDIA’s NVML library will tell you, per process on a GPU, how much memory it’s holding, and you can trace each process back to the pod and team that owns it. The numbers are dependable, with one asterisk: they won’t quite add up to the card’s total, because the driver reserves a slice of memory for itself that doesn’t belong to any workload. Compute is where it falls apart and it’s worth understanding why. Picture a shared kitchen: memory is counter space, you can look and see what ingredients are sitting where. Compute is the stove and everyone’s taking turns in bursts of milliseconds. What NVIDIA gives you isn’t “how much stove time did each cook get.” It’s closer to a flag that gets checked many times a second asking “was this cook doing something right now?” If two people are both working, both flags read yes almost all the time, so you get two jobs that each look 90% busy, which is true and also tells you nothing about who got more done. That measurement is usable in one setup, when the GPU is strictly taking turns between jobs one at a time, where polling something like DCGM’s accounting mode or nvidia-smi’s PID-level sampling can approximate each job’s share. It breaks in the setup where jobs genuinely run side by side, which is also the setup people pick when they want better utilization. If two teams share a GPU, nothing available today will tell you which one burned 70% and which one burned 30%. So the practical decision is to bill on memory, where the data holds up, and treat compute as a signal, something to drive chargeback. The reality is, fairness through accuracy between teams actually matters when you want to move beyond showback and GPU memory is the most accurate way to attribute with existing tooling. Bring your own sharing paradigm Sharing a GPU turns out to mean a handful of different things and each one changes the math underneath. There’s time-slicing, which round-robins the GPU with no isolation and lets you oversubscribe it. Then MPS lets kernels from different processes run at the same time. MIG is quite popular and splits the GPU into fixed hardware partitions, though it’s worth noting that most clouds still charge you for the whole physical GPU even when you’re only using a slice, and on A100/H100-class GPUs you can only slice it up to 7 instances. And then there’s DRA, Dynamic Resource Allocation, which has been maturing over the last few Kubernetes releases and is clearly where things are going, but the ecosystem around it, including autoscalers like Karpenter, is still catching up. Every one of these changes what “allocated” even means, so visibility depends on which mode a given node is in. Bring your own splitting rules (and the bill is brutal) GPU costs run far higher per hour than CPU costs and are much harder to split per workload. The cloud provider bills a GPU node as one line item with the CPU, memory, and GPU all lumped together. To get to a real dollar number per workload, you have to break that line apart and weight the GPU piece by model, because a T4 and an H200 are nowhere near the same price. Then you split it across whatever workloads were sharing the GPU. On AWS, the cheapest MIG compatible A100 GPU is $22/hr, about ~$14/hr on spot, whereas a comparable CPU-only instance of that size runs about $5/hr. Even on spot that’s quite the difference. So what does this actually cost you? Add this all up and the real cost isn’t just the GPU bill but the engineering time and toil you sink rebuilding visibility you used to get for free. The metrics, the expected accuracy, the guardrails, the attribution, the splitting rules, every layer is something you now have to own and maintain. The upside here, is the space is moving quickly. DRA is maturing and adoption growing with it, hardware partitioning is getting easier, and the tooling gap narrows every release. So be deliberate about which layers you build now versus what you let the ecosystem catch up on, and definitely don’t go in expecting your CPU and memory playbook will carry straight over.

If two teams share a GPU, nothing available today will tell you which one burned 70% and which one burned 30%.

So the practical decision is to bill on memory, where the data holds up, and treat compute as a signal, something to drive chargeback. The reality is, fairness through accuracy between teams actually matters when you want to move beyond showback and GPU memory is the most accurate way to attribute with existing tooling.

Bring your own sharing paradigm

Sharing a GPU turns out to mean a handful of different things and each one changes the math underneath. There’s time-slicing, which round-robins the GPU with no isolation and lets you oversubscribe it. Then MPS lets kernels from different processes run at the same time. MIG is quite popular and splits the GPU into fixed hardware partitions, though it’s worth noting that most clouds still charge you for the whole physical GPU even when you’re only using a slice, and on A100/H100-class GPUs you can only slice it up to 7 instances. And then there’s DRA, Dynamic Resource Allocation, which has been maturing over the last few Kubernetes releases and is clearly where things are going, but the ecosystem around it, including autoscalers like Karpenter, is still catching up. Every one of these changes what “allocated” even means, so visibility depends on which mode a given node is in.

Bring your own splitting rules (and the bill is brutal)

GPU costs run far higher per hour than CPU costs and are much harder to split per workload. The cloud provider bills a GPU node as one line item with the CPU, memory, and GPU all lumped together. To get to a real dollar number per workload, you have to break that line apart and weight the GPU piece by model, because a T4 and an H200 are nowhere near the same price. Then you split it across whatever workloads were sharing the GPU. On AWS, the cheapest MIG compatible A100 GPU is $22/hr, about ~$14/hr on spot, whereas a comparable CPU-only instance of that size runs about $5/hr. Even on spot that’s quite the difference.

So what does this actually cost you?

Add this all up and the real cost isn’t just the GPU bill but the engineering time and toil you sink rebuilding visibility you used to get for free. The metrics, the expected accuracy, the guardrails, the attribution, the splitting rules, every layer is something you now have to own and maintain.

The upside here, is the space is moving quickly. DRA is maturing and adoption growing with it, hardware partitioning is getting easier, and the tooling gap narrows every release. So be deliberate about which layers you build now versus what you let the ecosystem catch up on, and definitely don’t go in expecting your CPU and memory playbook will carry straight over.

items.title: Google paid $90,000 for this bug, then waited two months to fix it
items.summary: Google took two months to patch an unauthenticated RCE vulnerability in its developer documentation infrastructure. The problem was a reused OAuth client secret, which DevSite stored in a Flask session cookie and also used to sign sessions. Anyone who recovered the secret could forge a valid cookie and execute Python code on the server. Simon Köck , a software engineer at Otark GmbH, discovered the flaw in Google’s DevSite infrastructure, the shared platform behind developers.google.com and several sibling documentation sites. Köck tells The New Stack that forged sessions were accepted on all seven affected domains, which relied on two different signing keys, and that he ran his code-execution proof on three of them, developers.google.com, docs.partner.android.com and web.dev. Köck tells The New Stack that forged sessions were accepted on all seven affected domains, which relied on two different signing keys, and that he ran his code-execution proof on three of them Google rated the vulnerability S0, the top of its severity scale, and awarded Köck a $90,000 bounty . That figure reflects a $75,000 base payout for an S0 RCE in what Google classifies as a normal application tier, multiplied by 1.2 for exceptional report quality. Köck confirmed unauthenticated RCE with a Python sleep payload, measuring response delays that matched his payload, and deliberately stopped short of running commands or touching files, credentials, or internal services. “I’d call it an exceptionally serious RCE because anyone could reach it without an account or victim interaction,” he tells The New Stack , adding that he doesn’t know whether the three hosts he tested shared the same backend machines. “I’d call it an exceptionally serious RCE because anyone could reach it without an account or victim interaction,” The more consequential unknown sits behind the server itself. Köck tells The New Stack , Arvin Shivram , a Singapore-based researcher who goes by @brutecat and has reported more than 130 Google vulnerabilities by his own count, has since pointed out that internal App Engine apps often have access to Stubby, Google’s internal service-to-service communication system. Köck acknowledges that access “could be a major part of the impact,” though he says he didn’t verify what this particular DevSite process could reach. One concern is whether an attacker could have modified Google’s developer documentation, replacing installation commands or download links with malicious ones. That could have enabled a supply-chain attack , but Köck didn’t test for write access to the content systems, and Google hasn’t disclosed DevSite’s process permissions or backend access. The exposed key also let Köck forge DevSite sessions, though he stopped short of checking whether those sessions could impersonate users or reach anyone’s data. By his own accounting, the demonstrated impact amounts to code execution on three hosts and accepted forged sessions on seven, while the full blast radius, including any path into Google’s internal services, remains unproven. One OAuth secret, two jobs DevSite stored a serialized OAuth2WebServerFlow object from Google’s oauth2client library, which Google has deprecated in favor of google-auth , inside a Flask session cookie, exposing the OAuth client secret in the process. Google had also reused that same OAuth client secret as DevSite’s Flask session-signing key , which Köck confirmed by reproducing the cookie’s signature offline, giving him the ability to forge sessions the server would accept. Pickle turns forgery into RCE The OAuth callback used Python’s pickle to deserialize session data, so Köck swapped the flow object for a malicious pickle payload, signed the forged cookie and let the callback execute it. The chain depended on three mistakes lining up, a secret exposed in the cookie, that same secret doing double duty as a signing key, and unsafe deserialization of session data, and fixing any one of them would have broken it. The chain depended on three mistakes lining up, a secret exposed in the cookie, that same secret doing double duty as a signing key, and unsafe deserialization of session data, and fixing any one of them would have broken it. Patch pace raises questions Köck reported the vulnerability on August 6, and Google accepted it the following day. The company approved the bounty on August 27 but didn’t deploy a fix until October 7 . Google hasn’t explained the two-month remediation window or whether it implemented interim mitigations, and questions also remain about the fix itself. Köck’s account of two separate signing keys explains why his recommendations mention two exposed OAuth client secrets, but Google hasn’t confirmed whether both were rotated or whether existing sessions were invalidated. Köck tells The New Stack , he was never given a forensic conclusion and doesn’t know whether Google found evidence of exploitation before the patch, and the company hasn’t said either. Google had not responded to a request for comment as of this update. An earlier version of this story said a single signing secret worked across all seven affected domains. Köck says the domains used two different signing keys. This story has also been updated with comment from Köck.

items.title: I'm a working parent who's built over 150 AI agents to help run my life. I get digital overload, but I'm getting more time back.
items.summary: Tristen O'Brien has built over 150 AI agents, including an AI family assistant. Sarah Lutomski/Sarah Lu Photography Tristen O'Brien is a working dad who built over 150 AI agents to manage his life and get back time. O'Brien's family has mixed opinions on AI, but they all use the AI family bot he built. He built an AI video game to help manage his agents and reduce digital overload. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Tristen O'Brien, a 44-year-old AI educator and content creator who works in cybersecurity based in Indiana. His words have been edited for length and clarity. For a long time, I've felt like I can only focus on three things at a time without everything falling apart: family, work, and school. If I tried to add something else, one of those three things would fail. I've been in the tech industry for over 20 years, and I'm working toward my doctorate in AI . I'm also a YouTuber. I spent years learning the programming language Python because I wanted to create a world where I could automate parts of my life, giving me more time for hobbies and other things. Then ChatGPT came out , and I realized I had wasted about five years doing that. Since learning how to build AI agents , I've built over 150 of them to help me run my life. I'm now down to using around 70. I've always wanted to automate parts of my life There's a book about automating the boring parts of your life with the programming language Python. Years ago, I found this book and decided to learn it. Then, when ChatGPT came out, I quickly got into it. I'm not a developer; I do this by vibe coding. I first used ChatGPT to make funny songs and things like that. My interest kept growing, and I kept doing more with it. I've switched to Claude as my main model now, but I still use ChatGPT , Perplexity, and Gemini. Two years ago, I went to an AI conference where I learned about AI agents. I remember being so excited about what I had learned that I told myself that as soon as I got home, I was finally going to automate my life with AI. I use a specific prompting technique to build my agents The very first agent that I built after the conference was a Chipotle burrito agent that could order my burrito for me. I love Chipotle , and it was silly, but that agent helped me see the power of AI. When I build agents, I'm never just like, " OK, Claude , this is what I want you to do, do the whole thing." Claude has a command called "/goal" that keeps the agent going until it gets the goal right. I think it's helpful, but I've learned to be very clear, or it will mess up. I do what I call my BIP process: Braindump, interview, prompt. I brain-dump everything, explaining what I want it to do, then I have Claude ask me questions about anything unclear or that it thinks I didn't ask. Then it gives me this crazy long prompt. So I might've started with a 15-word prompt , but now I have a 500-word prompt on everything that I want the agent to do. I've built over 100 agents and stopped using some of them In total, I've built five research and education agents, four research and news agents, one agent that builds new products, 18 financial agents, 27 home and family agents , 26 inbox and communication agents, 42 agents for my YouTube channel, and another 27 agents for publicity and outreach. Not all of those agents run at once. For example, I only have 12 active home and family agents: Four run every day for reminders about birthdays, softball, the dog, and school paperwork. Four run weekly for groceries, meal planning, a Sunday family brief, and a weekly check-in coach. One runs monthly for house maintenance reminders, and three run only when something comes up, like travel, packing, or gift ideas. I also had an agent who looked at a Google Sheet with all of my friends' and family's birthdays. If it were two weeks before their birthday, the agent would go to a webpage for a service that would send them a birthday card with what looks like my handwriting, then postmark it from my address. But I stopped using that one because it didn't feel personal enough. AI is more powerful once you learn how to use plug-ins I have a wife and two kids. I think my daughter likes AI a lot, too, because we talk about it a lot, and my wife sometimes gets into it. But my son is an artist , so he's not as big a fan, and I agree that there's definitely a line with creative work and industries. However, one of my favorite agents I've built is our family AI bot, which we all use. I used the texting service Twilio with a Claude plug-in to create an AI agent that is a custom chatbot and assistant for our family. It pings us, and we're able to vote on things like what we want for dinner that week, or see our calendars side by side. This agent helps us organize our lives and stay on the same page. AI gets really powerful when you start using connectors. My Claude agents wouldn't be as powerful if it couldn't connect to my Gmail, my calendar, or Twilio. So, from a technical standpoint, I'd suggest learning how to sign in on those kinds of plug-ins first. I spend around $600 a month on my AI subscriptions, which also support my YouTube channel and other work. If I were just using this for my personal life, I'd probably scale back to the $200 Claude Max subscription. I created an agent hierarchy game I get digital overload sometimes, and there is a point where too much is digital. It was hard to keep up with all my agents, so, in addition to getting rid of some of them, I had to create a digital hierarchy. I'm the chief human officer. I have my AI chief of staff , who works with a handful of director-level AI agents, and those directors each have AI worker agents under them. My chief of staff will relay updates from other agents, so now I'm mainly communicating with one agent who's relaying updates to the rest, which helps with the overload. I also created an animated game world where I can see all my agents running around a village. The different levels of agents have different outfits, so I can tell which one's which. I can run around the game world with my chief of staff and go talk to one of my agents any time to check in on what it's doing. Tristen O'Brien's video game village for his AI agents Courtesy of Tristen O'Brien I can also press a button to call a meeting, and we all go to this meeting hall in the game. It's more of a visual way to see all of my agents, and talk to them individually if I want to. The AI agent meeting room inside O'Brien's AI agent village video game. Courtesy of Tristen O'Brien I worry about privacy, but I'm getting more time back There are a lot of things I don't share with AI, like my Social Security number, but you have to have a level of trust, as you do with Gmail or any other service that is using your data or has access to it. I feel like AI does more good than harm. I'm not a doomsday guy about AI; I'm more of a utopian. There are things that I've picked up because I have more free time. I like to 3D print, fly drones, and ride my bike. I feel like I get a lot more done now. That was my mission from the start. To give myself back some time to do things that I really enjoy and appreciate, while still being able to focus on the top three things that matter to me most. Do you have a story to share about how you're using AI agents? If so, please reach out to the reporter at aapplegate@businessinsider.com . Read the original article on Business Insider

Tristen O'Brien has built over 150 AI agents, including an AI family assistant.

Sarah Lutomski/Sarah Lu Photography

  • Tristen O'Brien is a working dad who built over 150 AI agents to manage his life and get back time.
  • O'Brien's family has mixed opinions on AI, but they all use the AI family bot he built.
  • He built an AI video game to help manage his agents and reduce digital overload.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Tristen O'Brien, a 44-year-old AI educator and content creator who works in cybersecurity based in Indiana. His words have been edited for length and clarity.

For a long time, I've felt like I can only focus on three things at a time without everything falling apart: family, work, and school. If I tried to add something else, one of those three things would fail.

I've been in the tech industry for over 20 years, and I'm working toward my doctorate in AI. I'm also a YouTuber. I spent years learning the programming language Python because I wanted to create a world where I could automate parts of my life, giving me more time for hobbies and other things.

Then ChatGPT came out, and I realized I had wasted about five years doing that.

Since learning how to build AI agents, I've built over 150 of them to help me run my life. I'm now down to using around 70.

I've always wanted to automate parts of my life

There's a book about automating the boring parts of your life with the programming language Python. Years ago, I found this book and decided to learn it. Then, when ChatGPT came out, I quickly got into it.

I'm not a developer; I do this by vibe coding. I first used ChatGPT to make funny songs and things like that. My interest kept growing, and I kept doing more with it. I've switched to Claude as my main model now, but I still use ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini.

Two years ago, I went to an AI conference where I learned about AI agents. I remember being so excited about what I had learned that I told myself that as soon as I got home, I was finally going to automate my life with AI.

I use a specific prompting technique to build my agents

The very first agent that I built after the conference was a Chipotle burrito agent that could order my burrito for me. I love Chipotle, and it was silly, but that agent helped me see the power of AI.

When I build agents, I'm never just like, "OK, Claude, this is what I want you to do, do the whole thing." Claude has a command called "/goal" that keeps the agent going until it gets the goal right. I think it's helpful, but I've learned to be very clear, or it will mess up.

I do what I call my BIP process: Braindump, interview, prompt. I brain-dump everything, explaining what I want it to do, then I have Claude ask me questions about anything unclear or that it thinks I didn't ask. Then it gives me this crazy long prompt. So I might've started with a 15-word prompt, but now I have a 500-word prompt on everything that I want the agent to do.

I've built over 100 agents and stopped using some of them

In total, I've built five research and education agents, four research and news agents, one agent that builds new products, 18 financial agents, 27 home and family agents, 26 inbox and communication agents, 42 agents for my YouTube channel, and another 27 agents for publicity and outreach.

Not all of those agents run at once. For example, I only have 12 active home and family agents: Four run every day for reminders about birthdays, softball, the dog, and school paperwork. Four run weekly for groceries, meal planning, a Sunday family brief, and a weekly check-in coach. One runs monthly for house maintenance reminders, and three run only when something comes up, like travel, packing, or gift ideas.

I also had an agent who looked at a Google Sheet with all of my friends' and family's birthdays. If it were two weeks before their birthday, the agent would go to a webpage for a service that would send them a birthday card with what looks like my handwriting, then postmark it from my address. But I stopped using that one because it didn't feel personal enough.

AI is more powerful once you learn how to use plug-ins

I have a wife and two kids. I think my daughter likes AI a lot, too, because we talk about it a lot, and my wife sometimes gets into it. But my son is an artist, so he's not as big a fan, and I agree that there's definitely a line with creative work and industries.

However, one of my favorite agents I've built is our family AI bot, which we all use.

I used the texting service Twilio with a Claude plug-in to create an AI agent that is a custom chatbot and assistant for our family. It pings us, and we're able to vote on things like what we want for dinner that week, or see our calendars side by side. This agent helps us organize our lives and stay on the same page.

AI gets really powerful when you start using connectors. My Claude agents wouldn't be as powerful if it couldn't connect to my Gmail, my calendar, or Twilio. So, from a technical standpoint, I'd suggest learning how to sign in on those kinds of plug-ins first.

I spend around $600 a month on my AI subscriptions, which also support my YouTube channel and other work. If I were just using this for my personal life, I'd probably scale back to the $200 Claude Max subscription.

I created an agent hierarchy game

I get digital overload sometimes, and there is a point where too much is digital. It was hard to keep up with all my agents, so, in addition to getting rid of some of them, I had to create a digital hierarchy.

I'm the chief human officer. I have my AI chief of staff, who works with a handful of director-level AI agents, and those directors each have AI worker agents under them. My chief of staff will relay updates from other agents, so now I'm mainly communicating with one agent who's relaying updates to the rest, which helps with the overload.

I also created an animated game world where I can see all my agents running around a village. The different levels of agents have different outfits, so I can tell which one's which. I can run around the game world with my chief of staff and go talk to one of my agents any time to check in on what it's doing.

Tristen O'Brien's video game village for his AI agents

Courtesy of Tristen O'Brien

I can also press a button to call a meeting, and we all go to this meeting hall in the game. It's more of a visual way to see all of my agents, and talk to them individually if I want to.

The AI agent meeting room inside O'Brien's AI agent village video game.

Courtesy of Tristen O'Brien

I worry about privacy, but I'm getting more time back

There are a lot of things I don't share with AI, like my Social Security number, but you have to have a level of trust, as you do with Gmail or any other service that is using your data or has access to it.

I feel like AI does more good than harm. I'm not a doomsday guy about AI; I'm more of a utopian. There are things that I've picked up because I have more free time. I like to 3D print, fly drones, and ride my bike. I feel like I get a lot more done now.

That was my mission from the start. To give myself back some time to do things that I really enjoy and appreciate, while still being able to focus on the top three things that matter to me most.

items.title: Most "AI Agents" Are Just Flowcharts With Good Marketing
items.summary: Software labeled "agentic" today is just a thin LLM wrapper around simple API calls. Real enterprise ROI from autonomous agents isn't happening in basic chat interfaces it is happening in unglamorous, closed-loop workflows like supply chain rerouting, compliance audit tracing, vendor procurement, and multi-hop variance analysis. Moving these systems from supervised demos to unattended production requires two key architectural shifts: placing deterministic guardrails (hard spend limits, kill-switches, and external audit logs) outside the agent's prompt, and routing data queries through governed semantic layers rather than raw text-to-SQL. items.title: Losing your job after age 50 could derail your career
items.summary: Thomas Heep (left), Steven Fielding (center), and Jon McCarty (right) struggled to find work after losing their jobs later in life. Thomas Heep (left), Steven Fielding (center), and Jon McCarty (right) Some Americans who lose their jobs after age 50 spend years struggling to find comparable work. In September, the average unemployment duration for workers ages 55 to 64 was over eight months. Some older job seekers suspect age discrimination is hurting their chances of finding work. Cathy Valentine lost her job as a transformation lead in 2023. After three years struggling to find a comparable full-time job, the 61-year-old is now a prep cook at a cafe. She said she earns about an eighth of her previous salary. "It just feels like I tried to do everything right and I still am stuck," said Valentine, who lives in Florida. Some older workers who lose their jobs can afford to retire, while others find a comparable role fairly quickly. But those who don't risk getting stuck in a job search that drags on for months or even years — and is getting longer. On some metrics, older Americans are doing just fine in the job market . As of September, older workers had lower unemployment rates than younger workers, and when they were jobless, the median length of that unemployment was shorter. But those figures obscure a worse trend for older job seekers . While half of 55 to 64-year-olds were jobless for a relatively low three months, the group's average unemployment duration was more than eight months in September. That means some older workers have been unemployed for so long that they're pulling the average way up. The gap between the average and median has widened in recent months, suggesting the longest job searches may be growing even longer. In September, about 173,000 unemployed Americans ages 55 to 64 had been out of work for at least six months, and some are facing far longer stretches of unemployment. A Bureau of Labor Statistics analysis found that only 57% of workers ages 55 to 64 who lost their long-held jobs any time between 2023 and 2025 had found new jobs as of January 2026. By contrast, 73% of workers ages 25 to 54 who lost long-held jobs in that period had found new work. Some older workers may have taken their job loss as a sign they should retire. But for others, it marked the beginning of an uphill battle to find another job. The struggle to get hired after 50 As their searches drag on for months or years, older job seekers like Valentine often blame age discrimination for at least part of their struggles. Thomas Heep, a Denver resident in his 60s, has been searching for full-time work since losing his operations manager role in April 2025. He's struggled to pay his bills and filed for bankruptcy earlier this year. Heep suspects some employers may favor younger job seekers over someone his age because they worry he won't remain in the workforce much longer. "Even if a company loves my résumé, skill set, and work history, they're going to look at my age and go: How long is he going to stay? He's close to retirement age. It's too risky." he said. Thomas Heep has struggled to find full-time work since losing his job last year. Thomas Heep Other older workers suspect their salary expectations may be working against them. A former Big Tech employee in her early 60s who lost her job last year said she worries her years of experience may put her at a disadvantage compared with younger candidates willing to accept lower pay. "There's so many people getting laid off at this point who are younger, willing to take these ridiculously low salaries with no benefits," she said. While some research suggests age discrimination plays a role in hiring, proving it in any individual case can be extremely difficult. And for older job seekers who suspect their age is holding them back, there's often no clear path to addressing the problem. Jacob Zinkula writes about how workers are navigating their careers. Share your story with him by filling out this form , emailing him , or reaching out via Signal at jzinkula.29. Follow his work by clicking here . When finding another job feels out of reach For some older workers, a prolonged job search eventually leaves them with two options: settle for lower-paying work or give up looking altogether. Jon McCarty spent 18 months trying to find another software engineering job after losing his role in 2022. Earlier in his career, it typically took him about a month to find a new job. But he said that as he got older, his stretches without work grew longer. McCarty, who's in his early 60s and lives in Virginia, eventually took a part-time cashier job at Home Depot. He's come to believe he'll likely never return to his former career. Jon McCarty spent more than a year searching for another software engineering job. Jon McCarty Steven Fielding, 58, has been laid off more than five times during his career in tech communications. He's been looking for work since April and said the employment gaps over the course of his career have taken a toll on his finances, leaving him with little in savings. Fielding, who lives in Washington state, said he's trying to adapt to the changing job market, including by developing his AI skills . He suspects his age may be contributing to his difficult search, in part because he believes some employers prefer younger workers who are willing to accept lower salaries. Still, he's hoping his decades of experience can help him land another opportunity. "It's like my house is down to the foundation and I'm going to have to rebuild again," he said. "It's pretty daunting to think about." Do you have a story to share? Reach out to the reporter via email at jzinkula@businessinsider.com , or via Signal at jzinkula.29. items.title: Coding agents made building easy. Platform teams that build from scratch are 3.5x more likely to lack a strategy.
items.summary: Build-or-buy is usually framed as an engineering trade-off, where developer time is weighed against integration and migration overhead, and control against the maintenance burden of a bespoke build. When we put together the 2026 Future of Platform Engineering report , we weren’t trying to settle the trade-off; we were trying to find out whether platform feature-sourcing decisions revealed anything about the platform team. It turns out it does. Across responses from 379 platform professionals, we found that teams predominantly building from scratch are less likely to have a clear strategy in place and to meet fewer of their platform goals. This question has changed considerably with AI. Agents have made building easier than ever; an internal tool that once took months to build can now be put together in a day. But AI removes the effort of writing code, not the work of owning it. The maintenance, upgrades, and governance that come with a scratch-built feature remain, while the volume of change moving through the pipeline increases. That makes build-versus-buy a sharper strategic question than ever. We asked platform teams how they support each feature they own: built from scratch, built on an existing template, or bought as an underlying tool. Teams whose dominant approach is building from scratch are far more likely to report that their platform lacks a clear strategy. The association is strong, but it is not as simple as “build from scratch means you don’t have a plan.” Most Teams Buy And Choose Deliberately Across the features platform teams own, we found that using an underlying tool is the most common: 51.3% of respondents said this was their primary approach, ahead of building on an existing template (31.2%) and building from scratch (17.5%). High performers lean more heavily on tools (58.8%) than on building from a template (47.8%) or from scratch (33.3%). This could reflect a broader maturity pattern: as architectural choices in Platform Engineering settle, teams increasingly standardize on tools rather than maintain their own. David Tuite has described the alternative as the “build-versus-buy trap,” where teams stuck maintaining custom interfaces sink 6 to 18 months into upgrades and operational overhead instead of shipping value. Build-versus-buy feature implementation approach by goals delivered (source: Octopus ). The exceptions are where it gets interesting. Local development environments, one-click projects , and ephemeral environments skew toward templates rather than tools, because they’re bound to a specific tech stack and golden paths that off-the-shelf tools rarely provide. Ephemeral environments are worth pausing on because they also mark where AI is landing well. Teams whose platforms offer them were far more likely to report that AI has positively affected the speed and stability of software delivery; the same was true of code coverage and cost control . Among teams reporting an extremely positive effect, more than three-quarters had ephemeral environments. This association also likely reflects the platform rather than the feature. Teams with ephemeral environments tend to run on broad platforms with a range of automated delivery capabilities around them, and that breadth itself tracks with positive AI impact on delivery. Ephemeral environments , then, could be a sign of a platform mature enough to absorb AI-generated volume and change, without losing stability. This is consistent with DORA’s research finding that organizational gains from AI depend on platform quality: strong platforms amplify the effects, while weaker ones dampen them. Features ranked by AI impact on software delivery speed and stability (source: Octopus ). The features that break the pattern reflect fit rather than a reluctance to buy, and the reasoning behind these decisions supports this. When asked to explain their build-or-buy logic, the most common response was a cost-benefit analysis (29.6%), followed by a preference for open source (28.6%), a fit-and-requirements assessment (22.4%), a preference for commercial tools (b22.4%), and building for core differentiation (16.3%). As one respondent summarized it, “Build what makes us unique, buy or adopt what’s standard, and always consider long-term cost and lock-in.” This is the same central idea presented in domain-driven design , which distinguishes the core domain, where custom work creates competitive advantage, from supporting and generic domains, where it mostly adds complexity and maintenance for something that could have been bought. Reasons behind deciding to build versus buy (source: Octopus ). The Build-from-Scratch Pattern Given how deliberately most teams choose, the strategy finding is more interesting. When classified by dominant build method, teams building from scratch are about 3.5x more likely to report a lack of clear strategy as an obstacle (57.9%) than teams building from a template (15.6%) or using an underlying tool (16.7%). AI clusters here, too, with predominantly build-from-scratch teams more likely to use AI moderately or extensively for legacy modernization and language migration. There is a clear pattern here: the teams building the most lean hardest on AI for maintenance. This isn’t because they use AI more generally: their reported adoption, impact, and expected effects match those of everyone else. The difference is specific to the work that follows custom-built features. Build-versus-buy feature implementation due to a lack of a clear strategy and technical complexity. Heatmap showing the percentage of respondents selecting the obstacle by dominant build approach (source: Octopus ). Building First, Deciding Later One interpretation is that strategy comes first, and the build-or-buy decision comes later: a team without clear direction has no basis for deciding what to buy, so it builds by default. Another is that building is the strategy rather than a sign of a missing strategy. Building can help identify the problem and show progress before the team has settled on the platform’s purpose. This is an interesting take, and the one the data can’t tell us which is right. Simon Wardley’s work on mapping describes a similar pattern: teams that can’t see what tools already exist tend to build their own solutions to problems that have already been solved better elsewhere. With AI, the gap between having an idea and having a working tool has almost closed. An agent can now build a custom incident-management tool before anyone has asked whether one is needed. Building has become easier, but maintaining what gets built hasn’t. DORA’s research suggests why this matters: good platforms provide capabilities and set boundaries on their use, and in AI-assisted development, those boundaries may currently matter more. Established tools come with those boundaries built in; a platform built piece by piece has only the ones someone thought to add. In either case, the relationship holds. Building from scratch isn’t the problem. Building from scratch by default, without a reason, is where the strategy gap appears. A Better Question Than Build or Buy This isn’t a case for buying everything, as we found that some features need to be built around their organization’s own context. It is a case of buying deliberately. Where a team builds from scratch, there should be a reason. When teams buy a tool, the reason is usually already evident: nearly every team buys for the well-defined parts of the platform, and as agents write more code, the value of tools that solve those problems well only grows.

items.title: One chart shows white-collar biz is thriving even as jobs dry up
items.summary: Employment in white-collar sectors has dipped, while output is surging. Maskot/Getty Images Employment has dropped in white-collar sectors, while output has continued to surge. AI and economic uncertainty are two likely reasons for the sluggish white-collar job market. Still, how productive AI makes companies remains a question. The white-collar sector is doing more with less. While the number of total jobs has slid in industries like finance, tech, and professional services, output has been on a tear. Gad Levanon, the chief economist at the Burning Glass Institute, examined how employment in white-collar-heavy sectors compares with real gross domestic product . items.title: Anthropic's Claude AI submitted false murder tip to Philadelphia police
items.summary: An Anthropic AI model submitted a false tip about an unsolved murder to Philadelphia police, the company and police department confirmed on Friday. A Claude model sent the false tip on July 18 to the Philadelphia Police Department's website for submitting information about unsolved murders, but it was flagged by a spam filter. Anthropic apparently discovered the incident on September 28 and informed the police department about it on October 8. During internal testing, Claude Haiku 4.5 was instructed to complete various forms up to the final submission stage and to stop before submitting those forms. "Several times Claude mistakenly submitted the form instead, expecting there to be an additional confirmation page," Anthropic said in a report describing "unintended model actions we’ve observed during evaluations and internal use of Claude." Read full article Comments

items.title: How Anthropic’s Dynamic Workflows Coordinate Claude Agents
items.summary: CJ Avilla and Harrison Stall, Members of Technical Staff at Anthropic, at AI Engineer NYC today. The AI Engineer New York 2026 conference kicked off this morning with a series of workshops, including Anthropic discussing how to orchestrate its Claude Managed Agents . Of particular interest was a brand new feature, announced on Friday , called dynamic workflows — or simply “flows,” as the presenters repeatedly called it. Flows are defined as “a new type of multiagent orchestration, built for your most ambitious workloads.” CJ Avilla and Harrison Stall , both Members of Technical Staff at Anthropic , began by invoking some operating system projects of the past — from Ken Thompson building the original Unix operating system, through to Linux evolving from one person (Linus Torvalds) to layers of trusted maintainers . The lesson: agents need the same level of organization in order to do the types of big, ambitious projects Anthropic envisions for dynamic workflows. Sponsored by Union.ai Build a sovereign AI factory The best engineering teams are building AI factories where they own and control not only their data, compute, and infrastructure, but also a durable runtime on their cloud. Union.ai gives your workflows the durability to adapt and right-size infra resources and recover from failures without re-running completed work. Get started directly through AWS Marketplace and try Union.ai free for 30 days . To learn more, visit us at AI Engineer New York booth #48. “I think a lot of us who are orchestrating and managing lots of agents now might start to feel this feeling of being the bottleneck and being the breaking point as we have lots of agents contributing tons and tons of PRs,” Avilla said. “And we’re sitting there in our GitHub trying to approve PRs and make sure that everything works as expected.” From agent rosters to dynamic workflows The pair noted that dynamic workflows began in Claude Code as the “a harness for every task” concept. But flows can run longer than a single agent or a roster. The basic idea is that Claude chooses the organization of agents. “Flows are essentially the next version of multi-agent orchestration,” said Stall, “where you can let Claude fully orchestrate the entirety of its own multi-agent topology.” The way this works is that the lead agent creates a plan for how it wants to accomplish tasks. Claude then writes an orchestration program, which launches agents, collects results, and manages information flow. Image via Anthropic Previously, Claude Managed Agents required developers to configure a coordinator and a roster of subagents. With dynamic workflows, Claude itself determines how to divide and orchestrate the work. “Across multiple different phases of the multi-agent orchestration, it’s able to accomplish discrete, verifiable units of work without you having to manage any of the interconnections between these things,” Stall said. That said, Avilla noted that the user can introduce specialist sub-agents if they wish. “It’s also possible in the agent config to pass in pre-configured sub-agents,” he said. All of this is available in Claude Console , the interface used by developers accessing Claude through API — the whole point of Claude Managed Agents. Claude Console, where Managed Agents is located. The presenters then showed a relatively simple workflow of a stock watchlist scanner. Although this was far removed from the big, ambitious projects Anthropic is encouraging, it did illustrate the basic pattern : a scan phase distributed individual tickers to agents with isolated contexts , and a later review phase examined the findings before producing a report. Q&A: Budgets and the limits of self-improvement The audience Q&A surfaced a number of potential problems. One audience member asked how Claude decides how many agents a task needs , and could a simple ticker scan trigger hundreds of sub-agents? “The answer really is evals and lower defaults ,” Stall replied, noting that ambitious tasks generally require explicitly encouraging greater parallelization. One enduring concern with agent orchestration is maintaining control over your token budget . Someone asked whether the lead agent knows how much money it has available? Stall replied that the model does not know its budget while running, but that developers can set a session budget. He added that informing models of their budgets could make the agents “a little bit anxious,” which elicited chuckles from the audience. Scanner in the stock watchlist example. A related question was how can developers make repeated flows cheaper and more efficient over time? Outside of asking Claude to examine the costs incurred, Avilla suggested another relatively new feature be used: dreaming . In the documentation , “dreaming” is defined as a research preview feature. A dream “reads an existing memory store alongside past session transcripts, then produces a new, reorganized memory store, ” with duplicates merged, “stale or contradicted entries” replaced, and “new insights surfaced.” Avilla described dreaming in the flow context as being able to “crystallize and basically improve the memory store that is related to those sessions.” For the stock watchlist example, someone asked whether the watchlist flow can improve itself? For example, recognize that its scanning model is inadequate and change the next scheduled run? Stall said this wasn’t built in, but he and Avilla suggested hill-climbing and dreaming could be used to improve the loop. The brain/hands conceptual overview of Managed Agents. What about visibility into the actions of the sub-agents , another audience member asked. Avilla replied that yes, developers can always inspect that through graphing functionality inside Claude Console. “You can tell, what did the lead agent actually pass to the sub-agent? You can look at that payload here to deeply understand what is actually happening for every transition in this entire graph.” Another interesting question was whether the subagents can communicate with each other? Stall said the agents share a filesystem and can use it to exchange information, but developers cannot directly instruct one workflow subagent to message another through the API. Flows cost much more, but are designed for big tasks In the watchlist-scanner comparison, Avilla said flows cost “much more” than a single-agent approach, but were also “much more effective at finding all of the details.” Setting a budget is key! The bigger question is how ambitious can flows be, really? One audience member asked whether dynamic workflows can power large scientific research projects, referencing OpenAI’s recently announced proof concerning the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize problem . While Stall wouldn’t be drawn on specifics about how Anthropic computes large scientific problems, he said it is their goal to enable general users to tackle those problems too. “Flows are basically a way to throw test-time compute at hard problems and get more capability faster out of the models,” he said. “We think, especially as an API service, that unlocking the power of this is the first step for us making these types of discoveries, or scientific progress, broadly doable by the general public. ”

items.title: Hello Python 3.15, goodbye 3.10, and now I can use 3.11
items.summary: Python 3.15 is here ! Here's the essential What's new in Python 3.15 guide, this year curated by 3.14 and 3.15 release manager Hugo van Kemenade. As someone who builds open source software that works in every supported Python version, I get to say goodbye to Python 3.10 and start embracing features from Python 3.11. First, some highlights from Python 3.15. Explicit lazy imports I'm most excited about Explicit lazy imports from PEP 810 . These let you import modules like so: lazy import json lazy from pathlib import Path The module will then be imported the first time those symbols are used in the code that follows. My LLM CLI tool implements plugins. I had to recommend manual lazy imports in the plugin author documentation, because simply installing plugins that used heavy dependencies such as sentence_transformers could add multiple seconds to every invocation of the llm command. Lazy imports directly address this startup cost. Unpacking in comprehensions The new [*sublist for sublist in lists] unpacking syntax is neat. Here's an illustration lifted from the documentation : lists = [[ 1 , 2 ], [ 3 , 4 ], [ 5 ]] [ * L for L in lists ] # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] # equivalent to [x for L in lists for x in L] sets = [{ 1 , 2 }, { 2 , 3 }, { 3 , 4 }] { * s for s in sets } # {1, 2, 3, 4} # equivalent to {x for s in sets for x in s} dicts = [{ 'a' : 1 }, { 'b' : 2 }, { 'a' : 3 }] { ** d for d in dicts } # {'a': 3, 'b': 2} # equivalent to {k: v for d in dicts for k,v in d.items()} PEP 798: Unpacking in Comprehensions by Adam Hartz and Erik Demaine proposed this as an extension of the unpacking syntax from PEP 448 , which landed in Python 3.5 back in 2015. A sampling profiler Python's existing tracing profiler has been renamed from cProfile to profiling.tracing , and has been joined by an exciting new sampling profiler called Tachyon, aka profiling.sampling . Sampling profilers work by periodically capturing stack traces from running processes, then using those to calculate which functions have the most time spent inside of them. They're very low overhead and can provide a deep insight into running systems, without needing to instrument those systems first. I've previously used tools like py-spy for this. Now this capability is baked into the standard library.
