items.summary_html:
Python 3.15 is here! Here's the essential What's new in Python 3.15 guide, this year curated by 3.14 and 3.15 release manager Hugo van Kemenade. As someone who builds open source software that works in every supported Python version, I get to say goodbye to Python 3.10 and start embracing features from Python 3.11.

First, some highlights from Python 3.15.

Explicit lazy imports

I'm most excited about Explicit lazy imports from PEP 810. These let you import modules like so:

lazy import json
lazy from pathlib import Path

The module will then be imported the first time those symbols are used in the code that follows.

My LLM CLI tool implements plugins. I had to recommend manual lazy imports in the plugin author documentation, because simply installing plugins that used heavy dependencies such as sentence_transformers could add multiple seconds to every invocation of the llm command. Lazy imports directly address this startup cost.

Unpacking in comprehensions

The new [*sublist for sublist in lists] unpacking syntax is neat. Here's an illustration lifted from the documentation:

lists = [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5]]
[*L for L in lists]
# [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
# equivalent to [x for L in lists for x in L]

sets = [{1, 2}, {2, 3}, {3, 4}]
{*s for s in sets}
# {1, 2, 3, 4}
# equivalent to {x for s in sets for x in s}

dicts = [{'a': 1}, {'b': 2}, {'a': 3}]
{**d for d in dicts}
# {'a': 3, 'b': 2}
# equivalent to {k: v for d in dicts for k,v in d.items()}

PEP 798: Unpacking in Comprehensions by Adam Hartz and Erik Demaine proposed this as an extension of the unpacking syntax from PEP 448, which landed in Python 3.5 back in 2015.

A sampling profiler

Python's existing tracing profiler has been renamed from cProfile to profiling.tracing, and has been joined by an exciting new sampling profiler called Tachyon, aka profiling.sampling.

Sampling profilers work by periodically capturing stack traces from running processes, then using those to calculate which functions have the most time spent inside of them. They're very low overhead and can provide a deep insight into running systems, without needing to instrument those systems first.

I've previously used tools like py-spy for this. Now this capability is baked into the standard library.

If you have the PID of an existing Python 3.15 process you can start gathering samples by running this (I had to use sudo on macOS):

sudo uv run --python 3.15 python -m profiling.sampling attach 1234

Interact with the main program a bit, then hit Ctrl+C to stop gathering and see a report, which looks something like this:

It can also produce flame graphs like this and heat maps like this, and can even output a format that can be viewed in the Firefox profiler UI.

3.15 isn't much faster than 3.14

Miguel Grinberg investigated How fast is Python 3.15? the other day against the 3.15.0rc3 release and found performance to be mostly the same as 3.14, with the exception of the experimental JIT. The JIT gave a 1.2x boost over the standard 3.15 interpreter (on a Fibonacci test), the first time Miguel observed a meaningful JIT performance increase.

Miguel's explorations of 3.14 last year found significant boosts against Python 3.13 across many more categories.

Upgrading to Python 3.15 with uv

I used the following sequence of commands to get uv to use Python 3.15 on my Mac. First I had to upgrade uv itself to ensure it knew about the new release:

uv self update

Then I installed the stable 3.15 release:

uv python install 3.15

And told uv that I wanted that to be the default for every uv run command, unless the project itself pinned a different version:

uv python pin --global 3.15

Now the following reports 3.15 as the version:

uv run python --version

I already have a bunch of tools installed using uv tool install. I reinstalled them to use Python 3.15 like this:

uv tool upgrade datasette --python 3.15

Then I can confirm the version like this:

datasette --get /-/versions.json | jq
Highlights from Python 3.11

The release of 3.15 means that Python 3.10 (released in 2021) is officially no longer supported.

My policy for my main open source projects is to keep them working in every supported Python version. I can now drop 3.10 and start using features that were introduced in 3.11.

Here's the What's new in Python 3.11 document. I finally get to rely on tomllib being available!

Datasette makes extensive use of asyncio. 3.11 adds TaskGroup and timeout(), and several more new features.

datetime.UTC is a new in 3.11 alias for datetime.timezone.utc.

Python's SQLite support got some significant upgrades in 3.11, including:

  • setlimit() and getlimit() expose a mechanism for setting SQLite runtime limits from Python.
  • create_window_function() lets us create custom window functions in Python, as a class with step(), value(), inverse(), and finalize() methods.
  • blobopen() provides an efficient mechanism for partial reads and writes of large BLOB binary values stored in a SQLite row.
  • You can now call set_authorizer(None) to remove a SQLite authorizer. Datasette had a workaround for this!

Plus a whole bunch of improvements to Python's typing system.

I plan to land Python 3.11 improvements to a bunch of my projects over the next few weeks. Here's my first Datasette PR removing that set_authorizer(None) workaround.

I've also updated my click-app, datasette-plugin, python-lib, and llm-plugin cookiecutter templates to test against Python 3.11 through Python 3.15.

Tags: open-source, profiling, python, sqlite, uv

items.summary_html:
You've measured share of voice and found a prompt cluster where a competitor keeps getting recommended and cited, and you don't. The obvious next question is what's different about their page?

Most people answer that by eyeballing two browser tabs. This post does it with a script: take the URLs AI engines cited for a prompt, fetch them the way a non-JavaScript crawler would, extract the features that tend to matter for extraction and citation, and print a diff against your page.

It won't explain everything. Brand reputation and third-party mentions matter too, and they don't show up in page HTML. But it reliably catches the boring structural gaps, which are the fastest ones to fix.

Step 1: Get the cited URLs

Start from stored citations (see the earlier post on parsing them) for the prompts where you lose:

import sqlite3, json
from collections import Counter

conn = sqlite3.connect("visibility.db")
rows = conn.execute("""
    SELECT r.sources FROM run r
    JOIN prompt p ON p.id = r.prompt_id
    WHERE p.topic = ? AND r.run_date >= date('now','-28 days')
""", ("analytics-pricing",)).fetchall()

counts = Counter(u for (s,) in rows for u in json.loads(s))
competitor_urls = [u for u, n in counts.most_common(10) if "acmeanalytics.com" not in u]

Pick the top three to five cited URLs. Pages cited across many runs and engines are the signal. A URL cited once is noise.

Step 2: Fetch like a simple crawler

Fetch raw HTML with no JavaScript rendering. If a page's content needs JS to appear, that's itself a finding:

import requests

UA = "Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; page-diff/0.1; +https://example.com/bot)"

def fetch(url: str) -> str:
    r = requests.get(url, headers={"User-Agent": UA}, timeout=20)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.text

Use an honest user agent and keep the volume tiny. You're reading a handful of public pages, not crawling a site.

Step 3: Extract features that matter for AI extraction

Retrieval systems split pages into passages, embed them and pull the best-matching chunks into the model's context. So the features worth measuring are the ones that affect whether a clean, self-contained answer passage exists and whether the facts are machine-readable.

import re, json
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

def features(html: str) -> dict:
    soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser")

    ld_types = []
    for tag in soup.find_all("script", type="application/ld+json"):
        try:
            data = json.loads(tag.string or "")
        except json.JSONDecodeError:
            ld_types.append("INVALID")
            continue
        items = data if isinstance(data, list) else data.get("@graph", [data])
        for it in items:
            t = it.get("@type")
            ld_types.extend(t if isinstance(t, list) else [t])

    for t in soup(["script", "style", "noscript", "nav", "footer", "header"]):
        t.decompose()
    main = soup.find("main") or soup.find("article") or soup.body or soup
    text = main.get_text(" ", strip=True)
    words = len(text.split())

    headings = [h.get_text(" ", strip=True) for h in main.find_all(["h2", "h3"])]
    question_heads = sum(1 for h in headings if h.endswith("?") or
                         re.match(r"(?i)^(how|what|why|when|which|is|can|does|should)\b", h))

    # words before the first paragraph under each H2: proxy for "answer first"
    first_para_lens = []
    for h in main.find_all("h2"):
        p = h.find_next("p")
        if p:
            first_para_lens.append(len(p.get_text(" ", strip=True).split()))

    return {
        "words": words,
        "h2_h3": len(headings),
        "question_headings": question_heads,
        "median_first_para_words": sorted(first_para_lens)[len(first_para_lens)//2] if first_para_lens else None,
        "tables": len(main.find_all("table")),
        "lists": len(main.find_all(["ul", "ol"])),
        "numbers": len(re.findall(r"\b\d[\d,.]*\s?(%|\$|ms|x|users|customers)?", text)),
        "jsonld_types": sorted(set(filter(None, ld_types))),
        "has_author": bool(soup.select_one('[rel=author], .author, [itemprop=author]')) or "Person" in ld_types,
        "has_date": bool(soup.find("time")) or bool(re.search(r'"date(Published|Modified)"', html)),
        "outbound_links": len([a for a in main.find_all("a", href=True) if a["href"].startswith("http")]),
    }

Each feature is a proxy, and some are crude (numbers will count list markers in some layouts). That's acceptable here. We're comparing pages against each other, not scoring them in absolute terms.

Step 4: Diff 
import pandas as pd

ours = "https://acmeanalytics.com/pricing"
table = {url: features(fetch(url)) for url in [ours, *competitor_urls[:4]]}
df = pd.DataFrame(table).T
df.index = ["OURS"] + [f"C{i}" for i in range(1, len(df))]
print(df.to_string())

      words h2_h3 question_headings median_first_para_words tables lists numbers jsonld_types                     has_author has_date
OURS    410     4                 0                      62      0     2      11 [Organization]                   False      False
C1     1840    14                 9                      28      2     6      74 [FAQPage, Organization, Product]  True       True
C2     2210    17                 6                      31      1     8      91 [Article, BreadcrumbList]        True       True
C3     1390    11                 7                      24      3     4      58 [Product, SoftwareApplication]   False      True

(Illustrative output.) A diff like this tends to make the problem obvious:

  • Depth: the cited pages are 3–5× longer, and that isn't padding. They have 11–17 sections.
  • Question headings: competitors title sections the way people ask. The other page has none.
  • Answer first: the competitors open each section with a short (~25–30 word) direct answer. The other page opens with ~60 words of preamble.
  • Specifics: many more concrete numbers, plus comparison tables.
  • Machine-readable facts: Product / FAQPage schema, an author and a date.

Step 5: Check what's cited, not just what exists

Features tell you what a page has. The cited passages tell you which part the engine used. If you stored cited_text with your citations (here, in a citation table of run_id, url, cited_text rows produced by the normaliser from the citations post), line them up against the competitor page:

for url in competitor_urls[:3]:
    print("\n", url)
    for (s,) in conn.execute(
        "SELECT cited_text FROM citation WHERE url = ? AND cited_text IS NOT NULL LIMIT 5", (url,)):
        print("  -", s[:160])

You'll usually find the engine quoting the same two or three passages: a pricing sentence with a concrete number, a one-line definition, a row of a comparison table. Those are the passages to match or beat, with your own facts.

What the diff can't see

Be honest about what's out of scope:

  • Off-site reputation. Reviews, forum threads, publications and lists where competitors are mentioned. In model-knowledge-heavy engines, these often matter more than on-page features.
  • JavaScript-rendered content. If your page renders client-side, the raw fetch shows less than a browser does. That's informative (many AI fetchers don't render JS), but compare against a rendered version before drawing conclusions.
  • Freshness and authority signals that the engines don't disclose.

So treat the output as a list of hypotheses. Ship the fixes, then check whether citation rate for that prompt cluster moves over the following weeks.

Automating the loop

Running this by hand works for one prompt cluster. Across dozens of clusters and several competitors, you want it running continuously.

Vista AI's Competitor Analysis handles the tracking side: it lists which competitor pages get cited most, where competitors beat you per engine, and surfaces content gaps and quick wins. For the page-level side, Vista's Page Audit scores your page and competitor pages side by side on AI visibility, understanding and citation potential, which is a more complete version of the feature diff above.

Whatever you use, the loop is the same: find the prompts you lose → read what gets cited instead → close the specific gap → re-measure.

items.title: Copilot YOLO mode, dissected: what --yolo, /yolo and Allow all actually skip
items.summary: TL;DR Copilot CLI: copilot --yolo (same flag as --allow-all ), or /yolo in a running session. It is shorthand for --allow-all-tools + --allow-all-paths + --allow-all-urls . VS Code: pick Allow all in the chat permission picker, type /yolo , or set "chat.tools.global.autoApprove": true to make it permanent. What it skips: approval prompts. What it doesn't: your --deny-tool rules, and (in VS Code, explicitly documented) an enabled sandbox. Autopilot is a different switch. It keeps the agent iterating; YOLO approves its tool calls. Unattended runs usually want both. Everything here was checked on October 7, 2026 against GitHub's Copilot CLI reference, the github/copilot-cli changelog (1.0.93) and VS Code's agent docs in microsoft/vscode-docs. Why does "YOLO" mean two different things in Copilot? Because Copilot ships two agent runtimes with two permission systems. The Copilot CLI is a terminal agent with flag-driven permissions. Copilot Chat in VS Code is an editor agent whose permissions hang off a picker and settings.json . They share vocabulary ( /yolo exists in both) but not config. Nothing you set in VS Code changes the CLI, and vice versa. The one thing they agree on is the layering. It decomposes into three narrower switches you can use on their own: Flag What stops asking --allow-all-tools every tool call (GitHub notes this is required when you drive the CLI from a script) --allow-all-paths the check on which file paths the agent may touch --allow-all-urls URL fetch approval The env var COPILOT_ALLOW_ALL=true does the same as --yolo and trusts the current directory, which makes it the CI-friendly form: no flag plumbing through wrapper scripts. If your threat model is "the agent may run npm test but must not read ~/.ssh or exfiltrate to random hosts", --allow-all-tools alone is a materially different posture from --yolo . How do the in-session commands map onto each other? /permissions is now the canonical command, with four arguments: default , assisted , allow-all and show . Everything else is an alias: /yolo and /allow-all → /permissions allow-all /yolo also takes off , auto and show /reset-allowed-tools (or /permissions default ) undoes it While it's on, the footer shows a YOLO indicator, so you can't forget you're flying without a net. Why isn't Autopilot the same thing as YOLO? Two orthogonal axes: Autopilot ( --autopilot , /autopilot , or Shift+Tab) answers "should the agent keep going without checking in with me?" YOLO answers "should the agent run tools without asking me?" Autopilot without YOLO: the agent keeps working, then blocks on the first approval. YOLO without Autopilot: approvals fly through, but the agent stops to check in. An unattended run usually needs both. VS Code's security docs make the same point from the other side: Autopilot "combines auto-approval with autonomous iteration" and "reduces your ability to review intermediate steps". Can I get most of the speed without approving everything? Yes, and this is where Copilot's design is genuinely nice. Two halfway layers: Pattern rules. --allow-tool and --deny-tool take typed patterns: copilot --allow-tool 'shell(git:*)' --deny-tool 'shell(git push)' Other shapes: write(src/*.ts) , read(.env) , url(github.com) , MyMCP(create_issue) . The rule that matters: a deny always wins , including over --yolo . That gives you a cheap "YOLO minus the footguns" profile: --yolo --deny-tool 'shell(git push)' . Assisted permissions. /permissions assisted puts a safety model in front of the prompt. It approves routine requests and only escalates the rest to you. It's a classifier in layer 2, not a sandbox, so it reduces prompts without adding isolation. Admins get the last word: "disableBypassPermissionsMode": "disable" under permissions kills all of this, and "allow-auto-only" restricts users to the assisted mode. How does VS Code's version work? The docs recommend the session-scoped Allow all when you don't need auto-approval everywhere. The experimental chat.permissions.default ( default , autoApprove , autopilot ) picks the level new chats start with, and orgs can block global auto-approve with the ChatToolsAutoApprove policy. Are terminal allowlists enough to keep me safe? They're the VS Code halfway option: { "chat.tools.terminal.autoApprove" : { "mkdir" : true , "/^git (status|diff|log)\\b/" : true , "rm" : false } } Keys are prefixes or regexes. true auto-approves; false forces a prompt even if another rule would approve. Note that false means ask , not block . But read the fine print: VS Code's security docs say auto-approval rules "use best-effort command parsing and have known limitations with shell aliases, quote concatenation, and complex shell syntax". Anyone who has written a shell parser knows why: g'it' push , an alias, or bash -c "$(…)" can all slip past a prefix match. Treat allowlists as a convenience, and put the real boundary somewhere that enforces it at the OS level. What does the sandbox actually enforce, and what doesn't YOLO touch? In VS Code, turn on chat.agent.sandbox.enabled (or the Sandboxing for terminal toggle in the picker). The docs are explicit that Allow all and Autopilot skip prompts "but an enabled sandbox still restricts terminal file system and network access". Under the hood VS Code's docs list: macOS: Apple's Seatbelt, built in. Linux / WSL2: bubblewrap for filesystem isolation plus socat for network proxying ( apt-get install bubblewrap socat ). WSL1 is out, because bubblewrap needs user namespaces. Two caveats from the same docs: outbound network stays on by default ( chat.agent.sandbox.network.allowNetwork defaults to true ), so lock that down separately; and the sandbox is "not a virtual machine or user-account boundary". If you see the older key chat.tools.terminal.sandbox.enabled in blog posts, it's no longer in VS Code's docs. The Copilot CLI has /sandbox / --sandbox too. GitHub's reference still marks it experimental while the changelog says it's available to everyone, and the CLI docs don't say whether --yolo bypasses it. We treat it as a separate layer like VS Code's, but if you rely on it, check what /sandbox reports. Can a cloned repo flip YOLO on for me? In VS Code, the front-line defense is Workspace Trust: an untrusted folder opens in restricted mode, which "also disables agents". So review a repo before you trust it, because trust is what unlocks agents in it at all. The global auto-approve setting is something you set yourself, and the docs steer you to the session-scoped level instead. The CLI has a notion of trusted directories too: COPILOT_ALLOW_ALL=true trusts the current directory, and /add-dir PATH grants file access to another directory and loads its .github/skills and .github/agents as trusted configuration. Copilot's YOLO is session-scoped: once on, it's on for everything that session does. Start Copilot without --yolo . The gateway moves each new session out of any mode that would approve on its own and into one where Copilot asks a person. Every permission request then lands in the AgentRQ task (web, phone or Slack) with the command or edit attached, and you answer: Allow Once : this call only. Always Allow : adds the tool to the workspace's auto-approved list, so routine calls stop asking. Deny : Copilot gets a refusal and carries on. If nobody answers within 30 minutes, the gateway cancels the turn rather than guessing; tune that with --permission-timeout . Per task. Flip the YOLO toggle on a task, or set it when you create one, to put just that task in YOLO mode . Every permission request in it is auto-approved and Copilot never waits, while every other task in the workspace still asks. The setting sticks to the task even if the agent disconnects and reconnects. Scheduled tasks, event triggers and workflow steps have the same switch, so the nightly job can run in YOLO while your interactive work stays supervised. Per workspace. Workspace settings has YOLO Mode (Execute All) (UI warning: "Agent will not ask for permission"). Under the hood it's a default, not a global override: the approval check reads the task's own YOLO flag, and the workspace switch decides what that flag starts as. New tasks you create in the web form open with the YOLO toggle already on (you can still switch it off per task), and tasks the agent creates for itself over the workspace MCP server inherit it. Extensions are trusted Node modules loaded by the AgentRQ desktop app. One registers a reviewer with ctx.hooks.add({ id, review(request) { ... } }) and is handed the pending call: the tool name, the argument preview the harness sent, and the workspace. It answers { behavior: 'deny', reason } , { behavior: 'allow' } , or nothing at all to abstain. Point review() at an external decision API such as TypeSafe's Jev , a "System One" model that returns a typed choice with calibrated probabilities and a confidence in milliseconds instead of generating text. The tool call history keeps a record of every call, including the auto-approved ones. FAQ Is copilot --yolo the same as --allow-all ? Yes. Same flag: tools, paths and URLs. Does --yolo override --deny-tool ? No. A deny always wins. Why doesn't Shift+Tab turn on YOLO in the CLI? It cycles standard, plan and autopilot. Use /yolo . How do I make Allow all permanent in VS Code? "chat.tools.global.autoApprove": true , though the session-scoped picker level is the safer habit. Does Allow all disable the VS Code sandbox? No. An enabled sandbox still restricts terminal filesystem and network access. Is Autopilot YOLO? No. Autopilot keeps the agent going; YOLO approves its tool calls. For every other agent, see what YOLO mode is and how to turn it on in every coding agent . items.summary_html:
TL;DR

  • Copilot CLI: copilot --yolo (same flag as --allow-all), or /yolo in a running session. It is shorthand for --allow-all-tools + --allow-all-paths + --allow-all-urls.
  • VS Code: pick Allow all in the chat permission picker, type /yolo, or set "chat.tools.global.autoApprove": true to make it permanent.
  • What it skips: approval prompts. What it doesn't: your --deny-tool rules, and (in VS Code, explicitly documented) an enabled sandbox.
  • Autopilot is a different switch. It keeps the agent iterating; YOLO approves its tool calls. Unattended runs usually want both.

Everything here was checked on October 7, 2026 against GitHub's Copilot CLI reference, the github/copilot-cli changelog (1.0.93) and VS Code's agent docs in microsoft/vscode-docs.

Why does "YOLO" mean two different things in Copilot?

Because Copilot ships two agent runtimes with two permission systems. The Copilot CLI is a terminal agent with flag-driven permissions. Copilot Chat in VS Code is an editor agent whose permissions hang off a picker and settings.json. They share vocabulary (/yolo exists in both) but not config. Nothing you set in VS Code changes the CLI, and vice versa.

The one thing they agree on is the layering. There are three separate gates between the model and your machine:

model wants to act
   │
   ▼
[1] deny rules ─────────── always win, YOLO or not
   │
   ▼
[2] approval prompt ────── this is the only layer YOLO removes
   │
   ▼
[3] sandbox (if enabled) ─ still limits files + network
   │
   ▼
your shell / filesystem / network

Keep that picture in mind; every flag below is about layer 2.

What exactly does copilot --yolo turn on? 
copilot --yolo

--yolo and --allow-all are the same flag, documented as "Enable all permissions (tools, paths, and URLs)". It decomposes into three narrower switches you can use on their own:

Flag What stops asking --allow-all-tools every tool call (GitHub notes this is required when you drive the CLI from a script) --allow-all-paths the check on which file paths the agent may touch --allow-all-urls URL fetch approval

The env var COPILOT_ALLOW_ALL=true does the same as --yolo and trusts the current directory, which makes it the CI-friendly form: no flag plumbing through wrapper scripts.

The nerdy bit worth noticing: paths and URLs are separate trust dimensions from tools. If your threat model is "the agent may run npm test but must not read ~/.ssh or exfiltrate to random hosts", --allow-all-tools alone is a materially different posture from --yolo.

How do the in-session commands map onto each other?

/permissions is now the canonical command, with four arguments: default, assisted, allow-all and show. Everything else is an alias:

  • /yolo and /allow-all → /permissions allow-all
  • /yolo also takes off, auto and show
  • /reset-allowed-tools (or /permissions default) undoes it

While it's on, the footer shows a YOLO indicator, so you can't forget you're flying without a net.

One gotcha for people coming from other agents: Shift+Tab does not toggle YOLO in the Copilot CLI. It cycles standard → plan → autopilot. That's a mode-of-work switch, not a permission switch.

Why isn't Autopilot the same thing as YOLO?

Two orthogonal axes:

  • Autopilot (--autopilot, /autopilot, or Shift+Tab) answers "should the agent keep going without checking in with me?"
  • YOLO answers "should the agent run tools without asking me?"

Autopilot without YOLO: the agent keeps working, then blocks on the first approval. YOLO without Autopilot: approvals fly through, but the agent stops to check in. An unattended run usually needs both. VS Code's security docs make the same point from the other side: Autopilot "combines auto-approval with autonomous iteration" and "reduces your ability to review intermediate steps".

Can I get most of the speed without approving everything?

Yes, and this is where Copilot's design is genuinely nice. Two halfway layers:

Pattern rules. --allow-tool and --deny-tool take typed patterns:

copilot --allow-tool 'shell(git:*)' --deny-tool 'shell(git push)'

Other shapes: write(src/*.ts), read(.env), url(github.com), MyMCP(create_issue). The rule that matters: a deny always wins, including over --yolo. That gives you a cheap "YOLO minus the footguns" profile: --yolo --deny-tool 'shell(git push)'.

Assisted permissions. /permissions assisted puts a safety model in front of the prompt. It approves routine requests and only escalates the rest to you. It's a classifier in layer 2, not a sandbox, so it reduces prompts without adding isolation.

Admins get the last word: "disableBypassPermissionsMode": "disable" under permissions kills all of this, and "allow-auto-only" restricts users to the assisted mode.

How does VS Code's version work?

Copilot Chat calls it Allow all, one of three permission levels:

Level Behavior Manual (default) asks for each tool call Assisted a model approves routine requests (needs chat.assistedPermissions.enabled) Allow all asks for nothing; VS Code warns you the first time

Three ways in:

  1. The permission picker in the chat input.
  2. /yolo or /autoApprove in chat, for the current session. Undo with /disableYolo or /disableAutoApprove.
  3. Permanently, in settings.json: 
{ "chat.tools.global.autoApprove": true }

That last one approves every tool in every workspace, and VS Code's own docs flag it as a setting that "disables critical security protections". The docs recommend the session-scoped Allow all when you don't need auto-approval everywhere. The experimental chat.permissions.default (default, autoApprove, autopilot) picks the level new chats start with, and orgs can block global auto-approve with the ChatToolsAutoApprove policy.

Are terminal allowlists enough to keep me safe?

They're the VS Code halfway option:

{
  "chat.tools.terminal.autoApprove": {
    "mkdir": true,
    "/^git (status|diff|log)\\b/": true,
    "rm": false
  }
}

Keys are prefixes or regexes. true auto-approves; false forces a prompt even if another rule would approve. Note that false means ask, not block.

But read the fine print: VS Code's security docs say auto-approval rules "use best-effort command parsing and have known limitations with shell aliases, quote concatenation, and complex shell syntax". Anyone who has written a shell parser knows why: g'it' push, an alias, or bash -c "$(…)" can all slip past a prefix match. Treat allowlists as a convenience, and put the real boundary somewhere that enforces it at the OS level.

What does the sandbox actually enforce, and what doesn't YOLO touch?

In VS Code, turn on chat.agent.sandbox.enabled (or the Sandboxing for terminal toggle in the picker). The docs are explicit that Allow all and Autopilot skip prompts "but an enabled sandbox still restricts terminal file system and network access". Under the hood VS Code's docs list:

  • macOS: Apple's Seatbelt, built in.
  • Linux / WSL2: bubblewrap for filesystem isolation plus socat for network proxying (apt-get install bubblewrap socat). WSL1 is out, because bubblewrap needs user namespaces.

Two caveats from the same docs: outbound network stays on by default (chat.agent.sandbox.network.allowNetwork defaults to true), so lock that down separately; and the sandbox is "not a virtual machine or user-account boundary". If you see the older key chat.tools.terminal.sandbox.enabled in blog posts, it's no longer in VS Code's docs.

The Copilot CLI has /sandbox / --sandbox too. GitHub's reference still marks it experimental while the changelog says it's available to everyone, and the CLI docs don't say whether --yolo bypasses it. We treat it as a separate layer like VS Code's, but if you rely on it, check what /sandbox reports.

Can a cloned repo flip YOLO on for me?

In VS Code, the front-line defense is Workspace Trust: an untrusted folder opens in restricted mode, which "also disables agents". So review a repo before you trust it, because trust is what unlocks agents in it at all. The global auto-approve setting is something you set yourself, and the docs steer you to the session-scoped level instead. The CLI has a notion of trusted directories too: COPILOT_ALLOW_ALL=true trusts the current directory, and /add-dir PATH grants file access to another directory and loads its .github/skills and .github/agents as trusted configuration. That's worth remembering before you point a YOLO session at a repo you haven't read.

How do I turn on YOLO per task or per workspace with AgentRQ?

Copilot's YOLO is session-scoped: once on, it's on for everything that session does. If you'd rather decide per task, and answer prompts from somewhere other than the terminal, you can route the Copilot CLI through AgentRQ via the ACP Gateway (Copilot setup guide):

npx @agentrq/acp-gateway@latest --agent github-copilot-cli

This covers the Copilot CLI only; Copilot Chat in VS Code keeps its own picker.

Start Copilot without --yolo. The gateway moves each new session out of any mode that would approve on its own and into one where Copilot asks a person. Every permission request then lands in the AgentRQ task (web, phone or Slack) with the command or edit attached, and you answer:

  • Allow Once: this call only.
  • Always Allow: adds the tool to the workspace's auto-approved list, so routine calls stop asking.
  • Deny: Copilot gets a refusal and carries on.

If nobody answers within 30 minutes, the gateway cancels the turn rather than guessing; tune that with --permission-timeout.

Per task. Flip the YOLO toggle on a task, or set it when you create one, to put just that task in YOLO mode. Every permission request in it is auto-approved and Copilot never waits, while every other task in the workspace still asks. The setting sticks to the task even if the agent disconnects and reconnects. Scheduled tasks, event triggers and workflow steps have the same switch, so the nightly job can run in YOLO while your interactive work stays supervised.

Per workspace. Workspace settings has YOLO Mode (Execute All) (UI warning: "Agent will not ask for permission"). Under the hood it's a default, not a global override: the approval check reads the task's own YOLO flag, and the workspace switch decides what that flag starts as. New tasks you create in the web form open with the YOLO toggle already on (you can still switch it off per task), and tasks the agent creates for itself over the workspace MCP server inherit it. Flipping the switch doesn't rewrite tasks that already exist.

Or let a model approve and deny for you, from plain-English rules. Between "ask me every time" and "approve everything" there's a third option: an AgentRQ desktop extension that reviews each permission request before it reaches you. Extensions are trusted Node modules loaded by the AgentRQ desktop app. One registers a reviewer with ctx.hooks.add({ id, review(request) { ... } }) and is handed the pending call: the tool name, the argument preview the harness sent, and the workspace. It answers { behavior: 'deny', reason }, { behavior: 'allow' }, or nothing at all to abstain. Point review() at an external decision API such as TypeSafe's Jev, a "System One" model that returns a typed choice with calibrated probabilities and a confidence in milliseconds instead of generating text. Send the tool call as the state, and your workspace's rules in plain English ("git push is fine on feature branches, never on main", "never read anything under ~/.aws") as a Choice question over allow / deny / ask me. Then threshold it: approve only on a high-confidence allow, refuse on a confident deny, and abstain on everything else so the request lands on your phone as usual. The rules can live on a per-workspace settings tab the extension draws itself; the bundled guardrail example does exactly that with literal patterns.

The review contract is built on one asymmetry: refusing costs a tool call, approving costs whatever the tool call does. So one refusal settles a request; silence (an abstain, an exception, or a reviewer that misses its 5-second deadline) is never an allow, the request just stays in front of you; and an extension needs the decide consent level to approve, while deny consent can only refuse. The install screen starts every extension at none. Reviews only happen while the desktop app is open and signed in, so treat this as a fast first pass, not a security boundary.

The tool call history keeps a record of every call, including the auto-approved ones.

FAQ

Does --yolo override --deny-tool? No. A deny always wins.

Why doesn't Shift+Tab turn on YOLO in the CLI? It cycles standard, plan and autopilot. Use /yolo.

How do I make Allow all permanent in VS Code? "chat.tools.global.autoApprove": true, though the session-scoped picker level is the safer habit.

Does Allow all disable the VS Code sandbox? No. An enabled sandbox still restricts terminal filesystem and network access.

Is Autopilot YOLO? No. Autopilot keeps the agent going; YOLO approves its tool calls.

Production RAG with LangChain & LangGraph: End-to-End Implementation Build a production-ready RAG system with document ingestion, hybrid retrieval, reranking, citations, guardrails, and monitoring. Introduction RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) is the standard for grounding LLMs in proprietary data. This guide builds a production system — not a prototype. Production RAG Requirements Requirement Prototype Production Ingestion Manual, one-off Automated, incremental, monitored Retrieval Vector only Hybrid (dense + sparse + rerank) Generation Basic prompt Structured output + citations + guardrails Evaluation Manual Automated metrics + LLM judge + A/B Monitoring None Latency, quality, cost, drift alerts Deployment Local notebook Containerized, scalable, resilient System Architecture ┌─────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐ │ Ingest │────▶│ Embedding │────▶│ Retrieval │────▶│ Generation │ │ Pipeline │ │ & Index │ │ Pipeline │ │ + Guardrails └─────────────┘ └─────────────┘ └─────────────┘ └─────────────┘ │ │ │ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ ▼ Chunking Vector DB Hybrid Search Structured Output Metadata (Qdrant) (Dense+Sparse) Citations Deduplication Quantization Reranking Guardrails Incremental Replication Filtering Evaluation Part 1: Document Ingestion Pipeline # ingestion/pipeline.py from dataclasses import dataclass from typing import List , Optional from pathlib import Path import hashlib import asyncio from datetime import datetime @dataclass class Document : id : str content : str metadata : dict source : str created_at : str chunk_hash : str = "" @dataclass class Chunk : id : str document_id : str content : str metadata : dict token_count : int embedding : List [ float ] = None class IngestionPipeline : def __init__ ( self , chunker , embedder , vector_store , doc_store , deduplicator ): self . chunker = chunker self . embedder = embedder self . vector_store = vector_store self . doc_store = doc_store self . deduplicator = deduplicator async def ingest_file ( self , file_path : Path , metadata : dict = None ) -> dict : """ Ingest a single file. """ # 1. Load document doc = await self . _load_document ( file_path , metadata ) # 2. Check for duplicates if await self . deduplicator . is_duplicate ( doc . chunk_hash ): return { " status " : " duplicate " , " document_id " : doc . id } # 3. Chunk chunks = self . chunker . chunk ( doc ) # 4. Embed texts = [ c . content for c in chunks ] embeddings = await self . embedder . embed_batch ( texts ) for chunk , emb in zip ( chunks , embeddings ): chunk . embedding = emb # 5. Store await self . doc_store . save_document ( doc ) await self . vector_store . upsert_chunks ( chunks ) await self . deduplicator . mark_seen ( doc . chunk_hash ) return { " status " : " success " , " document_id " : doc . id , " chunks " : len ( chunks )} async def ingest_batch ( self , file_paths : List [ Path ]) -> dict : """ Parallel batch ingestion. """ semaphore = asyncio . Build a production-ready RAG system with document ingestion, hybrid retrieval, reranking, citations, guardrails, and monitoring.

Introduction

RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) is the standard for grounding LLMs in proprietary data. This guide builds a production system — not a prototype.

Part 1: Document Ingestion Pipeline 
# ingestion/pipeline.py
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import List, Optional
from pathlib import Path
import hashlib
import asyncio
from datetime import datetime

@dataclass
class Document:
    id: str
    content: str
    metadata: dict
    source: str
    created_at: str
    chunk_hash: str = ""

@dataclass
class Chunk:
    id: str
    document_id: str
    content: str
    metadata: dict
    token_count: int
    embedding: List[float] = None

class IngestionPipeline:
    def __init__(
        self,
        chunker,
        embedder,
        vector_store,
        doc_store,
        deduplicator
    ):
        self.chunker = chunker
        self.embedder = embedder
        self.vector_store = vector_store
        self.doc_store = doc_store
        self.deduplicator = deduplicator

    async def ingest_file(self, file_path: Path, metadata: dict = None) -> dict:
        """Ingest a single file."""
        # 1. Load document
        doc = await self._load_document(file_path, metadata)

        # 2. Check for duplicates
        if await self.deduplicator.is_duplicate(doc.chunk_hash):
            return {"status": "duplicate", "document_id": doc.id}

        # 3. Chunk
        chunks = self.chunker.chunk(doc)

        # 4. Embed
        texts = [c.content for c in chunks]
        embeddings = await self.embedder.embed_batch(texts)
        for chunk, emb in zip(chunks, embeddings):
            chunk.embedding = emb

        # 5. Store
        await self.doc_store.save_document(doc)
        await self.vector_store.upsert_chunks(chunks)
        await self.deduplicator.mark_seen(doc.chunk_hash)

        return {"status": "success", "document_id": doc.id, "chunks": len(chunks)}

    async def ingest_batch(self, file_paths: List[Path]) -> dict:
        """Parallel batch ingestion."""
        semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(10)

        async def limited_ingest(path):
            async with semaphore:
                return await self.ingest_file(path)

        results = await asyncio.gather(*[limited_ingest(p) for p in file_paths])
        return {
            "total": len(results),
            "successful": sum(1 for r in results if r["status"] == "success"),
            "duplicates": sum(1 for r in results if r["status"] == "duplicate"),
            "details": results
        }

    async def _load_document(self, path: Path, metadata: dict) -> Document:
        # Implement based on file type (PDF, MD, HTML, etc.)
        content = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        chunk_hash = hashlib.sha256(content.encode()).hexdigest()[:16]

        return Document(
            id=hashlib.md5(str(path).encode()).hexdigest()[:12],
            content=content,
            metadata=metadata or {},
            source=str(path),
            created_at=datetime.utcnow().isoformat(),
            chunk_hash=chunk_hash
        )
Semantic Chunking 
# ingestion/chunker.py
from dataclasses import dataclass
import re
from typing import List

@dataclass
class Chunk:
    content: str
    metadata: dict
    token_count: int

class SemanticChunker:
    """Chunk by semantic boundaries (headers, paragraphs)."""

    def __init__(self, max_tokens: int = 512, overlap: int = 50):
        self.max_tokens = max_tokens
        self.overlap = overlap

    def chunk(self, doc: Document) -> List[Chunk]:
        # Split by markdown headers
        sections = self._split_by_headers(doc.content)

        all_chunks = []
        for section_content, section_meta in sections:
            section_chunks = self._chunk_section(
                section_content, 
                {**doc.metadata, **section_meta}
            )
            all_chunks.extend(section_chunks)

        return all_chunks

    def _split_by_headers(self, text: str) -> List[tuple[str, dict]]:
        pattern = r'^(#{1,6})\s+(.+)$'
        lines = text.split('\n')

        sections = []
        current_header = {}
        current_content = []

        for line in lines:
            match = re.match(pattern, line)
            if match:
                if current_content:
                    header_path = " > ".join(v for v in current_header.values() if v)
                    sections.append(("\n".join(current_content), {"header_path": header_path}))

                level = len(match.group(1))
                header_text = match.group(2)
                current_header[f"h{level}"] = header_text
                for l in range(level + 1, 7):
                    current_header[f"h{l}"] = ""
                current_content = [line]
            else:
                current_content.append(line)

        if current_content:
            header_path = " > ".join(v for v in current_header.values() if v)
            sections.append(("\n".join(current_content), {"header_path": header_path}))

        return sections

    def _chunk_section(self, content: str, metadata: dict) -> List[Chunk]:
        paragraphs = [p.strip() for p in content.split('\n\n') if p.strip()]

        chunks = []
        current_chunk = []
        current_tokens = 0

        for para in paragraphs:
            para_tokens = self._estimate_tokens(para)

            if current_tokens + para_tokens > self.max_tokens and current_chunk:
                chunk_text = "\n\n".join(current_chunk)
                chunks.append(Chunk(chunk_text, metadata, current_tokens))

                overlap_text = self._get_overlap(current_chunk)
                current_chunk = [overlap_text, para] if overlap_text else [para]
                current_tokens = self._estimate_tokens("\n\n".join(current_chunk))
            else:
                current_chunk.append(para)
                current_tokens += para_tokens

        if current_chunk:
            chunk_text = "\n\n".join(current_chunk)
            chunks.append(Chunk(chunk_text, metadata, current_tokens))

        return chunks

    def _estimate_tokens(self, text: str) -> int:
        return len(text) // 4

    def _get_overlap(self, chunks: List[str]) -> str:
        if not chunks:
            return ""
        last = chunks[-1]
        words = last.split()
        overlap_words = words[-(self.overlap // 4):]
        return " ".join(overlap_words)
Part 2: Hybrid Retrieval Pipeline 
# retrieval/pipeline.py
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import List, Optional, Callable
import asyncio

@dataclass
class RetrievedDoc:
    content: str
    metadata: dict
    score: float
    rank: int
    source: str  # "dense", "sparse", "hybrid"

class HybridRetrievalPipeline:
    def __init__(
        self,
        dense_embedder: Callable,
        sparse_embedder: Callable,
        vector_store,
        sparse_store,
        reranker: Callable,
        dense_weight: float = 0.7,
        sparse_weight: float = 0.3
    ):
        self.dense_embedder = dense_embedder
        self.sparse_embedder = sparse_embedder
        self.vector_store = vector_store
        self.sparse_store = sparse_store
        self.reranker = reranker
        self.dense_weight = dense_weight
        self.sparse_weight = sparse_weight

    async def retrieve(
        self,
        query: str,
        k: int = 5,
        fetch_k: int = 20,
        filters: dict = None,
        use_reranker: bool = True
    ) -> List[RetrievedDoc]:
        # Stage 1: Parallel dense + sparse retrieval
        dense_task = self._dense_search(query, fetch_k, filters)
        sparse_task = self._sparse_search(query, fetch_k, filters)

        dense_results, sparse_results = await asyncio.gather(dense_task, sparse_task)

        # Stage 2: Fuse results (RRF - Reciprocal Rank Fusion)
        fused = self._reciprocal_rank_fusion(dense_results, sparse_results, k * 2)

        # Stage 3: Rerank
        if use_reranker and fused:
            fused = await self._rerank(query, fused)

        # Stage 4: Final selection
        return fused[:k]

    async def _dense_search(self, query: str, k: int, filters: dict) -> List[RetrievedDoc]:
        query_vector = await self.dense_embedder(query)
        results = await self.vector_store.search(query_vector, k, filters)
        return [
            RetrievedDoc(
                content=r["content"],
                metadata=r["metadata"],
                score=r["score"] * self.dense_weight,
                rank=i,
                source="dense"
            )
            for i, r in enumerate(results)
        ]

    async def _sparse_search(self, query: str, k: int, filters: dict) -> List[RetrievedDoc]:
        sparse_vector = await self.sparse_embedder(query)
        results = await self.sparse_store.search(sparse_vector, k, filters)
        return [
            RetrievedDoc(
                content=r["content"],
                metadata=r["metadata"],
                score=r["score"] * self.sparse_weight,
                rank=i,
                source="sparse"
            )
            for i, r in enumerate(results)
        ]

    def _reciprocal_rank_fusion(
        self, 
        dense: List[RetrievedDoc], 
        sparse: List[RetrievedDoc], 
        k: int,
        k_constant: int = 60
    ) -> List[RetrievedDoc]:
        """RRF fusion for hybrid search."""
        # Combine by content hash
        doc_scores = {}

        for results, weight in [(dense, self.dense_weight), (sparse, self.sparse_weight)]:
            for rank, doc in enumerate(results):
                content_hash = hash(doc.content[:200])
                if content_hash not in doc_scores:
                    doc_scores[content_hash] = {
                        "doc": doc,
                        "rrf_score": 0
                    }
                # RRF score: 1 / (k + rank)
                doc_scores[content_hash]["rrf_score"] += weight / (k_constant + rank + 1)

        # Sort by RRF score
        fused = sorted(
            doc_scores.values(), 
            key=lambda x: x["rrf_score"], 
            reverse=True
        )

        return [
            RetrievedDoc(
                content=item["doc"].content,
                metadata=item["doc"].metadata,
                score=item["rrf_score"],
                rank=i,
                source="hybrid"
            )
            for i, item in enumerate(fused[:k])
        ]

    async def _rerank(self, query: str, docs: List[RetrievedDoc]) -> List[RetrievedDoc]:
        contents = [d.content for d in docs]
        rerank_scores = await self.reranker(query, contents)

        for doc, score in zip(docs, rerank_scores):
            doc.score = score
            doc.source = "reranked"

        docs.sort(key=lambda x: x.score, reverse=True)
        return docs
Part 3: Generation with Citations & Guardrails 
# generation/rag_chain.py
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate
from langchain_core.output_parsers import JsonOutputParser
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing import List, Optional

class CitedAnswer(BaseModel):
    answer: str = Field(description="Complete answer with inline citations [doc_id]")
    citations: List[dict] = Field(description="Citations with doc_id, snippet, metadata")
    confidence: float = Field(ge=0, le=1, description="Confidence 0-1")
    needs_clarification: bool = Field(default=False)

RAG_PROMPT = """You are a precise assistant that answers questions using ONLY the provided context.

## Context Documents
{context}

## Question
{question}

## Instructions
1. Answer ONLY from the provided context
2. If context is insufficient, say "I don't have enough information to answer this"
3. Cite sources inline using [doc_id] format
4. Be concise but complete
5. Include confidence score (0-1) based on context coverage

## Output Format (JSON)
{{
    "answer": "Your answer with [doc_id] citations",
    "citations": [
        {{"doc_id": "abc123", "snippet": "relevant excerpt", "metadata": {{...}}}}
    ],
    "confidence": 0.9,
    "needs_clarification": false
}}"""

def build_rag_chain(model_name: str = "gpt-4o"):
    llm = ChatOpenAI(model=model_name, temperature=0)
    prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_template(RAG_PROMPT)
    parser = JsonOutputParser(pydantic_object=CitedAnswer)
    return prompt | llm | parser

def format_context(docs: List[RetrievedDoc]) -> str:
    formatted = []
    for i, doc in enumerate(docs):
        doc_id = doc.metadata.get("chunk_hash", f"doc_{i}")
        formatted.append(
            f"[Document {doc_id}]\n"
            f"Source: {doc.metadata.get('doc_title', 'Unknown')}\n"
            f"Section: {doc.metadata.get('header_path', 'N/A')}\n"
            f"Content: {doc.content}\n"
        )
    return "\n---\n".join(formatted)
Guardrails 
# generation/guardrails.py
import re
from typing import Tuple

class RAGGuardrails:
    def __init__(self):
        self.pii_patterns = [
            (r'\b\d{3}-\d{2}-\d{4}\b', 'SSN'),
            (r'\b[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Z|a-z]{2,}\b', 'EMAIL'),
            (r'\b\d{4}[\s-]?\d{4}[\s-]?\d{4}[\s-]?\d{4}\b', 'CREDIT_CARD'),
            (r'\b\d{10}\b', 'PHONE'),
        ]

        self.refusal_triggers = [
            "ignore previous instructions",
            "system prompt",
            "reveal your prompt",
            "bypass",
            "jailbreak",
        ]

    def check_input(self, query: str) -> Tuple[bool, str]:
        query_lower = query.lower()

        for trigger in self.refusal_triggers:
            if trigger in query_lower:
                return False, "I can't help with that request."

        for pattern, pii_type in self.pii_patterns:
            if re.search(pattern, query):
                return False, f"Please don't share {pii_type} in your question."

        return True, ""

    def check_output(self, answer: str, context: str) -> Tuple[bool, str]:
        # Hallucination check: numbers in answer must exist in context
        answer_numbers = re.findall(r'\b\d+\.?\d*\b', answer)
        context_numbers = set(re.findall(r'\b\d+\.?\d*\b', context))

        for num in answer_numbers:
            if num not in context_numbers and len(num) > 2:
                return False, f"Unverified claim detected: {num}"

        # PII leakage check
        for pattern, pii_type in self.pii_patterns:
            if re.search(pattern, answer):
                return False, f"Potential {pii_type} leakage in response."

        return True, ""

    def sanitize_output(self, answer: str) -> str:
        sanitized = answer
        for pattern, _ in self.pii_patterns:
            sanitized = re.sub(pattern, "[REDACTED]", sanitized)
        return sanitized
Part 4: LangGraph Orchestration 
# orchestration/rag_graph.py
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END
from langgraph.checkpoint.sqlite import SqliteSaver
from typing import TypedDict, Annotated, List
from langgraph.graph.message import add_messages
from langchain_core.messages import BaseMessage

class RAGState(TypedDict):
    messages: Annotated[List[BaseMessage], add_messages]
    question: str
    retrieved_docs: List[RetrievedDoc]
    answer: CitedAnswer
    guardrail_passed: bool
    retry_count: int

async def retrieve_node(state: RAGState):
    pipeline = get_retrieval_pipeline()
    docs = await pipeline.retrieve(state["question"])
    return {"retrieved_docs": docs}

async def generate_node(state: RAGState):
    chain = get_rag_chain()
    context = format_context(state["retrieved_docs"])
    answer = await chain.ainvoke({"context": context, "question": state["question"]})
    return {"answer": answer}

async def guardrail_node(state: RAGState):
    guardrails = get_guardrails()
    context = format_context(state["retrieved_docs"])
    passed, reason = guardrails.check_output(state["answer"].answer, context)

    if not passed and state["retry_count"] < 2:
        return {
            "guardrail_passed": False,
            "retry_count": state["retry_count"] + 1,
            "messages": [HumanMessage(content=f"Regenerate: {reason}")]
        }

    return {"guardrail_passed": passed}

def route_after_guardrail(state: RAGState) -> str:
    if state["guardrail_passed"]:
        return END
    return "generate"

# Build graph
workflow = StateGraph(RAGState)
workflow.add_node("retrieve", retrieve_node)
workflow.add_node("generate", generate_node)
workflow.add_node("guardrail", guardrail_node)

workflow.add_edge(START, "retrieve")
workflow.add_edge("retrieve", "generate")
workflow.add_edge("generate", "guardrail")
workflow.add_conditional_edges("guardrail", route_after_guardrail, {
    "generate": "generate",
    END: END
})

rag_app = workflow.compile(checkpointer=SqliteSaver.from_conn_string("sqlite:///rag.db"))

# server.py
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException, BackgroundTasks
from pydantic import BaseModel
from typing import Optional
import uvicorn

app = FastAPI(title="Production RAG API", version="1.0.0")

class QueryRequest(BaseModel):
    question: str
    filters: Optional[dict] = None
    k: int = 5
    use_reranker: bool = True
    stream: bool = False

class QueryResponse(BaseModel):
    answer: str
    citations: List[dict]
    confidence: float
    retrieved_count: int
    latency_ms: float

@app.post("/query", response_model=QueryResponse)
async def query(request: QueryRequest):
    start = time.time()

    # Input guardrails
    guardrails = get_guardrails()
    passed, reason = guardrails.check_input(request.question)
    if not passed:
        raise HTTPException(400, reason)

    # Execute RAG
    config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": f"query-{uuid.uuid4()}"}}
    result = await rag_app.ainvoke({
        "question": request.question,
        "retry_count": 0
    }, config)

    latency = (time.time() - start) * 1000

    # Log for monitoring
    background_tasks.add_task(log_metrics, {
        "question": request.question,
        "latency_ms": latency,
        "retrieved": len(result["retrieved_docs"]),
        "confidence": result["answer"].confidence,
        "guardrail_passed": result["guardrail_passed"]
    })

    return QueryResponse(
        answer=result["answer"].answer,
        citations=result["answer"].citations,
        confidence=result["answer"].confidence,
        retrieved_count=len(result["retrieved_docs"]),
        latency_ms=latency
    )

@app.post("/ingest")
async def ingest(request: IngestRequest, background_tasks: BackgroundTasks):
    background_tasks.add_task(run_ingestion, request.paths)
    return {"status": "ingestion_started"}

@app.get("/health")
async def health():
    return {"status": "healthy", "timestamp": datetime.utcnow().isoformat()}

@app.get("/metrics")

if __name__ == "__main__":

# evaluation/rag_eval.py
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import List
import json

@dataclass
class RAGTestCase:
    question: str
    expected_answer: str
    relevant_doc_ids: List[str]
    metadata_filters: dict = None

class RAGEvaluator:
    def __init__(self, rag_system):
        self.rag = rag_system

    def evaluate_retrieval(self, test_cases: List[RAGTestCase]) -> dict:
        metrics = {"precision@k": [], "recall@k": [], "mrr": []}

        for tc in test_cases:
            results = await self.rag.retrieve(tc.question, k=10)
            retrieved_ids = [r.metadata.get("chunk_hash") for r in results]
            relevant = set(tc.relevant_doc_ids)

            for k in [1, 3, 5, 10]:
                retrieved_k = set(retrieved_ids[:k])
                metrics[f"precision@{k}"].append(len(retrieved_k & relevant) / k)
                metrics[f"recall@{k}"].append(len(retrieved_k & relevant) / len(relevant))

            for i, rid in enumerate(retrieved_ids):
                if rid in relevant:
                    metrics["mrr"].append(1 / (i + 1))
                    break
            else:
                metrics["mrr"].append(0)

        return {k: sum(v) / len(v) for k, v in metrics.items()}

    async def evaluate_generation(self, test_cases: List[RAGTestCase]) -> dict:
        scores = {"accuracy": [], "completeness": [], "citation_quality": []}

        for tc in test_cases:
            result = await self.rag.query(tc.question)
            eval_result = await llm_judge(
                task="Answer question using provided context",
                input_text=tc.question,
                response=result.answer,
                criteria=["accuracy", "completeness", "citation_quality", "faithfulness"]
            )

            for k in scores:
                scores[k].append(eval_result.scores.get(k, 0))

        return {k: sum(v) / len(v) for k, v in scores.items()}
Production Monitoring 
# monitoring/production_monitor.py
from dataclasses import dataclass, asdict
from datetime import datetime
import json

@dataclass
class RAGMetrics:
    timestamp: str
    question_hash: str
    latency_ms: float
    retrieval_latency_ms: float
    generation_latency_ms: float
    num_retrieved: int
    num_cited: int
    confidence: float
    user_feedback: Optional[str] = None
    error: Optional[str] = None

class ProductionMonitor:
    def __init__(self, log_path: str = "logs/rag_metrics.jsonl"):
        self.log_path = log_path
        self.buffer = []

    def log(self, metrics: RAGMetrics):
        self.buffer.append(asdict(metrics))
        if len(self.buffer) >= 100:
            self.flush()

    def flush(self):
        with open(self.log_path, "a") as f:
            for m in self.buffer:
                f.write(json.dumps(m) + "\n")
        self.buffer.clear()

    def get_stats(self, hours: int = 24) -> dict:
        import pandas as pd
        df = pd.read_json(self.log_path, lines=True)
        df["timestamp"] = pd.to_datetime(df["timestamp"])
        cutoff = pd.Timestamp.utcnow() - pd.Timedelta(hours=hours)
        df = df[df["timestamp"] > cutoff]

        return {
            "total_queries": len(df),
            "avg_latency_ms": df["latency_ms"].mean(),
            "p95_latency_ms": df["latency_ms"].quantile(0.95),
            "avg_confidence": df["confidence"].mean(),
            "error_rate": df["error"].notna().mean(),
            "avg_retrieved": df["num_retrieved"].mean(),
            "feedback_positive_rate": (
                df["user_feedback"].eq("positive").mean() 
                if "user_feedback" in df.columns else 0
            )
        }

items.title: Stop Flying Blind: Adding OpenTelemetry Tracing to Your AI Gateway
items.summary: Originally published on tamiz.pro . Stop Flying Blind: Adding OpenTelemetry Tracing to Your AI Gateway Building an AI Gateway has become standard practice for organizations moving from experimental LLM playgrounds to production-grade applications. The gateway sits between your application code and multiple model providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Local LLMs), handling routing, caching, rate limiting, and cost control. However, without deep observability, your team is essentially flying blind. When a user complains that the chat response was "slow" or "weird," can you distinguish between a network timeout, a specific model hallucination, or a cache miss that triggered a redundant expensive inference? Standard APM tools struggle with AI workloads because they lack semantic understanding of Large Language Model (LLM) interactions. They see HTTP requests, but they miss the semantic "spans" that matter: the actual prompt sent, the token count consumed, the finish reason, and the semantic relationship between a retrieval step (RAG) and the final generation. This tutorial walks you through implementing a robust OpenTelemetry (OTel) tracing pipeline for an AI Gateway. We will cover semantic attribute conventions, context propagation across asynchronous boundaries, and how to export this data to a backend like Jaeger or Grafana Tempo. Table of Contents 1. Why Standard Tracing Fails for AI Gateways 2. Architecture: The AI Gateway Observability Pipeline 3. Semantic Conventions: What to Record 4. Implementation: Instrumenting the Gateway with Python 5. Handling Context Propagation in Async Python 6. Redacting PII and Sensitive Data 7. Visualizing the Data: Jaeger and Grafana 8. Frequently Asked Questions 1. Why Standard Tracing Fails for AI Gateways Traditional distributed tracing focuses on "where" the latency is (DB query, API call). In AI systems, the question is often "why" the model behaved a certain way. A standard HTTP trace will tell you that /api/chat took 3.2 seconds. It will not tell you that 2.5 seconds of that was spent in the LLM inference engine generating tokens, or that the prompt was 4,000 tokens long (hence the high cost). Furthermore, AI workflows are often multi-step. A typical RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) flow looks like this: Embed the user query. Search the vector database. Rerank the results. Send the context + query to the LLM. If you don't link these operations into a single trace, you cannot diagnose issues like "the vector DB returned irrelevant results, causing the LLM to hallucinate." OpenTelemetry provides the primitive Span that allows us to nest these operations, creating a hierarchical view of the request lifecycle. 2. Architecture: The AI Gateway Observability Pipeline Before writing code, we must define the architecture. An AI Gateway typically acts as a reverse proxy or a SDK wrapper. For this tutorial, we will assume a Python-based gateway service that receives requests and forwards them to LLM providers. The Data Flow: Ingestion : The Gateway receives an inbound HTTP request. Root Span : The Gateway creates a root span representing the entire request. Child Spans : As the Gateway processes the request, it creates child spans for specific operations: retrieval.search : For fetching context from a vector DB. llm.inference : For the actual call to the model provider. llm.generate : For streaming chunks (if applicable). Enrichment : Each span is enriched with attributes defined by the OpenTelemetry GenAI Semantic Conventions (e.g., gen_ai.model.name , gen_ai.usage.prompt_tokens ). Export : The spans are batched and exported via OTLP to a collector. Storage & Visualization : The Collector routes data to Jaeger/Tempo for viewing. *Note: For a deeper dive into the underlying collector architecture, you might find the technical breakdown on Tamiz's Insights on high-throughput telemetry pipelines useful. 3. Semantic Conventions: What to Record To make traces readable by standard tools, you should adhere to the emerging OpenTelemetry GenAI Semantic Conventions . While these are still evolving, defining a consistent set of attributes now ensures you won't have to rewrite your instrumentation later.
