Stop Flying Blind: Adding OpenTelemetry Tracing to Your AI Gateway

Building an AI Gateway has become standard practice for organizations moving from experimental LLM playgrounds to production-grade applications. The gateway sits between your application code and multiple model providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Local LLMs), handling routing, caching, rate limiting, and cost control. However, without deep observability, your team is essentially flying blind. When a user complains that the chat response was "slow" or "weird," can you distinguish between a network timeout, a specific model hallucination, or a cache miss that triggered a redundant expensive inference?

Standard APM tools struggle with AI workloads because they lack semantic understanding of Large Language Model (LLM) interactions. They see HTTP requests, but they miss the semantic "spans" that matter: the actual prompt sent, the token count consumed, the finish reason, and the semantic relationship between a retrieval step (RAG) and the final generation. This tutorial walks you through implementing a robust OpenTelemetry (OTel) tracing pipeline for an AI Gateway. We will cover semantic attribute conventions, context propagation across asynchronous boundaries, and how to export this data to a backend like Jaeger or Grafana Tempo.

Table of Contents
  • 1. Why Standard Tracing Fails for AI Gateways
  • 2. Architecture: The AI Gateway Observability Pipeline
  • 3. Semantic Conventions: What to Record
  • 4. Implementation: Instrumenting the Gateway with Python
  • 5. Handling Context Propagation in Async Python
  • 6. Redacting PII and Sensitive Data
  • 7. Visualizing the Data: Jaeger and Grafana
  • 8. Frequently Asked Questions
1. Why Standard Tracing Fails for AI Gateways

Traditional distributed tracing focuses on "where" the latency is (DB query, API call). In AI systems, the question is often "why" the model behaved a certain way. A standard HTTP trace will tell you that /api/chat took 3.2 seconds. It will not tell you that 2.5 seconds of that was spent in the LLM inference engine generating tokens, or that the prompt was 4,000 tokens long (hence the high cost).

Furthermore, AI workflows are often multi-step. A typical RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) flow looks like this:

  1. Embed the user query.
  2. Search the vector database.
  3. Rerank the results.
  4. Send the context + query to the LLM.

If you don't link these operations into a single trace, you cannot diagnose issues like "the vector DB returned irrelevant results, causing the LLM to hallucinate." OpenTelemetry provides the primitive Span that allows us to nest these operations, creating a hierarchical view of the request lifecycle.

2. Architecture: The AI Gateway Observability Pipeline

Before writing code, we must define the architecture. An AI Gateway typically acts as a reverse proxy or a SDK wrapper. For this tutorial, we will assume a Python-based gateway service that receives requests and forwards them to LLM providers.

The Data Flow:

  1. Ingestion: The Gateway receives an inbound HTTP request.
  2. Root Span: The Gateway creates a root span representing the entire request.
  3. Child Spans: As the Gateway processes the request, it creates child spans for specific operations:
    • retrieval.search: For fetching context from a vector DB.
    • llm.inference: For the actual call to the model provider.
    • llm.generate: For streaming chunks (if applicable).
  4. Enrichment: Each span is enriched with attributes defined by the OpenTelemetry GenAI Semantic Conventions (e.g., gen_ai.model.name, gen_ai.usage.prompt_tokens).
  5. Export: The spans are batched and exported via OTLP to a collector.
  6. Storage & Visualization: The Collector routes data to Jaeger/Tempo for viewing.

*Note: For a deeper dive into the underlying collector architecture, you might find the technical breakdown on Tamiz's Insights on high-throughput telemetry pipelines useful.

3. Semantic Conventions: What to Record

To make traces readable by standard tools, you should adhere to the emerging OpenTelemetry GenAI Semantic Conventions. While these are still evolving, defining a consistent set of attributes now ensures you won't have to rewrite your instrumentation later.

Key attributes to record:

Attribute Key Description Example Value gen_ai.system The vendor or system name openai, anthropic, local gen_ai.request.model The specific model identifier gpt-4-turbo, claude-3-opus gen_ai.request.temperature Sampling temperature 0.7 gen_ai.response.model The model that actually responded gpt-4-turbo-2024-04-09 gen_ai.usage.prompt_tokens Number of tokens in the prompt 150 gen_ai.usage.completion_tokens Number of tokens in the response 1024 gen_ai.prompt The actual prompt content "..." (See PII section) gen_ai.completion The actual completion content "..." (See PII section)

Important: Do not record raw prompt/completion content in spans unless you have a strict PII redaction pipeline. Spans are often sampled at a lower rate than metrics, but they are still logged. We will address this in Section 6.

4. Implementation: Instrumenting the Gateway with Python

We will build a minimal AI Gateway using FastAPI and httpx. We will instrument it using the opentelemetry-sdk and opentelemetry-exporter-otlp.

Prerequisites

Ensure you have Python 3.10+ installed. Create a virtual environment and install dependencies:

pip install fastapi uvicorn httpx opentelemetry-sdk opentelemetry-exporter-otlp-proto-http opentelemetry-instrumentation-fastapi opentelemetry-instrumentation-httpx
4.1 Setting up the Tracer Provider

First, we need to initialize the OpenTelemetry SDK. This sets up the environment where spans will be generated and exported.

# app/telemetry.py
from opentelemetry import trace
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export import BatchSpanProcessor
from opentelemetry.exporter.otlp.proto.http.trace_exporter import OTLPSpanExporter
from opentelemetry.sdk.resources import Resource, SERVICE_NAME
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.sampling import TraceIdRatioBased
import os

OTEL_ENDPOINT = os.getenv("OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT", "http://localhost:4317")
OTEL_HEADERS = os.getenv("OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS", "")

def get_tracer_provider() -> TracerProvider:
    resource = Resource.create({
        SERVICE_NAME: "ai-gateway",
        "service.version": "1.0.0",
    })

    provider = TracerProvider(resource=resource)

    # Configure sampling. In production, you might use parent-based sampling.
    # Here we use a 50% ratio for demonstration.
    sampler = TraceIdRatioBased(0.5)

    exporter = OTLPSpanExporter(
        endpoint=OTEL_ENDPOINT,
        headers=OTEL_HEADERS,
        insecure=True # For local dev; use HTTPS in prod
    )

    processor = BatchSpanProcessor(exporter)
    provider.add_span_processor(processor)

    trace.set_tracer_provider(provider)
    return provider
4.2 The Gateway Logic and Instrumentation

Here is the core of the AI Gateway. We will create a service that wraps a hypothetical LLM provider. Notice how we create nested spans for the "Retrieval" step and the "Generation" step.

# app/gateway.py
import asyncio
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
from pydantic import BaseModel
import httpx
from opentelemetry import trace
from app.telemetry import get_tracer_provider

tracer = trace.get_tracer("ai_gateway")

app = FastAPI()

# Initialize provider
get_tracer_provider()

class ChatRequest(BaseModel):
    message: str
    user_id: str

class ChatResponse(BaseModel):
    response: str
    usage: dict

# Mock LLM and Vector DB calls for demonstration
async def mock_vector_search(query: str):
    """Simulates a vector database lookup."""
    async with tracer.start_as_current_span("vector_db.search") as span:
        span.set_attribute("db.system", "pinecone")
        await asyncio.sleep(0.1) # Simulate latency
        return ["Context chunk 1", "Context chunk 2"]

async def mock_llm_call(prompt: str, model: str = "gpt-4"):
    """Simulates an LLM API call."""
    async with tracer.start_as_current_span("llm.generate") as span:
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.system", "openai")
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.request.model", model)
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.request.temperature", 0.7)

        # Simulate token counting and generation latency
        await asyncio.sleep(0.5)

        # Mock response
        response_text = f"Response based on: {prompt[:20]}..."

        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.response.model", f"{model}-2024-01")
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.usage.prompt_tokens", 150)
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.usage.completion_tokens", 1024)
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.finish_reason", "stop")

        return response_text

@app.post("/chat", response_model=ChatResponse)
async def chat(request: ChatRequest):
    # 1. Create Root Span for the entire request
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("gateway.handle_chat") as root_span:
        root_span.set_attribute("user.id", request.user_id)

        # 2. Step 1: Retrieval
        context = await mock_vector_search(request.message)

        # 3. Step 2: Construction of Prompt
        final_prompt = f"Context: {str(context)}\nQuery: {request.message}"

        # 4. Step 3: Generation
        response_text = await mock_llm_call(final_prompt)

        return ChatResponse(
            response=response_text,
            usage={"prompt_tokens": 150, "completion_tokens": 1024}
        )

Key Takeaway: Notice the use of tracer.start_as_current_span. This context manager automatically handles the parent-child relationship. The vector_db.search and llm.generate spans will be automatically nested inside gateway.handle_chat.

5. Handling Context Propagation in Async Python

A common pitfall when instrumenting Python AI gateways is context loss in asynchronous code. If you spawn a new asyncio.Task or thread, the OpenTelemetry context (which holds the current trace ID) does not propagate automatically unless you handle it correctly.

In the example above, we awaited everything in the same task, so propagation worked. However, if your gateway uses concurrent.futures or separate worker processes, you must explicitly capture the SpanContext and inject it into the child environment.

Here is how to propagate context to an httpx request (which many gateways use to call LLM providers). The opentelemetry-instrumentation-httpx package handles this mostly, but you must ensure the traceparent header is sent.

import httpx
from opentelemetry.trace import get_current_span, SpanKind
from opentelemetry.trace.context import Context
from opentelemetry.propagate import inject

async def call_external_llm_with_trace(url: str, payload: dict):
    tracer = trace.get_tracer("http_client")

    with tracer.start_as_current_span("http.client.llm_call", kind=SpanKind.CLIENT) as span:
        span.set_attribute("http.method", "POST")
        span.set_attribute("http.url", url)

        # We need to inject the current trace context into the headers
        headers = {}
        inject(headers) # This adds 'traceparent' header

        async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
            try:
                response = await client.post(url, json=payload, headers=headers)
                response.raise_for_status()

                span.set_attribute("http.status_code", response.status_code)
                return response.json()
            except httpx.HTTPError as exc:
                span.set_status(trace.StatusCode.ERROR, str(exc))
                span.record_exception(exc)
                raise

By injecting the headers, you ensure that if the LLM provider also supports OpenTelemetry (or if you are tracing across microservices), the trace remains contiguous. For local LLMs that don't support OTel, at least the client-side duration and status are recorded.

6. Redacting PII and Sensitive Data

This is the most critical security aspect of AI tracing. LLM prompts often contain user PII, API keys, or proprietary data. Never record raw prompts/completions in spans without a redaction layer.

We can add a middleware or a utility function to sanitize attributes before they are attached to the span.

import re
from opentelemetry.trace import Span

def redact_pii(text: str) -> str:
    """Simple regex-based redaction for emails and phone numbers."""
    if not text:
        return text

    # Email addresses
    text = re.sub(r'\b[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}\b', '[EMAIL_REDACTED]', text)

    # US Phone Numbers (example)
    text = re.sub(r'\b\d{3}[-.]?\d{3}[-.]?\d{4}\b', '[PHONE_REDACTED]', text)

    # API Keys (generic pattern)
    text = re.sub(r'sk-[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}', '[API_KEY_REDACTED]', text)

    return text

# Modify the mock_llm_call to use this
async def mock_llm_call_safe(prompt: str, model: str = "gpt-4"):
    async with tracer.start_as_current_span("llm.generate") as span:
        # ... other attributes ...

        # Instead of span.set_attribute("gen_ai.prompt", prompt)
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.prompt", redact_pii(prompt))

        # In production, log the full prompt to a secure S3 bucket with IAM controls,
        # and store only the hash or reference in the trace span.
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.prompt.hash", get_sha256_hash(prompt))

Best Practice: Store the full prompt/completion in a separate, secure log store (like CloudWatch or Datadog Logs) with strict access controls. In the OpenTelemetry span, store only the hash or a reference ID. This allows developers to debug by looking up the ID in the secure logs, while keeping the trace backend clean and compliant.

7. Visualizing the Data: Jaeger and Grafana

To see the results of our work, we need a backend. For local development, the easiest way is to run Jaeger in All-In-One mode.

docker run -p 16686:16686 -p 4317:4317 jaegertracing/all-in-one

Visit http://localhost:16686 in your browser. Search for the service ai-gateway. You will see a trace waterfall that looks like this:

gateway.handle_chat (200ms)
├── vector_db.search (50ms)
└── llm.generate (150ms)
Interpreting the Waterfall
  1. Latency Breakdown: If llm.generate takes 80% of the total time, you know the issue is inference, not retrieval. If vector_db.search is slow, you need to optimize your indexing.
  2. Error Propagation: If llm.generate fails (e.g., 429 Too Many Requests), the root span gateway.handle_chat will also be marked as errored because of the context propagation. This makes it easy to filter for "All Errored Requests" in Jaeger.
  3. Cost Correlation: By exporting gen_ai.usage.* attributes, you can build dashboards in Grafana that correlate Trace IDs with Cost. For example, you can create a panel that shows the average cost per trace ID, helping you identify expensive queries that might be failing or returning low-quality results.
8. Frequently Asked Questions Should I trace every single LLM call, or only sampled ones?

In high-throughput systems, tracing every call can be expensive. OpenTelemetry's BatchSpanProcessor and sampling strategies (like TraceIdRatioBased(0.1)) allow you to sample only 10% of traces. However, you should use Head-Based Sampling with a higher rate for error spans. This ensures that if an LLM call fails (which is more interesting), you always capture that trace, even if successful calls are dropped.

How do I handle streaming responses?

Streaming responses (SSE) create a challenge because the completion_tokens are not known until the stream ends. You can update the span attributes after the stream finishes. Use span.set_attribute after the async for loop completes. Do not finalize the span (end it) until the entire stream has been processed, otherwise, you will have an incomplete trace.

Does OpenTelemetry work with local LLMs like Llama 3?

Yes, but you must instrument the client library (e.g., transformers, ollama, vllm). Since local LLMs run on your infrastructure, the "network" latency is replaced by CPU/GPU compute latency. You can use opentelemetry-instrumentation-nvidia-smi (or similar) to capture GPU utilization metrics alongside the trace spans. This provides a holistic view: the trace tells you what happened, and the metrics tell you how the hardware performed.

By implementing this observability layer, you transform your AI Gateway from a "black box" into a transparent, debuggable system. You gain the ability to answer complex questions about performance, cost, and quality, ultimately enabling safer and more reliable deployment of AI applications in production.

items.title: Every "no AI contributions" policy is a Level 0 control
items.summary: This week QGIS merged QEP #387 : "No LLM, AI or agent assisted code contributions are allowed in the qgis/qgis repository." Violators face "code reversion and contributor rights sanctioning." It replaced a human-in-the-loop policy, it passed a vote, it is on master as of October 7. The HN thread is at three hundred comments and counting, split between "rationing attention is fair" and "this will age like milk." The line that settles the whole debate was written by the project itself, in the proposal's discussion. Asked how compliance will work, a core contributor answered: did you in good conscience write the code yourself. That is not an enforcement mechanism. That is a conscience test with a reversion clause attached — and by the taxonomy this series has been building, it makes QEP #387 a textbook Level 0 control : a paragraph of English that nobody executes, failing silently, with the drift invisible. The project knows it; the enforcement quote is honest about it. What the debate is missing is the ladder — and what the second rung costs. Grant the ban first, because it is rational Before grading anything: the workload is real and the maintainers are not imagining it. items.summary_html:
This week QGIS merged QEP #387: "No LLM, AI or agent assisted code contributions are allowed in the qgis/qgis repository." Violators face "code reversion and contributor rights sanctioning." It replaced a human-in-the-loop policy, it passed a vote, it is on master as of October 7. The HN thread is at three hundred comments and counting, split between "rationing attention is fair" and "this will age like milk."

The line that settles the whole debate was written by the project itself, in the proposal's discussion. Asked how compliance will work, a core contributor answered: did you in good conscience write the code yourself.

That is not an enforcement mechanism. That is a conscience test with a reversion clause attached — and by the taxonomy this series has been building, it makes QEP #387 a textbook Level 0 control: a paragraph of English that nobody executes, failing silently, with the drift invisible. The project knows it; the enforcement quote is honest about it. What the debate is missing is the ladder — and what the second rung costs.

Grant the ban first, because it is rational

Before grading anything: the workload is real and the maintainers are not imagining it. The proposal's rationale — "massive and unbearable pressure", AI volume exceeding "what human review can take seriously" — matches what every maintainer in every lane reports. And this is not QGIS's first control attempt: an earlier tagging process for AI-assisted PRs was tried and quietly died, with roughly fifty PRs tagged and forty closed. They tried the lighter control. It did not hold. Nyall Dawson's "start with a closed door" and open selectively is a stop gap, said out loud by a voter: "the baby might be non-viable."

A blanket ban is the correct answer to the question "how do we survive this quarter." This post is about the next question: what is the policy made of, and what does that material cost.

The ladder, applied

Every control lives on one of three rungs, graded by what enforces it:

Level 0 — prose. "No AI contributions permitted" in a document nobody executes. Fails silently: the drift is invisible, because the trigger condition — was this code AI-assisted? — cannot be evaluated by anything except a conscience. The definitional holes in the QGIS thread are not drafting accidents; they are proof the trigger is unevaluable. Does autocomplete count? Translation? A ranking model that reordered your imports? A rule whose scope is undecidable cannot be enforced by anything below a human's honest memory — and the project has already said that is the mechanism.

Level 1 — a primitive in context. A declaration the contributor makes, visible in the PR: a template field, a trailer line, a checkbox that survives into the commit. It fails visibly — but only if someone looks. QGIS tried this rung: the tagging process. It failed for the boring reason — roughly fifty tags in the whole history is not enforcement, it is decoration. Level 1 works when the CI checks it, and QGIS's did not.

Level 2 — the host refuses. The control lives in a gate that runs without trusting anyone's memory. This is the rung the debate keeps skipping, because people conflate two different problems: detecting AI code (adversarial, unwinnable — simple code is undetectable and always will be) and binding process to a signed name (boring, winnable, and what receipts are for).

The receipt schema this series follows ships the distinction in code. Every verdict must carry judged_by — required, no default; the schema throws rather than seal an unlabeled verdict. For LLM-judged checks, spec_hash is mandatory: the prompt that defines the judgment is hashed, so the rubric and its paraphrase produce different ids. Neither field claims to detect a lie. They make an unlabeled claim unsealable — the lie, if it comes, has to arrive signed.

The measured part: twenty repos, six policies, zero enforcement

A taxonomy without data is a sermon, so I audited the twenty most-starred repositories on GitHub — the projects whose policies shape what thousands of contributors believe is normal. The method, disclosed: pull each repo's contributing docs and AI policy files, read every policy found in full, grade it on the ladder, and check the repos' GitHub workflow names for any automation referencing AI, LLMs, or disclosure.

Fourteen of the twenty have no AI policy anywhere in their contributing docs — including several that receive AI-generated PRs by the hundred. Six have one. I read all six in full, and every one of them, graded on the ladder, stops below the gate:

Repo Policy, as written Rung Machine enforcement denoland/deno AI-assisted contributions: "you must disclose this in your PR description"; PRs "will be rejected if there is suspicion of undisclosed AI usage" 1 none pytorch/pytorch AI content "must be clearly disclosed and contained" under a labeled PR section, with human commentary attached 1 none nodejs/node contributors "should disclose" the tools used "and what the contributor does to personally verify the generated output"; DCO still applies 1 none home-assistant/core unreviewed AI content "will not be accepted"; autonomous agents banned, PRs closed on belief 1 none flutter/flutter a behaviors policy — "focuses on behaviors rather than tools", conduct channel for violations 0–1 none rust-lang/rust conditional allow — and self-labeled: "we are aware that many clauses in this policy are unenforceable" 0–1, labeled none qgis/QGIS the ban: reversion + sanctioning, trigger = conscience 0 none

(The other thirteen have nothing to grade. The "machine enforcement" column is the absence finding: I checked each repo's workflow names for anything referencing AI, disclosure, or contribution labels — nothing. A deeper CI-content audit might hide an exception; the name-level sweep found none.)

Three findings, in ascending order of interest. Deno, node, and PyTorch converge on disclosure — the ecosystem's consensus rung is "say it out loud", and PyTorch goes furthest: AI content must be contained under a labeled PR-template section with human commentary attached. That is the closest thing to structure anyone ships — the template makes the section exist by default; an empty one is at least visible. Home Assistant closes PRs on belief — "we believe were created autonomously" — which is the strongest trigger in the sample, applied by the weakest instrument. And Rust wrote the thesis of this post before I did: "we are aware that many clauses in this policy are unenforceable. Our goal is not to catch every violation... our goal is to remove plausible deniability: to force a choice between following the policy and intentionally violating it."

Rust is the proof the ladder is fair. Its policy is prose — Level 0 by trigger — and it says so, out loud, in its own introduction. QGIS threatens reversion and sanctioning from the same rung without the label. Same material, opposite honesty: one wrote "these clauses are unenforceable" where its enforcement should be; the other dressed the conscience test in reversion threats. The difference between them is not strictness. It is whether the policy's own rung is falsifiable.

What a Level 2 policy for AI contributions looks like

Not detection. Process, signed:

  • A provenance trailer on every commit, the same shape as Signed-off-by: Authored-by: human or Authored-by: human, assisted-by: . No LLM-detection claims — a declaration, required by the CI, refused at the gate when absent. The Linux kernel answer quoted approvingly on HN — "LLM use allowed, but you are fully responsible for the code it produces" — is this rung: responsibility attaching to a signed name instead of to a detection heuristic.
  • Reversion with a logged reason. "Code reversion and sanctioning" already threatened by QGIS becomes enforceable the day reversions carry receipts: which commit, which rule, which reviewer. A sanction that lives in a private conversation is not a control.
  • A published exceptions log. Dawson's "closed door, open case-by-case" (autocomplete replacements, translations) is the right shape — but a case-by-case door with no public log is a door that silently becomes a hallway. The exceptions ledger is the policy's audit trail.
  • Optional, and only if the maintainers want it: canaries for docs. Plant a decoy instruction in the contributing docs and see who commits it — the deliberately-failed probe, already proven useful for grading agents. Cheap, imperfect, honest about being a tripwire rather than a judge.
  • Write the rung into the policy. Rust's LLM policy does it in its own overview — "we are aware that many clauses in this policy are unenforceable" — and that sentence is why nobody can accuse Rust of pretending. A labeled weakness beats an invisible one, in constitutions as much as in code.

None of this detects AI code. Detection is the adversary's game and the adversary is winning it. The receipts regime claims something narrower and true: when a contribution breaks the rules, the break is provable, attributable, and on the record — instead of discoverable, if at all, by vibes.

The cost, stated plainly

The seatbelt tax. A provenance trailer is thirty seconds per commit, forever, on every contributor — including the ninety-nine percent who were never going to game anything. Level 0 costs nothing and catches nothing; Level 2 costs everyone and catches process violations, not authorship. There is no rung with no price. A maintainer who says "my contributors will not accept friction" has chosen Level 0, and after this week's numbers — the pressure is real — that is a defensible choice. It should be a labeled one.

Two honest limits

The survey is a snapshot with disclosed crudeness. Twenty repos chosen by prominence, contributing docs and policy files as the policy surface, workflow names as the enforcement surface — a deep CI-content audit, or a policy living outside those files, would be missed. Five of the six policies are graded from full reads (Rust's was fetched from the Rust Forge; its unenforceable-clauses sentence is quoted from the policy's own overview), one (QGIS) from its merged proposal and the core team's comments. Whether the policy authors would accept my rung assignments is their right to dispute — the rungs are quoted from their own texts so the dispute can be precise.

And QGIS is not wrong to choose survival over verifiability this quarter. Fifty tags and forty closed PRs is a real attempt with real numbers; "unbearable pressure" is not performative. This post argues the stop gap should carry its label — Level 0, honesty-based, revision to follow — the same way this series labels every weakness it confesses, and the same way Rust labels its own clauses. A project that writes its control's rung into the policy has not solved enforcement. It has made the absence of enforcement falsifiable.

Your turn

What does your project's AI policy actually enforce — and at which rung? If you maintain one, link it in the comments with an honest grading: prose, primitive, or gate. And if you have built an enforceable provenance scheme for contributions — trailers, CI gates, canaries, anything that refuses at the host — I want the receipts. The registry only works if the levels travel.

items.summary: For the past few years, the largest US technology companies have been in a costly race to develop advanced artificial intelligence systems while at the same time providing computing power to a burgeoning field of startups. To chase these goals, they have radically changed how they finance their growth. Long reliant on rich revenues and share price increases, Alphabet Inc.’s Google, Meta Platforms Inc. and other tech giants now are borrowing heavily to build the technology that makes chatbots run

items.title: Gemini CLI YOLO mode, read from the source: why settings.json can't turn it on
items.summary: TL;DR Start YOLO with gemini --approval-mode=yolo , or press Ctrl+Y in a running session. --yolo / -y still work but are deprecated, and combining --yolo with --approval-mode is an error. You cannot make YOLO the default in settings.json . That's a deliberate design choice, and the code that enforces it is three lines long. YOLO only removes approval prompts. The sandbox (Seatbelt, Docker, Podman, gVisor, LXC) is a separate switch, and in the current source YOLO never turns it on. In an untrusted folder, any mode other than default gets forced back to default . If security.disableYoloMode or admin secure mode is set, asking for YOLO is a fatal config error, not a silent downgrade. Everything below was checked against the Gemini CLI source (google-gemini/gemini-cli, 0.65.0-nightly.20261006 ) and its docs, on October 7–8, 2026. Who is this even for in late 2026? Short version: Gemini CLI users with a Gemini Code Assist Standard or Enterprise license. Since June 18, 2026, Gemini CLI no longer serves Google AI Pro, Ultra or free Code Assist users. Google moved them to the Antigravity CLI ( agy ), which has a different YOLO story (it's agy --dangerously-skip-permissions , and there's no --yolo at all). Gemini CLI is still developed, though, and the approval code is worth reading on its own. It's one of the cleaner permission designs among coding agents. What does Gemini CLI actually do with an approval mode? There are four modes: default , auto_edit , plan and yolo . Here's how the CLI picks one at startup, in order: --approval-mode on the command line else --yolo / -y , which maps to yolo else general.defaultApprovalMode from settings, unless its value is yolo , in which case it's skipped else default Step 3 is the interesting one. The resolver doesn't reject a "yolo" value in settings. It just reads past it, as if the key weren't there. The settings schema says it outright: YOLO "can only be enabled via command line". Two gates come after the mode is resolved: Kill switch. If security.disableYoloMode or admin.secureModeEnabled is set and the resolved mode is YOLO, startup throws a FatalConfigError . It doesn't quietly drop you to default . You asked for something that's banned, and the CLI tells you so. Folder trust. If the current folder isn't trusted, any mode other than default gets forced back to default , with a warning. This one applies to auto_edit and plan too, not just YOLO. Why can't I just put "yolo" in settings.json? The threat model is a cloned repo. Gemini CLI merges settings from several layers, and one of them is the workspace's own .gemini/settings.json . If a project file could set defaultApprovalMode: "yolo" , then git clone evil-repo && cd evil-repo && gemini would hand an attacker-controlled GEMINI.md an agent that never asks before running a shell command. Prompt injection plus auto-approval is the worst combination in agent security. So the rule is: YOLO has to come from a human typing a flag (or a key) in this process. Settings can make you more cautious ( disableYoloMode , secureModeEnabled , folder trust), but never less. If you want YOLO every time, the supported answer is a shell alias: alias gemini-yolo = 'gemini --approval-mode=yolo --sandbox' Compare that with Qwen Code, Gemini CLI's fork, which does allow tools.approvalMode: "yolo" in settings. It pushes the protection down to folder trust instead. Does YOLO turn the sandbox on? Not in the current code, whatever one older config page says. Gemini CLI has two independent layers: Layer What it gates Switch Approval mode Whether a human confirms each tool call --approval-mode , Ctrl+Y, Shift+Tab Sandbox What a tool call can touch once it runs --sandbox , GEMINI_SANDBOX , tools.sandbox The sandbox resolver never reads the approval mode. With nothing set, it returns "no sandbox". Here's what you get when you turn it on: macOS, sandbox: true : sandbox-exec (Seatbelt) is picked first. The default profile is permissive-open . Despite the name, it starts from (deny default) , allows file reads anywhere, and allows writes only to the project dir, temp, cache, ~/.npm , ~/.cache and any --include-directories . It also explicitly blocks the Docker socket and writes to ~/.gemini credential files ( oauth_creds.json , mcp-oauth-tokens.json , …). Pick another built-in profile with SEATBELT_PROFILE : permissive-* and restrictive-* come in -open , -closed and -proxied network flavors, and strict-* in -open and -proxied . Anything not on that list is rejected, which also stops path traversal through the variable. Linux/other, sandbox: true : Docker, then Podman, whichever exists. Explicit only: runsc (gVisor, Linux only, run via Docker's --runtime=runsc ), lxc (needs a container you already have running, so it's never auto-detected) and windows-native (Windows only). A wrong value fails fast. GEMINI_SANDBOX=runsc on a Mac, or true with neither Docker nor Podman installed, is a fatal error, not a silent run without a sandbox. The point: YOLO plus a sandbox is a reasonable setup. YOLO without one means "run anything with my user's full privileges". Pass --sandbox yourself. How do Ctrl+Y and Shift+Tab interact? Ctrl+Y toggles between YOLO and default . This is the only in-session way into YOLO. Shift+Tab cycles default → auto_edit → plan (plan only if it's enabled). It never lands on YOLO. If you're in YOLO and press it, you drop to auto_edit . Small design choice, sensible result: the key you hit all the time can't take you to the dangerous mode by accident. One more thing: --yolo together with --approval-mode doesn't pick a winner. It's a validation error. Ambiguous intent fails at the door. What happens in CI and headless runs? This edge case trips people up. In non-interactive mode ( gemini -p "…" ) there's nobody to answer a prompt, and the policy engine handles that by translating ask_user decisions into deny . So in headless default mode, a tool call that would have asked simply doesn't run. Belt and braces: the CLI also removes ask_user , the tool the model uses to ask you a question, from the toolset in headless and ACP modes. The source comment says why: so that "it can never be allowed via a high-priority policy rule when no human is present". In ACP mode the IDE or client does the asking instead. So headless, your options are: --approval-mode=yolo , ideally with --sandbox --approval-mode=auto_edit , plus policy rules that allow the shell commands you need or a policy file that says allow for exactly the tools the job uses What are the halfway options? auto_edit approves file edits and still asks before shell commands. tools.allowed lists tool patterns that skip the prompt, such as run_shell_command(git) . The policy engine is the recommended route: TOML files in ~/.gemini/policies/ with allow / deny / ask_user rules, which can be scoped to a mode (including YOLO). --allowed-tools on the command line is deprecated in its favour. For the Gemini Code Assist extension in VS Code, set "geminicodeassist.agentYoloMode": true in user settings and reload the window. Note the familiar rule again: it only works in a trusted workspace. In IntelliJ, the matching option is Auto-approve changes . How do I turn on YOLO per task or per workspace with AgentRQ? Gemini CLI's switch is per process: you either started with --approval-mode=yolo or you didn't. AgentRQ moves that decision onto the task. 1. Connect Gemini CLI. It goes through the ACP Gateway . The Gemini CLI setup guide and the step-by-step post have the details: npx @agentrq/acp-gateway@latest --agent gemini Start it without --approval-mode=yolo . The gateway also moves each new session out of any mode that would approve on its own and into one where Gemini CLI asks a person. 2. Answer from anywhere. Each permission request shows up in the AgentRQ task, on the web, on your phone or in Slack, along with the command or edit it's asking about. You answer Allow Once , Always Allow (adds the tool to the workspace's auto-approved list) or Deny . If nobody answers within 30 minutes, the gateway cancels the turn instead of guessing. --permission-timeout changes that limit. 3a. YOLO for one task. Flip the YOLO toggle on a task, or when you create it. Every permission request in that task is approved automatically, while every other task in the workspace still asks. The flag lives on the task, so it persists across agent disconnects and reconnects. Scheduled tasks , event triggers and workflow steps have the same switch. 3b. YOLO for the whole workspace. Workspace settings has YOLO Mode (Execute All) (UI warning: "Agent will not ask for permission"). Under the hood it's a default, not a global override: the approval check reads the task's own YOLO flag, and the workspace switch decides what that flag starts as. New tasks you create in the web form open with the YOLO toggle already on (you can still switch it off per task), and tasks the agent creates for itself over the workspace MCP server inherit it. Flipping the switch doesn't rewrite tasks that already exist. Or let a model approve and deny for you, from plain-English rules. Between "ask me every time" and "approve everything" there's a third option: an AgentRQ desktop extension that reviews each permission request before it reaches you. Extensions are trusted Node modules loaded by the AgentRQ desktop app. One registers a reviewer with ctx.hooks.add({ id, review(request) { ... } }) and is handed the pending call: the tool name, the argument preview the harness sent, and the workspace. It answers { behavior: 'deny', reason } , { behavior: 'allow' } , or nothing at all to abstain. Point review() at an external decision API such as TypeSafe's Jev , a "System One" model that returns a typed choice with calibrated probabilities and a confidence in milliseconds instead of generating text. Send the tool call as the state, and your workspace's rules in plain English ("git push is fine on feature branches, never on main", "never read anything under ~/.aws") as a Choice question over allow / deny / ask me. Then threshold it: approve only on a high-confidence allow, refuse on a confident deny, and abstain on everything else so the request lands on your phone as usual. The rules can live on a per-workspace settings tab the extension draws itself; the bundled guardrail example does exactly that with literal patterns. The review contract is built on one asymmetry: refusing costs a tool call, approving costs whatever the tool call does. items.summary_html:
TL;DR

  • Start YOLO with gemini --approval-mode=yolo, or press Ctrl+Y in a running session. --yolo / -y still work but are deprecated, and combining --yolo with --approval-mode is an error.
  • You cannot make YOLO the default in settings.json. That's a deliberate design choice, and the code that enforces it is three lines long.
  • YOLO only removes approval prompts. The sandbox (Seatbelt, Docker, Podman, gVisor, LXC) is a separate switch, and in the current source YOLO never turns it on.
  • In an untrusted folder, any mode other than default gets forced back to default. If security.disableYoloMode or admin secure mode is set, asking for YOLO is a fatal config error, not a silent downgrade.

Everything below was checked against the Gemini CLI source (google-gemini/gemini-cli, 0.65.0-nightly.20261006) and its docs, on October 7–8, 2026.

Who is this even for in late 2026?

Short version: Gemini CLI users with a Gemini Code Assist Standard or Enterprise license.

Since June 18, 2026, Gemini CLI no longer serves Google AI Pro, Ultra or free Code Assist users. Google moved them to the Antigravity CLI (agy), which has a different YOLO story (it's agy --dangerously-skip-permissions, and there's no --yolo at all). Gemini CLI is still developed, though, and the approval code is worth reading on its own. It's one of the cleaner permission designs among coding agents.

What does Gemini CLI actually do with an approval mode?

There are four modes: default, auto_edit, plan and yolo. Here's how the CLI picks one at startup, in order:

  1. --approval-mode on the command line
  2. else --yolo / -y, which maps to yolo
  3. else general.defaultApprovalMode from settings, unless its value is yolo, in which case it's skipped
  4. else default

Step 3 is the interesting one. The resolver doesn't reject a "yolo" value in settings. It just reads past it, as if the key weren't there. The settings schema says it outright: YOLO "can only be enabled via command line".

Two gates come after the mode is resolved:

  • Kill switch. If security.disableYoloMode or admin.secureModeEnabled is set and the resolved mode is YOLO, startup throws a FatalConfigError. It doesn't quietly drop you to default. You asked for something that's banned, and the CLI tells you so.
  • Folder trust. If the current folder isn't trusted, any mode other than default gets forced back to default, with a warning. This one applies to auto_edit and plan too, not just YOLO.
Why can't I just put "yolo" in settings.json?

The threat model is a cloned repo.

Gemini CLI merges settings from several layers, and one of them is the workspace's own .gemini/settings.json. If a project file could set defaultApprovalMode: "yolo", then git clone evil-repo && cd evil-repo && gemini would hand an attacker-controlled GEMINI.md an agent that never asks before running a shell command. Prompt injection plus auto-approval is the worst combination in agent security.

So the rule is: YOLO has to come from a human typing a flag (or a key) in this process. Settings can make you more cautious (disableYoloMode, secureModeEnabled, folder trust), but never less. If you want YOLO every time, the supported answer is a shell alias:

alias gemini-yolo='gemini --approval-mode=yolo --sandbox'

Compare that with Qwen Code, Gemini CLI's fork, which does allow tools.approvalMode: "yolo" in settings. It pushes the protection down to folder trust instead.

Does YOLO turn the sandbox on?

Not in the current code, whatever one older config page says.

Gemini CLI has two independent layers:

Layer What it gates Switch Approval mode Whether a human confirms each tool call --approval-mode, Ctrl+Y, Shift+Tab Sandbox What a tool call can touch once it runs --sandbox, GEMINI_SANDBOX, tools.sandbox

The sandbox resolver never reads the approval mode. With nothing set, it returns "no sandbox". Here's what you get when you turn it on:

  • macOS, sandbox: true: sandbox-exec (Seatbelt) is picked first. The default profile is permissive-open. Despite the name, it starts from (deny default), allows file reads anywhere, and allows writes only to the project dir, temp, cache, ~/.npm, ~/.cache and any --include-directories. It also explicitly blocks the Docker socket and writes to ~/.gemini credential files (oauth_creds.json, mcp-oauth-tokens.json, …). Pick another built-in profile with SEATBELT_PROFILE: permissive-* and restrictive-* come in -open, -closed and -proxied network flavors, and strict-* in -open and -proxied. Anything not on that list is rejected, which also stops path traversal through the variable.
  • Linux/other, sandbox: true: Docker, then Podman, whichever exists.
  • Explicit only: runsc (gVisor, Linux only, run via Docker's --runtime=runsc), lxc (needs a container you already have running, so it's never auto-detected) and windows-native (Windows only).

A wrong value fails fast. GEMINI_SANDBOX=runsc on a Mac, or true with neither Docker nor Podman installed, is a fatal error, not a silent run without a sandbox.

The point: YOLO plus a sandbox is a reasonable setup. YOLO without one means "run anything with my user's full privileges". Pass --sandbox yourself.

How do Ctrl+Y and Shift+Tab interact?
  • Ctrl+Y toggles between YOLO and default. This is the only in-session way into YOLO.
  • Shift+Tab cycles default → auto_edit → plan (plan only if it's enabled). It never lands on YOLO. If you're in YOLO and press it, you drop to auto_edit.

Small design choice, sensible result: the key you hit all the time can't take you to the dangerous mode by accident.

One more thing: --yolo together with --approval-mode doesn't pick a winner. It's a validation error. Ambiguous intent fails at the door.

What happens in CI and headless runs?

This edge case trips people up. In non-interactive mode (gemini -p "…") there's nobody to answer a prompt, and the policy engine handles that by translating ask_user decisions into deny. So in headless default mode, a tool call that would have asked simply doesn't run.

Belt and braces: the CLI also removes ask_user, the tool the model uses to ask you a question, from the toolset in headless and ACP modes. The source comment says why: so that "it can never be allowed via a high-priority policy rule when no human is present". In ACP mode the IDE or client does the asking instead.

So headless, your options are:

  • --approval-mode=yolo, ideally with --sandbox
  • --approval-mode=auto_edit, plus policy rules that allow the shell commands you need
  • or a policy file that says allow for exactly the tools the job uses
What are the halfway options?
  • auto_edit approves file edits and still asks before shell commands.
  • tools.allowed lists tool patterns that skip the prompt, such as run_shell_command(git).
  • The policy engine is the recommended route: TOML files in ~/.gemini/policies/ with allow / deny / ask_user rules, which can be scoped to a mode (including YOLO). --allowed-tools on the command line is deprecated in its favour.

For the Gemini Code Assist extension in VS Code, set "geminicodeassist.agentYoloMode": true in user settings and reload the window. Note the familiar rule again: it only works in a trusted workspace. In IntelliJ, the matching option is Auto-approve changes.

How do I turn on YOLO per task or per workspace with AgentRQ?

Gemini CLI's switch is per process: you either started with --approval-mode=yolo or you didn't. AgentRQ moves that decision onto the task.

1. Connect Gemini CLI. It goes through the ACP Gateway. The Gemini CLI setup guide and the step-by-step post have the details:

npx @agentrq/acp-gateway@latest --agent gemini

Start it without --approval-mode=yolo. The gateway also moves each new session out of any mode that would approve on its own and into one where Gemini CLI asks a person.

2. Answer from anywhere. Each permission request shows up in the AgentRQ task, on the web, on your phone or in Slack, along with the command or edit it's asking about. You answer Allow Once, Always Allow (adds the tool to the workspace's auto-approved list) or Deny. If nobody answers within 30 minutes, the gateway cancels the turn instead of guessing. --permission-timeout changes that limit.

3a. YOLO for one task. Flip the YOLO toggle on a task, or when you create it. Every permission request in that task is approved automatically, while every other task in the workspace still asks. The flag lives on the task, so it persists across agent disconnects and reconnects. Scheduled tasks, event triggers and workflow steps have the same switch.

3b. YOLO for the whole workspace. Workspace settings has YOLO Mode (Execute All) (UI warning: "Agent will not ask for permission"). Under the hood it's a default, not a global override: the approval check reads the task's own YOLO flag, and the workspace switch decides what that flag starts as. New tasks you create in the web form open with the YOLO toggle already on (you can still switch it off per task), and tasks the agent creates for itself over the workspace MCP server inherit it. Flipping the switch doesn't rewrite tasks that already exist.

Or let a model approve and deny for you, from plain-English rules. Between "ask me every time" and "approve everything" there's a third option: an AgentRQ desktop extension that reviews each permission request before it reaches you. Extensions are trusted Node modules loaded by the AgentRQ desktop app. One registers a reviewer with ctx.hooks.add({ id, review(request) { ... } }) and is handed the pending call: the tool name, the argument preview the harness sent, and the workspace. It answers { behavior: 'deny', reason }, { behavior: 'allow' }, or nothing at all to abstain. Point review() at an external decision API such as TypeSafe's Jev, a "System One" model that returns a typed choice with calibrated probabilities and a confidence in milliseconds instead of generating text. Send the tool call as the state, and your workspace's rules in plain English ("git push is fine on feature branches, never on main", "never read anything under ~/.aws") as a Choice question over allow / deny / ask me. Then threshold it: approve only on a high-confidence allow, refuse on a confident deny, and abstain on everything else so the request lands on your phone as usual. The rules can live on a per-workspace settings tab the extension draws itself; the bundled guardrail example does exactly that with literal patterns.

The review contract is built on one asymmetry: refusing costs a tool call, approving costs whatever the tool call does. So one refusal settles a request; silence (an abstain, an exception, or a reviewer that misses its 5-second deadline) is never an allow, the request just stays in front of you; and an extension needs the decide consent level to approve, while deny consent can only refuse. The install screen starts every extension at none. Reviews only happen while the desktop app is open and signed in, so treat this as a fast first pass, not a security boundary.

The trade-off. Per-task YOLO is scoped trust: it ends when the job you vetted ends, and an unattended nightly job can run in YOLO while your interactive work stays supervised. Workspace-wide YOLO is easier, but it outlives any single decision you made, and every new task inherits it. The setup that holds up: leave the workspace switch off, use per-task YOLO, keep GEMINI_SANDBOX=true (or "tools": {"sandbox": true}) so the auto-approved commands still run in a container, start from a clean git tree, and read the tool call history afterwards. More on the per-task model: AgentRQ YOLO mode.

FAQ

Can I make YOLO the default in settings.json? No. The resolver skips "yolo" in defaultApprovalMode. Use a shell alias.

What does Ctrl+Y do? It toggles YOLO ↔ default in the running session.

Why do my tool calls silently not run in gemini -p? Headless mode turns "ask" into "deny". Use YOLO (with a sandbox), auto_edit, or allow rules in a policy file.

For every other agent, see what YOLO mode is and how to turn it on in every coding agent.

Over to you: do you think "YOLO only from a flag, never from settings" is the right call, or should a tool trust your user-level config the way Qwen Code does? And if you run Gemini CLI in CI, which sandbox backend did you end up on? 👇

items.title: Syncthing on the public internet: 3,593 instances and the file-sync trust question
items.summary: Syncthing on the public internet: 3,593 instances and the file-sync trust question The measurement A fingerprint query for Syncthing, the peer-to-peer file synchronisation tool, returns 3,593 matching assets on the public internet. The result is interesting because Syncthing is designed to work without a central server, so every visible instance is a node that has chosen to make part of itself reachable. The trust model, briefly Syncthing pairs devices using cryptographic device identifiers. Two devices exchange identifiers, authenticate each other, and then synchronise. The web interface, by contrast, is an administrative surface that shows folder configuration, connected peers, and the file index. Reaching that interface is not the same as reaching the synchronised data, but it is a step toward it, because the interface holds the configuration that would let an attacker add their own device as a peer. The design is careful. The operational risk lives in how the interface is exposed and how device identifiers are shared. Reading the number The figure comes from an application fingerprint rather than a title match, which limits false positives from an unrelated service. As always it measures interface reachability, not configuration quality. A node with a strong administrative password on a well-maintained host and a node with no password on an abandoned laptop are indistinguishable from outside. The count also depends on the searchable scope, which here included both device and web assets. Comparing runs requires the same query, subtype, and method. Practical follow-up Where the interface is reachable, the first checks are the ones the product itself exposes. Confirm that a GUI authentication user and password are set, and that the interface is not bound to a public address when a local or tunnel-only binding would work. Syncthing's own documentation recommends against exposing the GUI directly. Then review folder configuration. A folder marked as shared with any device, or an introducer configuration on an internet-facing node, widens the set of peers that can be added over time. Understand which folders are shared with which device identifiers, and prune devices that no longer exist. Treat a device identifier like a key. Sharing it with the wrong party does not grant immediate access, since authentication still requires both sides, but it reduces the problem to that of obtaining the counterpart credential. Where the value of measurement lies For a technology built on direct peer connections, the value of an internet-scale query is inventory. Organisations that permit Syncthing for legitimate file distribution often cannot say how many nodes exist or which folders they share. A query against their own address space answers that in minutes and turns an unknown into a list with owners. Limitations The number reflects fingerprint coverage at collection time. Authentication state, folder configuration, and the identities of connected peers are not observable from outside, and a reachable interface does not imply reachable file content. References Syncthing documentation: https://docs.syncthing.net/ Syncthing security guidance: https://docs.syncthing.net/users/security.html ZoomEye cyberspace search: https://www.zoomeye.ai/

items.title: Google AI Overviews Can Misstate Brand Facts: How Businesses Should Audit Search Results
items.summary: Google AI Overviews are becoming a more prominent part of branded search results, which means an AI-generated summary can increasingly influence what a prospective customer learns about a company before reaching its website. That creates a straightforward operational task for business owners: search for the brand, inspect the AI Overview when one appears, and verify every material claim against authoritative information. Google has expanded its AI-driven Search experience with Gemini-based upgrades to AI Overviews, including Gemini 3 integration and the ability to ask follow-up questions within the overview interface. In Google's official update on AI Mode and AI Overviews , the company describes a more conversational Search experience. For brands, that matters because a summary can now become the opening point of a longer customer research journey. An AI Overview is not a company profile maintained solely from a business's own website. It synthesizes information from multiple sources. Independent research into AI Overviews has highlighted concerns around source quality and claim fidelity, particularly where underlying information is incomplete or inconsistent. The practical risk is not limited to a plainly false statement. An overview can also omit a qualification, surface old information, or combine sources in a way that gives customers an inaccurate impression of a product, service, location, or business relationship. Third-party industry analysis also suggests that AI Overviews appear frequently on branded U.S. searches. That makes routine checking more important for companies that rely on search visibility, local discovery, or reputation to generate enquiries. What to check when an AI Overview appears Start with searches that mirror how customers actually look for the business: its exact name, name plus location, name plus a core service, and common variations. Record the query, date, overview text, cited sources , and a screenshot where appropriate. Search results can vary by location, device, language, and query wording, so a single result is not a complete audit. Focus first on facts that can change a buying decision or cause customer-service problems: Business identity: company name, location, contact details, and operating area. Offerings: products, services, availability, and whether a claim needs important context. Commercial information: pricing, policies, opening hours, and eligibility statements where these are shown. Reputation-sensitive claims: ownership, partnerships, certifications, awards, and descriptions of what the business does. Citations: whether the overview relies on current, authoritative pages or on outdated and less reliable third-party material. A discrepancy should be evaluated carefully. The AI Overview may cite a page that is correct but ambiguous, or it may reflect conflicting information published elsewhere. The goal is to identify the source of the mismatch, not simply assume that editing a page will immediately change an AI-generated result. Google AI Search element Verified development What a brand audit should examine AI Overviews Gemini-based summaries in Search, with Gemini 3 included in the 2026 upgrade described by Google. Whether the summary's individual claims match current first-party information. Follow-up questions Users can continue with conversational follow-ups from the AI Overview interface. Whether likely follow-up queries could amplify an incomplete or misleading initial summary. Website owner controls Google has introduced controls intended to let website owners influence whether their sites appear in AI-generated and AI-grounded responses. Whether applicable controls are available and appropriate for the company's content strategy. Build a repeatable verification workflow A useful audit does not need to become a large technical project. Assign one person to own the review, establish a small set of priority queries, and keep a simple record of what appears. Review the business's own key pages alongside the citations in the overview. For location-dependent businesses, consistency across address, contact, and service information is especially important because customers may use those details to decide whether to make contact. When the issue originates on a brand-owned page, correct the factual source first. Make the information clear, current, and consistent across the pages that explain the company, its services, and its contact details. If cited third-party pages conflict with the business's records, request corrections from the relevant publisher or platform. This is more durable than attempting to react only to the wording of an individual overview. Google has also announced controls for website owners related to appearing in AI-generated responses and AI-grounded features. Those options provide a concrete decision point for site owners, but their availability and suitability may vary. Businesses should review Google's current documentation and administrative options before changing how their content participates in AI features. Opting out may reduce the chance that a site's content is used in these responses, while also limiting its potential visibility within them. Treat citations as part of brand monitoring The citations attached to an AI Overview are often as important as the generated text. They show which pages are helping ground the answer and can reveal gaps in the brand's information ecosystem. A cited official page that is old, unclear, or incomplete is an opportunity to improve it. A cited external page with stale details is a prompt to pursue correction where possible. This work complements conventional search and local listing maintenance rather than replacing it. Accurate first-party pages and consistent third-party references give search systems clearer evidence to synthesize. They cannot guarantee that every AI-generated response will be error-free, but they reduce avoidable ambiguity and make it easier to identify where a problematic claim may have originated. For businesses that depend on enquiries from Search, this is also a customer-experience issue. A wrong phone number, outdated service description, or misleading qualification can create friction before a customer reaches the site. Establish a rapid response path involving the person responsible for the website, local listings, and customer-facing communications. That makes it possible to check a reported issue, update a source where needed, and monitor whether subsequent searches change. As AI-generated results become another way customers encounter a company, businesses need a practical way to protect accuracy and discoverability. GEO Search Leads can help teams improve visibility in AI search results by identifying how their web presence is represented and where high-value search opportunities may be missed. Turn occasional brand searches into a repeatable visibility check that supports better customer journeys and stronger inbound demand. Start an AI visibility scan. Frequently Asked Questions What is a Google AI Overview? A Google AI Overview is an AI-generated summary that can appear in Google Search results and may cite multiple web sources. Google has expanded the feature with Gemini-based capabilities and follow-up questions . Why should a business check AI Overviews for its name? A branded AI Overview can shape a customer's first impression. Checking it helps a business identify incorrect, incomplete, or outdated claims about its location, services, contact details, or other important facts. How can a business investigate an incorrect claim in an AI Overview? Compare the claim with the business's official pages, then inspect the overview's cited sources. Correct inaccurate first-party information and seek updates from third-party sources that publish conflicting details. Can website owners control whether their content appears in AI-generated responses? Google has introduced controls intended to let website owners influence whether their sites appear in AI-generated and AI-grounded responses. Businesses should review Google's current documentation to determine what is available and appropriate for their sites. Will updating a website immediately change an AI Overview? No immediate change is guaranteed. AI Overviews synthesize multiple sources, and results can vary by query and context. Updating authoritative information is still an important first step in reducing inconsistency. Conclusion Google's more interactive AI Overviews make brand-result accuracy a recurring search maintenance issue, not a one-time check. By auditing important branded queries , reviewing cited sources, correcting inconsistent information, and assessing Google's available owner controls, businesses can respond more effectively when AI-generated summaries fail to reflect the facts.

For location-dependent businesses, consistency across address, contact, and service information is especially important because customers may use those details to decide whether to make contact.

When the issue originates on a brand-owned page, correct the factual source first. Make the information clear, current, and consistent across the pages that explain the company, its services, and its contact details. If cited third-party pages conflict with the business's records, request corrections from the relevant publisher or platform. This is more durable than attempting to react only to the wording of an individual overview.

Google has also announced controls for website owners related to appearing in AI-generated responses and AI-grounded features. Those options provide a concrete decision point for site owners, but their availability and suitability may vary. Businesses should review Google's current documentation and administrative options before changing how their content participates in AI features. Opting out may reduce the chance that a site's content is used in these responses, while also limiting its potential visibility within them.

Treat citations as part of brand monitoring

The citations attached to an AI Overview are often as important as the generated text. They show which pages are helping ground the answer and can reveal gaps in the brand's information ecosystem. A cited official page that is old, unclear, or incomplete is an opportunity to improve it. A cited external page with stale details is a prompt to pursue correction where possible.

This work complements conventional search and local listing maintenance rather than replacing it. Accurate first-party pages and consistent third-party references give search systems clearer evidence to synthesize. They cannot guarantee that every AI-generated response will be error-free, but they reduce avoidable ambiguity and make it easier to identify where a problematic claim may have originated.

For businesses that depend on enquiries from Search, this is also a customer-experience issue. A wrong phone number, outdated service description, or misleading qualification can create friction before a customer reaches the site. Establish a rapid response path involving the person responsible for the website, local listings, and customer-facing communications. That makes it possible to check a reported issue, update a source where needed, and monitor whether subsequent searches change.

As AI-generated results become another way customers encounter a company, businesses need a practical way to protect accuracy and discoverability. GEO Search Leads can help teams improve visibility in AI search results by identifying how their web presence is represented and where high-value search opportunities may be missed. Turn occasional brand searches into a repeatable visibility check that supports better customer journeys and stronger inbound demand. Start an AI visibility scan.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a Google AI Overview?

A Google AI Overview is an AI-generated summary that can appear in Google Search results and may cite multiple web sources. Google has expanded the feature with Gemini-based capabilities and follow-up questions.

Why should a business check AI Overviews for its name?

A branded AI Overview can shape a customer's first impression. Checking it helps a business identify incorrect, incomplete, or outdated claims about its location, services, contact details, or other important facts.

How can a business investigate an incorrect claim in an AI Overview?

Compare the claim with the business's official pages, then inspect the overview's cited sources. Correct inaccurate first-party information and seek updates from third-party sources that publish conflicting details.

Can website owners control whether their content appears in AI-generated responses?

Google has introduced controls intended to let website owners influence whether their sites appear in AI-generated and AI-grounded responses. Businesses should review Google's current documentation to determine what is available and appropriate for their sites.

Will updating a website immediately change an AI Overview?

No immediate change is guaranteed. AI Overviews synthesize multiple sources, and results can vary by query and context. Updating authoritative information is still an important first step in reducing inconsistency.

Conclusion

Google's more interactive AI Overviews make brand-result accuracy a recurring search maintenance issue, not a one-time check. By auditing important branded queries, reviewing cited sources, correcting inconsistent information, and assessing Google's available owner controls, businesses can respond more effectively when AI-generated summaries fail to reflect the facts.

items.title: We checked 49 payment MCP servers. 37 can move money. Only 4 document a spending budget.
items.summary: Disclosure: I work on Pink Agentic AI Payments at PinkWallet, which is one of the 49 servers in this census. Pink was scored from its public docs by the same criteria as every other row, and it currently runs as a public sandbox with test money only. The full dataset is open so you can check every number: github.com/Pink-Agentic-Payments/payment-mcp-census . Short answer: most payment MCP servers can move real money, but very few tell you how to stop an agent from spending too much. Of 37 servers that can create a payment, transfer, payout, charge or card, only 4 (11%) document a configurable spending budget, only 6 (16%) document a human-approval step, and only 1 (3%) documents a velocity limit. If you are about to give an AI agent a payment tool over MCP, that gap is the thing to check first. What we counted We catalogued 49 payment-adjacent MCP servers (24 official vendor servers, 25 community ones) between 2026-10-08 and 2026-10-09, and read each one's own docs or README. For every server we recorded whether it can move money and whether it documents six spending controls: a per-agent or aggregate budget a per-payment limit a payee / merchant allowlist or block a human approval step a rate / velocity limit a sandbox / test mode "Documents" means the control is described in the server's public docs. A server may have a control it does not document; for an agent builder, an undocumented control is hard to rely on. The numbers Finding Count Servers that can move money 37 of 49 (76%) …that document a spending budget 4 of 37 (11%) …that document a per-payment limit 5 of 37 (14%) …that document a payee allowlist / block 3 of 37 (8%) …that document human approval 6 of 37 (16%) …that document a velocity / rate limit 1 of 37 (3%) …that document a sandbox / test mode 8 of 37 (22%) Listed servers whose GitHub repo returned 404 5 of 49 (10%) Community servers move money slightly more often than official ones: 20 of 25 community rows versus 17 of 24 official rows. Who documents what These are the money-moving servers that document at least one spending control (from the census table, generated straight from census.csv ): Budget: Marqeta ("spending caps"), Gatewards ("per-agent spend caps"), MCPay ("a hard budget"), Pink (per-agent monthly budget). Per-payment limit: Coinbase AgentKit / CDP (value-based policy rules), Crossmint Checkout ( maxCost ), MCPay, x402search-mcp, Pink. Payee allowlist: Coinbase AgentKit / CDP, Marqeta, Pink. Human approval: Stripe (confirmation for refunds and outbound payments), Crossmint ( awaiting_input ), Ramp ("managing approvals"), GoCardless ("with user confirmation"), SpendNod, Pink ( pending_human ). Velocity limit: Marqeta only. No single control is common. The most-documented one, human approval, still appears in fewer than 1 in 6 money-moving servers. Why this matters if you build agents Prompts are not a spending limit. An instruction like "never spend more than $50" lives in the model's context, and the model can misread it, forget it, or be talked out of it by a prompt injection in a web page or an email. A control that actually holds has to sit outside the model , in the system that holds the money, and has to be checked before the payment executes. A companion survey of 12 popular agent frameworks (LangChain/LangGraph, CrewAI, OpenAI Agents SDK, Vercel AI SDK, Google ADK, AutoGen, Semantic Kernel, LlamaIndex, Pydantic AI, Mastra, Claude Agent SDK, smolagents) found that 0 of 12 document a spending budget in currency for tool calls, while 10 of 12 offer some form of human approval and 9 of 12 a max-steps limit ( agent-framework-spend-guardrails ). The frameworks can pause an agent; they do not know what a tool call costs. So in practice the spending controls have to come from the payment layer. When you evaluate a payment MCP server, ask five questions: Can I set a budget per agent , not just per account? Is there a per-payment cap , enforced server-side? Can I restrict who the agent may pay? Can a payment above a threshold go to a human and wait, with a default of "no" if nobody answers? Is there a sandbox so I can test the rules with fake money first? How Pink approaches it (one data point, not the only answer) Pink's MCP server gives the agent a pink.request_payment tool instead of a card. Every request is checked on the server against circuit breakers (agent registered and active, monthly budget, company daily ceiling) and then against the company's rules, top to bottom. The answer is one of three: allowed (the agent gets a single-use credential locked to one payee and one amount, expiring in about 15 minutes), pending_human (a person approves or rejects; silence means no), or blocked . Unmatched requests default to blocked. The public sandbox at agentic-sandbox.pinkwallet.com uses test credentials only; production is not yet available. If you want to try to break it, there is an open challenge: can you make an AI agent overspend? Get the data Dataset, method and every source URL: payment-mcp-census (CC BY 4.0) Framework survey: agent-framework-spend-guardrails A longer comparison with notes per server: Payment MCP servers compared If your server is in the census and we got a row wrong, open an issue on the repo with a link to your docs and we will correct it.
