Disclosure: I work on Pink Agentic AI Payments at PinkWallet, which is one of the 49 servers in this census. Pink was scored from its public docs by the same criteria as every other row, and it currently runs as a public sandbox with test money only. The full dataset is open so you can check every number: github.com/Pink-Agentic-Payments/payment-mcp-census.

Short answer: most payment MCP servers can move real money, but very few tell you how to stop an agent from spending too much. Of 37 servers that can create a payment, transfer, payout, charge or card, only 4 (11%) document a configurable spending budget, only 6 (16%) document a human-approval step, and only 1 (3%) documents a velocity limit.

If you are about to give an AI agent a payment tool over MCP, that gap is the thing to check first.

What we counted

We catalogued 49 payment-adjacent MCP servers (24 official vendor servers, 25 community ones) between 2026-10-08 and 2026-10-09, and read each one's own docs or README. For every server we recorded whether it can move money and whether it documents six spending controls:

  1. a per-agent or aggregate budget
  2. a per-payment limit
  3. a payee / merchant allowlist or block
  4. a human approval step
  5. a rate / velocity limit
  6. a sandbox / test mode

"Documents" means the control is described in the server's public docs. A server may have a control it does not document; for an agent builder, an undocumented control is hard to rely on.

The numbers
Finding Count Servers that can move money 37 of 49 (76%) …that document a spending budget 4 of 37 (11%) …that document a per-payment limit 5 of 37 (14%) …that document a payee allowlist / block 3 of 37 (8%) …that document human approval 6 of 37 (16%) …that document a velocity / rate limit 1 of 37 (3%) …that document a sandbox / test mode 8 of 37 (22%) Listed servers whose GitHub repo returned 404 5 of 49 (10%)

Community servers move money slightly more often than official ones: 20 of 25 community rows versus 17 of 24 official rows.

Who documents what

These are the money-moving servers that document at least one spending control (from the census table, generated straight from census.csv):

  • Budget: Marqeta ("spending caps"), Gatewards ("per-agent spend caps"), MCPay ("a hard budget"), Pink (per-agent monthly budget).
  • Per-payment limit: Coinbase AgentKit / CDP (value-based policy rules), Crossmint Checkout (maxCost), MCPay, x402search-mcp, Pink.
  • Payee allowlist: Coinbase AgentKit / CDP, Marqeta, Pink.
  • Human approval: Stripe (confirmation for refunds and outbound payments), Crossmint (awaiting_input), Ramp ("managing approvals"), GoCardless ("with user confirmation"), SpendNod, Pink (pending_human).
  • Velocity limit: Marqeta only.

No single control is common. The most-documented one, human approval, still appears in fewer than 1 in 6 money-moving servers.

Why this matters if you build agents

Prompts are not a spending limit. An instruction like "never spend more than $50" lives in the model's context, and the model can misread it, forget it, or be talked out of it by a prompt injection in a web page or an email. A control that actually holds has to sit outside the model, in the system that holds the money, and has to be checked before the payment executes.

A companion survey of 12 popular agent frameworks (LangChain/LangGraph, CrewAI, OpenAI Agents SDK, Vercel AI SDK, Google ADK, AutoGen, Semantic Kernel, LlamaIndex, Pydantic AI, Mastra, Claude Agent SDK, smolagents) found that 0 of 12 document a spending budget in currency for tool calls, while 10 of 12 offer some form of human approval and 9 of 12 a max-steps limit (agent-framework-spend-guardrails). The frameworks can pause an agent; they do not know what a tool call costs.

So in practice the spending controls have to come from the payment layer. When you evaluate a payment MCP server, ask five questions:

  1. Can I set a budget per agent, not just per account?
  2. Is there a per-payment cap, enforced server-side?
  3. Can I restrict who the agent may pay?
  4. Can a payment above a threshold go to a human and wait, with a default of "no" if nobody answers?
  5. Is there a sandbox so I can test the rules with fake money first?
How Pink approaches it (one data point, not the only answer)

Pink's MCP server gives the agent a pink.request_payment tool instead of a card. Every request is checked on the server against circuit breakers (agent registered and active, monthly budget, company daily ceiling) and then against the company's rules, top to bottom. The answer is one of three: allowed (the agent gets a single-use credential locked to one payee and one amount, expiring in about 15 minutes), pending_human (a person approves or rejects; silence means no), or blocked. Unmatched requests default to blocked. The public sandbox at agentic-sandbox.pinkwallet.com uses test credentials only; production is not yet available.

If you want to try to break it, there is an open challenge: can you make an AI agent overspend?

Get the data
  • Dataset, method and every source URL: payment-mcp-census (CC BY 4.0)
  • Framework survey: agent-framework-spend-guardrails
  • A longer comparison with notes per server: Payment MCP servers compared

If your server is in the census and we got a row wrong, open an issue on the repo with a link to your docs and we will correct it.

items.title: Meet the Anthropic Engineer Keeping Its AI Agent Trustworthy
items.summary: If you’ve ever wondered how Claude and similar AI agents can answer complex questions in seconds and where they get the information, you’re not alone. Gurmeet Saran works to find that answer every day as an engineer at Anthropic in San Francisco, the AI research company behind Claude. The IEEE senior member is developing an infrastructure to understand the mechanics behind the chatbot’s behavior and to ensure its underlying architecture produces reliable outputs. Gurmeet Saran Employer Anthropic in San Francisco Title Member of technical staff Member grade IEEE senior member Alma maters University of Kalyani, in India; Birla Institute of Technology and Science, in Pilani, India “My job is to make sure the data is accurate, structured, and trustworthy, and that private data stays private,” he says. “As I learned earlier in my career, privacy can’t be a layer you bolt on—it has to be part of the architecture from the start.” If you can’t trust the logic, he adds, you can’t make reliable claims about the behavior, and that has real safety implications. Safety is a priority for Anthropic, he says. According to Claude’s mission statement , the company wants the AI agent to be “genuinely helpful to the people it works with or on behalf of, as well as to society, while avoiding actions that are unsafe, unethical, or deceptive.” Crucial to the mission is ensuring that researchers can observe and understand how AI models behave, a challenge that is especially acute for large language models , Saran says. “We have decent tools to monitor databases and web services,” he says, “but for LLMs, we’re still figuring it out.” Solving data quality problems at Yahoo, Intuit, and Meta Saran’s interest in computing systems dates back to his childhood in Kolkata, where he logged as much time as he could in the school computer lab. “I remember the first time I used one of the computers,” he says. “What struck me was that you could write instructions, and the machine would follow them exactly. No ambiguity. “That felt magical to me.” After graduating from high school in 1999, he stayed in India to pursue advanced degrees. He earned a bachelor’s degree in electronics and telecommunication engineering in 2004 at the University of Kalyani . In 2010, he earned a master’s degree in software engineering from the Birla Institute of Technology and Science in Pilani. While a graduate student, he began his career in 2007 at Yahoo as a technical lead of the data team in Bengaluru, India. While there, he encountered the project that shaped his career trajectory: working on web analytics and business intelligence reporting solutions. “We kept running into a frustrating problem,” he recalls. “Different teams would calculate the same website metric—something like daily active site users—using slightly different logic, and end up with conflicting answers. It sounds like a small issue, but when leadership is making decisions about resource allocation and product development using that data, not knowing which number is correct becomes a problem.” The team built a central data repository with defined metrics, essentially serving as a single source of truth. Saran created a model that defined what “daily active site users” means, breaking down which events counted, how to handle edge cases (or when standard code fails), and more. With the new model, data teams across the company could rely on a standard method to determine the number of daily active users for the projects and sites they were responsible for and obtain comparable results using the same logic. From there, Saran and his team built Yahoo! Digits , an internal web analytics tool used for all the company’s products. Saran left Yahoo in 2010 to join Intuit as a staff engineer in Mountain View, Calif. He helped build the analytics infrastructure that unified data across the company’s products, including TurboTax and QuickBooks accounting software. During his tenure, Intuit developed a feature that detected fraudulent tax filings in real time. It required Saran and other engineers to build a system to protect taxpayer data while adhering to strict U.S. Internal Revenue Service policies. “IEEE operates in a lot of countries where engineers don’t have easy pathways into the global professional community. That kind of connection matters as AI development spreads beyond a handful of organizations.” “This taught me that privacy and governance can’t be layers you bolt onto software after the fact,” he says. “They have to be part of the architecture from the start.” Saran joined Meta (known as Facebook at the time) in 2016 as a lead software engineer in Menlo Park, Calif. The company was facing controversy over its video metrics: Meta publicly acknowledged an error that caused it to overstate the number of views for posted videos . “This wasn’t a coding bug; it was an architectural problem,” Saran says. He built a system that worked similarly to what he had developed at Intuit, whereby one single truth was defined to govern all video view metrics across the site. That system, Metric360 , eventually became part of the site’s architecture. By the time he left Meta in 2021, he says, Metric360 was being used across the company to calculate video metrics. He left the company to become a principal software engineer at Wealthfront , a financial services company in Palo Alto, Calif. He helped build the company’s data infrastructure. Building trustworthy AI systems at Anthropic Saran joined Anthropic in 2025 as a member of the technical staff. To describe the implications of his work, he uses a medical analogy: “Imagine a doctor is monitoring a patient’s vital signs and making treatment decisions based on those numbers. What if one or a few of the medical devices used were slightly miscalibrated? Even if most readings are fine, it’s a serious problem because the difficult decisions happen in the margins. “It’s the same with AI systems. My job is essentially to make sure the instruments are giving accurate readings—that the data means what it says it means.” His job comes with high stakes and complex problems to solve. “ AI agents are especially tricky to observe,” he says. “When a system is taking sequences of actions [generating conversational responses with different users], you need a way to capture what it did, what information it was working from, and whether outcomes matched what the end user expected. And you have to do all of that without exposing anyone’s private information—the systems are designed to recognize sensitive data and keep it protected as it flows through. It’s a much more demanding observability problem than anything I’ve worked on before.” Solving for system reliability while AI is still in its early days of adoption is both Saran’s passion and the problem that keeps him up at night, he says. “I think making AI systems genuinely auditable and transparent is one of the more important engineering problems of the next decade,” he says, “and it doesn’t get talked about as much as model capabilities do.” IEEE can play a role in shaping AI development Saran joined IEEE in March 2025. “After more than 20 years of building data infrastructure across organizations like Yahoo, Intuit, Meta, and Wealthfront,” he says, “I wanted to contribute back to the technical community through peer review, publishing, and engaging with the broader engineering research ecosystem.” He says he believes IEEE can play an essential role in shaping the future of AI through its standards work . “We have standards for everything, from building codes to software testing,” he says. “AI infrastructure needs something similar, and IEEE has the credibility and the reach to do that.” Another problem that IEEE can solve for, he says, is access: “IEEE operates in a lot of countries where engineers don’t have easy pathways into the global professional community. That kind of connection matters, especially as AI development spreads beyond a handful of organizations in a few cities.”

items.summary: Sakana AI's MASS method lets one language model improve itself by solving tasks, judging results, and refining workflows, reaching a win rate of nearly 70 percent against the base model after two rounds. But when the model misses the same errors across all three roles, it can mistake them for progress and reinforce them during training. items.summary: As startups scramble to get access to AI servers, more venture capital firms are finding ways to secure compute on their behalf. Andreessen Horowitz, which two years ago set up a cluster of 20,000 graphics processing units for its startups, is in talks to expand its offering, potentially via two data center companies it has backed, according to people familiar with its plans. Meanwhile, General Catalyst is building a data center to supply compute for its startups, said two other people. And several other VC funds have used brokers to find sought-after chips for their companies.

He said: The Royal College of Emergency Medicine estimates that 15,000 people across Britain died last year due to excess wait times for emergency treatment. This is a moral outrage, and it is a direct result of decisions made by Tory and Labour governments. I don’t think that’s because he wants to have a fight over the European Union. items.title: When AI is subject to less regulation than your fridge, something is startlingly wrong | Richard Hermer
items.summary: Let’s be clear: the risk to humanity is unprecedented. Without an urgent public debate and robust use of international law, we will lose control of the future In my two years as attorney general, I spent more time working on national security than any other issue. The range and gravity of the threats posed to our nation are multifold, from terrorism, armed conflicts and nuclear proliferation, to the impacts of financial insecurity and the climate crisis. All profound challenges, yet ones our superb intelligence and defence communities are well placed to counter. The risk from AI is of an altogether different magnitude, not only in scale, but also because there is a limited time window to address it. The risk is difficult to overestimate: it poses an existential risk to humanity. The lights are flashing red and we must act now before it’s too late. Although the extraordinary threats posed by AI have long been flagged by those closely involved in its creation, it was not until very recently, after the disclosure of the Hugging Face hack and the resignation of Jacob Coxon from Anthropic , that the issue at last started to gain traction in the public discourse. This moment is an opportunity, and to capitalise on it we desperately need increased urgency in international coordination to regulate frontier AI. There must also be meaningful public engagement with how AI should be shaped to benefit humanity, rather than entrench the power of a few. We cannot leave this to China, the US and big tech – we must all demand a voice in the debate.

items.title: Ukrainian soldiers are putting RPGs on robots for fights in the kill zone, a manufacturer says
items.summary: Ukrainian forces have used RPGs to fight Russia's invasion. Now, they're starting to put them on robots to attack. Roman Chop/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images Ukrainian troops are shifting another infantry weapon from soldiers to robots. RPGs are finding a new role as combat evolves and troops lean on emerging tech to mitigate risk. The change reflects how drones and robots are reshaping ground warfare. Ukrainian soldiers conducting operations in the kill zone have been putting anti-tank RPGs on ground robots, a robotic systems manufacturer told Business Insider, explaining that the battlefield has become too dangerous for troops to use the weapons the way they did earlier in the war. Rocket-propelled grenades are often used by infantry to defeat armored vehicles and weaken fortified positions, but the battlefield has changed, forcing new innovations. In the kill zone, "nobody knew how to use" an RPG "while staying safe himself," Oleg Fedoryshyn, the R&D director of Ukrainian robot maker DevDroid, told Business Insider. The kill zone along Ukraine's front is a perilous area, as deep as 50 kilometers in some areas, where drones are so heavily concentrated alongside other weaponry that any movement represents a significant risk. For many soldiers, simply getting within RPG range can be extremely difficult. The decision to move RPGs onto robots reflects a broader shift in the war. Early in Russia's full-scale invasion, RPGs were a common infantry weapon, used against Russian tanks and vehicles and to support infantry during fights in towns and cities. But cheap drones , in both surveillance and strike roles, have transformed ground combat, reducing the use of armored vehicles and changing infantry engagements. Ukraine's robot fleet can fire a growing array of weapons. Dmytro Smolienko/Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty Images DevDroid's ground robots aren't the only ones getting RPGs as the war evolves. Ukrainian UGV maker Temerland says its Gnom-VP ground robotic fire support platform carries two RPG-7 launchers, along with other weapons and mine-laying capabilities. Fedoryshyn said soldiers working with DevDroid started putting the RPGs on robots that were already armed with machine guns . The robots can drive close enough to targets and fire shorter-range weapons while keeping their operators much farther from danger. Fedoryshyn said a brigade came to the company and said they wanted to try putting RPGs on a robot, and they had "great" success using it. Now, the company is exploring "how to add support for this for everyone in the future," he said. Devdroid makes ground robots and a remote-controlled weapons station that allows operators to fire from safe distances, as well as electric triggers that allow operators to activate a weapon remotely. Requests from soldiers are often how Ukraine's new capabilities emerge . Arms makers work directly with front-line units, gathering feedback and rapidly modifying equipment. Fedoryshyn said DevDroid has 24/7 chat support available for every unit that uses its systems. He said that the company can design a new update, test it with a brigade, and roll it out across all deployed systems within a week. It designs its gear for easy updates, "like mobile phones or operating systems," he added. Robots have a growing role in Ukraine's fight against Russia's invasion. Oleksandr Klymenko/Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty Images The war is one of rapid innovation to field new capabilities and preserve the utility of older ones as the war changes. Mounting RPGs on ground robots is another sign of that evolution. Instead of discarding a weapon designed for a kind of fighting that is less common now, Ukrainian troops are changing who carries it to keep it in the fight. Other weapons, such as flamethrowers, grenade launchers, and machine guns, have also been mounted on robots. Fedoryshyn said his company is often surprised by how soldiers use its robots, including cases in which Russian soldiers have surrendered to them. Ukraine's experience, he said, shows Western militaries preparing for protracted wars should invest in large numbers of inexpensive, easily replaceable robots rather than relying solely on costly tanks and armored vehicles. items.title: The Secret to Getting Better AI Answers Might Be Hiding in a 1986 Aircraft Manual
items.summary: How ASD-STE100, an aerospace writing standard, can improve AI prompting and make LLM responses clearer, more concise, and easier to understand. An aerospace writing standard meets AI prompting, with surprising lessons in how to make complex ideas easier to understand. An aircraft mechanic stands in front of a maintenance panel. There’s a handle, and right beside it, one clear instruction: PULL . Yet somewhere in a manual hundreds of pages long, that simple action has a whole explanation devoted to it. AI has a similar habit. Ask a chatbot a simple question, and it can turn the answer into six paragraphs, three caveats, and a summary that repeats what you already read. The information is there; finding the answer in all that explanation is the hard part! Aerospace engineers have spent decades solving a version of this problem: making technical instructions clear enough to follow without ambiguity. One of their writing standards, Simplified Technical English , offers a set of rules that might help AI do the same. And you can try them in your next prompt. The aviation standard hiding in your next prompt In October 2026, Andrej Karpathy shared a collection of ideas for making language models easier to work with. One suggestion stood out: ask an LLM to explain something using ASD-STE100 , a controlled language standard originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. He also mentioned asking for output “80% of the way to ASD-STE100” because the full standard can be too restrictive. The idea is simple. Instead of telling a model to be concise , give it a writing system that already has rules for making technical language clearer. Andrej Karpathy’s original post on X for using ASD-STE110 for LLMs ASD-STE100 was developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. Its roots go back to the late 1970s, when the European aerospace industry worked on making technical instructions easier to understand for readers with different levels of English proficiency. The first guide appeared in 1986. Issue 9, released in January 2025, became an international standard for technical documentation. The reason for its existence is not to make writing elegant. It is to make instructions easier to understand correctly. The standard has two main parts: Writing rules: 53 rules covering word choice, grammar, sentence structure, and style. A controlled dictionary: approximately 900 approved general words, each with a defined meaning and part of speech, alongside guidance on words to avoid. Consider the number of ways English lets us express the same idea. We can start , commence , initiate , or begin something. In everyday conversation, that variety is useful. In technical documentation, unnecessary variation can make a reader stop and wonder whether the words mean different things. STE favours consistent choices. It also encourages direct sentences, active voice, and clear relationships between actions and objects. Instead of writing: “Prior to commencing the procedure, it is recommended that the operator verify the availability of the required components.” You could write: “Before you start the procedure, make sure that the required components are available.” The second version gets to the action without burying it in formal language. The official ASD-STE100 website explains the standard and provides access to the current issue. Of course, an LLM explaining prompt caching is not an aircraft mechanic following a safety-critical maintenance procedure. But both situations benefit from clear wording and consistent terminology. That is the connection worth exploring. Why “be concise” is a surprisingly weak instruction Most of us have tried telling an AI to “keep it short” or “explain it simply.” Sometimes it works. Sometimes the model removes a few sentences but leaves the explanation just as difficult to follow. The problem is that be concise describes the outcome we want without specifying how to achieve it. items.summary_html:
How ASD-STE100, an aerospace writing standard, can improve AI prompting and make LLM responses clearer, more concise, and easier to understand.An aerospace writing standard meets AI prompting, with surprising lessons in how to make complex ideas easier to understand.

An aircraft mechanic stands in front of a maintenance panel. There’s a handle, and right beside it, one clear instruction: PULL.

Yet somewhere in a manual hundreds of pages long, that simple action has a whole explanation devoted to it.

AI has a similar habit. Ask a chatbot a simple question, and it can turn the answer into six paragraphs, three caveats, and a summary that repeats what you already read. The information is there; finding the answer in all that explanation is the hard part!

Aerospace engineers have spent decades solving a version of this problem: making technical instructions clear enough to follow without ambiguity. One of their writing standards, Simplified Technical English, offers a set of rules that might help AI do the same. And you can try them in your next prompt.

The aviation standard hiding in your next prompt

In October 2026, Andrej Karpathy shared a collection of ideas for making language models easier to work with. One suggestion stood out: ask an LLM to explain something using ASD-STE100, a controlled language standard originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation.

He also mentioned asking for output “80% of the way to ASD-STE100” because the full standard can be too restrictive.

The idea is simple. Instead of telling a model to be concise, give it a writing system that already has rules for making technical language clearer.

Andrej Karpathy’s original post on X for using ASD-STE110 for LLMs

ASD-STE100 was developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. Its roots go back to the late 1970s, when the European aerospace industry worked on making technical instructions easier to understand for readers with different levels of English proficiency. The first guide appeared in 1986. Issue 9, released in January 2025, became an international standard for technical documentation.

The reason for its existence is not to make writing elegant. It is to make instructions easier to understand correctly.

The standard has two main parts:

  • Writing rules: 53 rules covering word choice, grammar, sentence structure, and style.
  • A controlled dictionary: approximately 900 approved general words, each with a defined meaning and part of speech, alongside guidance on words to avoid.

Consider the number of ways English lets us express the same idea. We can start, commence, initiate, or begin something. In everyday conversation, that variety is useful. In technical documentation, unnecessary variation can make a reader stop and wonder whether the words mean different things.

STE favours consistent choices. It also encourages direct sentences, active voice, and clear relationships between actions and objects.

Instead of writing: “Prior to commencing the procedure, it is recommended that the operator verify the availability of the required components.”

You could write: “Before you start the procedure, make sure that the required components are available.”

The second version gets to the action without burying it in formal language.

The official ASD-STE100 website explains the standard and provides access to the current issue.

Of course, an LLM explaining prompt caching is not an aircraft mechanic following a safety-critical maintenance procedure. But both situations benefit from clear wording and consistent terminology. That is the connection worth exploring.

Why “be concise” is a surprisingly weak instruction

Most of us have tried telling an AI to “keep it short” or “explain it simply.” Sometimes it works. Sometimes the model removes a few sentences but leaves the explanation just as difficult to follow.

The problem is that be concise describes the outcome we want without specifying how to achieve it. Should the model simplify its wording, remove repetition, or break a long sentence into smaller ideas?

ASD-STE100 offers more concrete guidance on these choices.

Take prompt caching as an example.

Example of the same idea explained two ways: verbose wording v/s clear, direct language.

Both answers explain the same concept, but they organise the information differently. The first packs the mechanism into a long sentence. The second explains what caching saves, when that content can be reused, and what benefit this provides.

The goal isn’t simply to use fewer words. It’s to make the explanation easier to follow without losing important information.

Why 80% might be better than 100%

If STE is designed to make technical language clearer, why not ask an AI to follow it completely?

Because the standard was built for a specific job.

Aircraft maintenance instructions need consistent terminology and carefully controlled wording. A conversation about neural networks has different demands. It may need a natural transition, a technical term that doesn’t fit neatly into a controlled vocabulary, or a longer explanation to make an unfamiliar concept click.

Apply a strict technical-writing standard to every conversation and the result can feel mechanical. You might get short sentences that are easy to read but awkward to follow as a whole.

Karpathy’s suggestion to aim for “80% of the way to ASD-STE100” acknowledges that trade-off.

The number is an informal prompting instruction, not an official compliance score or a measurable guarantee of clarity.

The aim is to borrow the useful constraints without forcing every explanation into the shape of a maintenance manual. The model should still be able to preserve important caveats, explain unfamiliar concepts, and sound natural.

Try it yourself!

You do not need to install a tool or build a custom workflow to test the idea. Start with a question you have asked an AI assistant before.

It could be about vector databases, attention mechanisms, API authentication, database indexing, or any other technical concept you find difficult to explain clearly.

Run the same question through three prompts.

A. Your normal prompt

Ask the question exactly as you usually would. Save the answer.

B. The generic clarity prompt

Ask the same question and add:

Explain this clearly and concisely. Avoid unnecessary details.

Save that answer too.

C. The STE-inspired prompt

Try this:

Explain [TOPIC] to [TARGET AUDIENCE].
Write about 80% of the way toward ASD-STE100
Simplified Technical English.
Use direct language and short sentences.
Prefer familiar words when they preserve the meaning.
Use active voice where appropriate.
Keep terminology consistent.
Put one main idea in each sentence.
Explain technical terms when they first appear.
Remove repetition and unnecessary introductory phrases.
Preserve important technical details, assumptions,
conditions, exceptions, and uncertainty.
Do not remove information only to make the answer shorter.
Prioritize clarity and accuracy over strict compliance
with the standard.
Use an example if it makes the concept easier to understand.

Now compare the three answers.

Which one gets to the point? Which is easiest to follow? Did any version remove a detail you needed, or explain something so simply that it became misleading?

For a less subjective comparison, ask someone else to read the answers without telling them which prompt produced each one. See which explanation they understand most easily.

Treat this as an experiment, not a foregone conclusion. Different models and topics may produce different results. The STE-inspired prompt may not win every comparison, and the shortest answer isn’t necessarily the best one.

What happened when I tried it?

I tried this with a question about API authentication. The usual prompt produced a sprawling explanation, while the generic clarity prompt cut it down to the basics. The STE-inspired version struck a middle ground, using clearer steps and definitions while retaining practical examples.

What if the explanation did not have to stay text?

What if AI could explain ideas through diagrams, interactive pages, or animated videos instead of text alone? As models get better at generating code, creating these custom explainers is becoming more accessible.

Favio Vazquez demonstrated this with a 3Blue1Brown-style explainer about ASD-STE100, using Manim for animation and Kokoro for local narration written in STE. The video ran on a single machine without API keys, using showtime, an open-source video studio for coding agents.

https://medium.com/media/5e123212b2fb692ef341b1aac9ea3769/href

The narration itself uses STE, so the video demonstrates the writing standard it explains. It is a neat example of how local tools can turn a writing principle into a visual explanation without relying on paid APIs.

But a polished animation doesn’t guarantee an accurate explanation. Video can help explain a process, while a short written answer may be enough for a definition. The format should serve the idea, not distract from it.

The catch: sounding clear isn’t the same as being correct

An AI can write short, tidy sentences and still get things wrong. It might even sound like it’s following STE without actually following its rules.

The ASD-STE100 community has warned that AI-generated text can look compliant without correctly applying the standard.

Clear writing doesn’t guarantee correct information, or true compliance with ASD-STE100.

For everyday explanations, borrowing STE’s principles can be useful. But safety-critical documentation needs the actual standard and human review. Clarity is not a fact-check.

Maybe better prompting is partly a writing problem

Technical writers have spent decades solving problems that LLMs still struggle with: ambiguity, inconsistent terminology, and unnecessary complexity.

ASD-STE100 wasn’t designed for AI, and borrowing its rules won’t guarantee accuracy. But it offers a useful starting point for making AI-generated explanations clearer.

Turns out, better AI instructions might have been hiding in an aircraft manual all along.

Before we teach AI to speak better, it might be worth learning from the people who taught machines how to be understood.

Sources & Further reading

Here are the resources behind this article, along with a few places to explore ASD-STE100 and its applications further:

  • Andrej Karpathy’s post on understanding LLM outputs
  • The official ASD-STE100 website
  • ASD-STE100 Issue 9: Simplified Technical English
  • Google’s guidance on using LLMs in technical writing
  • https://github.com/FavioVazquez/showtime

items.title: Simulating student learning for better AI tutoring
items.summary: At a glance StudentSim is a research system for evaluating and improving AI tutors before they are tested with real learners; it is not a product, is not deployed in classrooms, and is not intended to replace teachers AI tutoring tools need feedback from students to improve, but collecting that feedback through human studies is slow, costly, and difficult to scale StudentSim trains personalized AI student simulators from publicly available, de-identified learner records, with one simulator adapted to each student The work evaluates simulators along two education-grounded dimensions: whether they respond like a specific student, and whether they update after tutor guidance Across chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics, StudentSim outperforms leading baselines and provides a useful feedback signal for training an AI tutor In research settings, teams are exploring how AI-powered tutoring systems can help explain a math problem, suggest an edit to a writing assignment, or guide a learner through a chess position. Yet the quality of teaching cannot be measured only from the tutor’s answer. A tutor needs to know what happens after the guidance reaches a student. Did the student correct the original mistake? Did the hint help them reason toward the answer, or did it give away too much? Would a different student need a different kind of support? In today’s AI tutor research, answering these questions often requires real learner studies. Those studies are valuable, but they are slow and costly to run, which makes it hard to use student feedback during fast model iteration. StudentSim is an AI system that creates personalized simulators of individual students, modeling how they answer questions and how their answers change after receiving a tutor’s guidance. The goal is to make student feedback more available during AI tutor development. This research also introduces StudentSimEval, a benchmark and evaluation protocol spanning chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics. Importantly, the goal is not to replace teachers or classroom learning. Instead, StudentSim helps researchers evaluate and improve AI tutoring systems during the research and development process before testing them with real learners. The research uses only publicly available learner datasets released for research use with de-identified records; no personally identifying information is used at any stage. Figure 1: AI tutors need feedback from students to improve. Student simulators can approximate part of that feedback during research-stage training and evaluation. They provide an early-stage research signal, not a replacement for testing with real learners. Measuring what a student simulator needs to do A simple way to build a student simulator is to ask a large language model to role-play a learner. For example, a prompt might say, “You are an elementary-school student who struggles with math.” The model can change its tone and express uncertainty. The harder part is preserving the learner’s actual ability boundary. A model may speak in a young student’s voice while still relying on knowledge and reasoning far beyond that student’s level. For training an AI tutor, this can produce misleading feedback: the tutor may appear effective because the simulated student is too capable. Traditional student modeling approaches face a different limitation. Knowledge tracing and behavior prediction models are grounded in real learning records and can estimate a student’s current knowledge, skills, and learning habits. Many of these models, however, were not designed to take natural-language tutor guidance as input. They can help describe what a student has done, but they do not always tell us how a student would respond to a particular explanation, hint, or Socratic question. StudentSim defines the target through two dimensions inspired by education research. Educators often distinguish what a learner can do independently from what they can do with support. Vygotsky’s zone of proximal development captures this gap between current independent performance and performance with guidance. StudentSim turns this idea into two evaluation goals. Behavioral fidelity measures whether a simulator matches a specific student’s recorded responses on held-out problems. Guidance responsiveness measures whether the simulator updates its response after reading tutor guidance. Figure 2: StudentSimEval evaluates whether a simulator matches a student’s independent behavior and whether it responds to guidance. These two goals are complementary. A simulator that only matches past student behavior may be useful for prediction, but it does not show whether a teaching intervention helped. A simulator that always follows the tutor may respond fluently, but it may fail to represent a particular student’s strengths, weaknesses, and likely mistakes. AI tutor training needs both signals: the learner’s starting point and how guidance affects the learner’s performance. Training personalized simulators from sparse student records StudentSimEval is built entirely from publicly available learner datasets that are released for research use with de-identified records. The records carry no personally identifying information, and each personalized simulator is trained only on the de-identified records of the student it represents. Real student data is often sparse at the individual level. A learner may contribute only a small number of essays, answers, or interactions. Training a separate simulator from scratch for each student would risk overfitting and would require each model to relearn common patterns in the domain. StudentSim uses a two-stage training pipeline. In the first stage, the model trains on records pooled across many students in the same domain. This stage learns common response formats, common errors, and common ways students revise after guidance. In the second stage, the model is specialized on one student’s own records, producing a personalized simulator for that student. Figure 3: StudentSim first learns shared student behavior from pooled records, then adapts to each student’s own data. The evaluation covers three domains with different response types. In chess, the simulator predicts a player’s next move and how that player may revise after coaching. In second-language English writing, it generates essays with error patterns matching a learner and predicts corrections after teacher feedback. In mathematics, it predicts a student’s multiple-choice answer and whether the student updates after an explanation. Across these domains, StudentSimEval uses the same principle: compare all methods on the same per-student training records and the same held-out evaluation records. StudentSim outperforms leading baselines across the three domains. In chess, for example, StudentSim reaches behavioral fidelity of 0.5150 and guidance responsiveness of 0.9067. GPT-5.4 reaches 0.2316 and 0.7186, respectively. Maia2, a chess-specific human move prediction model, reaches 0.4535 and 0.2721. The comparison illustrates the difference between the baseline families: GPT-5.4 can respond to guidance but does not reliably match a specific student’s behavior, while Maia2 predicts human chess moves more closely but lacks a natural-language guidance pathway. Figure 4: In chess, StudentSim improves both behavioral fidelity and guidance responsiveness compared with leading baselines. Using simulated feedback to improve AI tutors The research also tests whether a trained student simulator can provide feedback for tutor optimization. In a chess tutor reinforcement learning study, the tutor receives a position and a real student’s previous wrong move, then generates guidance. The student simulator’s own parameters are held fixed during this process, and it reads the guidance and produces a revised move. The reward is based on the improvement in move quality from the student’s previous move to the simulator’s revised move, using Stockfish as an independent chess engine signal. Figure 5: StudentSim can provide feedback during AI tutor reinforcement learning by estimating how a student response changes after guidance. The study compares three conditions: a supervised fine-tuned tutor with no reinforcement learning, a tutor trained with GPT-5.4 as the simulated student reward source, and a tutor trained with StudentSim as the reward source. All conditions use the same tutor policy, supervised starting point, and reinforcement learning setup. Human chess experts then evaluate the tutor responses blind to condition. The StudentSim reward produces the highest-rated tutor on all reported dimensions. The tutor trained with StudentSim reaches 90.5% accuracy, compared with 75.7% for the no-RL baseline and 71.6% for the GPT-5.4 reward condition. It also receives higher ratings for guidance quality and personalization. The result is a proof of concept that student simulators trained on real learner data can provide useful feedback for improving AI tutors. Looking ahead StudentSim does not remove the need for real learners in education research. Human studies remain essential for measuring learning outcomes, safety, usability, and classroom fit. The role of student simulators is earlier in the development process: they can help researchers test tutor strategies, compare models, and refine training signals before moving to more expensive studies with real students. The broader direction is to build AI tutor systems that learn from student reactions, not only from expert-written explanations or static correctness labels. StudentSim shows one path: use real learning records to train personalized simulators, evaluate those simulators on both independent behavior and response to guidance, and use them as scalable feedback sources for tutor training. Future work can extend this approach to longer learning trajectories, additional subjects, richer student profiles, and studies that connect simulated feedback with real learning outcomes. The paper and the StudentSim training and evaluation code, including the StudentSimEval protocol, are publicly available. Sources Paper Code Opens in a new tab

AI tutor training needs both signals: the learner’s starting point and how guidance affects the learner’s performance. 

Training personalized simulators from sparse student records

StudentSimEval is built entirely from publicly available learner datasets that are released for research use with de-identified records. The records carry no personally identifying information, and each personalized simulator is trained only on the de-identified records of the student it represents.

Real student data is often sparse at the individual level. A learner may contribute only a small number of essays, answers, or interactions. Training a separate simulator from scratch for each student would risk overfitting and would require each model to relearn common patterns in the domain.  

StudentSim uses a two-stage training pipeline. In the first stage, the model trains on records pooled across many students in the same domain. This stage learns common response formats, common errors, and common ways students revise after guidance. In the second stage, the model is specialized on one student’s own records, producing a personalized simulator for that student. 

Figure 3: StudentSim first learns shared student behavior from pooled records, then adapts to each student’s own data. 

The evaluation covers three domains with different response types. In chess, the simulator predicts a player’s next move and how that player may revise after coaching. In second-language English writing, it generates essays with error patterns matching a learner and predicts corrections after teacher feedback. In mathematics, it predicts a student’s multiple-choice answer and whether the student updates after an explanation. Across these domains, StudentSimEval uses the same principle: compare all methods on the same per-student training records and the same held-out evaluation records. 

StudentSim outperforms leading baselines across the three domains. In chess, for example, StudentSim reaches behavioral fidelity of 0.5150 and guidance responsiveness of 0.9067. GPT-5.4 reaches 0.2316 and 0.7186, respectively. Maia2, a chess-specific human move prediction model, reaches 0.4535 and 0.2721. The comparison illustrates the difference between the baseline families: GPT-5.4 can respond to guidance but does not reliably match a specific student’s behavior, while Maia2 predicts human chess moves more closely but lacks a natural-language guidance pathway.

Figure 4: In chess, StudentSim improves both behavioral fidelity and guidance responsiveness compared with leading baselines. Using simulated feedback to improve AI tutors

The research also tests whether a trained student simulator can provide feedback for tutor optimization. In a chess tutor reinforcement learning study, the tutor receives a position and a real student’s previous wrong move, then generates guidance. The student simulator’s own parameters are held fixed during this process, and it reads the guidance and produces a revised move. The reward is based on the improvement in move quality from the student’s previous move to the simulator’s revised move, using Stockfish as an independent chess engine signal.  

Figure 5: StudentSim can provide feedback during AI tutor reinforcement learning by estimating how a student response changes after guidance.

The study compares three conditions: a supervised fine-tuned tutor with no reinforcement learning, a tutor trained with GPT-5.4 as the simulated student reward source, and a tutor trained with StudentSim as the reward source. All conditions use the same tutor policy, supervised starting point, and reinforcement learning setup. Human chess experts then evaluate the tutor responses blind to condition. 

The StudentSim reward produces the highest-rated tutor on all reported dimensions. The tutor trained with StudentSim reaches 90.5% accuracy, compared with 75.7% for the no-RL baseline and 71.6% for the GPT-5.4 reward condition. It also receives higher ratings for guidance quality and personalization. The result is a proof of concept that student simulators trained on real learner data can provide useful feedback for improving AI tutors. 

Looking ahead

StudentSim does not remove the need for real learners in education research. Human studies remain essential for measuring learning outcomes, safety, usability, and classroom fit. The role of student simulators is earlier in the development process: they can help researchers test tutor strategies, compare models, and refine training signals before moving to more expensive studies with real students. 

The broader direction is to build AI tutor systems that learn from student reactions, not only from expert-written explanations or static correctness labels. StudentSim shows one path: use real learning records to train personalized simulators, evaluate those simulators on both independent behavior and response to guidance, and use them as scalable feedback sources for tutor training. Future work can extend this approach to longer learning trajectories, additional subjects, richer student profiles, and studies that connect simulated feedback with real learning outcomes. 

The paper and the StudentSim training and evaluation code, including the StudentSimEval protocol, are publicly available.

items.title: Andrej Karpathy says only 5,000 people have seen what AI can really do
items.summary: OpenAI founding member Andrej Karpathy , who joined Anthropic in May , thinks most of the world has little idea of what AI can do, and in a Sunday post on X , he said the gap is getting wider. By his own napkin math, roughly 6 billion people have barely used an LLM, 1 to 2 billion use chatbots casually, about 20 million use frontier models professionally in math and code, and around 5,000 have access to frontier systems inside the labs. Box CEO Aaron Levie sees an opportunity in that gap. “This is a good way to understand how early we actually are in AI diffusion right now,” he wrote in his response on X . He argued that most people still think of AI as a chatbot or a next-generation search engine while barely exploring its more advanced opportunities. Box bets on agent swarms “Agent swarms represent possibly the ultimate form factor of what agents will do inside of our workflows,” Levie wrote, envisioning systems that divide complex work among agents running in parallel. “Agent swarms represent possibly the ultimate form factor of what agents will do inside of our workflows” For now, “less than a fraction of a fraction of the population uses AI in this way,” Levie noted, and he identified the obstacles keeping it that way. We’re still early. Models aren’t equally capable across every kind of work, running them at scale is expensive, and tools to manage multiple agents are still catching up. Most people don’t even have access to the most powerful models yet. Rethinking how work gets done with AI is a fraction of what companies have to consider. Connecting their data and figuring out security and compliance are just a few other challenges. Levie expects “a huge amount of change management” before most industries outside software and AI research can take advantage of these agents. That puts Box squarely in the conversation, since the company has been expanding its AI offerings with products such as Box Automate , which connects AI-powered automation to document-heavy business processes. Levie has also said Box doesn’t intend to compete directly with model providers . “A lot of this is where the applied layer of AI will really shine in the enterprise because of the domain specificity of this type of work,” Levie wrote, placing the opportunity with the companies building industry-specific applications and infrastructure on top of frontier models. Chatbots versus coding agents Karpathy sees casual users and developers as looking at opposite ends of the same technology. In his original April post , he contrasted OpenAI’s free voice mode, which he said “will fumble the dumbest questions in your Instagram’s reels,” with the company’s top-tier Codex model, which can spend an hour restructuring an entire codebase. Karpathy wrote that less than a year ago he was still writing code by hand, occasionally relying on autocomplete. By April, he was describing agents that “melt programming problems that you’d normally expect to take days/weeks of work.” Back in February, Karpathy moved beyond vibe coding to “agentic engineering,” with developers spending more time directing and reviewing agents than writing code. Why verifiable work wins “Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable,” Karpathy wrote. Coding and math are well suited to reinforcement learning because results can be tested and improvements measured. Writing and advice are harder to evaluate, and there’s more money to be made improving models for technical work. As Karpathy put it in April, “The goldmines are elsewhere, and the focus comes along.” “Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable.” Karpathy also thinks people aren’t giving these systems enough to do. “A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system,” he wrote. The real gains become apparent when agents can spend hours working through a problem, testing changes and trying again. In March, Karpathy’s AutoResearch project ran 50 experiments overnight on a single GPU, found a better learning rate and committed the change to Git. Each run produced a validation score, so the agent could tell whether a change was worth keeping and move on to the next experiment. From capability to deployment Karpathy calls it “the weirdness of the moment.” Most people still judge AI by their experiences with chatbots, while a small group of developers watches capabilities improve at a staggering pace. Levie sees the same gap, but from the enterprise side. Companies still have to figure out how to make these systems affordable, secure, and reliable enough to use at scale. For Box, that’s where the opportunity lies. Most people still judge AI by their experiences with chatbots, while a small group of developers watches capabilities improve at a staggering pace.

items.title: Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi counteroffensive is a proving ground for war robots
items.summary: Ground robots are being deployed in a variety of roles during Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi. Yevhen Titov/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images Ground robots are playing a key role in Operation Vivaldi, an ongoing Ukrainian counteroffensive. Ukrainian troops are using them to distract the Russians and carry out assaults behind enemy lines. Business Insider spoke with a commander whose unit is at the front of the robot operations. Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi is showcasing how ground robots are reshaping offensive warfare. In the opening stages of this complex operation, Ukrainian forces used uncrewed ground vehicles , or UGVs, as distractions. The robots drew Russian attention and exposed surveillance systems and firing positions while assault troops slipped through and seized key territory. Robots have also conducted airborne assaults, delivered explosives, attacked enemy command centers, and supported infantry operations amid this major counteroffensive in eastern Ukraine. NC13, a strike UGV unit within the Third Assault Brigade of the Third Army Corps, has played a leading role in Vivaldi. Mykola Zinkevych, the unit's commander, told Business Insider that his forces have used robots across a wide range of missions to inflict defeats on the Russians. Over the course of the operation, the robots evolved from diversions that enabled Ukrainian advances into armed strike platforms targeting Russian command posts, drone operators, and large troop concentrations in the rear. Ukraine is sending robots to distract and assault Russian positions. Yevhen Titov/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images Zinkevych, who goes by the call sign "Makar" and spoke through a translator, said these efforts disrupted Russian command and control and logistics, making it harder to bring in more soldiers and limiting Moscow's ability to conduct operations. Robots also carried out what the commander described as full-scale robotic assault operations , independently and in support of Ukrainian infantrymen. Most notably, NC13 used heavy bomber drones to carry armed robots over the front lines and drop them in enemy territory, surprising Russian troops and creating additional pressure, Zinkevych said. He added that it also affected their morale. Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi, commander of Ukraine's Third Army Corps, revealed the use of this tactic in late September and said that his forces had become the "first in the world" to operationally air-drop robots from drones in combat. Beyond explosive-laden robots, NC13 also deployed robots armed with grenade launchers , Zinkevych said, adding that the unit was the first to do so in combat. He said the Russians apparently mistook the UGVs for an infantry assault, which led to confusion and disorientation. Broadly, robots are playing an increasingly important role in Ukrainian combat operations. ZUMA Press Wire via Reuters Connect These innovative tactics come amid broader efforts by Kyiv's forces to integrate ground robots into combat operations. Ukrainian officials have said they want machines to replace humans in dangerous front-line missions, particularly in logistics and casualty evacuation roles. Vivaldi, which Ukraine launched over the summer to halt Russian advances in the northern part of the Donetsk region, has already seen Kyiv retake control of dozens of square miles of territory, according to analysts at the Institute for the Study of War, a US think tank. Zinkevych attributed Vivaldi's success in part to strike robots, but he also credited Biletskyi's planning and coordination. Conventional weaponry, specifically artillery, has played a key role, too, according to Western analysts and the Ukrainian military. The Third Army Corps said last week that Ukrainian artillery fire has prevented Moscow from bringing up reserve forces, equipment, and ammunition to regain positions it had lost. Drones assessed damage and eliminated remaining targets. Artillery was responsible for a larger share of casualties in the war's early stages, but drones are now the biggest killer. ISW analysts wrote in an October 9 battlefield assessment that artillery remains relevant even in a drone-dominated fight. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Andrej Karpathy says this AI gap is widening
items.summary: AI researcher Andrej Karpathy said the gap in AI diffusion that he observed in April is widening. Michael Macor/The San Francisco Chronicle via Getty Images OpenAI cofounder Andrej Karpathy says most of the world is still barely using large language models. Karpathy said of those who do use LLMs, most regard AI as a Google-esque tool. That's not the only gap that is growing amid AI diffusion, Karpathy wrote. OpenAI cofounder Andrej Karpathy says the world still barely knows AI. "The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems," Karpathy wrote on X on Sunday. "When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot." Karpathy said he was following up on his April observation about a growing gap among AI users. Just over six months later, the renowned AI researcher who coined the term "vibe coding" sees the widening gap less as "two groups of people speaking past each other," as he phrased it in April, and more as a "sharp funnel." Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel. - Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come… https://t.co/79xGhQdf1n — Andrej Karpathy (@karpathy) October 11, 2026 The situation, Karpathy said, is that based on his estimate, roughly 75% of the world's population "have barely come in contact" with large language models at all. As for everyone else, Karpathy said around 1 to 2 billion people, "are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products." There's a bigger gap between the chatbot users and those who, Karpathy said, are using frontier models to code, a group that he estimates is around 20 million people or 0.2% of the population. This group, he wrote, sees "large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt." The smallest group, which Karpathy estimates is just 5,000 people, consists of those with inside access to frontier AI systems, likely due to their employment at one of the leading companies. Karpathy said the OpenAI Hugging Face breach showed what's on the horizon. "It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics," he wrote. "Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work." The pace of AI advancement is so rapid, Karpathy said, that humans are struggling to review the outputs fast enough. "For example, people are still involved in the 'archeology' of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago," he wrote. "Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while." Box CEO Aaron Levie said Karpathy's post was "a good way to understand how early we actually are in AI diffusion." "The vast majority of people are using AI as a chatbot for simple interactions that approximate next-generation search," he wrote. "This is super useful but dramatically underrepresents the full capability of AI." Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan said now is the moment to join the AI labs. "Be part of the 5000 today," he wrote on X. "It's amazing." Read the original article on Business Insider
