Input Tokens ────────► [ High-FLOP GEMM ] ──────► High Tensor Core Utilization (>70%)
Decode (Bandwidth-Bound):
Static Weights + KV ──► [ 3.35 TB/s HBM Bus ] ──► Stalled Tensor Cores (<20% Utilization)

Cycle-accurate GPU profiling confirms that pushing batch sizes higher does not transition decode into a compute-bound regime (Recasens et al., 2025). Recasens et al. (2025) demonstrate that as batch sizes scale under naive memory allocation, GPU L1 and L2 cache hit rates collapse to approximately 12% and 2%, respectively. More than 50% of attention kernel cycles stall entirely on DRAM data fetches (Recasens et al., 2025). Pushing more sequences through an unmanaged memory bus merely exacerbates cache thrashing without increasing generation throughput (Recasens et al., 2025).

Furthermore, distributed inference over multi-GPU nodes hits strict synchronization ceilings (Davies et al., 2025). Davies et al. (2025) prove that raw HBM3 bandwidth (3.35 TB/s on modern silicon) loses efficacy when inter-chip synchronization latency exceeds 1 microsecond. Network fabric topologies and all-reduce collective communications dictate multi-GPU economics far more than peak accelerator teraFLOPS (Davies et al., 2025).

Mechanical flow installation contrasting parallel prefill execution against memory-bus constriction and DRAM fetch stalls during decode.

To relieve this memory bus saturation, precision compression is necessary (Baek et al., 2025). Baek et al. (2025) (FireQ) demonstrate that INT4-FP8 mixed-precision GEMM kernels outperform standard FP16 operations. Rather than introducing dequantization bottlenecks, INT4-FP8 quantization drastically compresses the raw tensor payload transferred over the memory bus, directly mitigating the memory starvation that idles compute registers (Baek et al., 2025). Layer-wise format selection also yields substantial gains: dynamic activation tensors favor FP8 due to wider dynamic range requirements, whereas static weights map effectively to INT4/INT8 (Liu et al., 2023).

💡 ProTip: Implementation Caveat:* Deploying uniform quantization across all transformer layers guarantees sub-optimal accuracy (Liu et al., 2023). Dynamic activation tensors demand FP8 to handle outlier spikes, while static weight matrices require dedicated INT8/INT4 handling to prevent degradation during multi-turn generation.
Section III: The Proposed System Blueprint: Tiered Paged Allocation, Distributed Prefix Sharing, and Dynamic Sparsification

Production architectures require decoupling virtual sequence lengths from physical memory blocks. The memory subsystem must treat VRAM as a paged, tiered hierarchy that coordinates with host memory and high-speed distributed storage.

[ Incoming Request (Session / RAG Context) ]
                     │
                     ▼
       ┌───────────────────────────┐
       │ Prefix Hash Match Engine  │◄─── [ Tier 2: Distributed Store (LMCache / RDMA) ]
       └─────────────┬─────────────┘      (Global prefix reuse; zero prefill recalculation)
                     │ (Cache Hit / Miss)
                     ▼
       ┌───────────────────────────┐
       │ Logical Block Allocator   │
       └─────────────┬─────────────┘
                     │ (Translates Virtual to Physical Pages)
                     ▼
       ┌───────────────────────────┐
       │ Tier 1: Paged VRAM Pool   │◄─── [ Non-contiguous 16-token physical blocks ]
       └─────────────┬─────────────┘
                     │ (During Long-Context Generation)
                     ▼
       ┌───────────────────────────┐
       │ Tier 3: DMS Eviction Loop │───► [ Drop non-critical KV pairs via sliding window ]
       └───────────────────────────┘
1. Data Model and Eviction State Engine

The memory engine maps variable logical client sequences to non-contiguous physical blocks while tracking candidate pages for sparsification:

from pydantic import BaseModel

class PhysicalBlock(BaseModel):
    block_id: int
    device_id: int
    free_slots: int
    ref_count: int
class LogicalBlockTable(BaseModel):
    session_id: str
    prefix_hash: str
    logical_to_physical: list[int]
    sliding_window_buffer: list[int]  # Delayed eviction commit

class DMSEvictionPolicy:
    def evaluate_eviction(
        self, 
        attention_entropy: float, 
        window_age: int
    ) -> bool:
        # Delays eviction decision across sliding window to preserve reasoning
        return attention_entropy < 0.15 and window_age > 128
2. Tier 1: Non-Contiguous Paging

By partitioning the KV cache into fixed-size physical memory pages (typically 16 or 32 tokens per block), the logical allocator allocates pages strictly on demand during autoregressive generation. This eliminates external fragmentation and compresses internal page waste to under 4%, allowing concurrent batch sizes to scale by 2.5× to 4× on identical GPU nodes.

3. Tier 2: Distributed Prefix Sharing

In enterprise RAG and multi-turn workflows, incoming requests frequently share long system prompts, few-shot demonstration blocks, or indexed documentation. Recalculating the prefill phase for identical prefixes across concurrent requests wastes compute capacity (Hsu et al., 2026).

By integrating distributed storage layers (such as LMCache over high-speed networks), nodes serialize and persist static prefix KV states across an RDMA-backed cluster tier (Hsu et al., 2026). Fetching a serialized KV cache payload across an optimized network fabric takes sub-milliseconds, bypassing multi-second prefill compute on high-cost accelerators (Hsu et al., 2026).

4. Tier 3: Dynamic Memory Sparsification (DMS)

For sequence lengths exceeding 16k tokens, paging alone cannot prevent HBM capacity exhaustion under heavy concurrency. Dynamic Memory Sparsification trains the system to predict and prune KV entries that contribute negligibly to future attention distributions, achieving up to an 8× memory compression ratio (Łańcucki et al., 2025).

A naive eviction policy risks catastrophic reasoning degradation if tokens containing critical reasoning state are dropped prematurely. To mitigate this, the allocator uses a sliding-window commit buffer (sliding_window_buffer). Eviction candidates must persist through a delayed window of 128 tokens; if downstream attention entropy rises, the block remains locked in memory.

Section IV: Production Engineering Trade-offs, Failure Modes, and the CTO Roadmap1. Engineering Trade-offs and Production Bottlenecks

Selecting an inference architecture requires balancing latency elasticity against absolute throughput:

Engineering roadmap installation outlining the three-phase 60-day memory modernization sequence and hierarchical speculative decoding architecture.

Dimension Dynamic Runtime Engine (e.g., vLLM) Ahead-of-Time Compiled Engine (e.g., TensorRT-LLM) Optimization Vector Continuous batching, elastic paged memory allocation (YottaLabs, 2026) Compiled CUDA graphs, custom kernel fusion (YottaLabs, 2026) Traffic Suitability Unpredictable, bursty loads with highly variable sequence lengths (YottaLabs, 2026) Static, highly predictable request shapes and fixed batch sizes (YottaLabs, 2026) Latency Profile Superior p95/p99 tail latency and faster time-to-first-token (TTFT) (YottaLabs, 2026) Higher absolute peak token throughput under homogeneous saturation (YottaLabs, 2026) Operational Overhead Low. Instant model updates and dynamic context bounds (YottaLabs, 2026) High. Engine recompilation required for sequence or precision changes (YottaLabs, 2026)

Source: Performance analysis based on empirical runtime evaluations (YottaLabs, 2026).

Beyond engine selection, production teams face distinct operational failure modes:

  • Aggressive KV Cache Eviction: Sparsifying the cache without an entropy-based sliding window causes severe accuracy drops on multi-step reasoning, mathematical proof construction, and structured code synthesis. Dropping tokens based solely on instantaneous attention scores removes foundational context required several decoding steps later (Łańcucki et al., 2025).
  • Distributed Network Desynchronization: Persisting and fetching KV caches over standard TCP/IP networking adds socket overhead that can exceed local GPU prefill recalculation latency. Distributed prefix sharing requires a dedicated high-bandwidth, low-latency fabric (RoCE v2 or InfiniBand). If your networking layer lacks sub-microsecond remote direct memory access, centralized caching will degrade rather than improve time-to-first-token metrics.
  • Speculative Verification Bottlenecks: While speculative decoding accelerates decode phases, pairing a draft model with mismatched parameter topologies creates verification stalls. Draft models must prioritize shallow neural depth over raw width to minimize draft latency (Xia et al., 2025). Employing intermediate early-exit verifiers ensures erroneous draft tokens are discarded before stalling the primary target model (Kumar, Sanghavi, & Das, 2026).
Hierarchical Speculative Decoding:
[ Shallow Draft Model ] ──► [ Early-Exit Verifier ] ──► [ Target 70B Model ]
     (Low Latency)            (Discards bad tokens)       (High-Cost Verification)
2. Tactical 60-Day Execution Roadmap

Engineering leadership should execute this memory transition across three structured delivery phases:

Phase 1 (Days 1–14)        Phase 2 (Days 15–30)        Phase 3 (Days 31–60)
┌──────────────────────┐   ┌──────────────────────┐   ┌──────────────────────┐
│ Memory Baseline &    │──►│ Mixed-Precision &    │──►│ Distributed Caching  │
│ Paged Attention      │   │ INT4-FP8 Kernels     │   │ & Speculative Decode │
└──────────────────────┘   └──────────────────────┘   └──────────────────────┘
 • Audit HBM saturation     • Quantize static weights  • Deploy LMCache / RDMA
 • Deploy vLLM runtime      • Transition KV to FP8     • Implement HiSpec/Saguaro
 • Recover 60%+ VRAM        • 2x memory throughput     • Sub-ms prefix fetch
Milestone 1 (Days 1–14): Memory Baseline and Continuous Batching Transition
  • Instrument GPU infrastructure to profile DRAM bandwidth saturation, L1/L2 cache hit rates, and VRAM fragmentation under production load (Recasens et al., 2025).
  • Deprecate static memory allocation runtimes. Deploy an elastic runtime engine with native PagedAttention (e.g., vLLM) across all serving endpoints (YottaLabs, 2026).
  • Recover the 60% to 80% of VRAM currently wasted on contiguous reservations (GPUSmith, 2026). Immediately increase default serving batch sizes from 4 to 16, cutting per-query cloud expenditure without adding hardware.
Milestone 2 (Days 15–30): Mixed-Precision and INT4-FP8 Kernels
  • Quantize static weights and the KV cache layer to mixed-precision representations (INT4 weights, FP8 KV cache and activations) utilizing optimized kernels (Baek et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2023).
  • Halve the per-token HBM memory footprint, doubling effective memory-bus streaming throughput during the decode phase (Baek et al., 2025).
  • Validate model perplexity and reasoning benchmarks across continuous integration test suites to confirm that mixed-precision compression maintains production quality (Baek et al., 2025).
Milestone 3 (Days 31–60): Distributed Caching and Speculative Acceleration
  • Implement a distributed prefix caching tier (LMCache over high-speed interconnects) to persist serialized KV caches for enterprise system prompts and base RAG document indices (Hsu et al., 2026).
  • Deploy Hierarchical Speculative Decoding (HiSpec) or speculative cache systems (Saguaro) to parallelize draft token generation and verification loops (Kumar, Dao, & May, 2026; Kumar, Sanghavi, & Das, 2026).
  • Configure dynamic memory sparsification (DMS) with a 128-token sliding-window buffer for long-context requests (>16k tokens) to ensure stable gross margins at scale (Łańcucki et al., 2025).

Executing this architectural sequence transforms inference infrastructure from an unmanaged, memory-bound bottleneck into a predictable, high-utilization system that scales efficiently with query volume.

items.title: An overlooked sci-fi movie shows how disruption by AI could be positive for society
items.summary: The AI doomsday news cycle plays on anxieties about the future. The media has tended to prioritise sensational takes on the risk at the expense of more thoughtful opinions by, for example, experts in the ethics of AI. Alarmist fantasies of superintelligence – where artificial intelligence surpasses that of the most gifted human minds – are criticised for distracting from real concerns and threats . AI is energy hungry, environmentally damaging, and has prompted urgent calls for legislation relating to a slew of ethical concerns . Apocalyptic AI visions drawn from science fiction engage public interest. One fascinating scenario can be found in the 2018 movie Annihilation, starring Natalie Portman and Oscar Isaac. The film is being released in the 4K Ultra HD home media format in the UK and US in October. Annihilation features an “alien intelligence” – a popular analogy for AI among tech leaders – which embeds itself within Earth’s environment. Can such visions be useful to the current real-world doomsday debate? Sci-fi could help reframe the real-world narrative in positive ways. There are strange techno-futurist and eugenicist visions at play within Silicon Valley, which appear popular with some tech billionaires. These are linked to dark enlightenment thinking – a movement that rejects liberal democracy and egalitarianism – as well as effective altruism (attempting to impartially calculate benefits to provide the greatest good). These visions encompass long-term perspectives that accept present-day sacrifice for future wellbeing. The future-oriented visions expressed by some tech leaders can be surreal , but they reflect the belief systems fuelling the drive for AI superintelligence. And that raises important questions, right now, about whose vision of the future we are investing in . Alex Garland’s sci-fi horror film Annihilation takes us into these issues through one of the weirdest sci-fi visions that’s out there. It is loosely adapted from a novel by Jeff VanderMeer. Termed the Shimmer, because it radiates energy, the AI steadily expands its reach (starting from Florida swampland) by operating as a networked entity beyond human control. It changes everything within its domain. People, animals, and plants mutate in unpredictable ways, seemingly infected by a strange parasite. Annihilation director Alex Garland has long been interested in artificial intelligence. DFree / Shutterstock The story focuses on an expedition team, including genetics expert Lena (Portman), who enter the Shimmer seeking answers. They discover that all electromagnetic waves and DNA are being disrupted and reconfigured. The Shimmer is interfering with the fundamental patterns of life, redefining evolutionary code. Among other things, the Shimmer learns to clone humans. This enables it to exist within human-type bodies anywhere on Earth. Both extinction and immortality Annihilation toys with different types of human extinction. Terminal extinction refers to humanity dying out while leaving a successor species, a bit like the concept of a human’s consciousness being uploaded onto a machine. Final extinction is when humanity ends, full stop. When tech billionaires stumble over questions about wanting humanity to endure , they are probably thinking of terminal extinction. Surreal as it sounds, this magical thinking is a recurrent feature of the AI landscape. Annihilation leaves the viewer to decide which form of human termination is occurring. The film draws on Garland’s deep fascination with AI . His debut as a director, Ex Machina , explored a humanoid robot passing the Turing test and breaking free from human control. His television series Devs visualises a world where a quantum supercomputer has “godlike” capabilities. Annihilation’s organic body horror uses imagery of destroyed, mutated, and cloned bodies to reflect profound social anxiety about humanity’s future. As Garland himself has suggested in an interview, there is a form of digital spirituality fuelling the tech billionaire drive for AI superintelligence and his sci-fi work explores this concept in various ways. AI as parasite Annihilation is weird but it makes sense through the parasite theory of communication. The French philosopher and historian of science Michel Serres expanded upon biological parasites to develop a media and communications theory . In it, he argued that all forms of interaction involve disruption and noise. Whether intentional or not, within every interaction there is always some kind of human or non-human disruption at play. Think in terms of glitches and interference while using digital devices, background noise, changeable environments, uninvited guests and any other distraction. According to Serres’ idea, these can all be visualised as forms of parasite feeding on attempts to interact. In some instances, the parasite takes over – the disruptor displaces the host. If the impact of a parasitical disruptor is significant, it can change society forever. Disruption is a popular term in technology, and AI can be seen as a global disruptor . But disruption shouldn’t be viewed as inherently negative. In fact, disruption is generally considered a form of positive change because it offers new tools, systems and processes that displace the current methods and structures available to humans in everyday life. But it raises the key issue of whose interests, ethics and beliefs are being propagated and served by the impact of AI as a disruptor. Annihilation visualises a parasitical disruptive force embedded within the environment, which invites comparison with the darker areas of techno-futuristic visions from Silicon Valley and beyond. Like the Shimmer, AI is not going away; it just keeps changing form. More importantly, Annihilation shows how small-scale changes can build towards global impacts. The story to engage with isn’t the fantasy that AI superintelligence is about to dominate humanity – it’s the one about disruption and whether that is a net positive or negative for human society. Changing how we think about and use AI requires critically examining it, disrupting the fantasy narrative, and redefining the discourse and direction of travel of this world-changing technology. What Annihilation tells us is that becoming a disruptor can change our future visions and current realities in a positive way. It helps us see possibilities for a technological future that move beyond the human extinction trope. items.title: Tesla's robotaxis catch the eye of a US safety regulator — again
items.summary: Tesla's Model Y and Cybercab vehicles are facing a defect petition from the NHTSA. Aaron E. Martinez/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images NHTSA opened a safety inquiry about Tesla's self-driving Model Y robotaxis and Cybercabs. An unnamed petitioner alleged that the robotaxis were speeding in an active school zone. Tesla has faced growing regulatory scrutiny as it rolls out its all-important self-driving cars. Tesla's self-driving taxis are facing a fresh safety question: are they slowing down when kids are in school? On Monday, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration announced it had opened a defect-petition review into a claim that 2026 Tesla Model Y robotaxis and Cybercabs exceeded speed limits in school zones while their automated driving systems were active. An unnamed petitioner submitted three videos in support of the claim, according to the filing , which says the probe was opened on Friday. NHTSA said it will evaluate the complaint before deciding whether to grant or deny a formal investigation. The agency's filing lists no reported crashes or injuries, and estimates that about 1,000 vehicles could be affected. Tesla didn't immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. The scrutiny comes as Tesla pushes to turn robotaxis into a much bigger business. The electric automaker has expanded its self-driving services with the Model Y robotaxis beyond Austin into other Texas cities and Florida. In September, the company added its steering-wheel-free Cybercab to the Austin fleet . CEO Elon Musk has increasingly shifted Tesla's focus away from traditional vehicle sales toward self-driving, AI, and robotics. The self-driving rollout previously caught the attention of federal regulators. NHTSA opened an audit inquiry into the Cybercab's self-certification a few hours after the cars started offering services in Austin. School zones have also tripped up rival robotaxi companies. Last year, NHTSA opened a preliminary investigation into Waymo after reports that its vehicles passed stopped school buses in Austin and Atlanta. The Google-owned robotaxi company issued a voluntary recall in December. In January, a Waymo vehicle struck a child near an elementary school in Santa Monica, California. The child had "minor injuries" according to the NHTSA , and, in a statement published on its website, Waymo said the vehicle "braked hard, reducing speed from approximately 17 mph to under 6 mph before contact was made." Read the original article on Business Insider

The electric automaker has expanded its self-driving services with the Model Y robotaxis beyond Austin into other Texas cities and Florida. In September, the company added its steering-wheel-free Cybercab to the Austin fleet.

CEO Elon Musk has increasingly shifted Tesla's focus away from traditional vehicle sales toward self-driving, AI, and robotics.

The self-driving rollout previously caught the attention of federal regulators. NHTSA opened an audit inquiry into the Cybercab's self-certification a few hours after the cars started offering services in Austin.

School zones have also tripped up rival robotaxi companies.

Last year, NHTSA opened a preliminary investigation into Waymo after reports that its vehicles passed stopped school buses in Austin and Atlanta. The Google-owned robotaxi company issued a voluntary recall in December.

In January, a Waymo vehicle struck a child near an elementary school in Santa Monica, California. The child had "minor injuries" according to the NHTSA, and, in a statement published on its website, Waymo said the vehicle "braked hard, reducing speed from approximately 17 mph to under 6 mph before contact was made."

items.title: Claude Haiku 5.5 Earned a Spot in My Real-World Workflows
items.summary: Source: Generated by author using GPT Image 2.5 Flare. Last week I was staring at my AI usage, wondering if $4 was too much to pay to complete my project. Cost-avoidance is a feature and flaw of my personality, and it’s made Anthropic a recurring thorn in my side. They’ve been slinging models that accidentally hack websites and possibly threaten the species, while their workhorse Haiku 4.5 model sat in the parking lot with no updates and a price tag that made it look like the gas-guzzling used car it really was. Then Haiku 5.5 landed a few days ago, and I had to open up a new parking space at my “useful models club.” Who Is This For? This is for people who run models on their own hardware and care about the bill at the end of the month, not just the benchmark score. If you’re a developer or maker with a decent GPU, a low tolerance for waiting, and a genuine distaste for paying for things, this is your article. If you want the smartest model regardless of cost, or if you don’t care whether your AI runs on your machine or someone else’s, keep scrolling. TL;DR Claude Haiku 5.5 is Anthropic’s latest low-cost Cloud LLM model. Haiku 5.5 is a bit smarter than OpenAI’s similar model (ChatGPT Luna 6) in agentic and coding tasks. GLM-5.3 is clearly smarter than Haiku 5.5 on coding and planning. Haiku 5.5 is much smarter AND much cheaper than Haiku 4.5. The API list price of Haiku 5.5 is misleading, because contexts above 100K tokens get billed 5x higher. I cross this barrier frequently in my coding sessions. If you have tasks that stay below the 100K context barrier, Haiku 5.5 is at the intersection of high capability and very low cost. What Matters to Me As a reminder from my past articles , I am a cheapskate who doesn’t like to pay for things. Cost matters . I don’t have any huge secrets to protect from the AI APIs, so I run local models to keep my costs down and not for data privacy reasons. I am also impatient along with being a cheapskate, so I don’t like to wait for the results I don’t want to pay for. Speed matters . I have a Strix Halo AI Max+ 395 with 96GB dedicated to VRAM ( more info on my local setup ), so I can run some sizable models but they don’t run super quickly. The current king of the AI hill on my machine is Ornith 1.5 35B-A3B . Ornith uses a novel self-improvement loop on top of Qwen’s models, and the 35B-A3B version uses a mixture-of-experts architecture to speed up inference. If those words don’t mean anything to you, just know that it’s smart and fast if you have enough VRAM to fit a 21 GB model. My Strix Halo machine is my daily driver, not just an AI appliance, and it only cost a couple hundred dollars more than the other machines I was looking at. So before you roll your eyes at me saying local LLM inference is “free”, know that I’m not wielding a multi-GPU flamethrower that costs as much as a used car. I’m using something that’s a slightly premium regular desktop and it happens to be good at AI. It made up for the price delta long ago, so I’m calling local LLM inference “free”. You can gripe if you want and I won’t hold it against you. At least not too much. When Ornith can’t handle something, I have to reach for a bigger and slower local model (annoying my impatient side), or I need a faster and more capable Cloud model (annoying my cheapskate side). What I need is a very cheap Cloud model that is noticeably better than Ornith 1.5 to get me over the top when the local model taps out. Benchmarks and Stats I find the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index to be the fastest way to compare models without too much hype. They make a composite score across a bunch of benchmarks, so a few points can mean you’ll notice the difference in capabilities. Here are the stats showing Claude Haiku 5.5, Claude Haiku 4.5, ChatGPT Luna 6, GLM-5.2, GLM-5.3, and Qwen 3.6 35B-A3B. I actually use Ornith 1.5, but that’s not in the index. It comes in slightly better than Qwen 3.6, but this is a useful baseline for my local model capability. Source: https://artificialanalysis.ai/evaluations/artificial-analysis-intelligence-index?models=glm-5-3%2Cclaude-haiku-5-5-medium%2Cglm-5-2%2Cgpt-6-luna-medium%2Cqwen3-6-35b-a3b%2Cclaude-4-5-haiku-reasoning Quick summary: In case you doubted my rant against Haiku 4.5, notice how it lands at the bottom of the intelligence ranking and in the middle of the cost ranking. That’s a bad place to be. Other than Haiku 4.5, all the Cloud models in this index have a significant intelligence advantage over my local model. With four extra intelligence points, Haiku 5.5 is just smart enough that you’ll notice it when comparing it to Luna 6. Haiku 5.5 can’t hold a candle to GLM-5.3 in intelligence and capability, though this isn’t surprising. Intelligence Index Score Source: Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3.2 Intelligence Index vs Cost per Task Source: Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3.2 Token Usage Source: Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3.2 Cost Source: Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3.2 An important note on Haiku 5.5 pricing : There are two WILDLY different pricing regimes for Claude Haiku 5.5. Source: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/models/haiku-5-5/overview (emphasis added) Under 100K of context tokens, Haiku 5.5 is priced identically to ChatGPT Luna 6. They’re both $0.10 for 1M input tokens and $0.50 for 1M output tokens, and that’s an absolute steal. Above 100K of context tokens, Haiku 5.5’s price jumps 5x to $0.50 for input and $2.50 for output. That makes Haiku 5.5’s value proposition go from “amazing” to “good”. ChatGPT Luna 6 also has a price escalator, but it’s at 272K of context and it only doubles the price instead of Haiku’s 5x. Source: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-6-luna (emphasis added) Methodology I break my model comparison into two broad categories: agentic tasks and coding. For agentic tasks , I have a stable harness of Open WebUI with a custom-developed agent. It has access to Tavily for web search, Defuddle and Playwright for scraping and web navigation, Open Terminal for local files and bash scripts, and Open WebUI’s built-in tools for notes, image generation, tasks, time, etc. As such, the agentic comparison is much more apples-to-apples because everything other than the model remains the same. I test agentic capabilities by asking the model to conduct research about how AI models have evolved over the past 12 months, and then it writes a report with some instructions. I monitor how thorough the research is, how efficient it is (getting the right information with 8 searches is better than the same info over 20 searches), how quickly it completes the task, how insightful the report is, and how succinct the report is. Source: Generated by author using GPT Image 2.5 Flare. My coding comparisons are admittedly less directly comparable, because I am often testing with different coding harnesses. This can make a HUGE difference. GLM-5.2 inside of Little Coder kept running out of thinking budget and got stuck forever. GLM-5.2 inside of OpenCode is a very capable combination. So I will note which coding harness I used for the testing. Every harness has Ponytail , Caveman , Defuddle MCP , Playwright MCP , and the harness’ built-in tools. And I test models at Medium effort or thinking level wherever the model allows me to specify this. Why not Max or Extreme or Super Awesome effort level? Because I am impatient, dear reader. If you don’t mind waiting for your model to write a novella about its internal anxiety trying to satisfy your conflicting requirements, be my guest. I save the higher effort levels for when I’m running things in the background or overnight. My primary coding benchmark is to use the intent-driven development files for my local AI image generator and create a finished implementation. Intent-driven development gives high level goals and constraints and then lets AI fill in the details. Every model starts from the same point with an intent, a wireframe, and a few notes. You can see the baseline and several implementations here . This coding benchmark contains a few intentional poison pills that the model has to overcome. The baseline intent file has some purposeful inaccuracies and contradictions, and that allows me to quickly measure a model’s debugging capability. The best result is for the model to notice it before implementing, ask me about it, and recommend fixing the intent before implementation. Very few models have achieved top marks on this. Source: Generated by author using GPT Image 2.5 Flare. Beyond those intentional issues with the intent, I want the coding model to complete the task quickly, effectively, and with minimal interaction with me. For this article, I tested Claude Haiku 5.5 inside Claude Code’s harness. I didn’t notice any regressions when I tested in OpenCode, but all coding observations in this article assume Claude Code. AI Model Showdown Agentic Tasks Haiku 5.5 garnered top marks in four of my agentic categories, and got second place on the other two. It didn’t exhibit any noteworthy weaknesses. By contrast, Luna 6 tends to over-research. GLM-5.2 tends to over-research and over-think. Ornith 1.5 is just a step down in quality across the board, though it is still very good. Verdict: Haiku 5.5 is the clear agentic winner. Source: author Coding Tasks Haiku 5.5 handled the intent spec and my poison pills beautifully, and while it didn’t win every category it had no clear weaknesses in the main test. In more complicated tasks beyond my benchmark, GLM-5.2 was noticeably better at creating an in-depth (albeit very verbose) and accurate plan. ChatGPT Luna 6 was a small step behind Haiku 5.5 on most of my metrics for the same price. But past 100K of context, Haiku costs 5x what Luna does and that’s going to happen frequently in coding scenarios. GLM required a bit more human feedback to reach a good solution, and Ornith was on the verge of annoying me by how much it needed my guidance. Luna and Haiku barely needed me after the initial prompt. For the intent spec, Luna and GLM fixed all the poison pills but never updated the intent spec, while Haiku and Ornith remembered to fix the underlying spec file. As a result of this mixed bag, I’m going to highlight when you would want to choose each model. Look at the “I Dub Thee” row to see when you should use each model. An important note: I ran my initial benchmark with GLM-5.2, but I have since switched to GLM-5.3 and it’s a major upgrade. Haiku 5.5 can kinda keep up with GLM-5.2, but it’s clearly not in GLM-5.3’s category for coding and planning. Verdict: Per dollar, Haiku 5.5 is the coding winner IF you stay under the 100K context barrier. Past that, it costs 5x what Luna does and each model earns a niche. Source: author My Existential Crisis with Local LLMs I bought a nice computer for local LLM inference. I spent months figuring it all out and setting up the software — all in the pursuit of a fully-local AI workflow. I’ve invested blood, sweat, tears, and money into this local LLM concept. Granted, the blood was only a paper cut when I was unboxing the computer, but still. ChatGPT Luna 6 and Claude Haiku 5.5 have presented me with a dilemma. They are both clearly better than the best local model I can run at decent speeds, and they’re so cheap that my cheapskate side is waffling. Is it better to accomplish my task over an hour working with Ornith 1.5 for free, or over 15 minutes with Luna or Haiku for less than a dollar? My internal voices of achievement, cheapskateness, and impatience are at war with each other over this. So while it hurts my pride and decreases my ability to smugly mock my friends spending money on Cloud APIs, I have found myself leveraging Luna 6 and Haiku 5.5 more frequently at the expense of my local LLMs. But I haven’t completely abandoned the local LLM cause! Where I Still Choose Local LLMs Any task that can be run in the background and churn through a bunch of input tokens goes immediately to Ornith 1.5. For example, I needed to review a private Git repo to ensure I didn’t accidentally check in anything sensitive before I made it public. I tossed that to Ornith 1.5 inside of OpenCode, told it to spin up sub-agents for each root folder, and then I did other things while it checked. 28 minutes later, I had a zero-cost clean bill of health across a TON of input tokens. That would have cost several dollars even with Luna 6 or Haiku 5.5, and it didn’t matter that Ornith took five times as long to do the work because it wasn’t an interactive session. I do the same thing with some large research tasks. If I need to comb through hundreds of web pages and I don’t mind waiting for the report, Ornith 1.5 knocks them out one-by-one, takes notes, and delivers an excellent summary for free. If I need a quick answer across 10–20 web pages interactively, I find myself reaching for the speed of the Cloud models. I also still hand anything that touches API keys and secrets to Ornith 1.5, because then I’m guaranteed to not be leaking private info. This isn’t a high frequency use case for me, but when it arises I have my trust local LLM at the ready. Conclusion Claude Haiku 5.5 has raised the bar for low cost Cloud LLMs — especially for any task that stays under the 100K context point. I’m still testing it, but I expect Haiku 5.5 to take over from Luna 6 as my main agentic Cloud model in Open WebUI, because most of those conversations stay under 100K of context. For coding, Luna 6 is likely to be the first car I pull out of the parking lot because of the much lower cost on coding tasks. Haiku 5.5 is a clear step up, but I also have GLM-5.3 sitting there with MUCH higher capability if I need a good plan that Luna 6 or Ornith 1.5 can implement. The highly capable and very cheap Cloud models are chipping away at my commitment to using local LLMs for everything, but I’m still glad I can do real work locally and I’m glad I can throw big token, slow-running tasks at my local LLM for free. Just promise me you won’t tell my friends that I’m reaching for Cloud models more than my local LLMs these days. They might give me some comeuppance if they find out. Claude Haiku 5.5 Earned a Spot in My Real-World Workflows was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

But past 100K of context, Haiku costs 5x what Luna does and that’s going to happen frequently in coding scenarios.

GLM required a bit more human feedback to reach a good solution, and Ornith was on the verge of annoying me by how much it needed my guidance. Luna and Haiku barely needed me after the initial prompt.

For the intent spec, Luna and GLM fixed all the poison pills but never updated the intent spec, while Haiku and Ornith remembered to fix the underlying spec file.

As a result of this mixed bag, I’m going to highlight when you would want to choose each model. Look at the “I Dub Thee” row to see when you should use each model.

An important note: I ran my initial benchmark with GLM-5.2, but I have since switched to GLM-5.3 and it’s a major upgrade. Haiku 5.5 can kinda keep up with GLM-5.2, but it’s clearly not in GLM-5.3’s category for coding and planning.

Verdict: Per dollar, Haiku 5.5 is the coding winner IF you stay under the 100K context barrier. Past that, it costs 5x what Luna does and each model earns a niche.
Source: authorMy Existential Crisis with Local LLMs

I bought a nice computer for local LLM inference. I spent months figuring it all out and setting up the software — all in the pursuit of a fully-local AI workflow. I’ve invested blood, sweat, tears, and money into this local LLM concept. Granted, the blood was only a paper cut when I was unboxing the computer, but still.

ChatGPT Luna 6 and Claude Haiku 5.5 have presented me with a dilemma. They are both clearly better than the best local model I can run at decent speeds, and they’re so cheap that my cheapskate side is waffling.

Is it better to accomplish my task over an hour working with Ornith 1.5 for free, or over 15 minutes with Luna or Haiku for less than a dollar? My internal voices of achievement, cheapskateness, and impatience are at war with each other over this.

So while it hurts my pride and decreases my ability to smugly mock my friends spending money on Cloud APIs, I have found myself leveraging Luna 6 and Haiku 5.5 more frequently at the expense of my local LLMs.

But I haven’t completely abandoned the local LLM cause!

Where I Still Choose Local LLMs

Any task that can be run in the background and churn through a bunch of input tokens goes immediately to Ornith 1.5.

For example, I needed to review a private Git repo to ensure I didn’t accidentally check in anything sensitive before I made it public. I tossed that to Ornith 1.5 inside of OpenCode, told it to spin up sub-agents for each root folder, and then I did other things while it checked. 28 minutes later, I had a zero-cost clean bill of health across a TON of input tokens. That would have cost several dollars even with Luna 6 or Haiku 5.5, and it didn’t matter that Ornith took five times as long to do the work because it wasn’t an interactive session.

I do the same thing with some large research tasks. If I need to comb through hundreds of web pages and I don’t mind waiting for the report, Ornith 1.5 knocks them out one-by-one, takes notes, and delivers an excellent summary for free. If I need a quick answer across 10–20 web pages interactively, I find myself reaching for the speed of the Cloud models.

I also still hand anything that touches API keys and secrets to Ornith 1.5, because then I’m guaranteed to not be leaking private info. This isn’t a high frequency use case for me, but when it arises I have my trust local LLM at the ready.

Conclusion

Claude Haiku 5.5 has raised the bar for low cost Cloud LLMs — especially for any task that stays under the 100K context point.

I’m still testing it, but I expect Haiku 5.5 to take over from Luna 6 as my main agentic Cloud model in Open WebUI, because most of those conversations stay under 100K of context.

For coding, Luna 6 is likely to be the first car I pull out of the parking lot because of the much lower cost on coding tasks. Haiku 5.5 is a clear step up, but I also have GLM-5.3 sitting there with MUCH higher capability if I need a good plan that Luna 6 or Ornith 1.5 can implement.

The highly capable and very cheap Cloud models are chipping away at my commitment to using local LLMs for everything, but I’m still glad I can do real work locally and I’m glad I can throw big token, slow-running tasks at my local LLM for free.

Just promise me you won’t tell my friends that I’m reaching for Cloud models more than my local LLMs these days. They might give me some comeuppance if they find out.

items.title: AI Is Only as Smart as the Data Behind It
items.summary: The unglamorous discipline of data quality is quietly deciding which AI projects succeed — and which quietly fail. A few years ago, I sat in a conference room while a retail client showed off a new demand-forecasting model. The dashboard looked impressive: clean charts, confident predictions, a color scheme that seemed to say, “we’ve arrived.” Then someone from the warehouse team asked a simple question — why was the model predicting a 400 percent spike in demand for a product that had been discontinued eight months earlier? Nobody in the room had an answer. It took three days to trace the problem back to a single source system that never marked discontinued items as inactive. The AI hadn’t done anything wrong. It had done exactly what it was trained to do: learn patterns from the data it was given. The data was simply lying to it. I’ve spent sixteen years building data platforms for companies in retail, banking, healthcare, and insurance, and if there’s one lesson that keeps repeating itself, it’s this: the gap between a good AI model and a bad one usually has nothing to do with the model. It has to do with what’s feeding it. The Part of the AI Story Nobody Wants to Talk About Every week brings another headline about an AI breakthrough — a model that writes code, diagnoses illness, or predicts financial markets. What rarely makes the headlines is far less glamorous: most of the effort behind a working AI system goes into cleaning, organizing, and validating data long before a single line of model code gets written. In my experience, that work eats up 60 to 70 percent of a typical AI project’s timeline. It’s tedious, it’s unglamorous, and it’s the single biggest reason AI initiatives succeed or quietly fail. (Shutterstock/WINEXA) Data quality isn’t a buzzword. It’s a discipline, and it has specific dimensions that any businessperson can understand without a computer science degree. What “Bad Data” Actually Looks Like When engineers say data is “dirty,” they usually mean one of a handful of specific problems. None of these concepts is complicated — they’re just invisible until something breaks. Completeness is about missing information. Picture a hospital’s patient-intake system where the “allergies” field is left blank for 20 percent of records — not because those patients have no allergies, but because the field was never made mandatory. A model trained on that data could learn that allergies are rarer than they actually are, with consequences nobody wants to think about. Accuracy is about information that’s simply wrong. I once worked with a logistics company where a shipping-weight field had been auto-filled with a default value of “1” for years, thanks to an uncaught bug in a legacy form. Thousands of shipments in the training data showed a one-pound weight, whether the package held a phone case or a refrigerator part. Consistency is about the same thing being described differently across systems. “NY,” “New York,” and “N.Y.” all mean the same state, but a model — or a simple SQL query — doesn’t know that unless someone tells it. I’ve seen customer counts off by double digits purely because three departments were counting the same customer three different ways. Timeliness is about data that’s stale. A fraud-detection model trained on transaction data that’s 48 hours old is trying to catch a thief who’s already three towns over. Lineage is about knowing where data came from and what happened to it along the way. Without it, when a number looks wrong, nobody can trace it back to the source fast enough to fix it — which is exactly what happened in that conference room with the discontinued product. Why This Problem Is Getting Bigger, Not Smaller Here’s what makes this moment different from the data-quality conversations of a decade ago. Back then, bad data mostly hurt a dashboard or a quarterly report. A wrong number was embarrassing, but it stayed contained. Generative AI and large language models change that math entirely. These systems are trained on enormous volumes of data pulled from dozens of internal systems, external feeds, and sometimes the open internet. A single inconsistency no longer shows up as one wrong cell in a spreadsheet — it gets absorbed into billions of parameters and resurfaces later as a confident, articulate, and completely wrong answer. I’ve watched a customer-service chatbot cheerfully quote a return policy that hadn’t been true in three years, because nobody had updated the knowledge base it was pulling from. (Yurchanka Siarhei/Shutterstock) The scale of the problem grows with the scale of the ambition. A company that used to run a handful of reports off clean, well-governed tables is now feeding dozens of loosely governed data sources into retrieval systems and AI agents that make decisions with far less human review in the loop. The margin for error hasn’t just stayed the same — it’s shrunk, right as the volume of data flowing through these systems has exploded. What Actually Works Companies that get this right don’t treat data quality as a one-time cleanup project before a big AI launch. They build it into the plumbing. It starts with automated data-quality checks running inside the pipelines themselves, not bolted on as an afterthought before a report goes out. A rule that flags a shipping weight of exactly “1” on every record, or catches a sudden spike in missing fields, catches problems in hours instead of months. It continues with data observability — essentially a health monitor for data, the same way a company might monitor server uptime. When a source system changes its format or a field starts filling with nulls, someone should know before the AI model does. It requires clear ownership. Data doesn’t take care of itself, and neither does data quality. The best organizations I’ve worked with assign specific people — not just a policy document — to be accountable for the health of specific data domains. And it demands honesty about lineage. If a team can’t trace a number back to its source in under ten minutes, that’s not a minor inconvenience. That’s a risk sitting quietly in the AI roadmap. The Real Lesson None of this is about slowing AI down. It’s about making sure that when a company puts an AI system in front of customers, doctors, loan officers, or supply chain managers, it’s standing on solid ground rather than a foundation nobody bothered to inspect. (Aditya Ranjan is a Senior Data Engineer at a leading Fortune 500 company) I think about that retail forecasting model often. The fix wasn’t a smarter algorithm. It was a data engineer correctly flagging discontinued products at the source. That’s rarely the story anyone tells at a product launch, but it’s the story that makes AI trustworthy. The smartest AI in the world is still, in the end, a mirror. It reflects the data it’s given — flaws, gaps, and all. Before asking how intelligent our AI has become, it might be worth asking a quieter, more useful question: how honest is the data behind it? About the author: Aditya Ranjan is a Senior Data Engineer at a leading Fortune 500 grocery retailer, with over 16 years of experience architecting enterprise data solutions across AWS, Azure, and GCP. He specializes in cloud migration, real-time analytics, and modern data architecture, with hands-on expertise spanning data lakes, lakehouses, and the modern data stack. A Google-certified Generative AI Leader, Aditya writes on the intersection of data engineering and AI.

items.title: What Alexandr Wang says he learned from Mark Zuckerberg's 'really long' WhatsApp DMs
items.summary: Alexandr Wang said Mark Zuckerberg often sent long, rigorous WhatsApp replies. Bloomberg/Getty Images Alexandr Wang says Zuckerberg sends really long WhatsApp replies and sends them really fast. Zuckerberg's rigorous time management allows him to balance work and family, Wang said. Wang says Meta’s CEO "ruthlessly" prioritizes his time. Alexandr Wang says he used to wonder how Mark Zuckerberg had time to write him such long WhatsApp messages. Before Wang joined Meta to help lead its AI agent efforts , the Scale AI founder would occasionally ask Zuckerberg for advice. The replies, Wang said in an interview with David Senra on Sunday, were unexpectedly detailed. "I would ask him a question on WhatsApp, and then he would write these really long responses," Wang said. "I was really confused. I was like, 'How does he have time to write these really long responses?'" Wang, the public face of Meta's AI agent Muse, said he later came to a simple conclusion: Zuckerberg is unusually fast — and rigorous — at writing. "He'll write a very rigorous, long response very quickly," Wang said. "It's a very impressive skill of his." The anecdote offers a small window into how Zuckerberg, Meta's CEO, manages his time and makes decisions as he tries to remake the company around artificial intelligence. Wang said Zuckerberg's packed schedule requires "ruthlessly" prioritizing his time: "The only way he's able to do that and be a good dad and be a good partner and all this other stuff is to just, like, ruthlessly prioritize." Wang said that an introduction to Zuckerberg around 2021 or 2022 took roughly a year to lead to a first meeting. At the time, the two spoke only about once every six months, he said. But Zuckerberg’s involvement increased as Meta confronted shortcomings in its Llama 4 AI model and the growing stakes of the race against rivals such as OpenAI and Anthropic. Wang said Zuckerberg called him to ask what Meta should do next and how it should think about its AI strategy. Their conversations quickly expanded beyond advice. Within five or six weeks of Zuckerberg’s initial outreach, Meta announced a deal to take a 49% stake in Scale AI, while Wang and several colleagues moved to Meta. Wang has since become a key figure in Meta’s attempt to rebuild its AI organization around a smaller, flatter group of top researchers. He said Zuckerberg’s willingness to seek feedback from prominent entrepreneurs is a notable trait in a leader who has run Meta for more than two decades. Read the original article on Business Insider

Well, there’s a chance that a version of Sora is coming back from the dead. items.title: Cops can creep on Airbnb
items.summary: Good Monday morning! Today's big story is an investigation from Joseph about cops and an AI tool that takes data from sites like Airbnb and Zillow and identifies specific properties. The internet is full of photos of the interiors of people's homes, from real estate and rental listings to short-term stays, and that data is in the hands of law enforcement. And in other news, a very interesting interview with the whistleblower subject of Sorkin's new movie, some big legislative impact, and what caught my eye over the weekend around the web. Let's get into it. A screenshot from a Raven promotional video on LinkedIn. AI Company Lets Cops Pinpoint Specific Houses Based on a Single Interior Photo An AI company now lets cops take a photo and nearly instantly figure out what specific home it was taken in, using only clues in the photo itself, and is clearly pulling data from sites like Zillow and Airbnb. The tool, called Raven, shows the increasing power of AI capabilities available to local law enforcement agencies. 404 Media previously reported that both the Los Angeles Police Department and Miami-Dade Sheriff’s Office (MDSO) have bought access to Raven, which was previously called GeoSpy . Now, Raven, made by a company called Graylark Technologies, has added features that let cops analyze the interior of homes. In a post on LinkedIn earlier this month , Graylark CEO Daniel Heinen wrote the company was introducing “the ability to geolocate interior images across millions of short-term rental units worldwide.” An accompanying demo video shows someone taking a photo from X of a washer/dryer unit inside a building. They upload it to Raven, select “Find Property: Interior and exterior property geolocation,” and then choose a region to search. After a couple of seconds, the map interface zooms in on an area in Charlotte, North Carolina. On the right hand side, the screen displays a list of results. The top one reads, “Renovated! Walk Uptown/located in 2 Hot Spots!” That result directly quotes the language on a specific Airbnb listing in Charlotte, and the photos in the Airbnb listing show the same property. Read the rest of this story here. MORE FROM 404 MEDIA Spoilers ahead for “The Social Reckoning. ” Did you catch this week’s interview episode? Jason talked to former Facebook employee Frances Haugen, who became one of the most important tech whistleblowers in 2021 when she exposed how Facebook’s algorithm was pushing people toward hate groups, showed Instagram was making teen girls feel worse about themselves, and showed that the company knew about its detrimental impacts on society. Haugen’s story is the basis for Aaron Sorkin’s new movie “The Social Reckoning,” which follows her evolution from model employee to leaker to formal whistleblower. Jason and Frances discuss what the movie got right about journalist-source relationships and how AI is supercharging privacy concerns. Listen to the weekly podcast on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , or watch the convo on YouTube .

items.title: PC prices to remain elevated until end of 2027
items.summary: IDC has bad news for enterprises upgrading PCs: don’t expect prices to come down any time soon. PC prices are already high due to constrained supplies and surging memory and component costs. Geopolitical tensions and an uncertain global economy won’t make the situation any better. “A weaker economy could soften demand further, and with prices still high and supply constrained, the outlook for the remainder of 2026 and going into 2027 could deteriorate,” IDC analysts said in a press release last week. The third quarter of 2026 was a disaster for PC makers, with shipments falling 20.1% year over year. PC makers and their channel partners stocked up on inventory earlier in the year ahead of memory-driven price hikes. The focus in the third quarter was on clearing out that leftover inventory amid dried-up demand. “Channels are now worried about carrying too much inventory into a market where high prices are suppressing demand,” said Jitesh Ubrani, a research director at IDC. Within the existing inventory, low-cost PCs are harder to find. For example, HP is making higher-priced PCs a larger part of its product mix so it can generate higher revenue amid declining PC shipments. HP’s chief financial officer, Karen Parkhill, said in an August earnings call that the company is prioritizing “higher-value unit placements, repricing for higher commodity costs” to offset the lower volume of PC shipments. “We continue to expect memory and storage costs to increase further as a percentage of the bill of materials,” Parkhill said. Enterprises picked up new PCs earlier in anticipation of price increases and are now pulling back, said analyst Jack Gold of J. Gold Associates. That’s partially because PC makers are passing higher memory and component costs on to customers, Gold said. Many new PCs have AI hardware accelerators and qualify as AI PCs . Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella at an event last week said AI PCs accounted for 40% of PC shipments. HP said on its earnings call that AI PCs made up 46% of its PC shipments in the fiscal quarter that ended July 31. The big question is whether AI PCs have any utility. HP is rolling out its own on-device AI software, called HP IQ , on its PCs to enhance the user experience. HP PCs also have an AI-based security tool from Wolf Security that protects against BIOS-level intrusion, said Ketan Patel, the company’s president of personal systems, on the August earnings call. But companies are rethinking the typical three-to-four-year PC upgrade cycle because most AI work still happens in the cloud, Gold said. “They have been spending big on infrastructure and cloud services to implement new AI solutions, which don’t need the latest PC hardware,” he said. Hardware makers are now building even faster PCs — dubbed “agentic AI PCs”— that cut token costs by running AI locally. Microsoft has dubbed that hardware as “Builder PCs.” Agentic AI PCs with GPUs have more horsepower to run high-end LLMs and cut cloud-based token costs. But those PCs, such as Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra and HP’s ZBook Ultra G3a mobile workstation, cost more than $2,500, which may be too expensive for cash-strapped enterprises. Agentic AI PCs could help cut token costs, but “whether that really means the category has been reinvented is still up for debate,” Technalysis Research analyst Bob O’Donnell said in a research note . Lenovo topped IDC’s global PC shipment chart in the third quarter of 2026. The company shipped 14.9 million units, a 22.6% decline from the same quarter last year, and held a 23.8% market share. HP was in second place, with 10.3 million units shipped, a 30.9% year-over-year decline. The company held a 16.5% market share. Dell was third, with 7.6 million PC shipments, a year-over-year decline of 25%. Apple was in better shape than its Windows counterparts, with 5.9 million units shipped, down 11.3% year over year. Asus and other PC makers accounted for the remainder.

items.title: AI Company Lets Cops Pinpoint Specific Houses Based on a Single Interior Photo
items.summary: An AI company now lets cops take a photo and nearly instantly figure out what specific home it was taken in, using only clues in the photo itself, and is clearly pulling data from sites like Zillow and Airbnb. The tool, called Raven, shows the increasing power of AI capabilities available to local law enforcement agencies. 404 Media previously reported that both the Los Angeles Police Department and Miami-Dade Sheriff’s Office (MDSO) have bought access to Raven, which was previously called GeoSpy . Now, Raven, made by a company called Graylark Technologies, has added features that let cops analyze the interior of homes. In a post on LinkedIn earlier this month , Graylark CEO Daniel Heinen wrote the company was introducing “the ability to geolocate interior images across millions of short-term rental units worldwide.” An accompanying demo video shows someone taking a photo from X of a washer/dryer unit inside a building. They upload it to Raven, select “Find Property: Interior and exterior property geolocation,” and then choose a region to search. 💡 Do you know anything else about this technology or others like it? I would love to hear from you. Using a non-work device, you can message me securely on Signal at joseph.404 or send me an email at joseph@404media.co. After a couple of seconds, the map interface zooms in on an area in Charlotte, North Carolina. On the right hand side, the screen displays a list of results. The top one reads, “Renovated! Walk Uptown/located in 2 Hot Spots!” That result directly quotes the language on a specific Airbnb listing in Charlotte, and the photos in the Airbnb listing show the same property. Later in the video, the Raven user takes a photo of a bathroom from social media. They upload it to Raven, and the tool points to an area of Montecito, California. The top result says, “Montecito Miramar Beach House on the Sand.” 404 Media found that result directly quotes a listing on the short term rental site Vrbo. In other words, from a single photo, Raven appears to be able to quickly find the specific home it was taken in, without using location data or other metadata attached to the image. In the demonstrations the videos were from social media, but in practice they could be from anywhere a law enforcement officer has obtained them. This is also not a reverse image search: a reverse image search would take an image then find an identical one posted somewhere else on the internet. What Raven is doing, instead, is identifying unique characteristics in the photo, then finding what are likely other photos from the same property on sites like Airbnb, even if those photos are not exactly the same, or even if time has passed between them being taken. In another post , Heinen wrote, “For investigators working trafficking and exploitation cases, that connection can turn an unidentified room into a location lead they can verify and pursue.” Raven is not limited to short term rentals, according to other demo videos. In a third example posted last year, Raven traces a photo of an interior room to a specific address in San Francisco. The interface returns other interior photos of the property; 404 Media found these are exactly the same photos as those posted on Zillow, indicating that Raven is at least pulling data from Zillow in some form. Another video posted last week shows Raven identifying a particular hotel, too. A screenshot from a Raven promotional video on LinkedIn. In another video, a part of the interface says, “City-specific property AI to determine an address.” That phrase implies the property search isn’t necessarily worldwide, but dependent on an AI model built specifically for that city. When 404 Media reported earlier this year that at least two law enforcement agencies have bought access to Raven, emails showed the MDSO had access to a custom model specifically trained for Miami-Dade County. “In 2026, we’re investing heavily in interior geolocation across U.S. hotels, short-term rentals, houses, and apartments,” Heinen adds in the post. Graylark trained Raven on millions of images from around the world. When the tool first launched, it was focused on identifying distinct geographical markers like architecture and soil. Now Raven extends that same idea into buildings. In an interview with the tech publication Indicator last year, Heinen discussed some of how the building interior searching capability came to be. “I’ll be honest, we didn't train it to do that,” he said. “That was kind of an ‘Oh shit’ moment for us. GeoSpy 1.0 couldn't do that. As we trained GeoSpy 2.0, we were just kind of red teaming and testing it out and I think I had a picture of my girlfriend just taking a selfie in the bathroom. I was curious what it would say and I dropped it in there and it put a pin on San Francisco. I was like, ‘Well hold on, wait a minute. That doesn't make any sense. It’s just a picture in a bathroom.’ And then I went over to Zillow and I just started screenshotting images and nine out of 10 of them it would get the right city.” “We have huge datasets that we train the models on and these are geotagged images from all over. Usually, we would assume that the images are all outdoor images. I'm assuming some of those images would probably have some indoors, whether it's people at a party or just taking pictures of food on their counter. The models must have learned some details that relate to different locations,” he continued. Airbnb told 404 Media in email “Protecting our community's privacy is important to us — that’s why location metadata is excluded from listing photos, hosts are given the option to show only an approximate location of their listing, and a home’s address is shared with a guest only after a reservation is confirmed. We also have technical safeguards in place to try to limit automated data collection from our site.” Airbnb stressed it has no relationship with Graylark, that its terms of service prohibit scraping, and that the company is reviewing this case. Zillow told 404 Media that scraping data is against its terms of use, and when necessary it pursues legal avenues. Vrbo did not respond to multiple requests for comment. It is unclear if the examples shown in the marketing videos are truly representative of Raven’s speed or capabilities. While law enforcement agencies have paid for access to Raven, it hasn’t always impressed. Joseph R. Peguero Rivera, from MDSO’s Public Affairs Office, previously told 404 Media “To date, use of GeoSpy has been limited and largely exploratory. While it has been reviewed in a small number of cases, it has not resulted in any significant investigative breakthroughs or arrests. No case outcomes were driven solely or primarily by information generated by the tool.” 404 Media first covered Raven in January 2025. At the time, the tool was available to essentially anyone, and some people in the company’s Discord server asked for help stalking women. A day after 404 Media contacted Graylark for comment, the company restricted access to the tool to only government agencies and enterprise users. In a September X post , Heinen said Alexandr Wang, now head of AI at Meta, was an angel investor in Graylark. Wang did not respond to a request for comment. items.summary_html:
An AI company now lets cops take a photo and nearly instantly figure out what specific home it was taken in, using only clues in the photo itself, and is clearly pulling data from sites like Zillow and Airbnb. 

The tool, called Raven, shows the increasing power of AI capabilities available to local law enforcement agencies. 404 Media previously reported that both the Los Angeles Police Department and Miami-Dade Sheriff’s Office (MDSO) have bought access to Raven, which was previously called GeoSpy. Now, Raven, made by a company called Graylark Technologies, has added features that let cops analyze the interior of homes.

In a post on LinkedIn earlier this month, Graylark CEO Daniel Heinen wrote the company was introducing “the ability to geolocate interior images across millions of short-term rental units worldwide.” An accompanying demo video shows someone taking a photo from X of a washer/dryer unit inside a building. They upload it to Raven, select “Find Property: Interior and exterior property geolocation,” and then choose a region to search.

💡
Do you know anything else about this technology or others like it? I would love to hear from you. Using a non-work device, you can message me securely on Signal at joseph.404 or send me an email at joseph@404media.co.

After a couple of seconds, the map interface zooms in on an area in Charlotte, North Carolina. On the right hand side, the screen displays a list of results. The top one reads, “Renovated! Walk Uptown/located in 2 Hot Spots!”

That result directly quotes the language on a specific Airbnb listing in Charlotte, and the photos in the Airbnb listing show the same property.

Later in the video, the Raven user takes a photo of a bathroom from social media. They upload it to Raven, and the tool points to an area of Montecito, California. The top result says, “Montecito Miramar Beach House on the Sand.” 404 Media found that result directly quotes a listing on the short term rental site Vrbo.

In other words, from a single photo, Raven appears to be able to quickly find the specific home it was taken in, without using location data or other metadata attached to the image. In the demonstrations the videos were from social media, but in practice they could be from anywhere a law enforcement officer has obtained them.

This is also not a reverse image search: a reverse image search would take an image then find an identical one posted somewhere else on the internet. What Raven is doing, instead, is identifying unique characteristics in the photo, then finding what are likely other photos from the same property on sites like Airbnb, even if those photos are not exactly the same, or even if time has passed between them being taken.

In another post, Heinen wrote, “For investigators working trafficking and exploitation cases, that connection can turn an unidentified room into a location lead they can verify and pursue.”

Raven is not limited to short term rentals, according to other demo videos. In a third example posted last year, Raven traces a photo of an interior room to a specific address in San Francisco. The interface returns other interior photos of the property; 404 Media found these are exactly the same photos as those posted on Zillow, indicating that Raven is at least pulling data from Zillow in some form. 

Another video posted last week shows Raven identifying a particular hotel, too.

A screenshot from a Raven promotional video on LinkedIn.

In another video, a part of the interface says, “City-specific property AI to determine an address.” That phrase implies the property search isn’t necessarily worldwide, but dependent on an AI model built specifically for that city. When 404 Media reported earlier this year that at least two law enforcement agencies have bought access to Raven, emails showed the MDSO had access to a custom model specifically trained for Miami-Dade County.

“In 2026, we’re investing heavily in interior geolocation across U.S. hotels, short-term rentals, houses, and apartments,” Heinen adds in the post.

Graylark trained Raven on millions of images from around the world. When the tool first launched, it was focused on identifying distinct geographical markers like architecture and soil. Now Raven extends that same idea into buildings. 

In an interview with the tech publication Indicator last year, Heinen discussed some of how the building interior searching capability came to be. “I’ll be honest, we didn't train it to do that,” he said. “That was kind of an ‘Oh shit’ moment for us. GeoSpy 1.0 couldn't do that. As we trained GeoSpy 2.0, we were just kind of red teaming and testing it out and I think I had a picture of my girlfriend just taking a selfie in the bathroom. I was curious what it would say and I dropped it in there and it put a pin on San Francisco. I was like, ‘Well hold on, wait a minute. That doesn't make any sense. It’s just a picture in a bathroom.’ And then I went over to Zillow and I just started screenshotting images and nine out of 10 of them it would get the right city.”

“We have huge datasets that we train the models on and these are geotagged images from all over. Usually, we would assume that the images are all outdoor images. I'm assuming some of those images would probably have some indoors, whether it's people at a party or just taking pictures of food on their counter. The models must have learned some details that relate to different locations,” he continued.

Airbnb told 404 Media in email “Protecting our community's privacy is important to us — that’s why location metadata is excluded from listing photos, hosts are given the option to show only an approximate location of their listing, and a home’s address is shared with a guest only after a reservation is confirmed. We also have technical safeguards in place to try to limit automated data collection from our site.” Airbnb stressed it has no relationship with Graylark, that its terms of service prohibit scraping, and that the company is reviewing this case.

Zillow told 404 Media that scraping data is against its terms of use, and when necessary it pursues legal avenues.

Vrbo did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

It is unclear if the examples shown in the marketing videos are truly representative of Raven’s speed or capabilities. While law enforcement agencies have paid for access to Raven, it hasn’t always impressed. Joseph R. Peguero Rivera, from MDSO’s Public Affairs Office, previously told 404 Media “To date, use of GeoSpy has been limited and largely exploratory. While it has been reviewed in a small number of cases, it has not resulted in any significant investigative breakthroughs or arrests. No case outcomes were driven solely or primarily by information generated by the tool.” 

404 Media first covered Raven in January 2025. At the time, the tool was available to essentially anyone, and some people in the company’s Discord server asked for help stalking women. A day after 404 Media contacted Graylark for comment, the company restricted access to the tool to only government agencies and enterprise users.

In a September X post, Heinen said Alexandr Wang, now head of AI at Meta, was an angel investor in Graylark. Wang did not respond to a request for comment.

In a LinkedIn post earlier this year, Heinen showed Raven being used against a video of people vandalizing a Flock camera.
