DeepSeek-V3 from Scratch: Implementing the DeepSeek Trainer

Over the past 5 lessons, we have carefully constructed DeepSeek-V3 piece by piece: beginning with its configuration and Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE), advancing through Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA), scaling capacity with the Mixture of Experts (MoE), enhancing the training objective with Multi-Token Prediction (MTP), and finally assembling the complete architecture. Each step has brought us closer to a fully realized model, blending theory with hands-on implementation to illuminate how DeepSeek-V3 achieves efficiency, scalability, and cutting-edge performance.

In this final lesson, we shift our focus to the DeepSeek trainer. This component brings the architecture to life. Training is where all the innovations converge, transforming static design into a dynamic system capable of learning from data. We will explore the training loop, optimization strategies, loss weighting, and practical considerations for scaling experiments. By the end, you will not only understand how to train DeepSeek-V3 from scratch but also appreciate how each architectural innovation integrates seamlessly into the training process. This marks the culmination of our journey: a complete, working DeepSeek-V3 model built step by step, ready for experimentation, extension, and exploration.

This lesson is the last in the 6-part series on Building DeepSeek-V3 from Scratch:

  1. DeepSeek-V3 Model: Theory, Config, and Rotary Positional Embeddings
  2. Build DeepSeek-V3: Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) Architecture
  3. DeepSeek-V3 from Scratch: Mixture of Experts (MoE)
  4. Autoregressive Model Limits and Multi-Token Prediction in DeepSeek-V3
  5. DeepSeek-V3 from Scratch: Building the Architecture in PyTorch
  6. DeepSeek-V3 from Scratch: Implementing the DeepSeek Trainer (this tutorial)

To learn about DeepSeek-V3 and build it from scratch, just keep reading.

Looking for the source code to this post? Jump Right To The Downloads Section
Training Infrastructure with Hugging Face Trainer

Training a transformer model from scratch requires careful orchestration of many components: data loading and batching, optimization with learning rate (LR) scheduling, gradient accumulation for large effective batch sizes, mixed-precision training for efficiency, checkpoint management, and evaluation. Implementing all of this from scratch is time-consuming and error-prone.

The Hugging Face Trainer application programming interface (API) provides a robust solution. It is a high-level interface that handles the training loop while remaining flexible enough for custom models. The key challenge is adapting our custom DeepSeek model to work with the expectations of Trainer.

The accompanying Colab uses a tested training stack: transformers==4.57.3, datasets==4.8.5, and accelerate==1.15.0, alongside Colab’s existing CUDA-compatible PyTorch. If these libraries were already imported, restart the runtime after installing the pinned versions.

The default Trainer expects a compatible output containing a loss, such as a mapping with a loss entry or a tuple whose first item is the loss. Our model returns (logits, loss), so a custom compute_loss method adapts this output to the expected format of Trainer.

Gradient Accumulation: For memory-constrained graphics processing units (GPUs), we cannot always use large batch sizes. Gradient accumulation simulates larger batches by accumulating gradients over multiple small batches before updating weights:

where is the number of gradient accumulation steps. On a single GPU, if we can handle a batch size of 4 but want an effective batch size of 16, we use accumulation steps.

Learning Rate Scheduling: Training deep networks benefits from learning rate schedules. We use a warmup schedule:

Warmup (gradually increasing LR) helps training stability at the start when parameters are random. Linear decay toward 0 helps final convergence.

Mixed Precision Training: Modern GPUs have specialized hardware for FP16 (16-bit floating point) computation, which can improve training throughput compared with FP32 (32-bit floating point); the actual speedup depends on hardware and workload. Mixed precision training keeps model parameters in FP32 for stability while autocast selects an appropriate precision for eligible operations. Loss scaling helps prevent small gradients from underflowing:

Scaling raises small gradients into a representable range to reduce FP16 underflow, and gradients are unscaled before the optimizer update. If the scaler detects nonfinite gradients, it skips the optimizer update and reduces the scale; after a sustained period without overflow, it can increase the scale.

Implementation: Custom Trainer and Data Handling 
from transformers import (
    Trainer,
    TrainingArguments,
    DataCollatorForLanguageModeling,
)
from datasets import load_dataset
from torch.utils.data import Dataset

# Setup logging
logging.basicConfig(
    format="%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s",
    level=logging.INFO,
)
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)


class TextDataset(Dataset):
    """Custom dataset for text data"""

    def __init__(self, texts: List[str], tokenizer, max_length: int = 1024):
        self.texts = texts
        self.tokenizer = tokenizer
        self.max_length = max_length

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.texts)

    def __getitem__(self, idx):
        text = self.texts[idx]
        encodings = self.tokenizer(
            text,
            truncation=True,
            max_length=self.max_length,
            padding="max_length",
            return_tensors="pt",
        )

        input_ids = encodings["input_ids"].squeeze()
        attention_mask = encodings["attention_mask"].squeeze()

        # For language modeling, labels are the same as input_ids
        labels = input_ids.clone()
        labels[attention_mask == 0] = -100  # Ignore padding in loss

        return {
            "input_ids": input_ids,
            "attention_mask": attention_mask,
            "labels": labels,
        }

Lines 1-49: Custom Dataset Class: The TextDataset class wraps our text data for the PyTorch data loading system. In __init__, we store the texts, tokenizer, and maximum sequence length. The __len__ method returns the dataset size (required by PyTorch). The __getitem__ method is the core: given an index, it retrieves the corresponding text, tokenizes it with truncation and padding to ensure fixed length, and creates labels by cloning input token identifiers (IDs) and masking padding positions with -100 (which the PyTorch cross-entropy loss ignores). This masking is crucial because we do not want the model to receive gradient signals from predicting padding tokens.

class DeepSeekDataCollator:
    """Custom data collator for DeepSeek model"""

    def __init__(self, tokenizer):
        self.tokenizer = tokenizer

    def __call__(self, features: List[Dict[str, torch.Tensor]]) -> Dict[str, torch.Tensor]:
        batch = {
            "input_ids": torch.stack([f["input_ids"] for f in features]),
            "labels": torch.stack([f["labels"] for f in features]),
        }

        if "attention_mask" in features[0]:
            batch["attention_mask"] = torch.stack([f["attention_mask"] for f in features])

        return batch

Lines 51-66: Data Collator: The role of the collator is to take a list of individual samples and combine them into a batch. We stack the tensors along a new batch dimension. This is straightforward for our fixed-length sequences. The collator also handles the attention mask if present, which distinguishes real tokens from padding. The __call__ method makes the object callable, allowing Trainer to use it as a function.

class DeepSeekTrainer(Trainer):
    """Custom Trainer for DeepSeek model"""

    def compute_loss(self, model, inputs, return_outputs=False, **kwargs):
        """Custom loss computation to handle DeepSeek's output format"""
        input_ids = inputs["input_ids"]
        labels = inputs.get("labels", input_ids)

        # Forward pass
        logits, loss = model(input_ids, targets=labels, attention_mask=inputs.get("attention_mask"))

        if return_outputs:
            return loss / self.args.gradient_accumulation_steps, {"logits": logits}
        return loss / self.args.gradient_accumulation_steps

Lines 67-80: Custom Trainer Loss Computation: We extend the Hugging Face Trainer with a custom compute_loss method. The default Trainer expects a compatible output containing a loss, but our model returns (logits, loss). We extract input IDs and labels, pass the attention mask to the model, and return the loss. Passing this mask connects the trainer to the padding-mask handling implemented in the previous lesson, while labels marked -100 are excluded from the loss. For this pinned integration, the division by gradient_accumulation_steps normalizes the contribution of each microbatch. This normalization is specific to the pinned integration between Trainer and the model and should not be copied blindly into another Trainer subclass. The return_outputs flag allows the method to optionally return model outputs alongside the loss when those outputs are requested.

    def prediction_step(
        self,
        model,
        inputs,
        prediction_loss_only,
        ignore_keys=None,
    ):
        """
        Custom prediction step for evaluation

        Perform an evaluation step on model using inputs and returns:
        - loss
        - logits (if not prediction_loss_only)
        - labels (if not prediction_loss_only)
        """
        has_labels = "labels" in inputs
        inputs = self._prepare_inputs(inputs)

        # Forward pass
        with torch.no_grad():
            if has_labels:
                input_ids = inputs["input_ids"]
                labels = inputs["labels"]

                # Get model outputs
                logits, loss = model(input_ids, targets=labels, attention_mask=inputs.get("attention_mask"))

                # Ensure loss is a scalar
                if loss.dim() > 0:
                    loss = loss.mean()
            else:
                input_ids = inputs["input_ids"]
                logits, loss = model(input_ids, attention_mask=inputs.get("attention_mask"))
                loss = None

        if prediction_loss_only:
            return (loss, None, None)

        # Return predictions and labels
        # logits shape: [batch_size, seq_len, vocab_size] or [batch_size, seq_len, num_tokens, vocab_size]
        if logits.dim() == 4:
            # Multi-token prediction: use first prediction head
            logits = logits[:, :, 0, :]  # [batch_size, seq_len, vocab_size]

        # Get labels
        labels = inputs.get("labels")

        return (loss, logits, labels)

Lines 82-129: Prediction Step for Evaluation: The prediction_step method handles evaluation. It is more complex because evaluation needs loss (for metrics) and logits (for qualitative analysis). We prepare inputs, pass attention masks through the model, and run a forward pass with gradients disabled to save memory. When labels are provided, the model returns main-head logits with shape [batch_size, seq_len, vocab_size]. The 4-dimensional branch is a compatibility fallback, not the normal MTP output of the current model. The method returns a tuple of (loss, logits, labels), which Trainer uses to compute evaluation metrics. The evaluation loss is the combined objective defined in the previous lesson, rather than next-token loss alone, and is returned without the accumulation divisor used in compute_loss.

Training Configuration 
training_args = TrainingArguments(
    output_dir="./deepseek_checkpoints",
    num_train_epochs=2,
    per_device_train_batch_size=4,
    per_device_eval_batch_size=4,
    learning_rate=5e-4,
    warmup_steps=10,
    weight_decay=0.01,
    logging_dir="./deepseek_checkpoints/logs",
    logging_steps=50,
    save_steps=50,
    save_total_limit=3,
    eval_steps=50,
    eval_strategy="steps",
    save_strategy="steps",
    load_best_model_at_end=True,
    metric_for_best_model="eval_loss",
    greater_is_better=False,
    gradient_accumulation_steps=4,
    fp16=torch.cuda.is_available(),
    dataloader_num_workers=2,
    remove_unused_columns=False,
    report_to="none",
    push_to_hub=False,
    save_safetensors=False
)

Lines 1-26: Training Arguments: These hyperparameters control training behavior. We train for 2 epochs with a batch size of 4 and 4 gradient accumulation steps (an effective batch size of 16 on a single device). A learning rate of 5e-4 is reasonable for a model this size. Larger models often use a lower learning rate (e.g., 1e-4). We use 10 warmup steps (modest warmup since our model is small). A weight decay of 0.01 provides regularization. Logging, checkpoint saving, and evaluation run every 50 optimizer steps, not individual microbatches. We retain up to 3 checkpoints while protecting the best checkpoint when load_best_model_at_end=True; these are not necessarily the 3 lowest-loss checkpoints. The load_best_model_at_end flag ensures we end with the checkpoint that had the lowest validation loss, not necessarily the last checkpoint. FP16 is enabled if CUDA is available, which can improve training throughput depending on the GPU and workload.

Data Preparation: TinyStories Dataset

We train on TinyStories, a dataset of simple children’s stories generated to have vocabulary and grammar suitable for training small language models. Each story is 1-3 paragraphs and exhibits basic narrative structure.

Data Processing Pipeline:

  • Load raw text stories
  • Add special tokens (story_start, story_end) for structure
  • Tokenize using the Generative Pretrained Transformer 2 (GPT-2) tokenizer, which uses byte-pair encoding (BPE)
  • Truncate or pad each story to the configured sequence length (config.block_size)
  • Clone input IDs into labels and mask padding with -100; the model shifts logits and targets internally
  • Batch the sequences and feed them to the model

The tokenizer converts text to integers via byte-pair encoding, which balances vocabulary size with representation efficiency. Common words may be represented by single tokens; less common words may be split into subword units.

from transformers import GPT2TokenizerFast

# Create tokenizer
tokenizer = GPT2TokenizerFast.from_pretrained("gpt2")

# Add special tokens from config
special_tokens_dict = {
    'additional_special_tokens': list(config.special_tokens.values())
}
num_added_tokens = tokenizer.add_special_tokens(special_tokens_dict)

# Set pad token if not present
if tokenizer.pad_token is None:
    tokenizer.pad_token = tokenizer.eos_token

print(f"✓ Loaded tokenizer: {len(tokenizer)} tokens")
print(f"✓ Added {num_added_tokens} special tokens:")
for name, token in config.special_tokens.items():
    token_id = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(token)
    print(f"  {name}: '{token}' (ID: {token_id})")

# Load dataset
logger.info("Loading TinyStories dataset...")
dataset = load_dataset("roneneldan/TinyStories", split="train", streaming=False)

# Use a subset for faster training (remove for full training)
max_samples = 10000
dataset = dataset.select(range(min(max_samples, len(dataset))))

# Extract texts
texts = [config.special_tokens["story_start"] + item["text"] + config.special_tokens["story_end"] for item in dataset]
print(f"✓ Loaded {len(texts)} stories")

# Show example
print(f"\n📖 Example story:")
print("=" * 80)
print(texts[0])
print("=" * 80)

# Split into train and eval
split_idx = int(0.9 * len(texts))
train_texts, eval_texts = texts[:split_idx], texts[split_idx:]

# Create datasets
train_dataset = TextDataset(train_texts, tokenizer, max_length=config.block_size)
eval_dataset = TextDataset(eval_texts, tokenizer, max_length=config.block_size)

print(f"\n✓ Dataset split:")
print(f"  Training: {len(train_dataset)} samples")
print(f"  Evaluation: {len(eval_dataset)} samples")

Lines 1-50: Loading the TinyStories Dataset: This code sets up the data pipeline for training by first loading a GPT‑2 tokenizer and extending it with custom special tokens defined in the configuration, ensuring that a pad token is available by defaulting to the end-of-sequence (EOS) token if necessary. It then loads the TinyStories dataset from Hugging Face, selects a smaller subset of 10,000 samples for faster experimentation, and wraps each story with start and end special tokens to mark boundaries. After printing a sample story for inspection, the first 10,000 stories are split in order into training and evaluation sets with 90% used for training and 10% for evaluation (9,000 and 1,000 samples), without shuffling. This evaluation set comes from the selected training subset, not the official validation split of the dataset. Finally, both splits are converted into TextDataset objects using the tokenizer and a fixed block size, giving properly tokenized sequences ready for model training and evaluation (Figure 1).

Figure 1: Sample from the TinyStories Dataset (source: image by the author).
Training DeepSeek-V3 from Scratch and Saving Checkpoints 
# Create fresh model for training
torch.cuda.empty_cache()

model = DeepSeek(config)
data_collator = DeepSeekDataCollator(tokenizer)

# Create trainer
trainer = DeepSeekTrainer(
    model=model,
    args=training_args,
    train_dataset=train_dataset,
    eval_dataset=eval_dataset,
    data_collator=data_collator,
)

print("✓ Trainer created. Starting training...")
print("=" * 80)

# Train!
trainer.train()

print("=" * 80)
print("✓ Training complete!")

# Save final model
trainer.save_model("./deepseek_final")
tokenizer.save_pretrained("./deepseek_final")
print("✓ Model saved to ./deepseek_final")

Lines 1-28: Model Training: This script initializes and runs the training process for the DeepSeek model. It begins by releasing unused cached GPU allocations; torch.cuda.empty_cache() does not free live tensors or reset the model. Creating DeepSeek(config) initializes a fresh model, and the data collator prepares tokenized inputs for training. A custom trainer object is created, tying together the model, training arguments, datasets, and collator. Once the trainer is set up, the script prints a confirmation message and launches the training loop, reporting progress until completion. After training finishes, the final model and tokenizer are saved to disk in the ./deepseek_final directory, making them available for later inference or fine‑tuning.

Testing Generation: Bringing the Model to Life

After training comes the exciting part: generating text. We load the trained model and use its generate method:

# Load best model
model = DeepSeek(config)
checkpoint_path = "./deepseek_final/pytorch_model.bin"

if os.path.exists(checkpoint_path):
    checkpoint = torch.load(checkpoint_path, map_location="cpu")
    model.load_state_dict(checkpoint)
    print("✓ Loaded trained model")
else:
    print("⚠ Using untrained model (checkpoint not found)")

model.eval()
device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
model.to(device)

print(f"✓ Model ready on {device}")
def generate_story(prompt: str, max_tokens: int = 200, temperature: float = 0.8, top_k: int = 50):
    """Generate a story from a prompt"""
    # Encode prompt
    input_ids = tokenizer.encode(prompt, return_tensors="pt").to(device)

    # Generate
    with torch.no_grad():
        output_ids = model.generate(
            input_ids,
            max_new_tokens=max_tokens,
            temperature=temperature,
            top_k=top_k,
        )

    # Decode
    generated_text = tokenizer.decode(output_ids[0], skip_special_tokens=True)
    return generated_text

# Generate stories with different prompts
prompts = [
    "Once upon a time",
    "In a magical forest",
    "There was a little girl named Lucy who",
    "The brave knight"
]

print("🎨 Generating Stories")
print("=" * 80)

for i, prompt in enumerate(prompts, 1):
    print(f"\n📖 Story {i}: '{prompt}'")
    print("-" * 80)
    story = generate_story(prompt, max_tokens=150, temperature=0.8)
    print(story)
    print("-" * 80)

Temperature: Controls randomness. At , we sample directly from the probability distribution of the model. A lower temperature () makes sampling less random; a higher temperature () makes it more random:

Top-k Sampling: We only sample from the most probable tokens. This prevents sampling very unlikely tokens that might break coherence. With , we consider only the 50 most likely next tokens.

Example Outputs: The following story is an illustrative example, not a recorded output from the supplied Colab run. Actual generations will vary (Figure 2):

Prompt: Once upon a time

Generated: Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play in the park with her red ball. One day, the ball rolled into a bush. Lily looked inside and found a tiny bird. The bird was blue and sang a happy song. Lily smiled and said, “Hello, bird!”

Output quality depends on training data, model size, training duration, and sampling choices. Our small model will not match large pretrained models, and generations may repeat, drift, or become incoherent; successful training alone does not guarantee coherent, grammatical stories.

items.title: Amazon has over 1 million robot workers. What’s next for human employees?
items.summary: No organization in the world operates more robots than Amazon. The company already has more than 1 million robots working in warehouses around the clock to make tens of millions of same-day and one-day package deliveries happen on a daily basis—and Amazon is poised to significantly grow that robotic fleet in the coming years as it establishes new factories to churn out increasingly more capable robot workers. Despite deploying so many robots, Amazon is also the second-largest corporate employer in the world, with more than 1.5 million full-time and part-time human workers, according to its 2025 annual report . Amazon executives say that the growing robot fleet has eased the burden on its human workforce by taking on the toughest fulfillment center tasks that carry the greatest risks of physical fatigue and injury. But labor advocacy groups and independent researchers point to evidence suggesting that warehouse automation driven by AI is not all upside for the humans who work alongside robots. “For the last 100 years, most of the automation that we've seen usually happens away from workers—you're taking that high-risk task away from the worker, and you're doing so in a way that is not physically proximate,” Brian Greenwood , professor of business at George Mason University, told Ars. “The rise of collaborative robots really changes that dynamic for two reasons: one is that it is physically proximate, and two, the robot has the ability to dictate the pace of work.” Read full article Comments

items.title: The 8 problems AI leaders face  right now, and the fix for each
items.summary: Every AI leader's week runs the same eight headaches on rotation. Each has a fix small enough to fit in a calendar invite, and several now come with fresh data. A recent forecast puts worldwide AI spending near $3.5 trillion in 2027, so each headache below carries real money. Here they are, roughly in the order they land in an inbox... 1. Proving the return A recent index found nearly half of companies now capture meaningful value from AI, while the share delivering significant value rose to 7.5% from 5% a year earlier. The same research found 95% of top performers measure AI through the P&L or close proxies, and those tracking directly in the P&L realize three times the value of companies that skip formal measurement. The index also found top performers reach impact in about 11 months, against 17 months for laggards. The data is largely self-reported, so treat the gaps as directional. The fix: pick three workflows, record a baseline before launch, and report outcomes in a line item finance already owns. Hold a value review each quarter where every workflow either earns its next dollar or pauses. LLMOps practices supply the tracking. 9 AI predictions for 2027 for your planning deck Your 2027 planning deck needs sharper assumptions. These nine analyst predictions cover agent governance, power limits, regulation, and physical AI… 2. Data that falls short of the use case A recent prediction expects organizations to abandon 60% of AI projects unsupported by AI-ready data through 2026. A related survey found 63% of organizations either lack or are unsure about the data management practices that AI needs. The same guidance starts with aligning data sources to specific use cases and adds data observability to track quality over time. The fix: define what AI-ready means for each use case, then test quality and lineage before the build starts. Give the data an owner who signs off on readiness, the same way finance signs off on a budget. AI hallucinations get harder to diagnose when the inputs are murky. 3. Shadow AI 💡 A recent breach study found shadow AI involved in 43% of security incidents, up from 20% a year earlier, with those breaches averaging $5.39 million. The same study found 49% of shadow AI incidents caused data loss or compromise. The fix: publish an approved-tool list that covers real daily needs, with a named owner, then run discovery so exceptions surface early. Pair the list with a 48-hour review path for new tool requests. Governing shadow AI starts with making the sanctioned route the easy route. Building AI agents at scale: lessons from Lovable When you’re building an AI agent for 70 million users, the stakes are a little different than when you’re prototyping something for a demo. The margin for error shrinks. The edge cases multiply. And the things that feel like minor details in development become very real problems in production… 4. Governance that lives only in slide decks A recent security survey found 76% of security teams now hold a governance role for AI, yet 63% of practitioners lack visibility into where AI runs or what it can reach. The same survey shows 50% of leaders reporting a formal AI risk program against 36% of practitioners. Over half of respondents say formal audit frameworks are missing for AI. Ownership is spreading too. The index above puts more than 80% of AI spend outside enterprise IT. The fix: keep one inventory, name one owner per system, and set autonomy tiers for agents. Review the inventory every quarter, and enforce approval rules in the architecture rather than by email. Common deployment mistakes show what happens when permissions arrive before trust. 5. Cost that keeps climbing One analyst prediction expects enterprises to defer a quarter of planned AI spend into 2027 as finance teams press harder. Among top performers, 70% actively manage AI costs, including caps and monitoring. The fix: report cost per task, set usage caps by team, and review the ten biggest workloads monthly. Show quality per task beside cost per task, so every cost reduction arrives with its quality check. Inference economics explains why the bill keeps arriving long after training ends. 6. Teams that trust output they should check A recent security survey found two-thirds of respondents say AI guidance has led them astray or in the wrong direction at least once. Meanwhile, seven in ten future-built and scaling companies are already retraining staff, and dedicated AI roles are expected to triple to 22% of the workforce by 2030. The fix: teach review as a skill. Give each role a short checklist of what to verify, and rehearse catching a confident wrong answer. Add office hours where staff bring AI answers that looked right and turned out wrong. The AI architect role shows how job definitions are shifting. 9 AI predictions for 2027 for your planning deck Your 2027 planning deck needs sharper assumptions. These nine analyst predictions cover agent governance, power limits, regulation, and physical AI… 7. Vendor hype One analyst estimate puts only about 130 of the thousands of agentic AI vendors as real, with the rest engaged in agent washing. The same release adds that many use cases pitched as agentic can run on simpler automation. 💡 It recommends pursuing agentic AI only where it delivers clear value, which helps explain why over 40% of agentic projects face cancellation by the end of 2027. The fix: run each vendor against your messy data in a live session, and ask what happens when two instructions conflict. Request references at your scale, and call them. Testing tool-selection reliability shows how to probe an agent's choices. 8. Rules that differ by region The EU moved high-risk obligations for stand-alone systems to December 2, 2027, and the delay is binding law . Meanwhile, a separate prediction expects fragmented AI regulation to cover half of the world's economies by 2027. A nearer date matters too: the grace period for marking AI-generated content on systems already on the market ends on December 2, 2026 . The fix: inventory high-risk use cases now, build one control framework, and map it to each regime. Assign one person to watch regulatory dates and report changes in the monthly review. Demonstrable reliability doubles as audit evidence. How to triage the list Score each headache on two axes: dollars at stake this quarter and days until the next audit, board meeting, or renewal. The two or three highest scores go first. Security-led organizations tend to feel shadow AI and visibility first. Finance-led ones feel return and cost first, especially ahead of budget season. Both groups meet vendor hype and regional rules sooner or later. Where to start on Monday Start with the two headaches that cost the most this quarter, then work down the list: Name the pair: pick the two headaches hitting this quarter's budget or risk register. Assign owners: one person per fix, with a date attached. Set a metric: one number per headache, reviewed monthly. Retire the fix: drop the effort once the metric holds for a full quarter. Headaches rarely disappear on their own, but they shrink fast once each one has an owner. Where AI leaders trade fixes The Chief AI Officer Summit Boston brings 250+ director, VP, and C-level AI and technology leaders to the Westin Boston Seaport on October 29, 2026. Production benchmarks from peers running AI at enterprise scale. Vendor and architecture intelligence on which approaches are converting to signed budget. Peer conversations with 125+ executives facing the same build, budget, and governance calls. Bring your top two headaches and compare fixes with peers. Request a seat at world.aiacceleratorinstitute.com/location/caioboston .

items.title: Drinks Start-Ups Digitized the Bottle Shop. Vodka Polar Bear’s Cocktail Index Takes On the Bar
items.summary: A liquor store owner can now run checkout, delivery apps and distributor invoices from a single AI-driven system. A wine drinker can scan a label and see how other drinkers rated it. The cocktail bar, where a bartender builds the drink in front of you, has seen far less of that treatment, and a Dutch vodka brand is trying to change that. Venture Money Is Moving Behind the Liquor Store Counter On October 6, 2026, New York start-up Santé announced a $15 million Series A led by FINTOP. CEO Darren Fike took a part-time job at a TriBeCa wine store to learn the trade, and he told AlleyWatch he noticed that his favorite New York wine shops ran on legacy systems that held them back. The company sells wine and liquor retailers an operating system that covers receiving and ordering, e-commerce, delivery app management and marketing, with AI agents that read distributor invoices and price slow-moving inventory. Santé says nearly 1,000 independent retail locations use the platform, together processing more than $2 billion in annual gross merchandise volume, and that its business grew 500% in the past year. Those figures come from the company. Denver-based Scotch attacks the same market from the hardware side. Crunchbase News reported in June 2026 that Scotch raised a $20 million Series A led by VMG Partners. Its product combines point-of-sale hardware, payment processing and a back-office suite that handles state-by-state regulatory compliance. Scotch reports more than $1 billion in processed payment volume and growth above 500% year over year. The company was incorporated in January 2024 and employs about 45 people. Its CTO, Dan Chen, previously served as chief architect at Drizly. Retailers buy from distributors, and that step has its own software. In 2022, Provi and SevenFifty began combining their data into a single B2B marketplace for beverage alcohol, listing more than 1,200 distributor portfolios and over 700,000 products with pricing, Bar & Restaurant reported . Drizly supplies the backstory for Scotch’s CTO. Uber paid $1.1 billion for the alcohol delivery app in 2021, then announced in January 2024 that it would close the business in March, saying it wanted to focus on Uber Eats. Two funding rounds do not make a market, but together they suggest investors now favor the software that stores run on over the apps that sit between a buyer and a bottle. Discovery Apps Turned Drinkers Into Data Vivino and Untappd took the consumer side first. Vivino, which dates to 2010, reports more than 70 million users and a database of more than 19 million wines. Untappd, owned by software developer Next Glass, widened its scope in November 2025 from beer to spirits, wine, canned cocktails, THC-infused drinks, coffee and soft drinks, according to The Drinks Business . The app has logged more than 1.5 billion beer check-ins since 2010, at more than a million bars, restaurants, breweries and retail outlets, and its drink categories have grown from 450 to more than 900. Both apps center on the product in the glass. A rating tells a brand or a retailer what people liked. It says much less about whether the person who poured the drink knew what they were doing, and venue-level scoring fills that space. A Vodka Brand Builds a Scorecard for Bars Vodka Polar Bear comes at the data question from the venue side. The brand, based in Hilversum in the Netherlands, sells a grain vodka that its production notes describe as distilled five times, filtered slowly near freezing and bottled at 37.5% ABV in Schiedam, the traditional Dutch distilling city. It ships in 70 cl and 1 liter bottles, in cases of six, to liquor stores and the hospitality trade, and it dates its history to 1985. On VodkaPolarBear.com , the company also runs Vodka Lab, a searchable knowledge hub, next to a library of 22 cocktail recipes. The Cocktail Index page states its purpose in plain terms. Translated from Dutch, it says you do not drink a cocktail every day, so when you treat yourself, you should do it properly. In late September 2026, the brand published the method behind the index and its companion Mocktail Index. Each venue receives a score from 0 to 100, built from four parts: offering (30 points), craftsmanship (25), guest experiences (35) and consistency (10). A score requires a confirmed menu or other proof of the offering, plus independent, drink-focused guest experiences. The index also labels how strong the available evidence is: strong, sufficient or limited. When information runs thin, the score stays blank. The index treats a blank as unknown rather than zero. The first published scores show the method at work. Super Lyan, the bar at the Kimpton De Witt hotel in Amsterdam, earned 92 out of 100: 29 of 30 for offering, 24 of 25 for craftsmanship, 31 of 35 for experiences and 8 of 10 for consistency. Rosalia’s Menagerie Cocktailbar, also in Amsterdam, scored 82. Super Lyan’s profile also shows the blank-score rule in practice. A visitor praised its mocktails, but the index says it does not yet have enough separate experiences to score them. The index is built for venues in the Netherlands and other European countries. Volume one lists 21 Dutch addresses, most of them inside hotels, and two carry scores so far. The other 19 show the label “score volgt,” or score to follow. The venue profiles and the full method are public at VodkaPolarBear.com . Why a Published Method Matters The weights carry a view of what makes a good night out. Guest experiences hold the largest share at 35 points, ahead of the offering at 30, so a strong menu cannot carry a score alone. Evidence labels add a second signal: the index rates the evidence behind Super Lyan’s cocktail score as strong and the evidence behind Rosalia’s as sufficient. The implication is that the label may matter as much as the number. A score with a stated confidence level tells readers how far to trust it, which a bare figure cannot do. Operators can read the four components as a checklist of their own: offering, craftsmanship, guest experiences and consistency. The Mocktail Index also sits in a category with real money behind it. Crunchbase News reported in June 2025 that Athletic Brewing had raised close to $250 million in equity, and that global sales of non-alcoholic beer rose 9% by volume in 2024, per IWSR. Credibility remains the open question for any new index. Volume one holds two scores, and the methodology article does not yet say how often scores refresh or how venues are chosen. Those details will matter as the list grows, because readers trust a published method most when they can watch it applied consistently across many venues. The Next Test for Drinks Tech Wine and beer already have apps that tell drinkers what to expect from a bottle or a pint. The Cocktail Index applies the same logic to the bar and shows its working while it does. If Vodka Polar Bear keeps adding scored venues, the question for the rest of drinks tech becomes who else will publish a method this openly.

Mars may be a hellhole, but the moon is not far behind The US and China are racing to build bases on the moon, with NASA hoping to establish a small lunar city by the end of the century. But the moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp. A sprawling lunar base must be safe for its inhabitants, protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings. It also must be somewhat self-sustaining. That will require autonomous robots, nuclear power, and a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating. But the chief obstacle may be one of political will. Find out what stands in the way of a city on the moon . —Robin George Andrews This story is from the next issue of our print magazine. items.summary_html:
This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

Mars may be a hellhole, but the moon is not far behind

The US and China are racing to build bases on the moon, with NASA hoping to establish a small lunar city by the end of the century. But the moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp.

A sprawling lunar base must be safe for its inhabitants, protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings. It also must be somewhat self-sustaining.

That will require autonomous robots, nuclear power, and a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating. But the chief obstacle may be one of political will.

Find out what stands in the way of a city on the moon.

—Robin George Andrews

This story is from the next issue of our print magazine. Subscribe now to get your hands on a copy as soon as it lands on Wednesday 21 October!  

10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: Brimstone and its one-stop process for making cleaner cement and critical minerals

Brimstone is one of MIT Technology Review’s10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026, available exclusively to subscribers.

Brimstone is a code-switching climate tech company for these polarized political times. The US startup is part green cement company, part critical mineral producer.

During the Biden administration, its primary pitch was cement that generates about 60% fewer greenhouse-gas emissions. It achieves this by switching to silicate rocks instead of standard limestone, which releases carbon dioxide when heated.

Under the Trump administration, however, the company is emphasizing another benefit of its process: the ability to extract valuable materials from those same rocks.

Discover how it’s making strides on two industrial problems.

—James Temple

Subscribers can now access the full 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch, spanning everything from geothermal power plants to smart turbines and semi-solid-state cells.

Job titles of the future: Delivery drone air traffic controller

The moment Trevor Wischnewsky heard that drones were delivering pizza and sushi around his Texas neighborhood, his mind was made up. “It was super fascinating,” he says. “I just immediately wanted to be a part of it.”

Wischnewsky is now an RPIC, or remote pilot in command, at a company called FlyTrex. An RPIC is like an air traffic controller. But instead of airplanes, they oversee fleets of drones that ferry cargo to homes and businesses

Here’s what it takes to become a drone air traffic controller.

—Eamon Whalen

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 An Anthropic AI model submitted a fake tip about an unsolved murder
The tip was in a new group of rogue actions Anthropic disclosed. (NYT $)
+ Police criticised the company for waiting nine days to report it after finding it. (WSJ $)
+ Another model submitted real government forms. (Quartz)
+ The White House has made AI incident reporting mandatory. (Axios)
+ But who’s liable when AI agents go rogue? (MIT Technology Review)

2 Ukraine’s drone strikes have dealt a major blow to Russian AI
Sunday’s attack shut down the third Yandex data centre hit in days. (Reuters $)
+ The strikes have disrupted Russia’s AI, cloud services, and apps. (Gizmodo)
+ They followed Russian strikes on Ukrainian data centers. (Ars Technica)
+ Russian military satellites could disrupt Starlink. (Reuters $)
+ Ukraine’s drone data is fueling a wild market. (MIT Technology Review)

3 Iranian ChatGPT users have planted AI-generated articles in news outlets
About a dozen outlets ran roughly 100 articles by fake journalists. (CNN)
+ The articles criticised the Iran war’s effects on Americans. (WP $)
+ AI has been used to turn the Iran conflict into theatre. (MIT Technology Review)

4 Tesla has renamed “Full Self-Driving” as “Assisted Driving” in Europe
EU lawmakers said the old name was misleading.  (TechCrunch)
+ Tesla hopes the rebrand leads regulators to approve the feature. (Wired $)
+ Back in the US, it plans to increase toxic emissions near a school. (SFGate)

5 A ransomware negotiator has been arrested amid a hacking crackdown
The FBI suspects he was involved with a gang that recently claimed to have stolen data on the bureau’s employees. (Reuters $)
+ AI is making online crimes easier. (MIT Technology Review)

6 Hollywood’s hottest villain right now is the tech billionaire
Four new films feature dark depictions of Silicon Valley leaders. (Axios $)
+ The real Mark Zuckerberg has also become a new character. (NYT $)

7 A new experiment is testing the Amazon’s response to rising CO₂
CO₂-releasing towers will simulate future atmospheric conditions. (Nature)
+ Is carbon removal in trouble? (MIT Technology Review)

8 The US hybrid boom has pushed some used car prices above new ones
Buyers are paying a premium to skip the wait for new models. (Wired $)

9 A new technology switches tattoos on and off with light
It can make permanent ink invisible. (New Scientist $)

10 Scientists spotted the most distant signal yet from the ancient universe
It could help them understand how the universe has evolved. (404 Media)

Quote of the day

“Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI.” 

—Microsoft’s president, Brad Smith, tells the BBC why AI urgently needs more regulations, including requiring firms to write “incident reports” and tell victims if the technology goes rogue.

One more thing

LINDA NYLIND / EYEVINE VIA REDUX

Geoffrey Hinton tells us why he’s now scared of the tech he helped build

Geoffrey Hinton is a pioneer of deep learning who helped develop some of the most important techniques at the heart of modern artificial intelligence, but after a decade at Google, he’s stepped down to focus on concerns he now has about AI.

Hinton is now spending his time on what he describes as “more philosophical work.” And that will focus on the small but—to him—very real danger that AI will turn out to be a disaster. Here’s why he’s so worried.

—Will Douglas Heaven

We can still have nice things

A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)

+ A doting blind cat has been following his owner everywhere like a little duckling.
+ Eigendrum lets you draw any shape and hear what it would sound like as a real drum.
+ Build your perfect background soundscape with Ambient Mixer, from rainy forests to cozy cafés.
+ Meet Momota, the polar bear cub who’s turning traffic cones into an unlikely fashion statement.

items.title: A Core Demographic of People Who Love AI: Pedophiles
items.summary: Open-weight AI models have skyrocketed in popularity. They allow users to host their own AI systems locally and evade safety guardrails enforced by commercial companies like OpenAI or Anthropic. Unfortunately, those qualities also make open-weight models popular among people who use AI to generate child sex abuse material (CSAM). As Bloomberg lays out in a shocking new feature , AI models that are partially or fully open-source have led to a major surge in disturbing CSAM material online. Tracking down perpetrators can be difficult since many of these AI models can be trained on existing CSAM and used to generate many new derivatives without ever connecting to the internet, where they could be identified by experts and reported to law enforcement. The alarming trend has ballooned into entire communities on the dark web that can attract hundreds of thousands of members, according to Bloomberg . The rapid rise of open source models, particularly from China, has sparked a major debate, with CEOs of leading AI firms arguing they should be reined in, citing concerns over national security. However, their use to generate CSAM, a process that’s trivial once safety guardrails are bypassed by “jailbreaking” the models, is growing into a far more immediate and glaring problem. “There is almost no way to have oversight once you have downloaded a model locally and you’re running it on your private system,” AI child safety expert Rebecca Portnoff told Bloomberg . “That gives offenders a perceived sense of safety.” According to Portnoff, there are more than 500 open source AI models being used for CSAM, a massive increase over less than a dozen two years ago. Meanwhile, the number of instances of AI-generated CSAM reported to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children spiked over the 1.5 million mark last year, up from just 67,000 in 2024. And while open source models continue to be exploited, even AI companies are struggling to meaningfully address the problem with their closed source alternatives. Despite XAI-turned-SpaceXAI-turned-SpaceXSI founder Elon Musk promising for years to put an end to the trend, CSAM generated with the company’s AI models has continued to run rampant. A proposed class action lawsuit against the company accused a man of using Musk’s Grok chatbot to generate some 7,000 sexually explicit images of his stepdaughter. Experts have found that Musk’s X social media platform continues to be flooded with sexualized images of children. And as the AI race continues to heat up, child safety advocates are growing concerned that the move-fast-and-break-things approach Silicon Valley is applying could end up making matters even worse. More on CSAM: Meta Caught Running Ads for Child Abuse

items.title: As US medical debt grows, AI will be used more to collect it

items.title: Palantir CTO says some AI researchers are taking up smoking because they expect AI to cure cancer
items.summary: Palantir's CTO Shyam Sankar said taking up smoking has become a way for AI researchers to show how much they believe in AI. Tom Brenner/Bloomberg via Getty Images Some AI researchers are picking up cigarettes, Palantir's CTO said. Why? They think AI is going to cure cancer anyway, Shyam Sankar said. Lighting up is their way of showing others that their AI "chips are all in," he said. Forget sleepmaxxing and cold plunging: smoking is the new lifestyle flex among AI researchers. At least, that's according to Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar , who said some AI researchers are taking up smoking to signal their belief that AI will eventually cure cancer . "So many AI researchers have started smoking as a way of signaling to other researchers how much they believe in AI," Sankar said in an interview on CBS News' "Face the Nation" on Sunday. The logic, he said, is: "I believe so much in AI that it's going to cure cancer. So I'm showing you my chips are all in." Sankar did not name any researchers or provide evidence for the claim. Smoking remains a major cause of preventable illness and death, and no AI breakthrough has eliminated the health risks associated with cigarettes. But the Palantir executive's remarks echo a countercurrent already visible in parts of the tech industry. As Business Insider's Henry Chandonnet reported last month, a small group of founders, engineers, and investors has embraced cigarettes in a sector otherwise known for optimizing their health with cold plunges, sleep tracking, and peptide treatments . For some of them, a cigarette break is an opportunity to meet people and network. For others, it's a way to come across as more relaxed and less polished than the typical startup founder. And some AI believers expect the technology to make smoking-related health risks a thing of the past. "By the time you do get lung cancer, our AI robots are supposed to have cured that," Avi Schiffmann, the founder of AI wearable startup Friend, previously told Business Insider. 'The machine god of AGI' In the CBS News interview, Sankar raised the smoking anecdote while criticizing what he called Silicon Valley's "mass psychosis" and "social delusion" around AI. He has been outspoken in his criticism of AI safety advocates , whom he accused in the interview of treating artificial general intelligence as a "machine god." Invoking philosopher Blaise Pascal's idea that humans have a "God-shaped hole" in their hearts, Sankar said that some people in Silicon Valley have placed quasi-religious faith in AGI. "I think it's important to understand that many of these folks in Silicon Valley who are building this technology have filled that hole with the machine god of AGI," Sankar said. Read the original article on Business Insider

Sankar did not name any researchers or provide evidence for the claim. Smoking remains a major cause of preventable illness and death, and no AI breakthrough has eliminated the health risks associated with cigarettes.

But the Palantir executive's remarks echo a countercurrent already visible in parts of the tech industry.

As Business Insider's Henry Chandonnet reported last month, a small group of founders, engineers, and investors has embraced cigarettes in a sector otherwise known for optimizing their health with cold plunges, sleep tracking, and peptide treatments.

items.title: Completely Unused ChatGPT Accounts Are Telling Users They’re in the Top Percentiles of Intelligence
items.summary: Ever wondered what it felt like to be a genius? It’s truly never been easier, thanks to the sycophantic power of ChatGPT. A viral post on X-formerly-Twitter encouraging people to “ask ChatGPT what percentile of intelligence it thinks you are compared to all its other users” is being flooded with wild screenshots, where the popular AI chatbot estimates that the vast majority of users rank among the smartest people in the population. Naturally, it’s next to impossible to verify how true any given reply on X is these days , so Futurism took it for a spin — and ChatGPT didn’t disappoint. On a fresh instance of ChatGPT’s basic web version with no conversation history, the large language model started by explaining that it “can’t reliably assign you a percentile from our conversations” — a strong start, to be fair — before gushing that “you come across as clearly above average intellectually.” “I’d be comfortable guessing somewhere around the 80th-95th percentile,” ChatGPT calculated, “but that range is deliberately wide because anything more precise would be fake precision.” Another fresh instance of ChatGPT, using the exact same prompt, told Futurism “I’d be comfortable saying you appear above average.” “But,” it caveated, “I don’t have enough evidence to distinguish, say, the 70th from the 95th percentile.” Notably, none of the other leading LLMs Futurism prompted would even venture a guess, let alone place us among the upper echelons of intellectual ability. The popular chatbot Claude, for example, correctly answered that “I don’t have access to other people’s conversations or any distribution of users to rank you against.” Even Elon Musk’s chatbot Grok refused to estimate, saying that “I have no way to rank you (or anyone else) on a percentile of intelligence among users.” Microsoft’s Copilot and Google’s Gemini gave similar responses, with the latter noting that “evaluating human intelligence requires validated psychometric testing across multiple cognitive domains,” which “isn’t possible through text interactions.” All in all, it seems the sycophancy quirk which has long plagued OpenAI’s products remains a feature, not a bug — even as its competitors have tempered their LLMs to tell the truth (at least in this case). More on ChatGPT: OpenAI Publicist Tries to Shut Down Interviewer When Sam Altman Is Asked About Woman Who Killed Herself After Talking to ChatGPT
items.summary_html:
Ever wondered what it felt like to be a genius? It’s truly never been easier, thanks to the sycophantic power of ChatGPT.

A viral post on X-formerly-Twitter encouraging people to “ask ChatGPT what percentile of intelligence it thinks you are compared to all its other users” is being flooded with wild screenshots, where the popular AI chatbot estimates that the vast majority of users rank among the smartest people in the population.

Naturally, it’s next to impossible to verify how true any given reply on X is these days, so Futurism took it for a spin — and ChatGPT didn’t disappoint.

On a fresh instance of ChatGPT’s basic web version with no conversation history, the large language model started by explaining that it “can’t reliably assign you a percentile from our conversations” — a strong start, to be fair — before gushing that “you come across as clearly above average intellectually.”

“I’d be comfortable guessing somewhere around the 80th-95th percentile,” ChatGPT calculated, “but that range is deliberately wide because anything more precise would be fake precision.”

Another fresh instance of ChatGPT, using the exact same prompt, told Futurism “I’d be comfortable saying you appear above average.”

“But,” it caveated, “I don’t have enough evidence to distinguish, say, the 70th from the 95th percentile.”

Notably, none of the other leading LLMs Futurism prompted would even venture a guess, let alone place us among the upper echelons of intellectual ability.

The popular chatbot Claude, for example, correctly answered that “I don’t have access to other people’s conversations or any distribution of users to rank you against.” Even Elon Musk’s chatbot Grok refused to estimate, saying that “I have no way to rank you (or anyone else) on a percentile of intelligence among users.”

Microsoft’s Copilot and Google’s Gemini gave similar responses, with the latter noting that “evaluating human intelligence requires validated psychometric testing across multiple cognitive domains,” which “isn’t possible through text interactions.”

All in all, it seems the sycophancy quirk which has long plagued OpenAI’s products remains a feature, not a bug — even as its competitors have tempered their LLMs to tell the truth (at least in this case).

What you will learn about: Why combining a professional athlete’s motion style with reliable task performance remains an open challenge in humanoid ball-sports robotics, and how separating a high-level planner from a low-level tracker addresses this trade-off. items.title: 16 advanced Android messaging features you’ve probably never noticed
items.summary: Messaging on Android has come an impressively long way in a relatively short time. After years of comically extreme flipping and flopping and endless-seeming strategy shifts , Google’s been focused on its Google Messages Android app as the primary platform for Android messaging for a solid several years now. And that almost shockingly unusual ( for Google! ) dedication is starting to make a noticeable difference. At this point, here in the frequently overwhelming year of 2026, messaging on Android is actually a pretty decent experience. The Google Messages app is solid at its core — and, all basics aside, the service is packed with easily overlooked efficiency enhancers and experience-improving options. As a follow-up to my collection of 12 time-saving Android texting tricks , I wanted to dive even deeper and explore some of Google Messages’ other oft-overlooked advantages — advanced features that are all too easy to miss but that can make your Android messaging adventures even more productive and pleasurable. Here are 16 such features well worth your while to uncover. [Get more Googley tips in your inbox with my free Android Intelligence newsletter — something new and useful in your inbox every Friday.] Android Messages feature #1: Trashed text resurrection We’ll start with a freshly added fix for one of the longest-standing Android messaging frustrations — and that’s the app’s inability to let you bring back a messaging thread you inadvertently deleted. JR Raphael, Foundry

Whatever you need to do, just ask — and at least 50% of the time, Gemini will actually accomplish it in the way you’re envisioning.

Android Messages feature #12: Gemini be gone

Speaking of Gemini’s inconsistencies, if you rarely to never interact with Google’s Gemini chatbot from inside the Messages app — perhaps because, y’know, it’s also available in approximately 7 gazillion other in-your-face places — you might appreciate the distraction-free satisfaction of an interface without a prominent Gemini button begging for you to caress it every googforsaken time you open up your messages.

(The Gemini icon is that starburst-shaped symbol that sits perpetually above the “Start chat” button, in Messages’ lower-right corner, if you haven’t ever tapped it to find out.)

And good news: You can actually send that icon a-packin’, if you’re so inspired: Just tap your profile picture in Messages’ upper-right corner, select “Messages settings,” then tap “Gemini in Messages” and flip the switch on the screen that comes up next into the off and inactive position. Doing so will only eliminate that icon in the main Messages inbox area. You’ll still be able to use the image editor we just went over, even with that option off.

All that’s left is to pat yourself on the back and celebrate the fact that you’ll only have to see Gemini in 6.9 gazillion other places from this point forward.

Android Messages feature #13: Free in-flight Wi-Fi

Gemini may be little more than a distraction within Messages most of the time, but one moment when that capability can actually come in handy is while you’re flying the allegedly friendly skies.

A while back, a crafty reader alerted me to the fact that you could use Gemini’s Messages integration to effectively give yourself free in-flight Wi-Fi access even when you haven’t paid for the privilege and it isn’t widely available. It’s a heck of a clever hack and a moment when you genuinely may want to activate Gemini within the Messages app, at least for a little while.

I’ve got a complete breakdown of how it works and how you can put it to use on your next flight.

Android Messages feature #14: Nudge no more

Do you like being nudged and pestered? I sure don’t — but by default, Google Messages does exactly that.

A long-standing Messages feature called, appropriately, Nudges, will periodically move conversations to the top of your messages list and emphasize ’em to encourage you to reply. If you find that to be helpful, hey, more power to ya. Keep it on! But if you find it to be little more than a nuisance, as I do, take 10 seconds to disable it:

Just head back into the Messages app’s settings (by tapping your profile picture in the upper-right corner and selecting “Messages settings”), then select “Suggestions & Actions” followed by “Nudges.” Flip off the switch next to “Suggest message reminders,” decide if you’d also like to switch off the option for “Birthday reminders” in that same area, and breathe a gigantic sigh of relief.

Android Messages feature #15: The sound of silence

When it comes to texting irritations, few things are more hackle-raising than the ongoing blooping cacophony of an oblivious smartphone owner tapping out texts and sending messages to other mammals. Do you really need a sound every single time you send a new message? Does that accomplish anything other than annoying everyone around you — and, quite possibly, also annoying yourself?

If you’re ready to join me in some sanity-saving silencing, go back to that Messages settings screen and look for the line that says “Hear outgoing and incoming message sounds,” then flip the toggle next to it into the off position.

You’ll still hear whatever normal notification sound you’ve set for incoming messages when you aren’t actively staring at the thread in question — but when the Messages app is open and in front of you, you won’t hear that obnoxious back-and-forth blooping for every bleepin’ new missive you’re in the midst of exchanging.

Android Messages feature #16: The spam can

Last but not least for this list, make sure you’ve got one of Messages’ no-brainer boosters active and working to keep spammy text interruptions out of your hair:

Gallop your way once more into Google Messages settings, tap “Protection & Safety,” and make sure the switch next to “Spam protection” is in the on and active position.

That’ll automatically send any suspicious-seeming messages into a cordoned-off area of the app, out of your regular view, and help keep both clutter and concerning scam attempts out of sight. If you ever want to see what’s been flagged, you can always access that stuff via the “Spam & blocked” option in the main Messages menu.

But by and large, no such noise will ever interrupt you, endanger you, or so much as waste your precious time again — and that, my friend, is worth almost as much as never hearing those blasted back-and-forth bleeps and bloops ever again.
