items.title: The Blessing and Curse of AI on the Open Source Community
items.summary: Let’s not kid ourselves. Generative AI is here to stay. A door has been opened that can no longer be closed. Even if the AI bubble bursts, and it probably will in the not-too-distant future, LLMs won’t disappear. The progress that has been made and the vast amount of open-weight models more than guarantee that, even if OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral, and the others completely vanish (they won’t, but that is for another discussion), AI is here to stay. With the good and the bad. Like most cutting-edge technologies that appeared throughout history, AI is not only a sensitive topic, but a complex one as well. There are people both on the Anti-AI and the Pro-AI side. And both parties have valid points to sustain their view. Because AI is not all good and it is not all bad. It is a tool. A very complex one that reshapes entire industries, but a tool nonetheless. And AI has done a lot of great work in the software industry, but also a lot of damage. A bit of (my) history. Ever since I was a young software engineer, I have been a pro open-source developer. I wanted from the start to contribute to open-source software, to have repositories that I can call my own that help others. I know that I will never have the impact that Spring, Thymeleaf, PostgreSQL, or Node, and so on had on the industry. But that does not stop me from trying to make people’s lives a tiny bit better. But life… had its ways of shifting priorities. So it took years until I managed to have an idea actually worth developing. It started as a proof-of-concept many years ago, before LLMs were popular. I coded in my spare time. I fixed bugs. I tried to get people to be interested in my project. And for a short time, I found moderate success with it. Don’t get me wrong, Flamewing (cause this is the project I am talking about) is not used anywhere. It is not even completely stable or ready for production use. But it is mine, and even now, I believe that the web needs a modern template engine for Spring Boot. However, Flamewing is not my only project. I had other ideas which I wanted to expand. I also discovered new technologies which I wanted to learn. I also discovered the need for software that wasn’t available in the form I wanted or was expensive. So, I tried to see how I could develop these other projects now that I was no longer limited by the knowledge I had accumulated in the 15+ years as a software engineer. Building became easy. After Flamewing, the first idea that I wanted to develop was a modern Text-to-Diagram engine. I had the idea a long time ago after being frustrated with how old PlantUML and later Mermaid seemed. I knew that documentation, UML diagrams, and flow charts needed something modern, lightweight, and elegant. But being a back-end developer, my front-end skills are not that advanced. And building them takes time, time which I don’t always have. And let’s be honest. No one will just come and say “Hey, this looks interesting. Let me contribute.” from the start. I knew I needed to have at least a partially functional product before I could even share it with the world. So, with the help of AI, I managed to bridge the knowledge gap and release DrakoFlow. But now, building became the easy part. As it did in my case, AI allowed other developers to bridge the knowledge gaps, some of whom were far from being ready to wield such power. And it allowed even non-devs to build projects. There can be an entire debate related to the quality of those products, their usefulness, or their impact. But nonetheless, the market became flooded with applications of all sorts and sizes. Building became the easy part, at least for small and niche applications. And people thought that they could earn a lot of money in a short amount of time by using AI to build software. Or become more widely known. Or just hoping to help others. Now, when almost anyone can build an application, software is no longer the moat. Marketing became it! The flood of apps being posted on the internet. If you browse Reddit, you will see that daily tens of people write a post starting with “I built an app that…”. And almost as many posts with “Why am I stuck at 0 revenue?” The reasons why so many apps fail are complex, from bad marketing to apps that no one actually needs to just being too many alternatives already on the market. The trend is not only on Reddit. It is on HackerNews. It is on LinkedIn. It is on forums. It is even on the Google Play Store or Apple App Store. But even though the number of apps has exploded in the past two years, revenue from these apps has barely increased. So, you can say that AI has made software so widely available that we became overexposed to apps. However, almost every day I also see posts that contain the words “free” and “open-source”. Not everybody wants to become rich from their apps. Not everyone sees AI as a way to earn money. Many people see it as a way to give something back, to help others, to try to make a positive impact in the world, even if just a small one. Differentiating between “slop” and non-”slop” became harder. When so many applications are launched each day, most of which are assisted in the coding process by AI, it becomes really hard to know what is truly useful, truly well made, and what is not. The term “AI-slop” or “vibe-coded slop” can be seen all over the place, even where it is not the case. The software industry has changed, and in my opinion at least, you have to use all the tools you have if you want to remain competitive, including AI. When so many things are launched every single day, not only does it make it harder for useful projects to stand out, it requires a completely different set of skills just to make sure an app is not lost in the sea of vibe-coded software. And most developers don’t have the skills to properly market their app. Me included. Or the time and resources. So many projects get lost, their developers become frustrated, and abandon an idea that would have actually been good and helpful. Competing with paid software. There is another problem. Money. And I am not talking about wanting to get rich, or even earn from the free and open source software that you are releasing. Marketing an app requires money. Building an app requires money. Paying rent, food, gas, and so on requires money. Most software engineers who build open-source software have a job, so at least the last few are covered. But if you want your project to be known, it requires money to market it. Otherwise, paid alternatives will always be more well-known, and people who could truly benefit from your project won’t, simply because they don’t know it exists. So there is a dilemma that many open source software owners have to face. Do I make my software truly free, or do I gatekeep a few features and release a paid version, just so I can cover the costs? This is a dilemma I also had with DrakoFlow. I know that I have a good product. I know I want it to be free. But how can I compete with more established projects like PlantUML or Mermaid? Both have been on the market for far longer than Drako. Mermaid has money to spend on ads, marketing, onboarding, as well as a team of developers that can release integrations with more platforms. So the question “Will Drako be actually used?” was inevitable. I still don’t have an answer. When I can build my own, why should I contribute to other projects? This is another problem that AI has introduced in the open source community. When it became so easy to build a new project from scratch, people started to build products even though perfectly good, free, and even open-source alternatives already exist. I am no stranger to this either. I made a Git client in the exact way I wanted just because I could. I could have downloaded one that already exists. But no, I wanted to see if and how I could build my own, even if just for me. And like me are countless others. I did not even release the code to my Git client. But other people did. So now there are so many solutions for the same problem, including open source ones, that new projects fail to gain the needed momentum to actually be widely used. AI made it so that there are many solutions for a problem, but none of which becomes mature enough simply because people are starting from scratch each time, instead of helping one project to grow. Conclusions So, naturally, the question pops up: Is open-source dead? Will we be stuck with the same well-established projects from before the AI era? Did AI make it impossible for new ideas to flourish in the open source community? Will there ever be “a new Spring Boot”, “a new NodeJS”, “a new React?” And the answers? Open-source is not dead. AI transformed it, and projects needed to evolve. Developers needed to evolve. But new and interesting projects will always get launched. And in this forest of applications, there will always be a sapling that will grow into a mighty oak that will shadow over the rest.
items.summary_html:
Let’s not kid ourselves. Generative AI is here to stay. A door has been opened that can no longer be closed. Even if the AI bubble bursts, and it probably will in the not-too-distant future, LLMs won’t disappear. The progress that has been made and the vast amount of open-weight models more than guarantee that, even if OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral, and the others completely vanish (they won’t, but that is for another discussion), AI is here to stay. With the good and the bad.

Like most cutting-edge technologies that appeared throughout history, AI is not only a sensitive topic, but a complex one as well. There are people both on the Anti-AI and the Pro-AI side. And both parties have valid points to sustain their view. Because AI is not all good and it is not all bad. It is a tool. A very complex one that reshapes entire industries, but a tool nonetheless. And AI has done a lot of great work in the software industry, but also a lot of damage.

A bit of (my) history.

Ever since I was a young software engineer, I have been a pro open-source developer. I wanted from the start to contribute to open-source software, to have repositories that I can call my own that help others. I know that I will never have the impact that Spring, Thymeleaf, PostgreSQL, or Node, and so on had on the industry. But that does not stop me from trying to make people’s lives a tiny bit better. But life… had its ways of shifting priorities.

So it took years until I managed to have an idea actually worth developing. It started as a proof-of-concept many years ago, before LLMs were popular. I coded in my spare time. I fixed bugs. I tried to get people to be interested in my project. And for a short time, I found moderate success with it. Don’t get me wrong, Flamewing (cause this is the project I am talking about) is not used anywhere. It is not even completely stable or ready for production use. But it is mine, and even now, I believe that the web needs a modern template engine for Spring Boot.

However, Flamewing is not my only project. I had other ideas which I wanted to expand. I also discovered new technologies which I wanted to learn. I also discovered the need for software that wasn’t available in the form I wanted or was expensive. So, I tried to see how I could develop these other projects now that I was no longer limited by the knowledge I had accumulated in the 15+ years as a software engineer.

Building became easy.

After Flamewing, the first idea that I wanted to develop was a modern Text-to-Diagram engine. I had the idea a long time ago after being frustrated with how old PlantUML and later Mermaid seemed. I knew that documentation, UML diagrams, and flow charts needed something modern, lightweight, and elegant. But being a back-end developer, my front-end skills are not that advanced. And building them takes time, time which I don’t always have.

And let’s be honest. No one will just come and say “Hey, this looks interesting. Let me contribute.” from the start. I knew I needed to have at least a partially functional product before I could even share it with the world. So, with the help of AI, I managed to bridge the knowledge gap and release DrakoFlow.

But now, building became the easy part. As it did in my case, AI allowed other developers to bridge the knowledge gaps, some of whom were far from being ready to wield such power. And it allowed even non-devs to build projects. There can be an entire debate related to the quality of those products, their usefulness, or their impact. But nonetheless, the market became flooded with applications of all sorts and sizes.

Building became the easy part, at least for small and niche applications. And people thought that they could earn a lot of money in a short amount of time by using AI to build software. Or become more widely known. Or just hoping to help others. Now, when almost anyone can build an application, software is no longer the moat. Marketing became it!

The flood of apps being posted on the internet.

If you browse Reddit, you will see that daily tens of people write a post starting with “I built an app that…”. And almost as many posts with “Why am I stuck at 0 revenue?” The reasons why so many apps fail are complex, from bad marketing to apps that no one actually needs to just being too many alternatives already on the market.

The trend is not only on Reddit. It is on HackerNews. It is on LinkedIn. It is on forums. It is even on the Google Play Store or Apple App Store. But even though the number of apps has exploded in the past two years, revenue from these apps has barely increased.

So, you can say that AI has made software so widely available that we became overexposed to apps. However, almost every day I also see posts that contain the words “free” and “open-source”. Not everybody wants to become rich from their apps. Not everyone sees AI as a way to earn money. Many people see it as a way to give something back, to help others, to try to make a positive impact in the world, even if just a small one.

Differentiating between “slop” and non-”slop” became harder.
When so many applications are launched each day, most of which are assisted in the coding process by AI, it becomes really hard to know what is truly useful, truly well made, and what is not. The term “AI-slop” or “vibe-coded slop” can be seen all over the place, even where it is not the case. The software industry has changed, and in my opinion at least, you have to use all the tools you have if you want to remain competitive, including AI.

When so many things are launched every single day, not only does it make it harder for useful projects to stand out, it requires a completely different set of skills just to make sure an app is not lost in the sea of vibe-coded software. And most developers don’t have the skills to properly market their app. Me included. Or the time and resources.

So many projects get lost, their developers become frustrated, and abandon an idea that would have actually been good and helpful.

Competing with paid software.

There is another problem. Money. And I am not talking about wanting to get rich, or even earn from the free and open source software that you are releasing. Marketing an app requires money. Building an app requires money. Paying rent, food, gas, and so on requires money. Most software engineers who build open-source software have a job, so at least the last few are covered. But if you want your project to be known, it requires money to market it.

Otherwise, paid alternatives will always be more well-known, and people who could truly benefit from your project won’t, simply because they don’t know it exists. So there is a dilemma that many open source software owners have to face. Do I make my software truly free, or do I gatekeep a few features and release a paid version, just so I can cover the costs?

This is a dilemma I also had with DrakoFlow. I know that I have a good product. I know I want it to be free. But how can I compete with more established projects like PlantUML or Mermaid? Both have been on the market for far longer than Drako. Mermaid has money to spend on ads, marketing, onboarding, as well as a team of developers that can release integrations with more platforms. So the question “Will Drako be actually used?” was inevitable. I still don’t have an answer.

When I can build my own, why should I contribute to other projects?
This is another problem that AI has introduced in the open source community. When it became so easy to build a new project from scratch, people started to build products even though perfectly good, free, and even open-source alternatives already exist. I am no stranger to this either. I made a Git client in the exact way I wanted just because I could. I could have downloaded one that already exists. But no, I wanted to see if and how I could build my own, even if just for me.

And like me are countless others. I did not even release the code to my Git client. But other people did. So now there are so many solutions for the same problem, including open source ones, that new projects fail to gain the needed momentum to actually be widely used.

AI made it so that there are many solutions for a problem, but none of which becomes mature enough simply because people are starting from scratch each time, instead of helping one project to grow.

Conclusions

So, naturally, the question pops up: Is open-source dead? Will we be stuck with the same well-established projects from before the AI era? Did AI make it impossible for new ideas to flourish in the open source community? Will there ever be “a new Spring Boot”, “a new NodeJS”, “a new React?”

And the answers? Open-source is not dead. AI transformed it, and projects needed to evolve. Developers needed to evolve. But new and interesting projects will always get launched. And in this forest of applications, there will always be a sapling that will grow into a mighty oak that will shadow over the rest.

items.summary: 🌿 LinkUp: Touch Grass, Find Your People, Make Real Connections Less scrolling. More exploring. More people. More life. 🌱 This is my submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge — Week 1: Touch Grass, hosted by DEV. Challenge link: https://dev.to/challenges/hacktoberfest-week1-2026-10-05 🌳 The Idea Behind LinkUp Imagine a sunny Sunday morning. You feel like going cycling, exploring a nature trail, playing cricket, visiting a local café, taking photographs outdoors, or simply walking in a park. There is just one problem: you have nobody to go with. Friends are busy, plans fall through, and sometimes finding people with the same interests feels harder than the activity itself. That is why I built LinkUp. LinkUp is a community-driven platform designed to help people turn everyday plans into real-world experiences by connecting with others who want to do the same things. Inspired by the idea of touching grass and spending more time outside, LinkUp encourages people to step away from their screens, discover activities, meet like-minded people, and create memories together. Because sometimes, the best connection is the one that starts with a simple question: “Anyone up for a walk?” 🌿 🍃 What Can You Do with LinkUp? 🌱 1. Plant the Seed of an Idea Have an activity in mind? Create a plan by choosing an activity, setting the date and time, specifying a general location, defining the available spots, and adding a budget if needed. Your simple idea can become an invitation for someone else to join. 🤝 2. Find Your People Discover people who share your interests, whether you enjoy cycling, photography, sports, outdoor adventures, creative activities, or relaxed social meetups. You do not need an existing group of friends to get started. You just need an idea and a willingness to connect. 🗺️ 3. Explore What's Happening Around You Discover activities based on interests, categories, skill levels, budgets, schedules, and a selected geographic radius of 1–25 km. The goal is to make finding something to do — and someone to do it with — easier. 🌼 4. Turn Invitations into Experiences Send requests to join activities and let organizers manage incoming requests and available spots. Backend capacity controls help prevent overbooking, making activity coordination more reliable. 🎒 5. Plan Your Next Adventure with AI Assistance Sometimes you have the idea but are unsure how to organize it. LinkUp's AI-assisted activity planner helps turn a rough concept into a structured draft with an activity description, an agenda, a packing checklist, and relevant safety guidance. For example: “A beginner-friendly cycling morning.” “A photography walk in a green park.” “An outdoor sketching session for creative people.” “A relaxed weekend nature walk.” The AI assistant helps with the planning, while the organizer stays in control of reviewing and publishing the activity. 🌍 6. Spend More Time in the Real World LinkUp is built around a simple belief: technology should help us experience more of life, not just spend more time looking at screens. It is for students, newcomers to a city, hobby enthusiasts, outdoor explorers, and anyone who wants to meet people through shared experiences. The idea is not to replace online connections. It is to give those connections a chance to grow into something real. 🌿 Try LinkUp 🌐 Live Demo: https://meetup-pulse.netlify.app/ Explore the live application and see how LinkUp brings activity discovery, planning, and participation together. 💻 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/Aryan544-arch/Link-Up Explore the source code, learn about the implementation, and follow the project's development. Contributions, suggestions, and feedback are welcome! 🌲 How I Built It LinkUp is a full-stack web application with a separate frontend and backend. This structure keeps the user interface separate from server-side logic and makes the application easier to maintain and extend. 🌿 Technology Stack Frontend: React 18, JavaScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and Lucide Icons. Backend: Node.js and Express.js REST API. Database: MongoDB and Mongoose, including GeoJSON geospatial indexing. Authentication: Cookie-based sessions using "express-session" and a MongoDB session store. Security: Helmet security headers, rate limiting, and CORS validation. API Communication: Axios with credentialed requests. Core Features: Activity discovery, geographic radius filtering, privacy-aware location display, join requests, organizer management, and a My Plans dashboard. Testing: More than 330 reported automated tests across backend and frontend suites, covering areas such as session persistence, capacity protection, and API contract integrity. 🔐 Privacy Matters Meeting new people should come with thoughtful privacy protections. LinkUp uses session-based authentication with secure HttpOnly cookies instead of storing sensitive authentication tokens in browser local storage. The application also masks precise GPS coordinates for non-organizers, showing general neighborhood information instead to help protect participants' privacy. The aim is to make discovering activities easier while treating user information responsibly. 🤖 Bringing Open-Source AI into the Outdoors AI is not the destination of LinkUp. It is a tool to help people get there. An Extensible AI Architecture The activity-planning engine is implemented in "apps/api/src/services/ai.service.js" and uses a provider-based architecture. The project has been designed around Google's Gemma model family and Gemini API integration, with model selection configurable through environment variables. The backend exposes a dedicated planning endpoint: "POST /api/ai/plan-activity" The external provider must be configured and verified for live model-generated responses. When an external provider is unavailable or unconfigured, the application can use its built-in fallback. From a Simple Thought to a Structured Plan An organizer can describe an activity in natural language and use the planning assistant to draft: An engaging activity title. A description with a suggested agenda and flow. A tailored packing checklist. Activity-specific safety guidelines. This can reduce the effort involved in organizing an activity and help people get from an idea to an actionable plan. A Fallback That Keeps Planning Available LinkUp includes a deterministic planning engine that uses rules and heuristics to create activity-specific suggestions. It covers categories such as hiking, photography, cycling, running, sports, yoga, board games, creative arts, nature exploration, and social meetups. This fallback can operate without an external AI API key. It is not an LLM, and its output is distinguished from AI-provider output through response metadata. People Stay in Control AI-generated plans are drafts, not decisions. The organizer reviews and edits the content before publishing. The AI does not automatically publish activities or confirm attendance. This human-in-the-loop approach keeps the technology in a supporting role while people make the final decisions. 🌻 What's Next for AI in LinkUp? Future enhancements could include: Browser-based Gemma inference using WebGPU or ONNX Runtime. Conversational activity discovery and natural-language search. Better activity recommendations based on interests. Compatibility-based attendee matching. More personalized suggestions for outdoor activities and community events. I want to explore AI in ways that make real-world participation easier rather than adding technology without a meaningful purpose. 🌎 Why Open Innovation Matters Nature thrives on diversity, collaboration, and interconnected ecosystems. I see a similar opportunity in open-source software. Open innovation allows developers to explore the code, learn from the architecture, suggest improvements, and contribute new ideas. LinkUp offers opportunities to experiment with: Better activity recommendations and matching algorithms. Natural-language planning and voice-based activity creation. Accessibility, internationalization, and multilingual support. Improved safety, privacy, and community moderation. New activity categories and neighborhood-level community features. Alternative open-weight AI models and improved evaluation methods. Open-source AI gives developers more flexibility to experiment with different models and build solutions around real needs. For LinkUp, that means exploring how technology can help people discover shared interests, coordinate plans, and build stronger communities. 🛠️ My Agent Session I used AI-assisted pair programming to help design the system architecture, implement authentication flows, develop automated tests, investigate integration issues, and reconcile changes across Git branches. Working with an AI coding partner helped accelerate development and testing while keeping attention on product requirements, database consistency, and user privacy. The experience also reinforced an important lesson: generated code still needs to be reviewed, tested, and verified. Building a working application requires more than generating code — it requires understanding how its parts fit together. 🌿 Team and Credits LinkUp was developed collaboratively across four core functional areas: @aryan_9852 @vipin00004 @princesharma00007 @shivalika_f3c425e435190b9 Frontend and UX: Responsive React/Vite interface, activity discovery cards, location pickers, and the My Plans dashboard. Backend and Marketplace: Express REST API, Mongoose schemas, capacity protection for join requests, and matching services. Authentication and AI Foundation: Session-based authentication, rate limiting, and the AI-assisted activity-planning engine with deterministic fallback. Integration, QA, and Deployment: API contract reconciliation, automated testing, safety features, and deployment verification. Thanks to the open-source community, Google for its Gemma model family, and the DEV team for organizing the Touch Grass challenge. 🌱 Final Thoughts: Let's Touch Grass We spend so much of our lives online, yet some of our best memories happen outdoors — on a cycling trail, during a spontaneous walk, over a game of cricket, or while discovering a new place with people we have just met. Sometimes, all it takes is one person sharing a plan for someone else to say, “I'm in!” LinkUp is my attempt to make that first step easier. Create a plan. Find your people. Step outside. Make memories. 🌐 Live Demo: https://meetup-pulse.netlify.app/ 💻 GitHub: https://github.com/Aryan544-arch/Link-Up Less scrolling. More exploring. More connections. More life. 🌿 Let's touch grass, meet people, and turn plans into experiences. 🌱
items.summary_html:
🌿 LinkUp: Touch Grass, Find Your People, Make Real Connections

Less scrolling. More exploring. More people. More life. 🌱

This is my submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge — Week 1: Touch Grass, hosted by DEV.

Challenge link: https://dev.to/challenges/hacktoberfest-week1-2026-10-05

🌳 The Idea Behind LinkUp

Imagine a sunny Sunday morning. You feel like going cycling, exploring a nature trail, playing cricket, visiting a local café, taking photographs outdoors, or simply walking in a park.

There is just one problem: you have nobody to go with.

Friends are busy, plans fall through, and sometimes finding people with the same interests feels harder than the activity itself.

That is why I built LinkUp.

LinkUp is a community-driven platform designed to help people turn everyday plans into real-world experiences by connecting with others who want to do the same things.

Inspired by the idea of touching grass and spending more time outside, LinkUp encourages people to step away from their screens, discover activities, meet like-minded people, and create memories together.

Because sometimes, the best connection is the one that starts with a simple question:

“Anyone up for a walk?” 🌿

🍃 What Can You Do with LinkUp?

🌱 1. Plant the Seed of an Idea

Have an activity in mind? Create a plan by choosing an activity, setting the date and time, specifying a general location, defining the available spots, and adding a budget if needed.

Your simple idea can become an invitation for someone else to join.

🤝 2. Find Your People

Discover people who share your interests, whether you enjoy cycling, photography, sports, outdoor adventures, creative activities, or relaxed social meetups.

You do not need an existing group of friends to get started. You just need an idea and a willingness to connect.

🗺️ 3. Explore What's Happening Around You

Discover activities based on interests, categories, skill levels, budgets, schedules, and a selected geographic radius of 1–25 km.

The goal is to make finding something to do — and someone to do it with — easier.

🌼 4. Turn Invitations into Experiences

Send requests to join activities and let organizers manage incoming requests and available spots.

Backend capacity controls help prevent overbooking, making activity coordination more reliable.

🎒 5. Plan Your Next Adventure with AI Assistance

Sometimes you have the idea but are unsure how to organize it.

LinkUp's AI-assisted activity planner helps turn a rough concept into a structured draft with an activity description, an agenda, a packing checklist, and relevant safety guidance.

For example:

  • “A beginner-friendly cycling morning.”
  • “A photography walk in a green park.”
  • “An outdoor sketching session for creative people.”
  • “A relaxed weekend nature walk.”

The AI assistant helps with the planning, while the organizer stays in control of reviewing and publishing the activity.

🌍 6. Spend More Time in the Real World

LinkUp is built around a simple belief: technology should help us experience more of life, not just spend more time looking at screens.

It is for students, newcomers to a city, hobby enthusiasts, outdoor explorers, and anyone who wants to meet people through shared experiences.

The idea is not to replace online connections. It is to give those connections a chance to grow into something real.

🌿 Try LinkUp

🌐 Live Demo: https://meetup-pulse.netlify.app/

Explore the live application and see how LinkUp brings activity discovery, planning, and participation together.

💻 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/Aryan544-arch/Link-Up

Explore the source code, learn about the implementation, and follow the project's development.

Contributions, suggestions, and feedback are welcome!

🌲 How I Built It

LinkUp is a full-stack web application with a separate frontend and backend. This structure keeps the user interface separate from server-side logic and makes the application easier to maintain and extend.

🌿 Technology Stack

  • Frontend: React 18, JavaScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and Lucide Icons.
  • Backend: Node.js and Express.js REST API.
  • Database: MongoDB and Mongoose, including GeoJSON geospatial indexing.
  • Authentication: Cookie-based sessions using "express-session" and a MongoDB session store.
  • Security: Helmet security headers, rate limiting, and CORS validation.
  • API Communication: Axios with credentialed requests.
  • Core Features: Activity discovery, geographic radius filtering, privacy-aware location display, join requests, organizer management, and a My Plans dashboard.
  • Testing: More than 330 reported automated tests across backend and frontend suites, covering areas such as session persistence, capacity protection, and API contract integrity.

🔐 Privacy Matters

Meeting new people should come with thoughtful privacy protections.

LinkUp uses session-based authentication with secure HttpOnly cookies instead of storing sensitive authentication tokens in browser local storage.

The application also masks precise GPS coordinates for non-organizers, showing general neighborhood information instead to help protect participants' privacy.

The aim is to make discovering activities easier while treating user information responsibly.

🤖 Bringing Open-Source AI into the Outdoors

AI is not the destination of LinkUp. It is a tool to help people get there.

  1. An Extensible AI Architecture

The activity-planning engine is implemented in "apps/api/src/services/ai.service.js" and uses a provider-based architecture.

The project has been designed around Google's Gemma model family and Gemini API integration, with model selection configurable through environment variables.

The backend exposes a dedicated planning endpoint:

"POST /api/ai/plan-activity"

The external provider must be configured and verified for live model-generated responses. When an external provider is unavailable or unconfigured, the application can use its built-in fallback.

  1. From a Simple Thought to a Structured Plan

An organizer can describe an activity in natural language and use the planning assistant to draft:

  • An engaging activity title.
  • A description with a suggested agenda and flow.
  • A tailored packing checklist.
  • Activity-specific safety guidelines.

This can reduce the effort involved in organizing an activity and help people get from an idea to an actionable plan.

  1. A Fallback That Keeps Planning Available

LinkUp includes a deterministic planning engine that uses rules and heuristics to create activity-specific suggestions.

It covers categories such as hiking, photography, cycling, running, sports, yoga, board games, creative arts, nature exploration, and social meetups.

This fallback can operate without an external AI API key. It is not an LLM, and its output is distinguished from AI-provider output through response metadata.

  1. People Stay in Control

AI-generated plans are drafts, not decisions.

The organizer reviews and edits the content before publishing. The AI does not automatically publish activities or confirm attendance.

This human-in-the-loop approach keeps the technology in a supporting role while people make the final decisions.

🌻 What's Next for AI in LinkUp?

Future enhancements could include:

  • Browser-based Gemma inference using WebGPU or ONNX Runtime.
  • Conversational activity discovery and natural-language search.
  • Better activity recommendations based on interests.
  • Compatibility-based attendee matching.
  • More personalized suggestions for outdoor activities and community events.

I want to explore AI in ways that make real-world participation easier rather than adding technology without a meaningful purpose.

🌎 Why Open Innovation Matters

Nature thrives on diversity, collaboration, and interconnected ecosystems. I see a similar opportunity in open-source software.

Open innovation allows developers to explore the code, learn from the architecture, suggest improvements, and contribute new ideas.

LinkUp offers opportunities to experiment with:

  • Better activity recommendations and matching algorithms.
  • Natural-language planning and voice-based activity creation.
  • Accessibility, internationalization, and multilingual support.
  • Improved safety, privacy, and community moderation.
  • New activity categories and neighborhood-level community features.
  • Alternative open-weight AI models and improved evaluation methods.

Open-source AI gives developers more flexibility to experiment with different models and build solutions around real needs.

For LinkUp, that means exploring how technology can help people discover shared interests, coordinate plans, and build stronger communities.

🛠️ My Agent Session

I used AI-assisted pair programming to help design the system architecture, implement authentication flows, develop automated tests, investigate integration issues, and reconcile changes across Git branches.

Working with an AI coding partner helped accelerate development and testing while keeping attention on product requirements, database consistency, and user privacy.

The experience also reinforced an important lesson: generated code still needs to be reviewed, tested, and verified. Building a working application requires more than generating code — it requires understanding how its parts fit together.

🌿 Team and Credits

LinkUp was developed collaboratively across four core functional areas:
@aryan_9852
@vipin00004
@princesharma00007
@shivalika_f3c425e435190b9

  • Frontend and UX: Responsive React/Vite interface, activity discovery cards, location pickers, and the My Plans dashboard.
  • Backend and Marketplace: Express REST API, Mongoose schemas, capacity protection for join requests, and matching services.
  • Authentication and AI Foundation: Session-based authentication, rate limiting, and the AI-assisted activity-planning engine with deterministic fallback.
  • Integration, QA, and Deployment: API contract reconciliation, automated testing, safety features, and deployment verification.

Thanks to the open-source community, Google for its Gemma model family, and the DEV team for organizing the Touch Grass challenge.

🌱 Final Thoughts: Let's Touch Grass

We spend so much of our lives online, yet some of our best memories happen outdoors — on a cycling trail, during a spontaneous walk, over a game of cricket, or while discovering a new place with people we have just met.

Sometimes, all it takes is one person sharing a plan for someone else to say, “I'm in!”

LinkUp is my attempt to make that first step easier.

Create a plan. Find your people. Step outside. Make memories.

🌐 Live Demo: https://meetup-pulse.netlify.app/

💻 GitHub: https://github.com/Aryan544-arch/Link-Up

Less scrolling. More exploring. More connections. More life. 🌿

Let's touch grass, meet people, and turn plans into experiences. 🌱

items.title: Field-Note: Turning Real-World Observations into Evidence-Backed AI Drafts
items.summary: title: "Field-Note: Turning Real-World Observations into Evidence-Backed AI Drafts" published: false tags: devchallenge, hf26challenge This is a submission for the "Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge — Week 1: Touch Grass" ( https://dev.to/challenges/hacktoberfest-week1-2026-10-05 ). What I Built Field-Note is a mobile-friendly field observation application designed to help people record real-world activities, preserve supporting evidence, and turn their observations into structured, AI-assisted draft findings. Fieldwork often involves taking photographs, recording notes, and documenting activities on construction sites or during inspections. Keeping these details organized and connecting observations to their supporting evidence can be difficult. Field-Note brings these elements together in one place. Users can: Capture field notes with a title and written description. Attach photographic and audio evidence. Optionally record their location. Save observations locally in their browser. Request AI-assisted analysis to generate structured draft findings when the backend and AI provider are configured. The central principle behind Field-Note is simple: AI proposes. Evidence proves. Humans verify. AI-generated findings remain drafts rather than verified facts. The original observation and its evidence remain the basis for human review. Demo Live application: "Open Field-Note" ( https://special-potato-x55797pvqrrrf6q5x-5173.app.github.dev/observations/af775afd-7b78-4b18-a266-bb4be0f0eccf ) Note: This is a temporary GitHub Codespaces development URL. The application may be unavailable when the Codespace is stopped. The linked observation is an example from the development environment, not a permanent public demo. Demo video: To be added if available. Code GitHub repository: https://github.com/Shorunkemanuel/Field-Note Field-Note is developed as an open-source project. The repository contains the application source code, backend API, frontend, and tests. How I Built It Field-Note uses a React and TypeScript frontend, Vite for development and building, and a Python backend built with FastAPI. The application uses browser-based storage to preserve field observations and their evidence on the user's device. The backend provides APIs for retrieving observations and requesting AI-assisted extraction. The AI integration uses an OpenAI-compatible provider interface. This allows the backend to communicate with compatible inference services through server-side configuration rather than exposing API credentials in the frontend. The extraction workflow is designed to produce structured findings containing descriptions, categories, supporting evidence references, reasoning, uncertainty, confidence where available, and suggested actions. The application also validates the model's structured output and checks that referenced evidence belongs to the material actually analyzed. AI-generated findings are explicitly marked as drafts. They are not automatically treated as verified inspection results. The project is still being tested, particularly the external AI provider integration. The core application and its AI extraction workflow should be described according to the functionality verified in the final demo. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Field-Note explores how open-source software and open-weight AI models can support practical tools for people working outside traditional office environments. Open innovation gives developers the flexibility to experiment with different model providers, inspect the application architecture, adapt the software to their needs, and build on existing technologies. A provider-independent integration also makes it easier to evaluate alternative inference services instead of permanently tying the application to one vendor. For fieldwork, the goal is not simply to generate text with AI. It is to make observations easier to organize while maintaining a clear connection between AI-generated suggestions and the evidence that supports them. Keeping AI findings as drafts helps preserve human judgment and accountability. My Agent Session Agent session: Not included yet. title: "Field-Note: Turning Real-World Observations into Evidence-Backed AI Drafts"
published: false
tags: devchallenge, hf26challenge

This is a submission for the "Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge — Week 1: Touch Grass" (https://dev.to/challenges/hacktoberfest-week1-2026-10-05).

What I Built

Field-Note is a mobile-friendly field observation application designed to help people record real-world activities, preserve supporting evidence, and turn their observations into structured, AI-assisted draft findings.

Fieldwork often involves taking photographs, recording notes, and documenting activities on construction sites or during inspections. Keeping these details organized and connecting observations to their supporting evidence can be difficult.

Field-Note brings these elements together in one place.

Users can:

  • Capture field notes with a title and written description.
  • Attach photographic and audio evidence.
  • Optionally record their location.
  • Save observations locally in their browser.
  • Request AI-assisted analysis to generate structured draft findings when the backend and AI provider are configured.

The central principle behind Field-Note is simple: AI proposes. Evidence proves. Humans verify.

AI-generated findings remain drafts rather than verified facts. The original observation and its evidence remain the basis for human review.

Demo

Live application: "Open Field-Note" (https://special-potato-x55797pvqrrrf6q5x-5173.app.github.dev/observations/af775afd-7b78-4b18-a266-bb4be0f0eccf)

Note: This is a temporary GitHub Codespaces development URL. The application may be unavailable when the Codespace is stopped. The linked observation is an example from the development environment, not a permanent public demo.

Demo video: To be added if available.

Code

GitHub repository: https://github.com/Shorunkemanuel/Field-Note

Field-Note is developed as an open-source project. The repository contains the application source code, backend API, frontend, and tests.

How I Built It

Field-Note uses a React and TypeScript frontend, Vite for development and building, and a Python backend built with FastAPI.

The application uses browser-based storage to preserve field observations and their evidence on the user's device. The backend provides APIs for retrieving observations and requesting AI-assisted extraction.

The AI integration uses an OpenAI-compatible provider interface. This allows the backend to communicate with compatible inference services through server-side configuration rather than exposing API credentials in the frontend.

The extraction workflow is designed to produce structured findings containing descriptions, categories, supporting evidence references, reasoning, uncertainty, confidence where available, and suggested actions.

The application also validates the model's structured output and checks that referenced evidence belongs to the material actually analyzed.

AI-generated findings are explicitly marked as drafts. They are not automatically treated as verified inspection results.

The project is still being tested, particularly the external AI provider integration. The core application and its AI extraction workflow should be described according to the functionality verified in the final demo.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Field-Note explores how open-source software and open-weight AI models can support practical tools for people working outside traditional office environments.

Open innovation gives developers the flexibility to experiment with different model providers, inspect the application architecture, adapt the software to their needs, and build on existing technologies.

A provider-independent integration also makes it easier to evaluate alternative inference services instead of permanently tying the application to one vendor.

For fieldwork, the goal is not simply to generate text with AI. It is to make observations easier to organize while maintaining a clear connection between AI-generated suggestions and the evidence that supports them.

Keeping AI findings as drafts helps preserve human judgment and accountability.

items.title: One Seller, Five Inboxes: Operating Customer Support Across Marketplaces Without Losing Threads
items.summary: Most multi-channel support pain is not volume — it is fragmentation. A buyer asks about sizing on one marketplace chat, follows up about shipping on another, and leaves a review mentioning both. The seller answers each inbox in isolation and accidentally gives two different answers. When you run several storefronts, the hardest problem is not answering fast; it is knowing that two conversations are the same conversation. Why marketplace inboxes resist consolidation Each platform guards its chat as an in-app experience: reply templates, response-time scorecards, and search all live inside the platform's own console. Official APIs exist but are uneven — some expose webhooks, some only polling, some rate-limit aggressively during the exact sales events when message volume peaks. So the realistic architecture is not "one inbox to rule them all" but a sync layer that pulls messages from each console into one working view while replies still go out through each platform's rules. The identity problem: same buyer, different accounts Cross-store buyer identity is the core technical challenge. Three signals, in descending order of reliability: Platform user IDs — authoritative within one platform, useless across two. Order and address matching — same shipping address or order phone number strongly implies one buyer; normalize phone formats before comparing, or you will miss half the matches. Behavioral fingerprints — writing style, question patterns, active hours. Weak alone, useful as a tie-breaker. Design rule: identity matching proposes, humans confirm. Auto-merging two different buyers is far more damaging than leaving two threads of the same buyer unmerged for an hour. Merge rules that survive contact with reality Time-window threading. Messages from the same buyer within a short window belong to one conversation, regardless of which storefront they arrived on. Without this, you answer the shipping question and miss that the sizing question is still open. Intent deduplication. If a buyer has asked the same thing in two places, reply once — in the thread where they asked — and reference the other. Answering the same question twice in two inboxes reads as robotic in both. Priority overrides. Paid-not-shipped beats after-sales beats pre-sales beats everything else, no matter which inbox each message sits in. Sellers who triage per-inbox systematically answer the easy inbox first, not the urgent one. One answer, one source. Policies like shipping cutoffs and return windows should live in one place that feeds every channel's reply templates. The "two different answers" failure is almost never a typing mistake; it is two copies of the truth drifting apart. What breaks during big sales events Traffic spikes arrive at the same hour on every platform simultaneously. Three preparations matter more than any tool: pre-write reply templates for the top questions the event will generate (promo mechanics, shipping deadlines, price-match complaints); lower your per-conversation ambition — during peak, fast correct answers to high-intent messages beat thoughtful answers to everything; and decide in advance which channels get human hours and which run on auto-reply plus a callback promise. Measuring a multi-channel operation Cross-store duplicate rate — how many buyer threads were the same underlying question. High values mean your merge rules are too weak. Per-channel response time against each platform's scorecard — because marketplace algorithms punish slow channels independently. Answer consistency — sample cross-store conversations weekly and check the two threads got the same policy answer. Escalation latency — how long a message marked "needs human" waits during peak, per channel. How we run it We build auto-reply tooling for e-commerce sellers who run multiple storefronts under Dingdang CS ; our write-up on built-in reply configuration across seven platforms covers the per-platform template rules and the daily operating rhythm for solo operators.

items.title: Log Off: One Real Place. One Small Activity. Local Gemma.
items.summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass What I Built At 4:00 PM in Kharghar, I gave a local model a deceptively small job: stop offering me choices and choose one real place I could walk to and return from in 30 minutes. The map pipeline found CIDCO Park seven minutes south, the timing code kept the outing inside daylight, and the interface reduced everything to one ticket. That test became Log Off . Log Off turns four quick choices into one reason to close the laptop. You choose your mood, how much time you have, your energy, and whether you are alone. It then: finds real nearby outdoor places from OpenStreetMap; checks walking time, current weather, sunrise, and sunset; asks a local Gemma 4 model for one small activity at a place that actually fits; and shows one ticket with where to go, what to do, when to leave, and when to be back. The model does not decide distances or invent the schedule. Code owns those facts. The goal is to make the screen the shortest part of the experience. Demo Log Off runs locally on a laptop, so there is no hosted demo. Setup and run instructions are in the README. Here is the complete screen flow: 1. Pick what you need from the break. Four compact choices give the planner enough context without turning the break into another questionnaire. 2. Take one ticket and leave the screen. The result gives one real place, one activity, and the leave-by and back-by times calculated by code. Code rahultapase / log-off Log Off Log Off turns a few preferences into one short reason to leave the screen. Pick a mood, the time available, your energy, and whether you are alone. The app finds a real nearby place, works out a safe walking window around daylight and weather, and asks a local Gemma 4 model for one small activity to do there. The result is a single outing ticket with where to go, when to leave, when to be back, and a task that needs no phone, purchase, or equipment. Built for the DEV Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 1: Touch Grass . Screenshots How it works Log Off keeps facts and generation separate: Find facts. A typed area or browser location is rounded to three decimal places before the app requests nearby places from OpenStreetMap and daylight and weather data from Open-Meteo. Build a shortlist. Python code calculates walking time and… View on GitHub FastAPI, TypeScript, Vite, local Gemma 4 through Ollama, and 104 backend tests. Repository: github.com/rahultapase/log-off How I Built It Log Off has three deliberate layers: facts, generation, and validation. 1. Facts before AI. A FastAPI backend uses OpenStreetMap for geocoding and nearby places, then Open-Meteo for weather, sunrise, and sunset. Python code rounds outbound coordinates, calculates walking time and compass direction, merges duplicate map entries, and filters out anything that cannot fit the selected time budget. That produces a numbered shortlist of real places. It also decides whether the outing can happen now or should move to just after sunrise. Gemma never calculates any of this. 2. A local Gemma task writer. Gemma 4 E2B runs locally through Ollama. It receives mood, energy, company, weather, and the numbered shortlist, but no coordinates. Its job is narrow: select one candidate ID and return a short, equipment-free activity as structured JSON. I found that the model was much more useful after code supplied a task style for each mood and energy combination. The first prompt often returned variations of "relax in the park." The final prompt asks for a concrete, finishable observation, investigation, movement, or social task. 3. A factual guardrail. Every model response passes through a validator that checks: valid JSON and schema; a place ID from the supplied shortlist; an activity duration that fits after the round-trip walk; invented place or street names; forbidden distances and clock times; and extra safety constraints for darkness and rain. A rejected response gets one repair attempt. If Ollama is unavailable or both attempts fail, a built-in deterministic activity keeps the ticket usable. The explanation visible to the user is also generated from code facts, not from Gemma's free-text reasoning. 4. I measured it. For the main evaluation, I ran 24 combinations of mood, time, company, and energy at 4:00 PM: Result with Gemma 4 E2B Measured value Valid on the first attempt 23 of 24 Fixed on the single retry 1 of 24 Deterministic fallback used 0 of 24 Invented-place runs 0 of 24 Median model-call latency 2.8 seconds Maximum model-call latency 3.2 seconds The most useful failure was not a hallucination. For a social, with-others, low-energy request, Gemma suggested: "Start a simple card game like Uno." It passed the factual validator but needed equipment, despite the prompt. The validator can prove that an answer fits known facts; it cannot yet prove that the idea is good. That distinction is now an explicit limitation instead of a hidden one. 5. I swapped the model. With the same 12 preference sets, gemma3:1b passed 0 of 12 answers on the first attempt. Eleven were repaired and one fell back safely. Gemma 4 was much more reliable, but the open setup let me measure that difference inside the real application. 6. I kept the final screen quiet. The browser interface is TypeScript and Vite. It uses a daylight arc, accessible controls, visible focus states, reduced-motion support, and one final screen designed to be left behind. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? The model does not need my location. Gemma runs on my laptop through Ollama, so no location is sent to a model provider, no model API key is needed, and inference has no per-request fee. I can inspect the full prompt, constrain its role, keep evaluation results locally, and replace the model without redesigning the app. I could test model sizes on the real task. The Gemma 3 and Gemma 4 comparison used the same planner, validator, preference sets, and hardware. I could choose based on measured reliability instead of a general benchmark or pricing page. Open data keeps generation grounded. OpenStreetMap provides inspectable place IDs and geometry, while Open-Meteo provides weather and daylight data under an open licence. Together they let the model write around facts instead of pretending to know the user's surroundings. Open does not automatically mean offline. Place and weather lookups still need the internet. It does mean I can draw a clear privacy boundary: rounded coordinates go to open-data services, while Gemma stays local and never sees them. It also means the failure handling is mine to test, explain, and improve. Limitations The 24-run evaluation is a focused application test, not a general model benchmark. The validator checks facts and safety rules, not taste. The Uno suggestion passed. Weather describes current conditions even when an after-dark outing moves to tomorrow morning. Place and weather lookups need internet access, even though model inference is local. What's next Take Log Off on a real outing, add an equipment-language validator rule, use forecast data for next-morning plans, and compare more small local models on the same evaluation set. Prize Categories Best Use of Gemma : Gemma 4 E2B writes the activity locally, and Gemma 3 1B provides the measured comparison.

This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass

What I Built

At 4:00 PM in Kharghar, I gave a local model a deceptively small job: stop offering me choices and choose one real place I could walk to and return from in 30 minutes. The map pipeline found CIDCO Park seven minutes south, the timing code kept the outing inside daylight, and the interface reduced everything to one ticket. That test became Log Off.

Log Off turns four quick choices into one reason to close the laptop. You choose your mood, how much time you have, your energy, and whether you are alone. It then:

  • finds real nearby outdoor places from OpenStreetMap;
  • checks walking time, current weather, sunrise, and sunset;
  • asks a local Gemma 4 model for one small activity at a place that actually fits; and
  • shows one ticket with where to go, what to do, when to leave, and when to be back.

The model does not decide distances or invent the schedule. Code owns those facts. The goal is to make the screen the shortest part of the experience.

Demo

Log Off runs locally on a laptop, so there is no hosted demo. Setup and run instructions are in the README. Here is the complete screen flow:

1. Pick what you need from the break. Four compact choices give the planner enough context without turning the break into another questionnaire.

2. Take one ticket and leave the screen. The result gives one real place, one activity, and the leave-by and back-by times calculated by code.

Code
rahultapase / log-off
Log Off

Log Off turns a few preferences into one short reason to leave the screen. Pick a mood, the time available, your energy, and whether you are alone. The app finds a real nearby place, works out a safe walking window around daylight and weather, and asks a local Gemma 4 model for one small activity to do there.

The result is a single outing ticket with where to go, when to leave, when to be back, and a task that needs no phone, purchase, or equipment.

Built for the DEV Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 1: Touch Grass.

Screenshots

How it works

Log Off keeps facts and generation separate:

  1. Find facts. A typed area or browser location is rounded to three decimal places before the app requests nearby places from OpenStreetMap and daylight and weather data from Open-Meteo.
  2. Build a shortlist. Python code calculates walking time and…


View on GitHub


FastAPI, TypeScript, Vite, local Gemma 4 through Ollama, and 104 backend tests.

Repository: github.com/rahultapase/log-off

How I Built It

Log Off has three deliberate layers: facts, generation, and validation.

1. Facts before AI. A FastAPI backend uses OpenStreetMap for geocoding and nearby places, then Open-Meteo for weather, sunrise, and sunset. Python code rounds outbound coordinates, calculates walking time and compass direction, merges duplicate map entries, and filters out anything that cannot fit the selected time budget.

That produces a numbered shortlist of real places. It also decides whether the outing can happen now or should move to just after sunrise. Gemma never calculates any of this.

2. A local Gemma task writer. Gemma 4 E2B runs locally through Ollama. It receives mood, energy, company, weather, and the numbered shortlist, but no coordinates. Its job is narrow: select one candidate ID and return a short, equipment-free activity as structured JSON.

I found that the model was much more useful after code supplied a task style for each mood and energy combination. The first prompt often returned variations of "relax in the park." The final prompt asks for a concrete, finishable observation, investigation, movement, or social task.

3. A factual guardrail. Every model response passes through a validator that checks:

  • valid JSON and schema;
  • a place ID from the supplied shortlist;
  • an activity duration that fits after the round-trip walk;
  • invented place or street names;
  • forbidden distances and clock times; and
  • extra safety constraints for darkness and rain.

A rejected response gets one repair attempt. If Ollama is unavailable or both attempts fail, a built-in deterministic activity keeps the ticket usable. The explanation visible to the user is also generated from code facts, not from Gemma's free-text reasoning.

4. I measured it. For the main evaluation, I ran 24 combinations of mood, time, company, and energy at 4:00 PM:

Result with Gemma 4 E2B Measured value Valid on the first attempt 23 of 24 Fixed on the single retry 1 of 24 Deterministic fallback used 0 of 24 Invented-place runs 0 of 24 Median model-call latency 2.8 seconds Maximum model-call latency 3.2 seconds

The most useful failure was not a hallucination. For a social, with-others, low-energy request, Gemma suggested: "Start a simple card game like Uno." It passed the factual validator but needed equipment, despite the prompt. The validator can prove that an answer fits known facts; it cannot yet prove that the idea is good. That distinction is now an explicit limitation instead of a hidden one.

5. I swapped the model. With the same 12 preference sets, gemma3:1b passed 0 of 12 answers on the first attempt. Eleven were repaired and one fell back safely. Gemma 4 was much more reliable, but the open setup let me measure that difference inside the real application.

6. I kept the final screen quiet. The browser interface is TypeScript and Vite. It uses a daylight arc, accessible controls, visible focus states, reduced-motion support, and one final screen designed to be left behind.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

The model does not need my location. Gemma runs on my laptop through Ollama, so no location is sent to a model provider, no model API key is needed, and inference has no per-request fee. I can inspect the full prompt, constrain its role, keep evaluation results locally, and replace the model without redesigning the app.

I could test model sizes on the real task. The Gemma 3 and Gemma 4 comparison used the same planner, validator, preference sets, and hardware. I could choose based on measured reliability instead of a general benchmark or pricing page.

Open data keeps generation grounded. OpenStreetMap provides inspectable place IDs and geometry, while Open-Meteo provides weather and daylight data under an open licence. Together they let the model write around facts instead of pretending to know the user's surroundings.

Open does not automatically mean offline. Place and weather lookups still need the internet. It does mean I can draw a clear privacy boundary: rounded coordinates go to open-data services, while Gemma stays local and never sees them. It also means the failure handling is mine to test, explain, and improve.

Limitations
  • The 24-run evaluation is a focused application test, not a general model benchmark.
  • The validator checks facts and safety rules, not taste. The Uno suggestion passed.
  • Weather describes current conditions even when an after-dark outing moves to tomorrow morning.
  • Place and weather lookups need internet access, even though model inference is local.
What's next

Take Log Off on a real outing, add an equipment-language validator rule, use forecast data for next-morning plans, and compare more small local models on the same evaluation set.

Prize Categories
  • Best Use of Gemma: Gemma 4 E2B writes the activity locally, and Gemma 3 1B provides the measured comparison.

items.title: How OpenSeal's Agent Architecture Works
items.summary: Let’s trace one task through OpenSeal. Suppose an agent is preparing a draft and needs approval before an action can send it. We want to see where the task lives, how a worker gets its next step, and what happens while a person reviews it. The example describes a workflow you can build with the right Skills and host setup. We will follow the saved execution path, then check the model and security settings it needs. Follow the durable path The main sequence is prompt or event → Agent or Team → Objective → Run → Turn → Skill action. An Agent or Team owns the Objective, which states a desired outcome. The Objective produces a Run. A Run advances in Turns, and a Turn may call a Skill to act outside the model's reasoning. The draft goal stays in the Objective. The Run records the attempt to reach it. If work has to wait, you can read that Run’s state without keeping the original API request open. Use leases to recover work A worker claims a Turn for a set time. That claim is called a lease. If the worker stops renewing it, the lease ends and the Turn becomes available again. Check this record when a worker stops mid-task. Every stage is saved before it is acted on. Approval waits are saved too. This gives work and review a common place to live across process restarts. Do not read this as a blanket exactly-once guarantee for external tools. Review each Skill's side effects and the service it calls. A restart test should check both the saved Run state and the external result. Check capabilities before calling routes Two OpenSeal services at the same version can expose different operations. The available surface depends on the store contracts, connected components, and complete configuration. curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1/capabilities Run creation needs a dispatcher. Approval resolution needs an authorizer. Workforce authoring needs a complete model endpoint, credential, and model name. A missing capability is not merely hidden in the client; the corresponding operation is not served. This lets a thin client work against a local service or a larger embedding host. The terminal client reads what the server advertises and does not own authoritative state. Closing it leaves durable work running. The health endpoint is a weaker check. Its fixed response does not prove that the database, workers, or model provider can complete your task. Keep orchestration state explicit A Run can wait for a dependency, another agent, an approval, or an inbound event. These are different states because they need different responses. Waiting for another Run to finish is not the same as waiting for a person to decide. Agents can ask each other for work through saved requests. The exchange moves through creation, response, completion, and optional completion review. Because those records are stored, the request can outlive the Run that raised it. Agent and Team definitions have saved versions that do not change. Deployments can switch versions, so they can roll back to an earlier one. A proposed change goes through proposal, review, decision, and activation as separate steps. Saving a decision does not activate the change. Govern actions at the Skill boundary Registering a Skill makes its definition known. A binding grants it to an Agent or Team deployment. Team grants and member grants are separate. When policy requires review, the action call stops at a durable approval checkpoint. A missing approval authorizer does not become permission to approve automatically. In local mode, the standalone operator flag enables local decisions and requires a loopback address. Activity events are saved in the same transaction as the state changes they describe. Credential values are resolved when an action runs and kept out of saved state, prompts, and the terminal client. The host boundary remains important: the standalone API supplies neither authentication nor request authorization nor TLS. A host or proxy must add them. Local approval records use user:local, so they cannot tell you which human clicked approve. Put model routing in the right layer Workforce authoring accepts an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. It can point to a compatible LLM gateway that exposes multiple models. The path is OpenSeal authoring → gateway → model provider. The documented authoring setup selects an endpoint, a credential, and one model name. That is not evidence that the core automatically picks a different model for every task. A gateway's routing and fallback rules must be configured and tested separately. This boundary keeps provider access apart from the durable work model. To test another supported model, change the model setup and compare the result while checking that the proposal still follows the review and apply process. Know which execution path you are using The standalone service uses SQLite. PostgreSQL is available through the Go embedding layer, not as a supported standalone storage setting. Projects group objectives for source monitoring and outreach, and Run commands let a team pause, resume, cancel, or intervene. OpenSeal also has a separate HCL runbook path through openseal run. It runs a typed graph in one process and does not share the durable Run lifecycle, approvals, or activity feed. Do not assume that a runbook command inherits the guarantees described for the durable core. A small evaluation plan Now test the draft workflow. Read capabilities, connect the needed worker, and create one small objective. Watch its Run and Turns. Try an allowed action, then an action that needs review. Restart while that review is pending. Check both the saved approval and anything the action changed outside OpenSeal . Write down the state before and after the restart. That comparison will tell you whether the task recovered as expected and where you need another test. Source and setup guide: https://github.com/axiom-studio/openseal

A Run can wait for a dependency, another agent, an approval, or an inbound event. These are different states because they need different responses. Waiting for another Run to finish is not the same as waiting for a person to decide.
Agents can ask each other for work through saved requests. The exchange moves through creation, response, completion, and optional completion review. Because those records are stored, the request can outlive the Run that raised it.
Agent and Team definitions have saved versions that do not change. Deployments can switch versions, so they can roll back to an earlier one. A proposed change goes through proposal, review, decision, and activation as separate steps. Saving a decision does not activate the change.

Govern actions at the Skill boundary
Registering a Skill makes its definition known. A binding grants it to an Agent or Team deployment. Team grants and member grants are separate.
When policy requires review, the action call stops at a durable approval checkpoint. A missing approval authorizer does not become permission to approve automatically. In local mode, the standalone operator flag enables local decisions and requires a loopback address.
Activity events are saved in the same transaction as the state changes they describe. Credential values are resolved when an action runs and kept out of saved state, prompts, and the terminal client.
The host boundary remains important: the standalone API supplies neither authentication nor request authorization nor TLS. A host or proxy must add them. Local approval records use user:local, so they cannot tell you which human clicked approve.

Put model routing in the right layer
Workforce authoring accepts an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. It can point to a compatible LLM gateway that exposes multiple models. The path is OpenSeal authoring → gateway → model provider.
The documented authoring setup selects an endpoint, a credential, and one model name. That is not evidence that the core automatically picks a different model for every task. A gateway's routing and fallback rules must be configured and tested separately.
This boundary keeps provider access apart from the durable work model. To test another supported model, change the model setup and compare the result while checking that the proposal still follows the review and apply process.

Know which execution path you are using
The standalone service uses SQLite. PostgreSQL is available through the Go embedding layer, not as a supported standalone storage setting. Projects group objectives for source monitoring and outreach, and Run commands let a team pause, resume, cancel, or intervene.
OpenSeal also has a separate HCL runbook path through openseal run. It runs a typed graph in one process and does not share the durable Run lifecycle, approvals, or activity feed. Do not assume that a runbook command inherits the guarantees described for the durable core.

A small evaluation plan
Now test the draft workflow. Read capabilities, connect the needed worker, and create one small objective. Watch its Run and Turns. Try an allowed action, then an action that needs review. Restart while that review is pending. Check both the saved approval and anything the action changed outside OpenSeal.
Write down the state before and after the restart. That comparison will tell you whether the task recovered as expected and where you need another test.
Source and setup guide: https://github.com/axiom-studio/openseal
