items.title: Salesforce Closes $3.6 Billion Fin Deal, Adding a Fast-Deploy AI Agent to Agentforce
items.summary: Salesforce now sells two ways to put an AI agent on customer support, and it agreed to pay about $3.6 billion to add the one it describes as fast to deploy. The company completed its acquisition of Fin, the Irish-founded business formerly known as Intercom, on September 10, 2026. What Salesforce Bought Fin sells an AI agent that handles customer queries from start to finish across live chat, email, WhatsApp, SMS, voice and Slack. Salesforce says more than 30,000 companies use it and that it resolves 76% of support volume on average. That 76% is Fin’s own figure. Fin’s help documentation defines its resolution rate as the percentage of conversations the agent resolves without human involvement, and it counts a resolution when the customer confirms the answer or exits without requesting further help. Fin renamed itself from Intercom in May 2026, with the Intercom name continuing as the label for its customer service software platform. CEO and co-founder Eoghan McCabe said at signing that he would stay on. He wrote that “little will practically change. I’ll still be CEO, Des will still be running R&D,” a reference to co-founder Des Traynor. Salesforce’s closing announcement says Fin will operate as part of its AI Labs, though Opus Research reports that responsibility for running the business sits within Service Cloud. Salesforce’s June announcement gave a price of approximately $3.6 billion, subject to customary purchase price adjustments, and no revenue figure. The Irish Times, citing Fin’s website, reported more than $400 million in recurring revenue. Simple division puts the price at no more than about nine times that number. An Early Close Ahead of Guidance Salesforce signed the agreement on June 15 and guided to a close in the fourth quarter of its fiscal 2027, which runs from November 2026 through January 2027. The deal closed 87 days after signing, in the third quarter. On its August 26 earnings report, Salesforce had told investors it expected Fin and the Contentful acquisition to close “in the coming weeks.” The same report put a number on what the two deals add. Salesforce said the pending Contentful and Fin acquisitions account for $200 million of the increase in its full-year fiscal 2027 revenue guidance, which now stands at $46.1 billion to $46.4 billion. Both deals close partway through the year, so that figure covers only a partial year of their revenue, and Salesforce did not split it between the two companies. Two Agents for Two Kinds of Buyer Salesforce draws the distinction itself. The closing announcement pairs Fin’s “fast-to-deploy AI agent” with “Agentforce’s deeply customizable platform.” At signing, Salesforce described Fin as offering “fast time-to-value options especially well-suited for SMB and some commercial organizations that need to launch quickly, integrate with existing systems, and deliver measurable outcomes.” Salesforce also has its own packaged service agent. Ten days after signing, on June 25, it announced Agentforce Help Agent with pay-per-resolution pricing, generally available in July. CIO reported a price of $2 per successful resolution, with a 1,000-resolution minimum for prepurchased packs. On September 11, it listed Casey, its “help agent,” and Fin, its “customer agent,” as separate, generally available agents among seven new “job-ready” Agentforce agents. Salesforce’s service page calls Casey its Help Agent. Fin’s website fills in the other side. It lists compatibility with Salesforce, HubSpot, Freshworks, Dixa, Front, Zoho, Sprinklr, Gorgias and custom help desks, says setup takes under an hour without a migration, and prices the agent at $0.99 per outcome, with a 50-outcome monthly minimum, when it runs on a customer’s existing help desk. Those are vendor claims. Set beside Help Agent’s reported $2, they invite a comparison, but the two prices are not like for like, because each vendor defines a billable outcome differently. Salesforce says it does not charge when a customer asks for a human or walks away unhappy. Fin does not bill escalations either, but it does count a customer who exits without asking for more help as an assumed resolution. Salesforce’s September 11 release adds one more number. It says 79% of Anthropic’s conversations that Fin sees are resolved autonomously, one customer’s result among several the release lists rather than a platform average, and it says Fin is powered by Operator, a customer operations agent, and Fin Apex, a set of custom models. Agentforce is growing quickly without help. Salesforce reported $1.2 billion in Agentforce annual recurring revenue in its first fiscal quarter, up 205% year over year, and more than $1.5 billion in the second, up over 240%. Those figures argue against reading the deal as a patch for a weak product. One way to read it instead is as coverage: Salesforce now has an answer for the buyer who wants an agent running without a build project. McCabe framed the gain as distribution. “The big strategic benefit of our decision to join Salesforce is magnitudes more businesses and their customers that we can bring it to,” he said in the closing announcement. Marc Benioff, Salesforce’s chair and CEO, put it this way in the same release: “The #1 customer agent meets the #1 CRM.” Both rankings are Salesforce’s own claims. What Salesforce Still Has to Answer The first question is neutrality. Fin’s website lists compatibility with help desks from other vendors, including HubSpot, Freshworks and Zoho, and Salesforce says Fin “works seamlessly with the help desks and systems companies already use.” The promise is in the present tense, and the closing announcement names no rival platform. Opus Research, writing on September 25, reported that Fin works with rivals such as Zendesk and that Salesforce will keep selling the Intercom help desk. The second is packaging. Salesforce now sells Help Agent and Fin side by side, and neither the closing announcement nor the September 11 agent launch says how the two will be priced against each other. Customers choosing between them will want that settled before they commit. The third is competition. Sierra, which builds AI agents for customer-facing work including support, raised $950 million at a $15 billion valuation in May, according to SiliconANGLE. A venture round and a full acquisition are different transactions, so the two figures do not compare directly. They do point to how much capital is moving into this category. What to Watch Next Salesforce’s fiscal third-quarter results are the first period in which Fin is part of the company. If Salesforce breaks out Fin’s contribution, that number will say more than any launch announcement about whether buyers want a customer service agent bought rather than built. For customers already running Fin on a help desk that Salesforce does not own, the practical test is whether the compatibility Salesforce describes today is still there when their contracts come up for renewal.

items.title: Microsoft Retires Themes by Copilot in Outlook Starting in Mid-October 2026
items.summary: Microsoft is retiring Themes by Copilot in Outlook worldwide, with the removal starting in mid-October 2026 and expected to finish by late October 2026, according to the Microsoft 365 Message Center post MC1492954, published on October 9. The change applies to users with a Copilot license on new Outlook for Windows , Outlook for Android, Outlook for iOS, Outlook for Mac, and Outlook on the web. Once the retirement reaches an account, Themes by Copilot is removed from Outlook's settings. Copilot themes can no longer be selected, and anyone who switches to a different theme cannot go back to a Copilot one afterward. Microsoft gives no reason for the retirement in the message. Outlook users without a Copilot license are not affected by the change. What Happens to Existing Copilot Themes in Outlook A Copilot theme that is already applied stays in place until the user changes it. Themes set to refresh automatically also remain applied, but they stop refreshing and keep the imagery they show at the moment of the retirement. Themes by Copilot was offered to Copilot Pro and Microsoft 365 Copilot subscribers in the Appearance settings of Outlook. Users could start from a weather type or a location, either their own or one of more than 100 curated destinations, and then choose a realistic, oil painting, or cartoon art style. Each generated theme combined a wallpaper, shown as the background on desktop or at the top of the mobile apps, with a matching accent color for the rest of the interface. Refresh intervals ranged from every few hours to daily, weekly, or monthly. Microsoft launched a separate collection of standard themes, which are not AI-generated, for all Outlook users regardless of license status, with color options such as green, red, and purple. The retirement notice covers only Themes by Copilot. What Copilot License Holders Should Check in Outlook The Message Center post states that no action is required. Users who like their current Copilot wallpaper should still keep the following in mind before the removal arrives: Leave the current Copilot theme applied if the imagery should stay, since switching to any other theme removes the option to return. Expect auto-refreshing Copilot themes to freeze on their current image once the retirement reaches the account. Pick a replacement from the standard theme collection in Outlook's Appearance settings if a frozen image is not wanted. The removal comes shortly after Microsoft announced plans to block .msix attachments in new Outlook in November. Microsoft is rolling the retirement out gradually across the mid to late October window, so Themes by Copilot remains visible in Settings on some accounts until the removal reaches them. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader.
items.summary_html:
Microsoft is retiring Themes by Copilot in Outlook worldwide, with the removal starting in mid-October 2026 and expected to finish by late October 2026, according to the Microsoft 365 Message Center post MC1492954, published on October 9.

The change applies to users with a Copilot license on new Outlook for Windows, Outlook for Android, Outlook for iOS, Outlook for Mac, and Outlook on the web.

Once the retirement reaches an account, Themes by Copilot is removed from Outlook's settings. Copilot themes can no longer be selected, and anyone who switches to a different theme cannot go back to a Copilot one afterward.

Microsoft gives no reason for the retirement in the message. Outlook users without a Copilot license are not affected by the change.

What Happens to Existing Copilot Themes in Outlook

A Copilot theme that is already applied stays in place until the user changes it. Themes set to refresh automatically also remain applied, but they stop refreshing and keep the imagery they show at the moment of the retirement.

Themes by Copilot was offered to Copilot Pro and Microsoft 365 Copilot subscribers in the Appearance settings of Outlook. Users could start from a weather type or a location, either their own or one of more than 100 curated destinations, and then choose a realistic, oil painting, or cartoon art style.

Each generated theme combined a wallpaper, shown as the background on desktop or at the top of the mobile apps, with a matching accent color for the rest of the interface. Refresh intervals ranged from every few hours to daily, weekly, or monthly.

Microsoft launched a separate collection of standard themes, which are not AI-generated, for all Outlook users regardless of license status, with color options such as green, red, and purple. The retirement notice covers only Themes by Copilot.

What Copilot License Holders Should Check in Outlook

The Message Center post states that no action is required. Users who like their current Copilot wallpaper should still keep the following in mind before the removal arrives:

  1. Leave the current Copilot theme applied if the imagery should stay, since switching to any other theme removes the option to return.
  2. Expect auto-refreshing Copilot themes to freeze on their current image once the retirement reaches the account.
  3. Pick a replacement from the standard theme collection in Outlook's Appearance settings if a frozen image is not wanted.

The removal comes shortly after Microsoft announced plans to block .msix attachments in new Outlook in November.

Microsoft is rolling the retirement out gradually across the mid to late October window, so Themes by Copilot remains visible in Settings on some accounts until the removal reaches them.

items.title: Building a Production-Grade Dimensional Model on Snowflake with Cortex Code using Skills
items.summary: How I designed, audited, and expanded an e-commerce star schema using an AI-powered skill — and what I learned about letting the machine enforce Kimball principles. The Problem: Dimensional Modeling Is Tedious, Not Hard Every data engineer knows the drill. You need a star schema for analytics. You know the theory — grain first, conformed dimensions, surrogate keys, the whole Kimball playbook. But the execution? That’s 200 lines of DDL, manual constraint wiring, zero-value rows you’ll forget, and clustering keys you’ll second-guess. What if you could encode those decisions into a reusable skill that enforces best practices every time — and then let an AI agent execute it? That’s what I built. This article walks through the full journey: creating a Cortex Code skill for dimensional modeling, testing it against a real e-commerce schema, auditing it against best practices, and expanding it with three additional fact tables. What We’re Building 12 tables. 8 dimensions. 4 fact tables. 28 constraints. 20,000+ rows of sample data. Step 1: The Skill — Encoding Kimball Into a Reusable Agent Instead of writing one-off DDL, I created a Cortex Code skill called snowflake-dimensional-modeling. A skill is a markdown file (SKILL.md) with YAML frontmatter that tells the AI agent when to activate and how to behave. Here’s the core workflow: Two approval gates, two revision loops: model first, then DDL, then execute. The skill supports three modes: Design New — describe a business process, get a star schema Review & Improve — point it at existing tables, get an audit report Expand — add more fact tables to an existing model What the Skill Enforces Every invocation, regardless of mode, applies these principles: Grain first — the skill refuses to design dimensions until the grain is stated as a business sentence Conformed dimensions — reuses DIM_DATE and DIM_GEOGRAPHY across all facts Zero-value rows — every dimension gets SK=0 for late-arriving facts Informational constraints — PK/FK on everything so BI tools discover relationships Queryable documentation — COMMENT on every table and key column Audit columns — ETL_LOADED_AT and ETL_SOURCE on every table Step 2: The Build — From Natural Language to Running Schema I told the skill: “I want to model an e-commerce business. We have orders, products, customers, and payments. Key questions: revenue by product category and region, monthly order trends, customer lifetime value.” What It Designed Grain: One row per order line item Dimensions: DIM_DATE - generated, 2020-2027, calendar + fiscal DIM_CUSTOMER - SCD Type 2 (address changes matter for LTV) DIM_PRODUCT - SCD Type 1 (overwrite is fine) DIM_PAYMENT_METHOD - SCD Type 1 Fact: FACT_ORDER_LINE Clustered by (DATE_SK, PRODUCT_SK) Measures: quantity, unit_price, discount, line_total, tax Two design decisions worth noting: SCD Type 2 for customers, Type 1 for products. The skill chose Type 2 for customers because the user asked about LTV — you need address history to track customer migration across regions. Products don’t need history for this use case. Clustering on (DATE_SK, PRODUCT_SK). Date first because “monthly order trends” is a time-series query. Product second because “revenue by category” groups through the product dimension. Step 3: The Audit — What the Skill Caught After building the initial model, I ran the skill in Review mode. It ran four diagnostic queries and produced a severity-ranked report: Six audit findings: one orphan table, three warnings, two suggestions. The orphan table was a leftover from a previous task. The skill caught it because it checks for tables with no FK relationships and no audit columns — a table that doesn’t participate in any star schema relationship is suspicious. The Fix The skill applied all fixes in one pass: Dropped the orphan table Added PAYMENT_METHOD_ID natural key Extended retention to 7 days Added search optimization Created conformed DIM_GEOGRAPHY Added shipping measures to the fact Step 4: The Expansion — Three New Fact Tables The real test of a dimensional model is whether it grows gracefully. I asked the skill to expand with returns, inventory snapshots, and customer sessions. Fact Design Decisions Transaction facts record events. Snapshots record state. The row counts show it. FACT_RETURN links back to the original order via ORDER_NUMBER (degenerate dimension). This enables return rate analysis: "Which products have the highest return rate by category?" FACT_INVENTORY_SNAPSHOT is a periodic snapshot — the key insight is that its measures are semi-additive . You can SUM quantity_on_hand across products (how much total stock in a warehouse?) but you must AVG across time (what's the average stock level this month?). The skill marks this in the column COMMENT so BI tools don't accidentally SUM across dates. FACT_CUSTOMER_SESSION captures web behavior without requiring a purchase. This enables funnel analysis: sessions → products_viewed → added_to_cart → converted . The IS_CONVERTED flag and optional ORDER_NUMBER bridge to FACT_ORDER_LINE for attribution. Conformed Dimensions in Action The expansion added three new dimensions (DIM_WAREHOUSE, DIM_RETURN_REASON, DIM_TRAFFIC_SOURCE) but reused four existing ones. This is conformed dimensions working as designed — DIM_DATE appears in all four fact tables, DIM_PRODUCT in three, DIM_CUSTOMER in three. items.summary_html:
How I designed, audited, and expanded an e-commerce star schema using an AI-powered skill — and what I learned about letting the machine enforce Kimball principles.The Problem: Dimensional Modeling Is Tedious, Not Hard

Every data engineer knows the drill. You need a star schema for analytics. You know the theory — grain first, conformed dimensions, surrogate keys, the whole Kimball playbook. But the execution? That’s 200 lines of DDL, manual constraint wiring, zero-value rows you’ll forget, and clustering keys you’ll second-guess.

What if you could encode those decisions into a reusable skill that enforces best practices every time — and then let an AI agent execute it?

That’s what I built. This article walks through the full journey: creating a Cortex Code skill for dimensional modeling, testing it against a real e-commerce schema, auditing it against best practices, and expanding it with three additional fact tables.

What We’re Building12 tables. 8 dimensions. 4 fact tables. 28 constraints. 20,000+ rows of sample data.Step 1: The Skill — Encoding Kimball Into a Reusable Agent

Instead of writing one-off DDL, I created a Cortex Code skill called snowflake-dimensional-modeling. A skill is a markdown file (SKILL.md) with YAML frontmatter that tells the AI agent when to activate and how to behave.

Here’s the core workflow:

Two approval gates, two revision loops: model first, then DDL, then execute.

The skill supports three modes:

  • Design New — describe a business process, get a star schema
  • Review & Improve — point it at existing tables, get an audit report
  • Expand — add more fact tables to an existing model
What the Skill Enforces

Every invocation, regardless of mode, applies these principles:

  1. Grain first — the skill refuses to design dimensions until the grain is stated as a business sentence
  2. Conformed dimensions — reuses DIM_DATE and DIM_GEOGRAPHY across all facts
  3. Zero-value rows — every dimension gets SK=0 for late-arriving facts
  4. Informational constraints — PK/FK on everything so BI tools discover relationships
  5. Queryable documentation — COMMENT on every table and key column
  6. Audit columns — ETL_LOADED_AT and ETL_SOURCE on every table
Step 2: The Build — From Natural Language to Running Schema

I told the skill: “I want to model an e-commerce business. We have orders, products, customers, and payments. Key questions: revenue by product category and region, monthly order trends, customer lifetime value.”

What It Designed
Grain: One row per order line item

Dimensions:
  DIM_DATE          - generated, 2020-2027, calendar + fiscal
  DIM_CUSTOMER      - SCD Type 2 (address changes matter for LTV)
  DIM_PRODUCT       - SCD Type 1 (overwrite is fine)
  DIM_PAYMENT_METHOD - SCD Type 1
  
Fact: FACT_ORDER_LINE
  Clustered by (DATE_SK, PRODUCT_SK)
  Measures: quantity, unit_price, discount, line_total, tax

Two design decisions worth noting:

SCD Type 2 for customers, Type 1 for products. The skill chose Type 2 for customers because the user asked about LTV — you need address history to track customer migration across regions. Products don’t need history for this use case.

Clustering on (DATE_SK, PRODUCT_SK). Date first because “monthly order trends” is a time-series query. Product second because “revenue by category” groups through the product dimension.

Step 3: The Audit — What the Skill Caught

After building the initial model, I ran the skill in Review mode. It ran four diagnostic queries and produced a severity-ranked report:

Six audit findings: one orphan table, three warnings, two suggestions.

The orphan table was a leftover from a previous task. The skill caught it because it checks for tables with no FK relationships and no audit columns — a table that doesn’t participate in any star schema relationship is suspicious.

The Fix

The skill applied all fixes in one pass:

  • Dropped the orphan table
  • Added PAYMENT_METHOD_ID natural key
  • Extended retention to 7 days
  • Added search optimization
  • Created conformed DIM_GEOGRAPHY
  • Added shipping measures to the fact
Step 4: The Expansion — Three New Fact Tables

The real test of a dimensional model is whether it grows gracefully. I asked the skill to expand with returns, inventory snapshots, and customer sessions.

Fact Design DecisionsTransaction facts record events. Snapshots record state. The row counts show it.

FACT_RETURN links back to the original order via ORDER_NUMBER (degenerate dimension). This enables return rate analysis: "Which products have the highest return rate by category?"

FACT_INVENTORY_SNAPSHOT is a periodic snapshot — the key insight is that its measures are semi-additive. You can SUM quantity_on_hand across products (how much total stock in a warehouse?) but you must AVG across time (what's the average stock level this month?). The skill marks this in the column COMMENT so BI tools don't accidentally SUM across dates.

FACT_CUSTOMER_SESSION captures web behavior without requiring a purchase. This enables funnel analysis: sessions → products_viewed → added_to_cart → converted. The IS_CONVERTED flag and optional ORDER_NUMBER bridge to FACT_ORDER_LINE for attribution.

Conformed Dimensions in Action

The expansion added three new dimensions (DIM_WAREHOUSE, DIM_RETURN_REASON, DIM_TRAFFIC_SOURCE) but reused four existing ones. This is conformed dimensions working as designed — DIM_DATE appears in all four fact tables, DIM_PRODUCT in three, DIM_CUSTOMER in three.

The payoff is cross-fact drill-across queries:

-- Net revenue: orders minus refunds, by product
SELECT
    p.PRODUCT_NAME,
    SUM(o.LINE_TOTAL) AS GROSS_REVENUE,
    SUM(r.REFUND_AMOUNT) AS TOTAL_REFUNDS,
    SUM(o.LINE_TOTAL) - SUM(r.REFUND_AMOUNT) AS NET_REVENUE
FROM DIM_PRODUCT p
LEFT JOIN FACT_ORDER_LINE o ON p.PRODUCT_SK = o.PRODUCT_SK
LEFT JOIN FACT_RETURN r ON p.PRODUCT_SK = r.PRODUCT_SK
WHERE p.PRODUCT_SK > 0
GROUP BY p.PRODUCT_NAME
ORDER BY NET_REVENUE DESC;

This query works because both facts share DIM_PRODUCT as a conformed dimension.

Step 5: The Automation — Lint, Test, Publish

I built three scripts to make the skill CI-friendly:

lint-skill.sh — validates SKILL.md structure (frontmatter, sections, checkpoints, placeholder consistency, balanced code fences). Zero errors, zero warnings on the final version.

test-skill.sh — integration tests against the live ECOMMERCE.ANALYTICS schema. Checks table existence (12 tables), row counts, constraint counts (28), zero-value rows in all dimensions, and a cross-fact join.

publish-skill.sh — orchestrates lint → test → publish. Supports --dry-run, --roles, and --private flags.

# Dry run: lint + test, don't publish
./scripts/publish-skill.sh --dry-run

# Publish to account, discoverable by everyone
./scripts/publish-skill.sh --roles PUBLIC

# Publish to specific roles only
./scripts/publish-skill.sh --roles ANALYST,DATA_ENG
What I Learned1. Skills Are Better Than Templates

A SQL template gives you structure. A skill gives you judgment. The skill chose SCD Type 2 for customers because the user asked about LTV. It chose Type 1 for products because history wasn’t needed. A template can’t make that call.

2. The Audit Checklist Is the Real Value

Designing a model from scratch is the easy part. Reviewing an existing one — finding the orphan tables, the missing natural keys, the DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS = 1 — that's where the skill earns its keep. The nine-item audit checklist catches things humans skip.

3. Semi-Additive Measures Need Documentation

Inventory snapshots are the most dangerous fact table type because they look additive but aren’t. Marking measures as semi-additive in the column COMMENT is a small thing that prevents significant downstream errors.

4. Conformed Dimensions Pay Off at Expansion Time

When I added three fact tables, the model grew from 6 tables to 12. But I only added 3 new dimensions — the other 5 were reused. That’s the Kimball promise delivered: the shared dimensions enable cross-fact queries that would be impossible with isolated schemas.

5. UNIFORM() Has Constant-Bound Requirements

Snowflake’s UNIFORM(min, max, RANDOM()) requires min and max to be constants, not column references. When generating sample data with dynamic bounds, you need to pre-compute random values in a CTE. A small gotcha that cost me one retry.

The Final Model
ECOMMERCE.ANALYTICS
├── 8 Dimensions (with zero-value rows, audit columns, informational constraints)
│   ├── DIM_DATE           — 2,922 rows (2020-2027, calendar + fiscal)
│   ├── DIM_CUSTOMER       — 21 rows (SCD Type 2, search optimized)
│   ├── DIM_PRODUCT        — 21 rows (SCD Type 1)
│   ├── DIM_GEOGRAPHY      — 21 rows (conformed, 6 regions)
│   ├── DIM_PAYMENT_METHOD — 9 rows (with natural key)
│   ├── DIM_WAREHOUSE      — 6 rows (5 fulfillment centers)
│   ├── DIM_RETURN_REASON  — 9 rows (3 categories)
│   └── DIM_TRAFFIC_SOURCE — 8 rows (6 mediums)
├── 4 Fact Tables (clustered, FK-constrained, grain-documented)
│   ├── FACT_ORDER_LINE         — 500 rows (transaction)
│   ├── FACT_RETURN             — 150 rows (transaction)
│   ├── FACT_INVENTORY_SNAPSHOT — 18,400 rows (periodic snapshot)
│   └── FACT_CUSTOMER_SESSION   — 1,000 rows (transaction)
└── 28 Constraints (8 PK + 20 FK)

The skill is published to the Snowflake account and available to anyone with the share URI. Type /snowflake-dimensional-modeling in Cortex Code to start.

Built with Cortex Code on Snowflake. The skill, scripts and DDL are available in the Github.

items.title: How Did I Write My First FlashAttention Kernel in CUDA ?
items.summary: From demystifying the online softmax trick to hitting a 41.6x speedup on an NVIDIA RTX 4050 GPU — a beginner’s hands-on journey into hardware-aware deep learning. Transformers have completely reshaped the landscape of artificial intelligence. At the beating heart of every Transformer model lies the self-attention mechanism. It empowers language models to capture intricate contextual relationships across sequences. Yet, self-attention is simultaneously a double-edged sword: its algorithmic complexity is 𝒪(N²) , meaning memory consumption and computation explode quadratically as sequence lengths grow. Over the years, numerous researchers attempted to alleviate this burden using algorithmic approximation ( Sparse Attention , Linformer , Performer , etc.). While mathematically clever, many failed to dominate in practice because the quality trade-offs were unacceptable or they were not hardware-friendly. When purely algorithmic solutions hit a ceiling, researchers looked at the hardware. In 2022, Tri Dao et al. introduced FlashAttention — an exact attention algorithm that redesigns attention around GPU memory hierarchy and IO-awareness. │ Note: Throughout my learning and debugging journey, I paired with Google Antigravity as my AI pair programmer, which helped me unravel the math and pinpoint subtle GPU memory pitfalls. 1. The Core Bottleneck: GPU Memory Hierarchy To understand why FlashAttention is necessary, we must look at how modern GPUs operate. A GPU is not just a massive compute engine, it is a hierarchy of memory spaces with vastly different bandwidths: HBM / Global Memory (VRAM): Large (e.g., 6GB–80GB), but relatively slow (~1.5–3 TB/s on modern architectures). SRAM / Shared Memory & Registers: On-chip, blisteringly fast (~19 TB/s), but minuscule (around 48KB–228KB per Streaming Multiprocessor). 2. The Standard Attention Trap Standard attention computes: In standard frameworks (naive PyTorch or CUDA implementations): Compute X = QKᵀ / √d ∈ ℝᴺˣᴺ → Written to Global Memory (HBM). Read X back, compute A = softmax(X) ∈ ℝᴺˣᴺ → Written to Global Memory (HBM). Read A back, compute O = AV ∈ ℝᴺˣᵈ → Written to Global Memory (HBM). For a sequence length of N = 16, 384, an N × N matrix contains over 268 million floating-point number (over 1 GB of memory for just a single attention head). The GPU spends nearly all its time waiting to transfer bytes across the memory bus rather than computing floating-point operations. It is overwhelmingly memory bound. FlashAttention solves this via Kernel Fusion: it never materializes the N × N matrix in Global Memory. Everything stays on-chip in SRAM. 3. The Mathematical Magic: From Safe Softmax to FlashAttention Why couldn’t we simply tile attention like regular matrix multiplication?Because Softmax is not naturally associative. Traditional softmax ( link ) Safe softmax ( link ) To compute the denominator, you traditionally need to see all N elements first. This normally requires 3 passes over the data: Pass 1: Find the maximum m (to avoid numerical overflow in float16/float32). Pass 2: Calculate the sum of exponentials d = ∑ eˣʲ⁻ᵐ . Pass 3: Divide each element aᵢ = eˣⁱ⁻ᵐ / d . The Online Softmax Trick (from 3 passes to 2 passes) In 2018, Milakov & Gimelshein proved that you can maintain a running maximum and running denominator dynamically. If you have processed tokens up to index i — 1 with running max mᵢ₋₁ and denominator d′ᵢ₋₁, and you encounter a new element xᵢ by following those steps: Update running maximum: mᵢ = max(mᵢ₋₁, xᵢ) Update running denominator using the recurrence relation: dᵢ stands for sum of row i-th ( link ) FlashAttention’s AHA Moment Tri Dao noticed something brilliant: we do not actually need the attention matrix A! We only care about the final output vector O = AV. By defining a surrogate running output vector o′ᵢ: oᵢ stands for updated vector i-th ( link ) As we sweep through the sequence, we continuously rescale our running output vector and blend in the new token’s contribution. When we reach the final token o′ₙ , is mathematically identical to standard attention — computed entirely in a single pass without ever writing N × N scores to VRAM! 4. The Tiled FlashAttention Algorithm: A Step-by-Step Walkthrough Before writing a single line of CUDA code, let’s look at the high-level algorithm. The genius of FlashAttention lies in transforming a global operation over huge N × N matrices into iterative tile-by-tile computations. Here is the pseudo-algorithm from the paper: FlashAttention paper ( link ) How the Algorithm Works in 5 Core Steps Partitioning the inputs: Divide the large input matrices Q , K , and V from HBM into smaller blocks fitting directly into SRAM. Q and O are split into row blocks of size Bᵣ × d , while K and V are split into blocks of size B꜀ × d . Statistics vectors m (row maximums) and ℓ (row sum of exponentials) are initialized to -∞ and 0 . 2. Loading blocks into SRAM: Execute a double loop over the tiles. The outer loop loads a column block Kⱼ , Vⱼ into fast on-chip SRAM once. The inner loop iterates over row blocks, streaming Qᵢ , the current accumulator Oᵢ , and local statistics mᵢ , ℓᵢ into SRAM to process tile by tile without writing intermediate full attention matrices to VRAM. 3. Computing local attention logits: Multiply the current query block with the key block directly in SRAM: Sᵢⱼ = QᵢKⱼᵀ This produces a tiny Bᵣ × B꜀ tile of raw attention scores rather than the massive N × N matrix. 4. Applying the online softmax update: Find the local row maximum m̃ᵢⱼ = rowmax(Sᵢⱼ) and compute unnormalized exponentials P̃ᵢⱼ = exp(Sᵢⱼ — m̃ᵢⱼ) along with their row sums ℓ̃ᵢⱼ . Update the global row statistics on-chip using online softmax: mᵢⁿᵉʷ = max(mᵢ, m̃ᵢⱼ) ℓᵢⁿᵉʷ = eᵐⁱ⁻ᵐⁱⁿᵉʷ ℓᵢ + eᵐ̃ⁱʲ⁻ᵐⁱⁿᵉʷ ℓ̃ᵢⱼ 5. Updating the output accumulator ( Oᵢ ): Rescale the previous partial output to align with the new max, add the contribution of the current tile P̃ᵢⱼVⱼ, and normalize by ℓᵢⁿᵉʷ : Oᵢ ← diag(ℓᵢⁿᵉʷ)⁻¹ (diag(ℓᵢ)eᵐⁱ⁻ᵐⁱⁿᵉʷ Oᵢ + eᵐ̃ⁱʲ⁻ᵐⁱⁿᵉʷ P̃ᵢⱼVⱼ) Write updated Oᵢ, mᵢ, and ℓᵢ back to HBM for the next iteration. 5. The CUDA Architecture: Mapping the cordinates & memory flow Translating the above theoretical algorithm to physical GPU hardware requires a rigorous understanding of the CUDA Memory Hierarchy and Thread Hierarchy: Generated by Gemini Who does what on the GPU ? The CUDA grid: Work distribution Tile-to-Block Mapping: Each CUDA block (blockIdx.x) processes exactly one row tile Qᵢ of size Bᵣ × d and computes its final output tile Oᵢ. Grid Sizing: For a sequence length N = 1024 with block size Bᵣ = 64, we launch a 1D grid of 1024 / 64 = 16 blocks. 2. Threads within a block: Collaborative parallelism Token Ownership: Each block contains Bᵣ = 64 threads (threadIdx.x = tid). Thread tid owns row tid of the Qᵢ tile, corresponding to one token in the sequence. Coalesced Tile Loading: All 64 threads cooperate to stream Q, K, and V tiles from global memory (HBM) into Shared Memory (SRAM) using aligned memory transactions. Race-Free Attention: Thread tid independently computes dot products between its query row and all key columns in Kⱼ, eliminating write conflicts and synchronization overhead. 3. Memory hierachy: Where data lives Shared Memory (SRAM — Block Scope): Holds tiles Qᵢ, Kⱼ, and Vⱼ (s_q, s_k, s_v). Total footprint: 3 × 64 × 64 × 4 bytes = 48 KB (fits comfortably within the on-chip budget). Registers (Private to Thread — Fastest): m_global: Running maximum (1 float). l_global: Running sum of exponentials (1 float). o[D]: Output accumulator vector (64 floats for d = 64). s_row[KV_SIZE]: Local attention logit tile. 6. The traps I fell into (And how I fixed them) Writing CUDA kernels is humbling. Here are the real bugs I encountered and resolved: Trap 1: Hardware shared memory limit Initially, I allocated four tiles directly in Shared Memory: s_q, s_k, s_v, and s_s (each 64 × 64 × 4 bytes = 16 KB), totaling 64 KB. When compiling, nvcc threw a hard fatal error: ptxas error : Entry function uses too much shared data (0x10000 bytes, 0xc000 max) The default hardware limit for statically allocated Shared Memory per thread block is 48 KB ( 0xc000) , but my kernel requested 64 KB ( 0x10000) . The Fix: Notice that thread tid only ever reads its own row of attention logits during the online softmax update. There was zero cross-thread communication needed for matrix S: Removed s_s from Shared Memory entirely. Stored the intermediate attention scores in a thread-private local register array (float s_row[64]). This eliminated 16 KB of SRAM, bringing total shared memory footprint to exactly 48 KB (3 × 16 KB) and fitting inside the default hardware budget. Trap 2: Loading K and V In my first draft, I attempted to load Key and Value rows into Shared Memory like this: s_k[tid][kv_idx] = K[global_kv_row * d + kv_idx]; // Bug! The Bug: Instead of copying the full head dimension vector ( d = 64 ), each thread copied only a single float at column kv_idx. This left the remaining 63 elements filled with uninitialized garbage data in Shared Memory, completely corrupting subsequent dot-product results. The Fix: I replaced the single assignment with an explicit loop across all d channels so each thread populates its complete row: for (int k = 0; k < d; k++) { s_k[tid][k] = K[global_kv_row * d + k]; s_v[tid][k] = V[global_kv_row * d + k]; } This guarantees the entire feature vector is loaded before computing attention scores. 6. The working CUDA kernel Here is the clean, working implementation of Tiled FlashAttention: #define D 64 // Head dimension #define Q_SIZE 64 // Block size for Q (Br) #define KV_SIZE 64 // Block size for K, V (Bc) __global__ void flash_attention( const float *Q, const float *K, const float *V, float *O, int N, int d ) { // 3 * 64 * 64 * 4 bytes = 48 KB (fits default Shared Memory limit) __shared__ float s_q[Q_SIZE][D]; __shared__ float s_k[KV_SIZE][D]; __shared__ float s_v[KV_SIZE][D]; int tid = threadIdx.x; // Each thread handles 1 row of Q int global_q_row = blockIdx.x * Q_SIZE + tid; int n_kv_blocks = (N + KV_SIZE - 1) / KV_SIZE; float scale = 1.0f / sqrtf((float)d); // Online Softmax statistics in registers float m_global = -1e30f; float l_global = 0.0f; float o[D] = {0.0f}; float s_row[KV_SIZE]; // Local attention logits for thread's row if (global_q_row < N) { // Step 1: Load Q tile into Shared Memory once for (int k = 0; k < d; k++) { s_q[tid][k] = Q[global_q_row * d + k]; } __syncthreads(); // Step 2: Loop over all KV blocks for (int kv_idx = 0; kv_idx < n_kv_blocks; kv_idx++) { int global_kv_row = kv_idx * KV_SIZE + tid; // Load K and V tiles into Shared Memory (with bounds check) if (global_kv_row < N) { for (int k = 0; k < d; k++) { s_k[tid][k] = K[global_kv_row * d + k]; s_v[tid][k] = V[global_kv_row * d + k]; } } else { for (int k = 0; k < d; k++) { s_k[tid][k] = 0.0f; s_v[tid][k] = 0.0f; } } __syncthreads(); // Step 3: Compute Q * K^T for thread's row for (int i = 0; i < KV_SIZE; i++) { float sum = 0.0f; for (int j = 0; j < d; j++) { sum += s_q[tid][j] * s_k[i][j]; } s_row[i] = sum * scale; } // Step 4: Find local maximum in current tile float m_local = -1e30f; for (int i = 0; i < KV_SIZE; i++) { if (s_row[i] > m_local) { m_local = s_row[i]; } } float m_new = fmaxf(m_local, m_global); // Step 5: Safe exponentiation and tile sum float l_local = 0.0f; for (int i = 0; i < KV_SIZE; i++) { float p = expf(s_row[i] - m_new); s_row[i] = p; l_local += p; } // Step 6: Online Softmax updates float alpha = (m_global <= -1e20f) ? 0.0f : expf(m_global - m_new); float l_new = l_global * alpha + l_local; // Step 7: Rescale previous output vector float rescale_old = (l_global * alpha) / l_new; for (int i = 0; i < d; i++) { o[i] *= rescale_old; } // Step 8: Accumulate (P * V) / l_new float rescale_new = 1.0f / l_new; for (int i = 0; i < KV_SIZE; i++) { float p_val = s_row[i] * rescale_new; for (int j = 0; j < d; j++) { o[j] += p_val * s_v[i][j]; } } m_global = m_new; l_global = l_new; __syncthreads(); } // Step 9: Write final output vector to Global Memory (HBM) for (int i = 0; i < d; i++) { O[global_q_row * d + i] = o[i]; } } } 7. Benchmarking & Evaluation I evaluated the implementation on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4050 Laptop GPU with a sequence length of N = 1024 and head dimension d = 64: Implementation | Execution Time (… | Speedup vs. CPU | Numerical Difference --------------------------|-------------------|-----------------|----------------------- CPU Standard Attention | 143.81 ms | 1.0x (Baseline) | 0.0 GPU Naive FlashAttention | 7.63 ms | 18.8x | 3.02 × 10⁻⁹ GPU Tiled FlashAttention | 3.45 ms | 41.6x | 6.40 × 10⁻⁹ 8. Lesson learned & Final thoughts Writing this kernel taught me three core lessons: Hardware awareness trumps raw FLOPs: Moving data costs significantly more latency and memory bandwidth than raw arithmetic. Minimizing round-trips to HBM is the defining factor behind high-performance deep learning systems. Build from first principles: Progressing systematically from 3-pass Softmax to Online Softmax and finally to 1-pass FlashAttention breaks down a complex paper into clear, manageable steps. Pair programming sharpens low-level engineering: Navigating hardware memory limits, thread synchronization, and floating-point stability can be daunting. Having an interactive thought partner to sanity-check equations and trace memory access patterns turns tedious debugging into a structured learning process. If you are diving into CUDA or exploring how high-throughput inference engines like vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, and FlashAttention operate under the hood, there is no substitute for writing a kernel from scratch and profiling the execution yourself. Happy coding! 9. Citations FlashAttention Original Paper: Dao, T., Fu, D. Y., Ermon, S., Rudra, A., & Ré, C. (2022). FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness . items.summary_html:
From demystifying the online softmax trick to hitting a 41.6x speedup on an NVIDIA RTX 4050 GPU — a beginner’s hands-on journey into hardware-aware deep learning.

Transformers have completely reshaped the landscape of artificial intelligence. At the beating heart of every Transformer model lies the self-attention mechanism. It empowers language models to capture intricate contextual relationships across sequences. Yet, self-attention is simultaneously a double-edged sword: its algorithmic complexity is 𝒪(N²), meaning memory consumption and computation explode quadratically as sequence lengths grow.

Over the years, numerous researchers attempted to alleviate this burden using algorithmic approximation (Sparse Attention, Linformer, Performer, etc.). While mathematically clever, many failed to dominate in practice because the quality trade-offs were unacceptable or they were not hardware-friendly.

When purely algorithmic solutions hit a ceiling, researchers looked at the hardware. In 2022, Tri Dao et al. introduced FlashAttention — an exact attention algorithm that redesigns attention around GPU memory hierarchy and IO-awareness.

│ Note: Throughout my learning and debugging journey, I paired with Google Antigravity as my AI pair programmer, which helped me unravel the math and pinpoint subtle GPU memory pitfalls.

1. The Core Bottleneck: GPU Memory Hierarchy

To understand why FlashAttention is necessary, we must look at how modern GPUs operate. A GPU is not just a massive compute engine, it is a hierarchy of memory spaces with vastly different bandwidths:

  • HBM / Global Memory (VRAM): Large (e.g., 6GB–80GB), but relatively slow (~1.5–3 TB/s on modern architectures).
  • SRAM / Shared Memory & Registers: On-chip, blisteringly fast (~19 TB/s), but minuscule (around 48KB–228KB per Streaming Multiprocessor).
2. The Standard Attention Trap

Standard attention computes:

In standard frameworks (naive PyTorch or CUDA implementations):

  1. Compute X = QKᵀ / √d ∈ ℝᴺˣᴺ → Written to Global Memory (HBM).
  2. Read X back, compute A = softmax(X) ∈ ℝᴺˣᴺ → Written to Global Memory (HBM).
  3. Read A back, compute O = AV ∈ ℝᴺˣᵈ → Written to Global Memory (HBM).

For a sequence length of N = 16, 384, an N × N matrix contains over 268 million floating-point number (over 1 GB of memory for just a single attention head). The GPU spends nearly all its time waiting to transfer bytes across the memory bus rather than computing floating-point operations. It is overwhelmingly memory bound.

FlashAttention solves this via Kernel Fusion: it never materializes the N × N matrix in Global Memory. Everything stays on-chip in SRAM.

3. The Mathematical Magic: From Safe Softmax to FlashAttention

Why couldn’t we simply tile attention like regular matrix multiplication?Because Softmax is not naturally associative.

Traditional softmax (link)Safe softmax (link)

To compute the denominator, you traditionally need to see all N elements first. This normally requires 3 passes over the data:

  • Pass 1: Find the maximum m (to avoid numerical overflow in float16/float32).
  • Pass 2: Calculate the sum of exponentials d = ∑ eˣʲ⁻ᵐ.
  • Pass 3: Divide each element aᵢ = eˣⁱ⁻ᵐ / d.
The Online Softmax Trick (from 3 passes to 2 passes)

In 2018, Milakov & Gimelshein proved that you can maintain a running maximum and running denominator dynamically. If you have processed tokens up to index i — 1 with running max mᵢ₋₁ and denominator d′ᵢ₋₁, and you encounter a new element xᵢ by following those steps:

  1. Update running maximum: mᵢ = max(mᵢ₋₁, xᵢ)
  2. Update running denominator using the recurrence relation:
dᵢ stands for sum of row i-th (link)FlashAttention’s AHA Moment

Tri Dao noticed something brilliant: we do not actually need the attention matrix A! We only care about the final output vector O = AV. By defining a surrogate running output vector o′ᵢ:

oᵢ stands for updated vector i-th (link)

As we sweep through the sequence, we continuously rescale our running output vector and blend in the new token’s contribution. When we reach the final token o′ₙ , is mathematically identical to standard attention — computed entirely in a single pass without ever writing N × N scores to VRAM!

4. The Tiled FlashAttention Algorithm: A Step-by-Step Walkthrough

Before writing a single line of CUDA code, let’s look at the high-level algorithm. The genius of FlashAttention lies in transforming a global operation over huge N × N matrices into iterative tile-by-tile computations.

Here is the pseudo-algorithm from the paper:

FlashAttention paper (link)How the Algorithm Works in 5 Core Steps
  1. Partitioning the inputs:

Divide the large input matrices Q, K, and V from HBM into smaller blocks fitting directly into SRAM. Q and O are split into row blocks of size Bᵣ × d, while K and V are split into blocks of size B꜀ × d. Statistics vectors m (row maximums) and ℓ (row sum of exponentials) are initialized to -∞ and 0.

2. Loading blocks into SRAM:

Execute a double loop over the tiles. The outer loop loads a column block Kⱼ, Vⱼ into fast on-chip SRAM once. The inner loop iterates over row blocks, streaming Qᵢ, the current accumulator Oᵢ, and local statistics mᵢ, ℓᵢ into SRAM to process tile by tile without writing intermediate full attention matrices to VRAM.

3. Computing local attention logits:

Multiply the current query block with the key block directly in SRAM:

Sᵢⱼ = QᵢKⱼᵀ

This produces a tiny Bᵣ × B꜀ tile of raw attention scores rather than the massive N × N matrix.

4. Applying the online softmax update:

Find the local row maximum m̃ᵢⱼ = rowmax(Sᵢⱼ) and compute unnormalized exponentials P̃ᵢⱼ = exp(Sᵢⱼ — m̃ᵢⱼ) along with their row sums ℓ̃ᵢⱼ. Update the global row statistics on-chip using online softmax:

mᵢⁿᵉʷ = max(mᵢ, m̃ᵢⱼ) ℓᵢⁿᵉʷ = eᵐⁱ⁻ᵐⁱⁿᵉʷ ℓᵢ + eᵐ̃ⁱʲ⁻ᵐⁱⁿᵉʷ ℓ̃ᵢⱼ

5. Updating the output accumulator (Oᵢ):

Rescale the previous partial output to align with the new max, add the contribution of the current tile P̃ᵢⱼVⱼ, and normalize by ℓᵢⁿᵉʷ:

Oᵢ ← diag(ℓᵢⁿᵉʷ)⁻¹ (diag(ℓᵢ)eᵐⁱ⁻ᵐⁱⁿᵉʷ Oᵢ + eᵐ̃ⁱʲ⁻ᵐⁱⁿᵉʷ P̃ᵢⱼVⱼ)

Write updated Oᵢ, mᵢ, and ℓᵢ back to HBM for the next iteration.

5. The CUDA Architecture: Mapping the cordinates & memory flow

Translating the above theoretical algorithm to physical GPU hardware requires a rigorous understanding of the CUDA Memory Hierarchy and Thread Hierarchy:

Generated by GeminiWho does what on the GPU ?
  1. The CUDA grid: Work distribution
  • Tile-to-Block Mapping: Each CUDA block (blockIdx.x) processes exactly one row tile Qᵢ of size Bᵣ × d and computes its final output tile Oᵢ.
  • Grid Sizing: For a sequence length N = 1024 with block size Bᵣ = 64, we launch a 1D grid of 1024 / 64 = 16 blocks.

2. Threads within a block: Collaborative parallelism

  • Token Ownership: Each block contains Bᵣ = 64 threads (threadIdx.x = tid). Thread tid owns row tid of the Qᵢ tile, corresponding to one token in the sequence.
  • Coalesced Tile Loading: All 64 threads cooperate to stream Q, K, and V tiles from global memory (HBM) into Shared Memory (SRAM) using aligned memory transactions.
  • Race-Free Attention: Thread tid independently computes dot products between its query row and all key columns in Kⱼ, eliminating write conflicts and synchronization overhead.

3. Memory hierachy: Where data lives

  • Shared Memory (SRAM — Block Scope):
  • Holds tiles Qᵢ, Kⱼ, and Vⱼ (s_q, s_k, s_v).
  • Total footprint: 3 × 64 × 64 × 4 bytes = 48 KB (fits comfortably within the on-chip budget).
  • Registers (Private to Thread — Fastest):
  • m_global: Running maximum (1 float).
  • l_global: Running sum of exponentials (1 float).
  • o[D]: Output accumulator vector (64 floats for d = 64).
  • s_row[KV_SIZE]: Local attention logit tile.
6. The traps I fell into (And how I fixed them)

Writing CUDA kernels is humbling. Here are the real bugs I encountered and resolved:

Trap 1: Hardware shared memory limit

Initially, I allocated four tiles directly in Shared Memory: s_q, s_k, s_v, and s_s (each 64 × 64 × 4 bytes = 16 KB), totaling 64 KB.

When compiling, nvcc threw a hard fatal error:

ptxas error : Entry function uses too much shared data (0x10000 bytes, 0xc000 max)

The default hardware limit for statically allocated Shared Memory per thread block is 48 KB (0xc000), but my kernel requested 64 KB (0x10000).

The Fix: Notice that thread tid only ever reads its own row of attention logits during the online softmax update. There was zero cross-thread communication needed for matrix S:

  • Removed s_s from Shared Memory entirely.
  • Stored the intermediate attention scores in a thread-private local register array (float s_row[64]).

This eliminated 16 KB of SRAM, bringing total shared memory footprint to exactly 48 KB (3 × 16 KB) and fitting inside the default hardware budget.

Trap 2: Loading K and V

In my first draft, I attempted to load Key and Value rows into Shared Memory like this:

s_k[tid][kv_idx] = K[global_kv_row * d + kv_idx]; // Bug!

The Bug:

Instead of copying the full head dimension vector (d = 64), each thread copied only a single float at column kv_idx. This left the remaining 63 elements filled with uninitialized garbage data in Shared Memory, completely corrupting subsequent dot-product results.

The Fix:

I replaced the single assignment with an explicit loop across all d channels so each thread populates its complete row:

for (int k = 0; k < d; k++) {
    s_k[tid][k] = K[global_kv_row * d + k];
    s_v[tid][k] = V[global_kv_row * d + k];
}

This guarantees the entire feature vector is loaded before computing attention scores.

6. The working CUDA kernel

Here is the clean, working implementation of Tiled FlashAttention:

#define D 64        // Head dimension
#define Q_SIZE 64   // Block size for Q (Br)
#define KV_SIZE 64  // Block size for K, V (Bc)

__global__ void flash_attention(
    const float *Q, 
    const float *K, 
    const float *V,
    float *O, 
    int N, 
    int d
) {
    // 3 * 64 * 64 * 4 bytes = 48 KB (fits default Shared Memory limit)
    __shared__ float s_q[Q_SIZE][D];
    __shared__ float s_k[KV_SIZE][D];
    __shared__ float s_v[KV_SIZE][D];

    int tid = threadIdx.x; // Each thread handles 1 row of Q
    int global_q_row = blockIdx.x * Q_SIZE + tid;
    int n_kv_blocks = (N + KV_SIZE - 1) / KV_SIZE;
    float scale = 1.0f / sqrtf((float)d);

    // Online Softmax statistics in registers
    float m_global = -1e30f;
    float l_global = 0.0f;
    float o[D] = {0.0f};
    float s_row[KV_SIZE]; // Local attention logits for thread's row

    if (global_q_row < N) {
        // Step 1: Load Q tile into Shared Memory once
        for (int k = 0; k < d; k++) {
            s_q[tid][k] = Q[global_q_row * d + k];
        }
        __syncthreads();

        // Step 2: Loop over all KV blocks
        for (int kv_idx = 0; kv_idx < n_kv_blocks; kv_idx++) {
            int global_kv_row = kv_idx * KV_SIZE + tid;

            // Load K and V tiles into Shared Memory (with bounds check)
            if (global_kv_row < N) {
                for (int k = 0; k < d; k++) {
                    s_k[tid][k] = K[global_kv_row * d + k];
                    s_v[tid][k] = V[global_kv_row * d + k];
                }
            } else {
                for (int k = 0; k < d; k++) {
                    s_k[tid][k] = 0.0f;
                    s_v[tid][k] = 0.0f;
                }
            }
            __syncthreads();

            // Step 3: Compute Q * K^T for thread's row
            for (int i = 0; i < KV_SIZE; i++) {
                float sum = 0.0f;
                for (int j = 0; j < d; j++) {
                    sum += s_q[tid][j] * s_k[i][j];
                }
                s_row[i] = sum * scale;
            }

            // Step 4: Find local maximum in current tile
            float m_local = -1e30f;
            for (int i = 0; i < KV_SIZE; i++) {
                if (s_row[i] > m_local) {
                    m_local = s_row[i];
                }
            }
            float m_new = fmaxf(m_local, m_global);

            // Step 5: Safe exponentiation and tile sum
            float l_local = 0.0f;
            for (int i = 0; i < KV_SIZE; i++) {
                float p = expf(s_row[i] - m_new);
                s_row[i] = p;
                l_local += p;
            }

            // Step 6: Online Softmax updates
            float alpha = (m_global <= -1e20f) ? 0.0f : expf(m_global - m_new);
            float l_new = l_global * alpha + l_local;

            // Step 7: Rescale previous output vector
            float rescale_old = (l_global * alpha) / l_new;
            for (int i = 0; i < d; i++) {
                o[i] *= rescale_old;
            }

            // Step 8: Accumulate (P * V) / l_new
            float rescale_new = 1.0f / l_new;
            for (int i = 0; i < KV_SIZE; i++) {
                float p_val = s_row[i] * rescale_new;
                for (int j = 0; j < d; j++) {
                    o[j] += p_val * s_v[i][j];
                }
            }

            m_global = m_new;
            l_global = l_new;
            __syncthreads();
        }

        // Step 9: Write final output vector to Global Memory (HBM)
        for (int i = 0; i < d; i++) {
            O[global_q_row * d + i] = o[i];
        }
    }
}
7. Benchmarking & Evaluation

I evaluated the implementation on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4050 Laptop GPU with a sequence length of N = 1024 and head dimension d = 64:

 Implementation           | Execution Time (… | Speedup vs. CPU | Numerical Difference
--------------------------|-------------------|-----------------|-----------------------
 CPU Standard Attention   | 143.81 ms         | 1.0x (Baseline) | 0.0
 GPU Naive FlashAttention | 7.63 ms           | 18.8x           | 3.02 × 10⁻⁹
 GPU Tiled FlashAttention | 3.45 ms           | 41.6x           | 6.40 × 10⁻⁹
8. Lesson learned & Final thoughts

Writing this kernel taught me three core lessons:

  • Hardware awareness trumps raw FLOPs: Moving data costs significantly more latency and memory bandwidth than raw arithmetic. Minimizing round-trips to HBM is the defining factor behind high-performance deep learning systems.
  • Build from first principles: Progressing systematically from 3-pass Softmax to Online Softmax and finally to 1-pass FlashAttention breaks down a complex paper into clear, manageable steps.
  • Pair programming sharpens low-level engineering: Navigating hardware memory limits, thread synchronization, and floating-point stability can be daunting. Having an interactive thought partner to sanity-check equations and trace memory access patterns turns tedious debugging into a structured learning process.

If you are diving into CUDA or exploring how high-throughput inference engines like vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, and FlashAttention operate under the hood, there is no substitute for writing a kernel from scratch and profiling the execution yourself.

Happy coding!

9. Citations
  • FlashAttention Original Paper: Dao, T., Fu, D. Y., Ermon, S., Rudra, A., & Ré, C. (2022). FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2022). arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135
  • Online Softmax & GPU Architecture Lecture Notes: University of Washington (CSE 599M: Systems and Machine Learning, Spring 2023). Lecture Notes: FlashAttention and Online Softmax. University of Washington CSE: https://courses.cs.washington.edu/courses/cse599m/23sp/notes/flashattn.pdf
  • Online Normalizer Foundation: Milakov, M., & Gimelshein, N. (2018). Online normalizer calculation for softmax. arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.02867
  • Sparse Attention (Sparse Transformer): Child, R., Gray, S., Radford, A., & Sutskever, I. (2019). Generating Long Sequences with Sparse Transformers. arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.10509
  • Linformer: Wang, S., Li, B. Z., Khabsa, M., Fang, H., & Ma, H. (2020). Linformer: Self-Attention with Linear Complexity. arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.04768
  • Performer: Choromanski, K., Likhosherstov, V., Dohan, D., Song, X., Gane, A., Sarlos, T., Hawkins, P., Davis, J., Belanger, D., Colwell, L., & Weller, A. (2020). Rethinking Attention with Performers. arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.14794

items.title: My cofounder and I were rivals at hackathons. At 21, I've put college on hold to build a startup with him.
items.summary: Raymond Loong Ng put his college plans on hold to build a startup in San Francisco. Provided by Raymond Loong Ng. At 21, Raymond Loong Ng put college on hold after his startup raised $250,000 from VC firm Afore Capital. He and his cofounder spent two months in a program in San Francisco, working on their startup. A subsequent investment brought their total funding to $1 million, and they're now back in Singapore awaiting O-1 visas. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Raymond Loong Ng, 21, the cofounder of Makeable, a San Francisco-based startup. It's been edited for length and clarity. I was born in Vietnam and moved to Singapore when I was 9. As a kid, I always had some kind of side hustle . In school, I sold toys, snacks, in-game currency, and sneakers to my classmates — anything that might earn me a little extra pocket money. When I was 16, I did an internship at an auditing firm, where I had the chance to speak with a lot of business owners. I began to see technology as a tool that could help me advance in the business world. I ended up getting a diploma in applied AI and analytics at a polytechnic after finishing secondary school. I was never the best at math or coding, but it offered me a way to turn my ideas into actual projects. Have you relocated abroad for career opportunities, retirement, or lower living costs? We want to hear from you. Fill out this short form to share your story. I always saw myself as the connector: I could spot a problem, form a vision, attract resources, then bring in my smartest classmates to make things happen. That was how I began building projects of my own. I built an AI tool that helps ex-offenders build résumés and find jobs. I also started a community of young AI builders that runs workshops for students across Singapore. From rivals to cofounders In school, the projects we built often felt theoretical. Participating in hackathons gave me the chance to build solutions under real-world market constraints. Although we had crossed paths earlier through a separate scholarship program, hackathons were also how I got to know the person who would later become my cofounder better. Ng and his cofounder started out on rival hackathon teams before deciding to work together. Provided by Raymond Loong Ng. We competed as rivals on different teams, but would often find ourselves among the only people still working at 2 or 3 a.m. Eventually, we decided we wanted to be on the same team. We started entering competitions together in late 2023 and went on a winning streak. We soon realized that full software solutions were becoming harder to differentiate in hackathons as AI tools and models advanced. We ventured into hardware because it gave AI a way to be deployed in the real world. At a medical technology hackathon in 2025, we built a device to help paralyzed patients communicate through brainwaves and eye blinks. That became our startup, Neural Drive. The product caught the attention of a local hospital and is set to undergo a clinical trial there. At the same time, I was trying to find my way to the US. I grew up fascinated by the people and stories of Silicon Valley . My favorite films were "Jobs" and "The Social Network," and they made me feel that if I wanted to build something that could change the world, I had to be there. While serving my two years of mandatory military service, I applied to several US colleges but was rejected by all. I ended up being accepted into the computer science program at the National University of Singapore, but I still wanted to go to the States. I kept reaching out to venture capital firms in the US, and Neural Drive eventually caught the attention of Afore Capital in June. In June, Afore Capital made a $250,000 pre-seed investment in Neural Drive. My cofounder and I then joined its two-month Founders-in-Residence program in San Francisco . Ng and his cofounder spent two months in San Francisco as part of Afore Capital's founders-in-residence program. Provided by Raymond Loong Ng. The timing was tricky. College was due to begin in August, so I had to defer my enrollment before classes started. My cofounder had to request a leave of absence from school, too. It wasn't an easy decision, but we took a bet on ourselves. I found a city that moved as fast as I did I had visited Shenzhen in China before and expected Silicon Valley to look even more futuristic. Instead, I was surprised by how ordinary it looked. Because we were scrimping on rent, we moved into a hacker house in San Francisco's Tenderloin neighborhood. Those two months in San Francisco were intense, but incredibly rewarding. We were often working until 4 a.m., but we made as much progress as we would have in two years in Singapore. The sheer density of talent inspired us: "What are you working on?" felt like the way people said hello. It was a city full of workaholics. I thought: This is my kind of place. Ng said he enjoyed the fast-paced lifestyle in Silicon Valley. Provided by Raymond Loong Ng. We went through several pivots before landing on Makeable, our startup that lets people build a physical product from an idea. All they have to do is describe their idea in a prompt. Makeable can generate everything from the 3D model to the electronics and code, then sends users a kit they can put together themselves, like Lego. items.summary_html:
Raymond Loong Ng put his college plans on hold to build a startup in San Francisco.

Provided by Raymond Loong Ng.

  • At 21, Raymond Loong Ng put college on hold after his startup raised $250,000 from VC firm Afore Capital.
  • He and his cofounder spent two months in a program in San Francisco, working on their startup.
  • A subsequent investment brought their total funding to $1 million, and they're now back in Singapore awaiting O-1 visas.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Raymond Loong Ng, 21, the cofounder of Makeable, a San Francisco-based startup. It's been edited for length and clarity.

I was born in Vietnam and moved to Singapore when I was 9. As a kid, I always had some kind of side hustle. In school, I sold toys, snacks, in-game currency, and sneakers to my classmates — anything that might earn me a little extra pocket money.

When I was 16, I did an internship at an auditing firm, where I had the chance to speak with a lot of business owners. I began to see technology as a tool that could help me advance in the business world.

I ended up getting a diploma in applied AI and analytics at a polytechnic after finishing secondary school. I was never the best at math or coding, but it offered me a way to turn my ideas into actual projects.

Have you relocated abroad for career opportunities, retirement, or lower living costs? We want to hear from you. Fill out this short form to share your story.

I always saw myself as the connector: I could spot a problem, form a vision, attract resources, then bring in my smartest classmates to make things happen.

That was how I began building projects of my own. I built an AI tool that helps ex-offenders build résumés and find jobs. I also started a community of young AI builders that runs workshops for students across Singapore.

From rivals to cofounders

In school, the projects we built often felt theoretical. Participating in hackathons gave me the chance to build solutions under real-world market constraints.

Although we had crossed paths earlier through a separate scholarship program, hackathons were also how I got to know the person who would later become my cofounder better.

Ng and his cofounder started out on rival hackathon teams before deciding to work together.

Provided by Raymond Loong Ng.

We competed as rivals on different teams, but would often find ourselves among the only people still working at 2 or 3 a.m. Eventually, we decided we wanted to be on the same team.

We started entering competitions together in late 2023 and went on a winning streak. We soon realized that full software solutions were becoming harder to differentiate in hackathons as AI tools and models advanced.

We ventured into hardware because it gave AI a way to be deployed in the real world.

At a medical technology hackathon in 2025, we built a device to help paralyzed patients communicate through brainwaves and eye blinks. That became our startup, Neural Drive. The product caught the attention of a local hospital and is set to undergo a clinical trial there.

At the same time, I was trying to find my way to the US.

I grew up fascinated by the people and stories of Silicon Valley. My favorite films were "Jobs" and "The Social Network," and they made me feel that if I wanted to build something that could change the world, I had to be there.

While serving my two years of mandatory military service, I applied to several US colleges but was rejected by all. I ended up being accepted into the computer science program at the National University of Singapore, but I still wanted to go to the States.

I kept reaching out to venture capital firms in the US, and Neural Drive eventually caught the attention of Afore Capital in June.

In June, Afore Capital made a $250,000 pre-seed investment in Neural Drive. My cofounder and I then joined its two-month Founders-in-Residence program in San Francisco.

Ng and his cofounder spent two months in San Francisco as part of Afore Capital's founders-in-residence program.

Provided by Raymond Loong Ng.

The timing was tricky. College was due to begin in August, so I had to defer my enrollment before classes started. My cofounder had to request a leave of absence from school, too.

It wasn't an easy decision, but we took a bet on ourselves.

I found a city that moved as fast as I did

I had visited Shenzhen in China before and expected Silicon Valley to look even more futuristic. Instead, I was surprised by how ordinary it looked. Because we were scrimping on rent, we moved into a hacker house in San Francisco's Tenderloin neighborhood.

Those two months in San Francisco were intense, but incredibly rewarding. We were often working until 4 a.m., but we made as much progress as we would have in two years in Singapore.

The sheer density of talent inspired us: "What are you working on?" felt like the way people said hello. It was a city full of workaholics. I thought: This is my kind of place.

Ng said he enjoyed the fast-paced lifestyle in Silicon Valley.

Provided by Raymond Loong Ng.

We went through several pivots before landing on Makeable, our startup that lets people build a physical product from an idea. All they have to do is describe their idea in a prompt.

Makeable can generate everything from the 3D model to the electronics and code, then sends users a kit they can put together themselves, like Lego.

In our final week of the program, Afore Capital made a follow-on investment, bringing our total funding to date to $1 million.

We flew back to Singapore to apply for our O-1 visas. While we're home, we're still working. The plan is to return to San Francisco for the next few years and keep building our company.

I probably have to extend my leave of absence. If it doesn't work out, I'll go back to school. I want to keep that option open. But honestly, I hope I don't have to.

items.title: AutoIndexer: Flexible-Order Decoding by Training Causal Models on Chains of Edits
items.summary: Autoregressive decoding is less suited to non-causally ordered data, e.g., cross-references or future dependencies, since their outputs cannot be revised post hoc, unlike iterative human reasoning. Diffusion LLMs partially mitigate this limitation but still cannot flexibly insert or remove arbitrary numbers of tokens from a pre-generated context. We design AutoIndexer as a generative model with a novel training and decoding mechanism that simulates a Chain of Edits, allowing the model to flexibly modify its prior outputs in hindsight via token insertions, substitutions, and deletions. The model learns to predict marker tokens for opening and closing edits, simultaneously moving a cursor to positions in the existing token sequence, analogous to a text editor. Training sequences are obtained by perturbing ground-truth labels with inverse chained edit operations, and the model learns to edit by undoing those inverses. The perturbation training allows AutoIndexer to be robust to erroneous context and adaptable to editing tasks such as code correction. We demonstrate that our method exhibits post-generation context-editing capabilities that most autoregressive and diffusion models lack without compromising performance on standard LLM benchmarks. The code is available at https://github.com/AutodeskAILab/autoindexer.

items.title: SWE-Duel: Towards a Self-Scaling Arena for Coding Agents
items.summary: Static coding benchmarks are fixed at release. Over time their tasks leak into training data, and stronger agents eventually saturate them. We argue that a benchmark should instead aim to be self-scaling: its tasks and oracles are created at evaluation time, so no content exists in advance to leak, and its difficulty is set by the participating agents rather than fixed at release. We introduce SWE-Duel, an arena in which two coding agents evaluate each other over mirrored Red-Blue turns. In each turn, the Red agent works on a real repository across three context-isolated sessions. It proposes and implements a new feature with feature tests, then embeds a subtle bug in that feature along with sealed bug-triggering tests. The resulting pull request is admitted only if (1) it passes the feature tests and the repository's existing tests while failing exactly the bug tests, and (2) a fresh session of the same agent can repair the bug blind, which rules out unsolvable tasks. The Blue agent then reviews the pull request without being told a bug exists. It wins only if its revision passes all three test suites, and then the two agents swap roles. We run a tournament among 11 model-harness participants on 15 repositories in five languages for 1,500 turns. The leaders win in different ways. GPT-5.5 with Codex CLI ranks first as the strongest solver, repairing 98.3% of the defects it reviews. Claude Opus 4.8 with mini-swe-agent ranks second as the strongest task author, with a 27.3% Red win rate. Finally, within one model family, tasks written by the newest version defeat a fixed-reference solver far more often than those of older versions (42.9% vs. 4.0%), giving preliminary evidence that task difficulty scales with task authoring capability.

items.title: Contextual Correction of Parallel Draftsfor Speculative Decoding
items.summary: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by using a lightweight drafter to propose multiple tokens that are subsequently verified in parallel by the target model. Recent diffusion-based drafters make this paradigm particularly attractive: deep attention-based neural backbones provide strong predictions, while drafting multiple future positions in parallel avoids the sequential cost of autoregressive generation. This parallelism, however, comes at a cost. Tokens within a draft block are predicted without access to the realized identities of preceding draft tokens, removing intra-block dependencies that would naturally be available under autoregressive generation. We introduce DCOCO (DFlash Contextual Corrector), a lightweight mechanism that restores these dependencies while preserving parallel drafting. Rather than committing to each position's top prediction, DCOCO retains multiple candidate tokens and evaluates their contextual compatibility across adjacent draft positions in parallel, enabling contextually informed token selection at low additional cost. Across four verifier backbones and ten benchmarks, DCOCO achieves the highest average throughput in every evaluated configuration, spanning greedy and stochastic decoding with and without extended reasoning, with speedups of up to 6.6x over vanilla decoding. Its advantage persists under concurrent serving: DCOCO outperforms the strongest competing method by 6-23% across 4-32 concurrent requests, while other sequential correctors fall below uncorrected DFlash at these loads. These results demonstrate that recovering intra-block dependencies through parallel contextual scoring delivers consistent acceleration across decoding regimes and serving loads.

items.title: CLUE: A Contrastive Learning Framework for Unsupervised Event Type Induction and Annotation
items.summary: Event ontology is the foundational framework for defining events in a dataset. Event type induction generally involves domain experts who define guidelines for creating event types and their names based on the dataset's domain and scope. However, this process is resource-intensive in terms of annotation costs and is prone to human biases. To alleviate the need for manual event ontology creation, we propose the CLUE framework for event type induction, naming, and annotation. Our main contributions in this work are: 1) designing a novel joint embedding representation for expressing both the verb-centric view and the semantic view of events; 2) event type induction using contrastive loss guided clustering; 3) event naming and refinement. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. Our code is available at https://github.com/PratikMaitra/CLUE.

items.title: One Model to Loop Them All: Elastic Latent Recurrence for Language Models
items.summary: A latent recurrent language model applies a shared block of layers repeatedly, so one checkpoint can trade inference compute for accuracy by changing the loop count. At one loop, however, such models typically fall well short of a non-recurrent model of the same size, a one-loop tax that makes a separate non-recurrent model the better choice whenever latency matters. We present Elastic Latent Recurrence (ELR), a recipe for training looped language models without this tax. At one loop, an ELR model costs the same to serve as a non-recurrent model of the same size and, trained on the same data, reaches similar accuracy. Each additional loop then buys more accuracy for more inference compute. Three choices make this work: a gated state update with a learned step size, loop counts mixed within each optimizer update, and conditioning each pass on its loop index and budget. The first two preserve one-loop accuracy, and the third lowers loss at every additional loop. Mixed depths can be introduced late in pretraining to limit the added training cost, and with zero-initialized conditioning added at the switch, this late schedule reaches lower loss than mixed-depth training from scratch. In MoE models, reusing first-loop expert routes on later loops cuts mixed-depth update time by 11.7% with no measurable change in accuracy. At inference, keeping only the last loop's attention KV cache holds attention KV memory at its one-loop level while retaining most of the gain from additional loops. On 4B dense and 30B-A3B MoE hybrid models, ELR at one loop is 0.52 points below and 1.04 points above its matched baseline on a ten-task average, and four loops add 7.25 and 4.75 points. Carried through post-training, the recipe yields Koi-4B, a single checkpoint that scores an estimated 18 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at one loop, matching Qwen3.5-4B, and 29 at four loops.

items.title: Reflective Prompt Optimization of a Deep-Research Agent: A Topic-Disjoint, Multi-Seed Protocol for Measuring Transferable Gains and Prompt-Level Overfitting
items.summary: Prompt optimization is an attractive alternative to reinforcement learning for adapting language-model agents, since it is cheap and produces human-readable artifacts. On factual tasks, however, it carries a failure mode that scalar-reward reinforcement learning does not. An optimizer that reads the training examples can write their answers into the prompt, so an in-distribution gain may be memorization rather than transferable behaviour. We apply reflective prompt evolution (GEPA) to the two system prompts of a multi-agent deep-research agent and evaluate it under a topic-disjoint split in which no topic is shared across train, validation, and test. Held-out citation reward rises by 0.079, from 0.702 to 0.781, with a bootstrap 95\% confidence interval of [0.051, 0.107], and the gain replicates across three seeds (mean 0.107). Nearly half of the winning prompt is a memorized answer key, yet a controlled ablation shows this content earns no reward even on the exact training questions it encodes. The large validation-minus-held-out gap is therefore small-sample selection under a noisy judge, not memorization. Varying the verifier isolates what makes the gain transfer. Decomposed per-dimension feedback is the causal ingredient, and collapsing it to a single scalar reward makes held-out transfer negative. The gain persists under an out-of-family judge and is largely reproduced by a hand-written version of the discovered recipe. Credible evaluation of prompt optimizers therefore requires held-out topics, multiple seeds, and verifier ablations. We release the candidate prompts, lineage diffs, figures, tables, and analysis.
