items.title: Shared Canonical Component Removal Beyond Expert Views
items.summary: In clinical practice, experts often begin by converting raw inputs into a set of expert features before making a decision. While black-box models trained on raw input can outperform models trained on expert views, it remains unclear what predictive signal the raw model exploits beyond what the expert view captures. We introduce an audit framework to quantify this gap using Shared Canonical Component Removal (SCCR). Unlike standard residualization or concept erasure, SCCR selectively removes only those directions strongly shared between learned raw and expert embeddings. Evaluations on synthetic data, coronary artery disease (CAD) detection, antidepressant treatment dropout prediction, and skin lesion classification using SkinCon annotations show that SCCR identifies the ways in which expert views are insufficient and recovers residual predictive signal while minimizing redundancy with the expert view.

items.title: On the Design Space of Continuous Diffusion Language Models
items.summary: Continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) promise to bring the benefits of continuous flow modelling to language, including accelerated sampling and controllable generation. The field has grown rapidly, and the capabilities of CDLMs have begun to rival those of discrete diffusion. Yet, unlike for continuous modalities such as images or videos, our grasp of the levers that matter when training CDLMs remains limited. In this work, we focus on two of these levers, namely self-conditioning and embedding geometry, and shed light on some of the mechanisms behind them, which in turn suggest cheaper and more effective designs. We begin by showing that self-conditioning corrects a train/inference mismatch by exposing the model to inference-like states that are otherwise rare during training. These gains can be recovered without an extra forward pass by a two-level interpolant, coined $\mathrm{DoubleCat}$, which improves TinyGSM accuracy more than threefold. Self-conditioning also aids in recognising tokens dominated by large-norm Gaussians$\unicode{x2013}$an issue known as token identifiability. To address it directly, we introduce discrete reveals to $\mathrm{DoubleCat}$, yielding $\mathrm{SemiCat}$, which achieves discrete diffusion-level performance on TinyGSM, reaching $49.94\%$ with standard training hyperparameters and a tuned sampler. At the $1.7$B scale, $\mathrm{SemiCat}$ outperforms discrete diffusion on four of six likelihood-based evaluations, and surpasses one-hot flows on unconditional generation. On embedded spaces, we find that cross-entropy drives embeddings towards a geometry whose decoding error rate closely matches the one-hot one. We briefly explore a range of further options, such as hybrid corruption processes and noise schedules, including asynchronous ones. We believe this exploration can help the community better understand and advance the design space of CDLMs.

items.title: Specialists Learn Faster: Knowledge Organization in Pre-training Shapes Knowledge Update Efficiency
items.summary: An ideal (language) model must continually update its knowledge. Existing work largely focuses on making these updates efficient after training. We investigate how the organization of time-varying knowledge during pre-training shapes the efficiency of subsequent updates. Models trained on chronologically ordered knowledge specialize in the most recently encountered knowledge; we call them specialists. In contrast, models trained on the same knowledge in randomly shuffled order perform well across all represented time periods; we call them generalists. Surprisingly, specialists require far fewer update steps than generalists to acquire new knowledge. To explain this advantage, we derive a law from first principles that relates update cost to the model's optimization dynamics and that closely predicts empirical results. Guided by these findings, we design a strategy for organizing pre-training data that preserves stable historical knowledge while enabling efficient updates to current knowledge. We also show that the benefits of temporal knowledge organization extend to real-world pre-trained models and existing knowledge update tools, and generalize to other knowledge orderings. Project page: https://horizon-lab.org/specialist/

items.title: Returning to Development States: When Full Sandbox Snapshots Help Coding Agents
items.summary: Coding agents often make useful progress before they fail, but retry-from-scratch discards the machine state created along the way. This makes failure recovery an interesting search problem: if intermediate environment states preserve meaningful progress, restoring and branching from them could outperform repeatedly restarting from the initial state. We implement Go-Explore-style search over full Daytona snapshots and find that higher and more efficient solve rates depend mainly on progress that sits outside the repository, such as databases, services, and other runtime state. Our results suggest that full-snapshot search is most effective when long-horizon coding work spans multiple services whose state cannot be reconstructed from a single diff.

items.title: Inference-Time Steering Across Scaffolds and Epitopes for Sample-Efficient De Novo Nanobody Design
items.summary: Generative molecular design typically relies on over-generation and post-hoc filtering. Inference-time steering methods like Feynman-Kac (FK) steering improve efficiency by biasing trajectories toward high-reward candidates, yet they optimize within a single fixed configuration. In de novo nanobody design, upfront commitment to conditioning choices like scaffold identity or target epitope creates a bottleneck. Since yield varies across these conditions, steering unpromising setups wastes compute. We recast generative condition selection as an inference-time resource-allocation problem. We propose two dynamic budget allocators: a joint Global Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) formulation that steers and allocates compute across configurations concurrently, and a decoupled approach adapting Batched Successive Elimination (BaSE). Empirically, these dynamic allocators increase the yield of designable candidates per GPU-hour nearly 5$\times$ without sacrificing diversity across distinct therapeutic targets and generative configurations.

items.title: Partially Informed Stochastic Optimization via Zeroth-Order Residual Tracking
items.summary: Many optimization problems provide direct access to only part of the gradient, while the remaining component must be inferred from function evaluations. This structure arises in performative prediction, performative reinforcement learning, and bilevel optimization with a black-box lower level. We introduce Partially Informed Stochastic Optimization (PISO), which combines the available gradient component with a running estimate of the residual. By centring each zeroth-order observation on this estimate, PISO makes the variance due to random probing depend on the tracking error rather than the residual's magnitude. This yields a randomized sketch iteration with an explicit contraction mechanism and a principled interpretation of momentum. For smooth nonconvex objectives, we establish convergence guarantees that depend on the residual's variation and initial magnitude, without requiring a uniform bound on the unavailable gradient component. With independently sampled function evaluations and Gaussian or spherical probes, PISO attains leading function-evaluation complexities of \(O(d^{2}\varepsilon^{-6})\) under Lipschitz gradients and \(O(d^{2}\varepsilon^{-5})\) under an additional Lipschitz-Hessian assumption. These rates require only one probe direction, two function samples, and one known-component sample per update. The analysis also quantifies how batching trades observations for fewer deployments. Across five settings, PISO variants improve on the tested baselines with comparable oracle access in three, reach a comparable solution faster in bilevel routing, and perform best among methods without response-model derivatives in performative reinforcement learning.

items.title: Prediction Is Not a Sufficient Memory State
items.summary: A memory that reproduces every current prediction may still have forgotten how to learn from the next observation. We characterize this distinction for exact cumulative learning and attention. For smooth convex residual losses with unrestricted real features and labels, a continuous recurrent state of fixed dimension exists exactly when the loss is polynomial. With ordinary, unweighted observations, degree $D$ requires precisely $r=\binom{d+D}{D}-1$ coordinates; even among histories with one fixed current predictor, exactly $r-d$ coordinates can remain necessary for continuation. Nonpolynomial losses have unbounded requirements on such equal-prediction histories. Bounded scalar logistic examples retain this obstruction after fixing any finite derivative jet. For ridge regression, the hidden evidence is the design matrix: the exact state costs $dp+d(d+1)/2$, versus $dp$ for the predictor. On a well-conditioned zero-prediction family, optimal $B$-bit compression has average one-update error of order $d^{-1}2^{-2B/s_d}$, $s_d=d(d+1)/2$, even with arbitrary randomized codes. Kernel attention gives a second exact closure classification. The results identify what future updates reveal, rather than proposing a new regression algorithm or asserting trained-model gains.

items.title: Revisiting Tabular Deep Regression: Objectives and the Limits of Global Early Stopping
items.summary: While deep learning models for tabular data have recently received significant research attention, the choice of objective functions for regression tasks remains an understudied degree of freedom. Several lines of research offer alternatives to the standard Mean Squared Error (MSE), but differences in datasets, backbones, and evaluation protocols make their practical benefits difficult to compare. In this work, we address this gap by performing a systematic re-evaluation of regression objectives across a broad collection of established tabular datasets and multiple neural backbones. Our comparison reveals that many proposed objectives provide limited or inconsistent gains over a properly tuned MSE baseline, while quantile loss yields consistent aggregate improvements over MSE across the tested backbones. We then identify a limitation that remains even with this strong objective: regions with different levels of target noise can reach their best predictive performance at different training epochs. Consequently, a single global early-stopping checkpoint can impose a compromise between uncertainty regions, even when the objective can represent heteroskedastic target distributions. Motivated by this limitation, we introduce a heteroskedasticity-aware extension of quantile loss that uses input-dependent label smoothing as a potential remedy and improves over quantile loss on several backbones. Overall, our results provide a modern empirical picture of regression objectives for tabular deep learning and highlight how differences in optimal stopping times across uncertainty regions can limit the effectiveness of global early stopping. The code is available at https://github.com/yandex-research/tabular-regression.

items.title: Designing Protein Structures from Natural Language
items.summary: A central challenge in de novo protein design is generating proteins with desired structural and functional properties. Existing design models typically require a dedicated input representation for each property, limiting the design objectives they support. We develop Prompteina, the first all-atom structure generation model that supports new and broader design objectives specified in natural language, analogous to text-to-image generation. To train Prompteina, we construct Prompteina-Data, a paired text--protein structure dataset of 1.8M structures and 50M+ captions describing global and residue-specific structural and functional properties. We adapt Proteina-Complexa, a pretrained structure generation model, through text-conditioned pretraining and finetuning that aligns residues with their corresponding text. Prompteina outperforms baselines on 15 of 18 structural properties and generates proteins that more closely match descriptions of their intended functions. In binder design, it leads baselines on at least 13 of 20 targets and improves interface confidence by 14\% over the strongest baseline. With iterative in silico feedback, Prompteina's gain over non-iterative generation is 57\% larger than the next-best baseline on the hardest targets. Finally, we experimentally validate Prompteina designs against GM2A, a target with no reported de novo binders. We identify nine binders, with the strongest at an apparent $K_{\mathrm{D}}$ of 107 nM. These results establish natural language as an effective and powerful conditioning interface for protein structure generation.

items.title: KL Before and After Mixing: A Round-Complexity Separation in Parallel Sampling
items.summary: A parallel sampler can choose at random which coordinates to generate together. For a target $p$ and the output law $q_U$ of a schedule $U$ drawn afresh for each output, we compare the schedule-averaged divergence $\mathbb{E}_U D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q_U)$ with the output-law divergence $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|\mathbb{E}_U q_U)$, in nats. Rounds commit independent draws from exact conditional marginals frozen at the round's start, each output's schedule is drawn before sampling from a finite mixture of schedules, and every scheduled round is charged. For the uniform distribution on binary strings of even length $n$ with $n/2$ ones, the least expected number of rounds at a fixed tolerance $\varepsilon>0$ is $\Theta_\varepsilon((\log n)^2)$ under the first criterion but $(e^{-\varepsilon}+o(1))\log_2\ln n$ under the second, and the double-logarithmic order is attainable with the same round count on every run. For this target, a count-state recursion gives the exact least output divergence at every round cap over all causal randomized policies. The separation extends to weighted fixed-count targets with bounded weight ratios and quota fractions bounded away from zero and one, without permutation symmetry, and to the full-support Beta$(1,1)$--Bernoulli target, where the sharp expected cost under the output-law criterion is $(e^{-\varepsilon}/2+o(1))\log_2\log_2n$, attained with rare $n$-round runs. Prior work implies the order of the schedule-averaged cost on the balanced target and its $O_\varepsilon((\log n)^2)$ upper bounds on both extensions.

items.title: AI Models Can Provably Hide Arbitrary Capabilities
items.summary: Capability evaluations aim to surface dangerous model behaviors before deployment, but their reliability depends on the assumption that hidden capabilities can be elicited. We show this assumption does not hold under adversarial conditions by constructing backdoor attacks that embed encrypted neural networks within host model weights, decrypting and executing them only upon receiving a secret trigger. Using digital lockers, these hidden circuits remain provably hard to elicit and interpret under cryptographic assumptions, even given full access to model weights, extending prior work from hiding fixed strings to arbitrary computations. We implement our proof of concept constructions in PyTorch and evaluate elicitation through fine-tuning, weight noising, gradient-based trigger search, and latent adversarial training on a small chemical reaction prediction task - a proxy for CBRN-relevant capabilities. Our results demonstrate resistance to these methods and, together with our cryptographic guarantees, reveal a limit of elicitation-based capability audits. We release our models to support the improvement of defenses.

items.title: TII Releases Falcon-ASR: 1.6B Arabic Speech Model Hits 20.92% WER
items.summary: The Technology Innovation Institute (TII) in Abu Dhabi has released Falcon-ASR , a 1.6B parameter Arabic speech recognition model. It focuses on the Emirati dialect and also transcribes English, French, Spanish and Portuguese. In TII’s evaluation, Falcon-ASR posts a 20.92% average word error rate (WER) across 6 Arabic test sets. That beats the best published entry in TII’s leaderboard snapshot by 2.25 points. For developers building Arabic voice products, the catch is access: today it runs only as a hosted demo. TL;DR Size: 1.6B parameters. Max audio context: Not disclosed (the demo accepts clips up to 60 seconds and 20 MB). Runs on: Not disclosed. No weights or quantized variants are published. Access is a Hugging Face demo, with API and native apps planned. Performance: Lowest Arabic and Emirati WER in TII’s own comparisons, with solid English results. Best: 20.92% average Arabic WER, 2.25 points below Audar-ASR-V1-Turbo (23.17%). Worst: 11.86% WER on Earnings-22, its weakest English test set. Bottom line (best): a compact 1.6B model leading larger Arabic systems in TII’s tests. Bottom line (worst): no weights, no license, no API yet, and all scores are self-reported. What is Falcon-ASR? Falcon-ASR is a speech-to-text model from TII that converts spoken Arabic and 4 other languages into text. All 5 languages share one set of weights. The model needs no language flag and outputs text in the language spoken. It also returns word-level timestamps , linking each word to its position in the audio. This is important for subtitling, searchable recordings and meeting notes. How does Falcon-ASR handle Arabic dialects? Dialectal Arabic has far fewer transcribed resources than Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). TII trained Falcon-ASR on Emirati, MSA, other Gulf and Arabic dialects, and English. The objective is everyday speech, including dialect forms and language switching. Training audio was augmented with background noise, overlapping speech, music, room reverberation and telephony effects. Speed and pitch were varied too. The same treatment was applied to Emirati recordings. The model builds on TII’s Falcon3-Audio work . That research describes audio-language models built on instruction-tuned LLMs and Whisper encoders, trained on under 30K hours of public audio. Our editorial and technical team at Marktechpost could not find any published Falcon-ASR’s exact architecture or training data size. How does Falcon-ASR score on Arabic benchmarks? TII followed the protocol of the Open Universal Arabic ASR Leaderboard , run by the ELM Research Center. It ranks systems by equal-weight average WER over 6 test sets. TII used the leaderboard’s pinned manifests. Competitor numbers are published leaderboard averages checked on 30 September 2026. Note that Falcon-ASR’s figure is TII’s own run, not a leaderboard entry. The Audar model card lists its own average CER as 9.20%. How does Falcon-ASR perform on Emirati speech? TII built an internal Emirati and Gulf test set from held-out recordings with human-validated transcripts. It complements the UAE subset of the public Casablanca dataset. items.summary_html:
The Technology Innovation Institute (TII) in Abu Dhabi has released Falcon-ASR, a 1.6B parameter Arabic speech recognition model. It focuses on the Emirati dialect and also transcribes English, French, Spanish and Portuguese. In TII’s evaluation, Falcon-ASR posts a 20.92% average word error rate (WER) across 6 Arabic test sets. That beats the best published entry in TII’s leaderboard snapshot by 2.25 points. For developers building Arabic voice products, the catch is access: today it runs only as a hosted demo.

TL;DR
  • Size: 1.6B parameters. Max audio context: Not disclosed (the demo accepts clips up to 60 seconds and 20 MB).
  • Runs on: Not disclosed. No weights or quantized variants are published. Access is a Hugging Face demo, with API and native apps planned.
  • Performance: Lowest Arabic and Emirati WER in TII’s own comparisons, with solid English results.
  • Best: 20.92% average Arabic WER, 2.25 points below Audar-ASR-V1-Turbo (23.17%).
  • Worst: 11.86% WER on Earnings-22, its weakest English test set.
  • Bottom line (best): a compact 1.6B model leading larger Arabic systems in TII’s tests.
  • Bottom line (worst): no weights, no license, no API yet, and all scores are self-reported.
What is Falcon-ASR?

Falcon-ASR is a speech-to-text model from TII that converts spoken Arabic and 4 other languages into text. All 5 languages share one set of weights. The model needs no language flag and outputs text in the language spoken. It also returns word-level timestamps, linking each word to its position in the audio. This is important for subtitling, searchable recordings and meeting notes.

How does Falcon-ASR handle Arabic dialects?

Dialectal Arabic has far fewer transcribed resources than Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). TII trained Falcon-ASR on Emirati, MSA, other Gulf and Arabic dialects, and English. The objective is everyday speech, including dialect forms and language switching.

Training audio was augmented with background noise, overlapping speech, music, room reverberation and telephony effects. Speed and pitch were varied too. The same treatment was applied to Emirati recordings.

The model builds on TII’s Falcon3-Audio work. That research describes audio-language models built on instruction-tuned LLMs and Whisper encoders, trained on under 30K hours of public audio. Our editorial and technical team at Marktechpost could not find any published Falcon-ASR’s exact architecture or training data size.

How does Falcon-ASR score on Arabic benchmarks?

TII followed the protocol of the Open Universal Arabic ASR Leaderboard, run by the ELM Research Center. It ranks systems by equal-weight average WER over 6 test sets. TII used the leaderboard’s pinned manifests. Competitor numbers are published leaderboard averages checked on 30 September 2026.

ModelParamsAvg WER (%)Avg CER (%)Falcon-ASR1.6B20.928.79Audar-ASR-V1-Turbo2.35B23.179.23Cohere Transcribe Arabic (07-2026)2.0B25.8711.80omniASR LLM 7B7.0B28.3212.52

Lower is better. Note that Falcon-ASR’s figure is TII’s own run, not a leaderboard entry. The Audar model card lists its own average CER as 9.20%.

How does Falcon-ASR perform on Emirati speech?

TII built an internal Emirati and Gulf test set from held-out recordings with human-validated transcripts. It complements the UAE subset of the public Casablanca dataset.

ModelParamsWER (%)CER (%)Falcon-ASR1.6B22.7310.19Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct30B (3B active)26.8012.72Audar-ASR-V1-Turbo2.35B27.8913.75Cohere Transcribe Arabic2.0B31.0518.07Qwen3-ASR-1.7B2.0B31.5213.35Audar-ASR-V1-Flash0.78B32.8715.36

Falcon-ASR leads by 4.07 WER points over Qwen3-Omni. This test set is private, so it cannot be reproduced. Audar reports 19.4% WER on a different Emirati set (Mixat), so the numbers are not directly comparable.

How good is Falcon-ASR at English?

On the 7 English test sets used by the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard, TII reports a 5.74% mean WER. Per-set scores range from 1.75% on LibriSpeech clean to 11.86% on Earnings-22. For context, Qwen3-ASR-1.7B lists 5.76% mean WER on that leaderboard. French, Spanish and Portuguese are supported, but TII published no scores for them.

Key Takeaways
  • Falcon-ASR is a 1.6B Arabic-first speech model from TII with an Emirati focus.
  • It reports 20.92% average Arabic WER, 2.25 points ahead of Audar-ASR-V1-Turbo.
  • On TII’s Emirati set it beats a 30B Qwen3-Omni by 4.07 WER points.
  • 1 set of weights covers 5 languages, with word-level timestamps.
  • No weights, license or API yet: test it via the 60-second demo.

Check out the Falcon-ASR blog, the Falcon3-Audio paper and try the demo. Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter. Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well.

items.title: Beyond the course: Reflections from the Bioconductor–Physalia sponsorship programme
items.summary_html:
[This article was first published on Bioconductor community blog, and kindly contributed to R-bloggers]. (You can report issue about the content on this page here) Want to share your content on R-bloggers? click here if you have a blog, or here if you don't.

What difference can a sponsored place on a bioinformatics course make? For some researchers, it means access to training they would otherwise struggle to afford. For others, it is an opportunity to explore a new field, work through unfamiliar analytical methods, or find new ways to approach an existing research question.

Through the Bioconductor–Physalia collaboration, Physalia offers two free places on eligible courses to researchers based in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). The Bioconductor Community Manager coordinates the application process and works with the Training Committee co-chairs on selecting participants, while Bioconductor helps promote the courses through its community channels. Between November 2025 and October 2026, the programme provided 18 sponsored places across nine courses, covering topics ranging from RNA-seq and proteomics to microbiome analysis, epigenomics and network biology.

The aim is to make specialist training more accessible to researchers who might otherwise miss out on these opportunities. We asked participants what they found useful about their courses and how they planned to use what they had learned. Their responses offer a glimpse into the different ways the training connects with their work.

Making training accessible

Access was a recurring theme in the feedback. For Blessing Chioma Oselu, a PhD student and Bioinformatics Research Assistant at Covenant University in Nigeria, the opportunity to attend the Single-cell RNA-seq Analysis with R/Bioconductor course meant learning directly from experts and having structured materials to return to afterward.

“The access to expert teaching and the structured materials were the most valuable parts for me,” she wrote.

Blessing plans to continue working through the recorded sessions at her own pace. For researchers balancing training with other commitments, being able to revisit course material can be just as useful as attending the live sessions.

Another participant, from Benin, came to the Epigenomics Data Analysis course without previous experience in the subject. The step-by-step walkthroughs of methods including ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq helped make the material more manageable.

“I left the course at a clearly higher level than I started, and I feel ready to work with my own data when the time comes,” the participant reflected.

They also noted that opportunities like this are rare where they are based, and that support from Bioconductor and Physalia made a real difference.

Taking new methods back to research

Participants also described how the training related to questions they were already working on, or hoped to explore.

For Amira M. F. Abozaid, a PhD student and Assistant Lecturer at Alexandria University and E-JUST in Egypt, the RNA-seq data analysis with R/Bioconductor course provided a deeper understanding of the RNA-seq workflow, from quality control and normalization to differential expression and visualization.

Amira wrote that she had already started applying the workflows to her cancer genomics projects and sharing the skills with colleagues and students at her home institutions.

Other participants were looking at different applications. Idris Ishola Adejumobi, a Research Associate at the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture in Nigeria, described how the Epigenomics Data Analysis course broadened his understanding of how epigenetic variation can influence complex traits and complement genomic information in crop improvement. He also identified further training in the integration of epigenomic, genomic, and transcriptomic data as a useful next step for agricultural and plant-breeding research.

Rabiath Adigoun, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Abomey-Calavi in Benin, highlighted the relevance of Orchestrating Microbiome Analysis with Bioconductor to her ongoing and future research on plant microbiomes.

“The expertise and methodological skills I have acquired will substantially strengthen my ongoing and future research on the plant microbiome in Benin and across Africa,” she wrote.

Sally Karimi Kinyua, a Research Assistant based in Kenya, attended the Network Analysis in Systems Biology with R/Bioconductor course. She hopes to apply what she learned about gene networks to research into mutations associated with malaria resistance. Sally also highlighted how the sponsored place gave her access to training that would otherwise have been out of reach because of limited resources.

These examples span different fields, but the underlying theme is similar: participants are looking for ways to connect computational methods with the biological questions they want to answer.

Learning to work with unfamiliar data

Sometimes, what matters most is finding a way into a subject that initially seems difficult.

A participant in the Statistical Methods for Metatranscriptomics course described how the practical sessions helped make complex concepts easier to follow. They particularly appreciated the explanations of foundational terminology before moving on to more technical material.

The course also introduced them to ways of analysing microbial gene expression data using computational tools and reproducible workflows. Coming from a bachelor’s degree background, they described it as one of their first deeper exposures to this area of bioinformatics.

Another participant, Binod Rayamajhee, a Research Fellow at the Kathmandu Research Institute for Biological Sciences in Nepal, highlighted the course’s combination of conceptual teaching and practical work with Bioconductor tools.

The training relates directly to his work in microbiome data analysis, and he anticipates applying the methods to study host–microbe interactions in bowel disease models.

Binod also hopes to share what he learned through workshops and one-to-one mentoring with colleagues and junior researchers, particularly those working in resource-limited settings.

Sharing what comes next

Knowledge sharing appeared in several participants’ reflections, whether through helping colleagues, teaching students, or bringing new analytical approaches into research groups.

Sandra Achieng Otieno, an MSc student at icipe in Kenya, attended the microbiome analysis course. She was particularly interested in learning how to structure microbiome data using TreeSummarizedExperiment and how different transformations can affect downstream analyses, including diversity estimation and ordination.

She hopes to apply these skills to research combining microbiome data with target gene expression and elemental analysis.

As Sandra put it, the course gave her “a clearer framework for integrating multi-omics biological data in a structured and reproducible way.”

For others, training may also open the door to contributing to Bioconductor itself. Marco Antonio Campanário Sampaio, a PhD student in Brazil who attended the Developing R/Bioconductor Packages for Genomics course, wrote, “I hope to become a contributor to the Bioconductor community soon.”

These are plans at different stages, and their longer-term outcomes remain to be seen. Still, it is useful to hear participants identify specific methods they want to try, datasets they want to analyse, and colleagues with whom they hope to share their knowledge.

Continuing the conversation

The feedback collected so far gives us a better sense of what participants value in specialist bioinformatics training. Expert teaching and well-organised materials matter, as do practical exercises that make unfamiliar methods easier to approach. Just as importantly, participants want to connect what they learn to their own research.

We would like to thank everyone who shared their reflections, along with the instructors and organisers who contributed to the courses. We’d also like to thank Laurah Nyasita Ondari for helping promote these opportunities through Bioconductor’s social media channels.

We hope to hear from participants again as they put their new skills into practice. In the meantime, their experiences offer a useful reminder of why access to training matters: it gives researchers more opportunities to learn new methods, explore their research questions, and contribute to the scientific communities around them.

For the full list of the Physalia courses and workshops, please visit www.physalia-courses.org. To find out more about the collaboration, explore the Bioconductor-Physalia course listings, including upcoming courses and how to apply for a sponsored place.

Interested in developing or teaching a Bioconductor-related course? Physalia welcomes ideas from potential instructors and is happy to discuss possible topics, content and formats. Get in touch with Physalia to explore an idea.
